choices: Saw directly through the middle of the bone.
Pull the skin off before locating the joint.
Bend it outward to find and cut through the joint.
quiz.question: How do you separate a bird leg in this method?

quiz.because: Clean cuts follow the structure and use controlled strokes.
choices: Neat slices and joints separating without sawing.
Ragged slices with crushed edges.
Bone splinters through every portion.
quiz.question: What suggests a clean carving stroke?

quiz.because: Changing direction shortens the fibres in the resulting slices.
choices: Make longer slices along the same fibres.
Cut across the fibre direction.
Use short crushing strokes along the grain.
quiz.question: Slices feel chewy after cutting along visible fibres. What should change?

cues.text: The skin is blackened and blistered all over, and the vegetable has sagged.
A deep, smoky, sweet smell.
The flesh gives completely when pressed with the tongs.

technique/char.does: Burns the skin of a whole vegetable black over an open flame or a fierce heat, so that the flesh inside turns soft, smoky and sweet, and the charred skin can be peeled away.
how: Set the whole vegetable directly on a gas flame, on a hot grill or on a barbecue.
Turn it now and then with tongs, until the skin is blackened and blistered all over and the flesh has gone soft and collapsed.
Move it to a bowl and cover it, so that the steam loosens the skin.
When it is cool enough to handle, peel off the skin and lift out the stem and seeds. Do not rinse it, or the smoky taste is lost.
Drain off the juices, or keep them for the dish, as it asks.

intro.what: Whole vegetables blacken and blister over strong heat before their skins are removed.
intro.why: Here the dark skin is a temporary layer. The goal is soft smoky flesh rather than keeping the burnt outer surface.

mistakes.fix: Keep turning it until the skin is black all over and the vegetable has collapsed.
mistakes.mistake: Taking it off while the skin is only blistered in patches, so that the flesh stays firm and the skin clings.

mistakes.fix: Wipe or pull the skin off by hand.
mistakes.mistake: Rinsing the vegetable under the tap to remove the skin, which washes away the smoke.

mistakes.fix: Cover it while it steams and cools.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it uncovered, so that the skin sticks.

quiz.because: The skin takes the direct heat and is peeled away to reveal the flesh.
choices: The blackened skin as the main part of the finished vegetable.
Firm flesh with all the smoky juices washed away.
The softened smoky flesh beneath the skin.
quiz.question: What is kept after charring the whole vegetable?

quiz.because: Steam beneath the cover makes the blackened skin easier to remove.
choices: Trapped steam helps loosen the skin.
The cover dries the skin onto the flesh.
The cover crisps the blackened skin before peeling.
quiz.question: Why cover the vegetable after taking it off the heat?

quiz.because: The intended change includes both the outer skin and the softened interior texture.
choices: Pale tight skin and rigid flesh.
Blistered dark skin and sagging soft flesh.
A dry hollow centre with crisp flesh.
quiz.question: What combination of cues belongs to this method?

quiz.because: Removing the skin without rinsing retains more of the smoky flavour.
choices: Rinse longer under stronger running water.
Soak the peeled vegetable before using it.
Wipe or pull the loosened skin away by hand.
quiz.question: Rinsing removed much of the smoky taste. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The whole, unpeeled vegetable sits straight on the flame and its skin is burnt black on purpose, then peeled away, so that the smoky soft flesh is what is kept.

cues.text: The container is cold to the hand all over, with no warm core.

technique/chill.does: Brings hot food down to the cold of the fridge quickly, so that it keeps well and so that a cold dish is truly cold.
how: Move the hot food out of its pot into a wide, shallow container.
Stand the container in iced water and stir now and then.
Put it in the fridge, uncovered, once it has stopped steaming.
Cover it when it is cold. Taste a cold dish again before serving, because cold dulls salt.

intro.what: Food is cooled in shallow containers, with an iced-water bath assisting the temperature change.
intro.why: Container shape affects how heat leaves the food. Cold dishes also need tasting at their serving temperature.

mistakes.fix: Divide it into shallow containers and cool them in iced water.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving a large pot of stock to cool by itself on the stove, where its middle stays warm for a long time.

mistakes.fix: Taste it again when it is cold.
mistakes.mistake: Seasoning a soup while it is hot and serving it cold.

quiz.because: Shallower containers reduce the depth of food that heat must travel through.
choices: Heat can leave more readily than from a deep pot.
The shallow shape helps a surface skin trap heat inside.
A shallow layer holds its centre warm for longer.
quiz.question: Why move food into shallow containers?

quiz.because: Cold water around the container helps remove heat; stirring distributes temperature within the food.
choices: It is poured into the food to dilute it.
It draws heat from the container while the food is stirred.
It warms the container before refrigeration.
quiz.question: How does the iced-water bath assist this method?

quiz.because: An evenly cold container is the handling observation described here; it does not measure the food’s centre temperature.
choices: The rim feels cold while the base stays warm.
Steam continues rising from the centre.
It feels cold across its surface.
quiz.question: What handling cue is described for the chilled container?

quiz.because: Cold changes flavour perception, so seasoning should be assessed again for the cold dish.
choices: Taste it again at its serving temperature.
Assume the hot tasting still describes it exactly.
Warm it solely to avoid tasting it cold.
quiz.question: A cold soup tastes underseasoned after being seasoned hot. What should you do?

cues.text: Pieces of roughly one size, still dry and separate on the board.

technique/chop.does: Cuts food into small, uneven pieces, where the exact shape does not matter.
how: Gather the food into a low pile.
Hold the tip of the knife on the board with your free hand.
Rock the blade up and down while swinging it across the pile.
Scrape the pile back together and go over it again until it is as fine as you want.

intro.what: Food is cut into small pieces when a precise geometric shape is unnecessary.
intro.why: Stopping at the intended fineness preserves distinct pieces and avoids turning delicate ingredients into paste.

mistakes.fix: Dry the herbs well first, and stop as soon as they are fine enough.
mistakes.mistake: Chopping wet herbs, which turns them to a dark paste.

mistakes.fix: Cut it by hand with a sharp knife: slices, then strips, then small cubes.
mistakes.mistake: Chopping meat for a tartare in a machine, which smears it.

quiz.because: Chopping controls fineness without requiring the repeated geometry of a precise dice.
choices: When every piece must be a perfect cube.
When small pieces matter more than exact shape.
When the aim is a completely smooth puree.
quiz.question: When is chopping useful?

quiz.because: Gathering the pile lets repeated rocking cuts reach the pieces evenly.
choices: Press the blade flat to crush the pile.
Chop only the centre without gathering outer pieces.
Rock the knife across it, then gather it together again.
quiz.question: How is the pile worked in this method?

quiz.because: Separate pieces indicate cutting without excessive bruising and moisture.
choices: Small distinct pieces that remain dry and separate.
A dark wet paste smeared on the board.
Whole leaves mixed with crushed stems.
quiz.question: What should chopped herbs look like?

quiz.because: Drying and limiting the cutting reduce the tendency to bruise herbs into paste.
choices: Chop them wetter and work them longer.
Dry them before chopping and stop when fine enough.
Crush them against the board before cutting.
quiz.question: Wet herbs turned into a dark paste. What should change?

comes_after.why: A stock is skimmed clean before it is clarified. Clarifying is the last and finest step.

cues.text: The liquid seen through the hole is as clear as tea.

technique/clarify.does: Clears a cloudy stock by simmering it with egg white and minced meat, which rise as a raft and trap what clouds it.
how: Mix egg white, minced lean meat and finely cut vegetables into a cold stock with no fat on it.
Heat slowly, stirring gently, until the mixture starts to rise and clump.
Stop stirring the moment a raft forms on top.
Make a small hole in the raft and simmer very gently, so that the liquid bubbles up through it.
Ladle the clear liquid out through the hole and strain it through a cloth.

intro.what: A raft of egg white and minced ingredients traps particles from cloudy stock.
intro.why: Clarity depends on letting that raft stay intact, showing why gentle heating can matter more than repeated stirring.

mistakes.fix: Leave it alone and keep the heat very low.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring after the raft has formed, or letting it boil, which breaks the raft and clouds the stock again.

mistakes.fix: Chill the stock and lift off all the fat first.
mistakes.mistake: Starting with a warm or fatty stock.

quiz.because: The raft gathers the suspended material so clear liquid can be drawn away.
choices: It thickens the stock into a cloudy sauce.
It breaks the cloudy particles into smaller suspended pieces.
It traps particles that cloud the stock.
quiz.question: What does the raft do during clarification?

quiz.because: An intact raft can trap particles; stirring or boiling breaks it apart.
choices: Stop stirring and keep the simmer gentle.
Stir harder to distribute the raft.
Bring the stock to a vigorous boil.
quiz.question: What changes when a raft forms?

quiz.because: Clear liquid in the opening shows the suspended particles have been gathered away.
choices: Opaque with floating crumbs.
Clear like tea.
Greasy with a thick cloudy layer.
quiz.question: What should the liquid visible through the raft opening look like?

quiz.because: Protecting the raft prevents trapped particles from being dispersed again.
choices: Beat the raft into smaller fragments.
Increase the boil to break it down.
Leave the formed raft undisturbed over gentle heat.
quiz.question: Stirring broke the raft and clouded the stock again. What would you change on the next attempt?

cues.text: The shells are closed and clean, with no tufts left sticking out.
They smell fresh, of clean sea water.

technique/clean-mussels.does: Scrubs the shells of mussels and pulls off the tuft of fibres at the hinge, which is called the beard, so that nothing gritty reaches the pot. Mussels are cleaned just before they are cooked.
how: Tip the mussels into a bowl of cold water and lift them out by the handful, leaving the grit in the bottom of the bowl.
Tap any open shell on the side of the bowl. Leave out any that stays open.
Scrape off barnacles and dirt with the back of a knife.
Take the tuft of fibres at the hinge between a thumb and the knife blade and pull it firmly towards the hinge end until it comes away.
Rinse once more and keep the mussels cold until they go into the pot.

intro.what: Shells are scrubbed and the fibrous beards removed before mussels enter the pot.
intro.why: Careful cleaning separates grit from the shellfish and shows why direction matters when removing an attached fibre.

mistakes.fix: Rinse them quickly in cold water and cook them soon after.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the mussels to soak for a long time in fresh water, which weakens them.

mistakes.fix: Pull towards the hinge end.
mistakes.mistake: Pulling the beard the wrong way, towards the point of the shell, which can tear the mussel.

quiz.because: Cleaning removes exterior debris and fibres before they reach the pot.
choices: Shell grit and the attached fibrous beard.
The entire shell before cooking.
The hinge that joins the shell.
quiz.question: What is the cleaning step intended to remove?

quiz.because: Pulling toward the hinge avoids the tearing associated with pulling the other way.
choices: Toward the pointed end.
Toward the hinge end.
Straight away while twisting the shell apart.
quiz.question: In which direction should the beard be pulled?

quiz.because: Looking at the hinge area checks whether the attached tuft remains.
choices: The beard remains stretched along the shell.
Fibres still hang below a polished shell.
No fibrous tuft projects from the hinge area.
quiz.question: What visual cue shows beard removal?

quiz.because: Lifting the mussels away separates them from debris that has settled below.
choices: Lift the mussels out and leave the settled grit behind.
Pour the whole bowl through the mussels again.
Stir the sediment up before lifting them.
quiz.question: Grit from the bowl ends up back with the mussels. What should change?

variant_of.differs: Clams are left to stand in salted water so that they give up their sand. Mussels hold little sand, so they are scrubbed, bearded and cooked soon after, and are never left to stand.

comes_after.why: The meat is seasoned first, because the coat shuts the seasoning off once it is on.

cues.text: An even coat of crumbs on every side, with no bare patch.
The crumbs hold when the piece is picked up and do not rain off.

technique/coat.does: Covers a piece of meat in a layer of breadcrumbs over a sticky coat of mustard or beaten egg, which turns into a crisp crust when the piece is cooked.
how: Pat the pieces dry and season them.
Brush a thin, even layer of mustard or beaten egg over every side, so that the crumbs have something to hold to.
Tip the crumbs into a shallow dish. Press each piece into them, turn it, and press again.
Shake off the loose crumbs and lay the pieces on a rack, so that the coat sets before cooking.

intro.what: A thin layer of mustard or egg holds breadcrumbs around a piece of meat.
intro.why: The surface must support the crumbs without becoming slippery. This makes preparation as important as pressing the coating on.

mistakes.fix: Brush on a thin, even layer.
mistakes.mistake: Brushing on a thick layer of mustard, which slides off with the crumbs.

mistakes.fix: Pat the meat dry first.
mistakes.mistake: Coating wet meat, so that the crumbs go soggy and fall off.

quiz.because: The sticky film connects the dry crumbs to the prepared surface.
choices: Gives the breadcrumbs a surface to cling to.
Keeps the crumbs dry by preventing any adhesion.
Makes the crumbs slide freely over the meat.
quiz.question: What does the mustard or egg layer do here?

quiz.because: A dry starting surface helps the binder and crumbs adhere.
choices: Wet the pieces thoroughly.
Pat the pieces dry.
Pack crumbs onto the unprepared surface.
quiz.question: What comes before applying the binder?

quiz.because: Clinging crumbs show that the binder and coating have made contact.
choices: The coating slides away in a wet sheet.
Most crumbs fall from bare patches.
The crumbs stay attached.
quiz.question: What should happen when the coated piece is lifted?

quiz.because: Excess binder becomes a slippery layer rather than an adhesive film.
choices: Apply a thinner even film.
Add a thicker mustard layer.
Wet the meat before brushing.
quiz.question: A thick mustard layer slides off with the crumbs. What should change?

variant_of.differs: Dredging dusts the piece with dry flour. Here a wet coat of mustard or egg goes on first and crumbs are pressed into it, to make a thick crisp crust.

cues.text: The crust is an even layer of dry flakes with no bare spots.
The flakes cling when the piece is lifted and do not fall away.

technique/coat-in-panko.does: Covers a cutlet in layers, first flour, then beaten egg and then coarse panko flakes, which fry into a light, shaggy, golden crust that stays crisp.
how: Season the meat and pat it dry.
Set out trays in a row: flour, beaten egg and panko.
Dust the meat in flour and tap off the extra, so that only a thin film is left.
Draw it through the egg so that every side is wet, and let the extra drip off.
Lay it in the panko and press the flakes on lightly with a dry hand, covering the faces and the edges. Do not pack them down.
Shake off the loose flakes and fry soon, before the coat turns damp.

intro.what: Flour, egg and panko form a layered coating with loose coarse flakes.
intro.why: Each layer helps the next cling. A light touch keeps the panko texture open instead of pressing it into a dense crust.

mistakes.fix: Press lightly and let the flakes stay loose.
mistakes.mistake: Pressing the panko down hard, which makes a dense, heavy crust.

mistakes.fix: Let the extra egg drip off before the flakes go on.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving thick egg on the meat, which makes a gummy coat.

mistakes.fix: Coat just before frying.
mistakes.mistake: Coating well ahead of the oil, so that the flakes soak up the egg and turn soft.

quiz.because: Heavy pressure compacts the coating instead of retaining its loose texture.
choices: Hard pressure creates more air spaces between the flakes.
Loose flakes make the intended light shaggy crust.
Packing firmly keeps the same light texture while making the crust thicker.
quiz.question: Why avoid packing panko tightly?

quiz.because: Flour prepares the surface, egg wets it, and panko clings to the outer layer.
choices: Panko, then flour, then egg.
Egg, then panko, then flour.
Flour, then egg, then panko.
quiz.question: Which coating order is used here?

quiz.because: Even dry coverage gives the crust its intended texture across the piece.
choices: Dry flakes covering the faces and edges without bare spots.
Wet egg pooling between tightly crushed crumbs.
Bare edges around a thick central mound.
quiz.question: What should the coated piece look like before frying?

quiz.because: Draining excess egg prevents a thick wet layer from weighing down the coating.
choices: Add more egg over the finished crumbs.
Let excess egg drip off before adding panko.
Press the wet flakes harder against the food.
quiz.question: The coating became gummy with thick egg between the flakes. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The crumbs are panko, coarse, dry flakes, and not fine breadcrumbs, and the coat is flour, then egg, then panko, with no mustard. It fries lighter and more shaggy and stays crisp longer.

cues.text: The coating is thin, dry and even, with no wet spots.
The piece crackles in the oil.

technique/coat-in-starch.does: Dusts a piece of food, often after it has been marinated, in a thin layer of potato starch or cornstarch just before frying. It fries to a crisp, light, pale crust.
how: Pat the food dry and shake off any marinade that is dripping.
Tip the starch into a tray and turn each piece in it, pressing lightly.
Tap off the loose starch, as too much turns pasty in the oil.
Fry straight away, before the starch dampens and turns gluey.

intro.what: Food receives a thin dry starch coating immediately before frying.
intro.why: The amount and timing of coating matter: loose starch or absorbed moisture can turn a light crust heavy and gluey.

mistakes.fix: Shake off the loose starch.
mistakes.mistake: Coating too thickly, which turns gluey and heavy.

mistakes.fix: Coat right before the oil.
mistakes.mistake: Coating long before frying, so that the starch gets wet.

quiz.because: A thin starch film fries differently from a heavy damp coating.
choices: A thick gluey layer.
A soft soaked paste.
A light crisp crust.
quiz.question: What crust is this coating intended to produce?

quiz.because: Removing excess and frying promptly help keep the coating thin and dry.
choices: Tap away loose starch and fry promptly.
Pile on more starch and leave it standing.
Soak the coated food before frying.
quiz.question: What should happen after turning the food in starch?

quiz.because: A dry even film shows the starch has not become a heavy wet layer.
choices: Thick ridges with damp clumps.
Thin, dry and even without wet patches.
A glossy paste sliding off the food.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches the intended coating?

quiz.because: Moisture reaches the starch as it waits, so timing the coating near frying preserves its texture.
choices: Coat earlier so it absorbs more moisture.
Leave the pieces pressed together after coating.
Coat closer to frying.
quiz.question: The starch turned wet while waiting. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The coat is starch, not flour, so it fries thinner, crisper and paler.

cues.text: The fat shivers and gives off a bubble now and then. The food does not sizzle.
A knife or skewer slips into the thickest part with no resistance.

technique/confit.does: Cooks food slowly while it lies covered in fat held far below a simmer, so that it turns tender and silky and the fat takes up its flavour. The food is lifted out and the scented fat is kept.
how: Season or cure the food first if it needs it, and dry it well.
Choose a pot just big enough for the food to lie in one snug layer, with the fat covering it.
Warm the fat over the lowest heat, or in a low oven, until it shivers and gives only the odd bubble. It must never fry.
Add the food and keep the fat at that heat until a knife slips into the thickest part with no resistance. Garlic needs less time than a duck leg, and a piece of fish least.
Lift the food out with a slotted spoon and drain it. Keep the fat.

intro.what: Food cooks gently while submerged in fat that barely moves.
intro.why: Confit treats fat as a gentle cooking medium rather than a fierce frying bath, developing a tender texture without the same browning.

mistakes.fix: Use the lowest heat, and lift the pan off the heat for a moment if the fat bubbles.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the fat get hot enough to fry, which toughens fish and browns garlic bitter.

mistakes.fix: Use a smaller pot, so that the fat covers the food.
mistakes.mistake: Using too little fat, so that part of the food sticks out and dries.

quiz.because: Confit relies on restrained heat instead of the active heat used to form a fried crust.
choices: The food is exposed above the fat to brown.
The fat stays gentle rather than sizzling around the food.
The fat is kept at a vigorous boil.
quiz.question: How does this confit method differ from frying?

quiz.because: A snug pot helps provide full coverage without exposed parts drying.
choices: So widely that much of the food stays exposed.
With the food packed above the fat line.
Snugly enough for the fat to cover it.
quiz.question: How should the pot fit the food?

quiz.because: Subtle movement is the cue for gentle fat rather than frying.
choices: A slight shiver with occasional bubbles.
A vigorous rolling boil.
A surface spitting around a browned crust.
quiz.question: What should the fat look like during cooking?

quiz.because: Reducing the heat restores the gentle medium this method requires.
choices: Raise the heat to deepen the crust.
Lower the heat and move the pan off it briefly if needed.
Expose more of the food above the fat.
quiz.question: The food starts sizzling and browning. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The food lies under fat and not under water, at a heat low enough that the fat barely stirs, so it gives its juices to the fat and takes the fat's flavour in return.

comes_after.why: The rolled round has to be thin and even or it will not puff.

cues.text: Bubbles rise on the upper face, then the bread swells like a ball on the flame, with brown flecks.
The finished bread is soft and flexible, not stiff or leathery.
A warm, toasty scent of wheat rises, with no burnt smell.

technique/cook-a-chapati.does: Cooks a thin round of atta dough for a short time on each face on a dry, hot iron plate, then lays it straight on the open flame, where the steam inside swells it into a soft ball. The finished bread is brushed with ghee and kept soft under a cloth.
how: Heat the iron plate until it is hot all over. A dusting of flour dropped on it should brown at once.
Lay the rolled round on the hot plate. When small bubbles show on the top, turn it.
Cook the second face until it has pale brown spots.
Using tongs, lift the bread off the plate and lay it straight on the open flame. It puffs up in moments.
Turn it over for a moment, then take it off. Brush it with ghee if wanted and stack the finished breads in a cloth, so that they stay soft.

intro.what: A thin atta round cooks on a hot dry plate before puffing over an open flame.
intro.why: The bread needs enough heat to puff without drying on the plate. Steam gives the soft bread its inflated shape.

mistakes.fix: Turn it as soon as bubbles show, and keep each side short.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking it too long on the plate, so that it dries out and will not puff.

mistakes.fix: Heat the plate until a dusting of flour browns at once.
mistakes.mistake: Putting it on a plate that is not hot enough, so that it turns leathery.

mistakes.fix: Hold it there for moments only and turn it.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the bread on the flame, where it chars to ash.

quiz.because: Steam expands between the bread surfaces and produces the puff.
choices: The flour dusting inflates as it browns.
Fat applied after cooking creates the internal puff.
Steam forming inside the bread.
quiz.question: What makes the chapati swell over the flame?

quiz.because: Early bubbles signal the change used for turning before the bread dries out.
choices: When small bubbles appear on top.
After it has dried into a rigid sheet.
Before any surface change appears.
quiz.question: When should the first face be turned on the plate?

quiz.because: The intended bread bends rather than becoming rigid from prolonged plate cooking.
choices: Stiff and leathery.
Soft and flexible.
Brittle and dry throughout.
quiz.question: What texture should the finished chapati have?

quiz.because: Excess drying on the plate works against the later steam puff.
choices: Keep it on the plate until it becomes stiffer.
Use a cooler plate and extend the cooking.
Turn promptly when bubbles appear and avoid prolonged plate cooking.
quiz.question: A chapati dried on the plate and would not puff. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: After the dry plate the bread is lifted off and held directly on the open flame, where trapped steam puffs it into a ball. A griddled flat bread is left on the hot surface from start to end.

comes_after.why: The vegetables go into a masala base that has already been fried until its fat parts.

cues.text: The pieces are tender and coated in a thick, dry spice paste, with a little browned crust on some.
A piece breaks easily under a spoon and a fork goes in with no resistance.

technique/cook-a-dry-vegetable-dish.does: Cooks cut vegetables in spiced fat with no added water, under a lid over a low heat, so that they soften in their own steam and end up coated in a thick spiced paste, with no gravy left in the pan.
how: Cut the vegetables into pieces of an even size and pat them dry.
Start the pan with a tempering of whole spices and a masala base cooked until its fat parts.
Add the vegetables and stir until they are coated. Add salt.
Cover the pan and cook over a low heat, lifting the lid and stirring now and then, so that the steam from the vegetables does the cooking. Sprinkle in a spoonful of water only if the pan catches.
Take off the lid at the end and stir over a higher heat for a short time, until any moisture has gone and the spices cling to the pieces.

intro.what: Vegetables soften in spiced fat and their own steam before moisture is released from the pan.
intro.why: The lid is useful early and removed later: containing moisture softens the vegetables, while releasing it makes the spices cling.

mistakes.fix: Trust their own moisture and add only a spoonful if the pan catches.
mistakes.mistake: Adding water at the start, so that the vegetables boil and the dish turns into a watery stew.

mistakes.fix: Stir gently and seldom, and use a wide pan.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring hard, so that soft vegetables break into mush.

mistakes.fix: Take the lid off for the end of the cooking and let the moisture cook away.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the lid on to the end, so that the dish is damp and not dry.

quiz.because: The final uncovered stage removes loose moisture and leaves a coating of spices.
choices: Spices cling to the vegetables without a pool of gravy.
The vegetables float in a thin broth.
The vegetables are drained of their spice coating before serving.
quiz.question: What distinguishes this dish from a watery stew?

quiz.because: The changing use of the lid manages moisture differently at each stage.
choices: Uncovered throughout to prevent any steam.
Covered for gentle softening, then uncovered to dry the finish.
Tightly covered even after moisture needs to leave.
quiz.question: How is the pan covered during this method?

quiz.because: The intended result retains vegetable pieces with a concentrated coating.
choices: Vegetables submerged in clear water.
A smooth paste with no remaining pieces.
Distinct pieces coated in a thick spice paste.
quiz.question: What should the finished vegetables look like?

quiz.because: Soft vegetables need gentle movement to preserve their shape.
choices: Stir more gently and less often.
Mash the pieces more firmly against the base.
Keep stirring vigorously as they soften.
quiz.question: The softened vegetables broke into mush during stirring. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: No liquid is added, and the pieces are not browned first. The vegetables cook in their own steam under a lid and the dish ends dry, with a coat of spices, and not in a sauce.

comes_after.why: The dough must be risen before it is stretched and cooked.

cues.text: Large bubbles lift across the top and the underside is speckled with brown, not black all over.
The naan is soft and bends without cracking when it is lifted.
A toasty, buttery smell as the ghee meets the hot bread.

technique/cook-a-naan.does: Stretches a rested ball of naan dough by hand into a teardrop, cooks it on a very hot iron plate until it puffs and blisters, then holds it for a moment over the open flame to char it in spots. The finished bread is brushed with ghee and kept soft under a cloth.
how: Divide the risen dough into equal balls, cover them, and let them rest for a short while.
Flatten a ball on a floured board, then pull and press it by hand into a teardrop, a little thicker than a chapati.
Heat the iron plate until a drop of water skips on it. Wet one face of the naan lightly and lay it on the plate wet side down, so that it sticks and steams.
Cook until bubbles rise across the top and the underside is spotted with brown.
Turn the naan with the tongs and hold the top over the open flame for a moment, until it is blistered in dark spots.
Brush at once with melted ghee and keep the naan wrapped in a cloth while the rest are cooked.

intro.what: Rested naan dough is stretched by hand, cooked on a hot plate and blistered over a flame.
intro.why: Keeping its body and cooking it briskly supports a soft bread with raised bubbles and charred spots.

mistakes.fix: Let the plate heat well first and cook quickly.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking on a plate that is not hot enough, so that the naan dries and turns leathery before it puffs.

mistakes.fix: Keep it a little thick and stretch it by hand.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling the dough thin like a chapati, so that it does not puff or stay soft.

mistakes.fix: Hold it over the flame only for a moment, turning it with tongs.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it on the flame too long, so that it chars to a cinder.

quiz.because: This method preserves more dough thickness for a puffy, flexible bread.
choices: A thinner sheet holds more moisture through a longer cooking.
Its thicker stretched shape helps retain the intended soft body.
A thicker shape should prevent the surface from blistering.
quiz.question: Why avoid rolling this naan as thinly as a chapati?

quiz.because: The wetted face sticks to the plate and supports the cooking described in this method.
choices: The face already coated in melted ghee.
A face covered with a thick flour crust.
The lightly wetted face.
quiz.question: Which face meets the hot plate first?

quiz.because: Blisters and spotted browning accompany the soft bread rather than an all-over burnt surface.
choices: Raised bubbles and brown spots, with a flexible texture.
A flat pale sheet that cracks when bent.
A uniformly black and brittle crust.
quiz.question: What does the intended naan look and feel like?

quiz.because: A properly heated plate encourages quick bubbling before the bread loses too much moisture.
choices: Start on a cooler plate and cook more slowly.
Heat the plate thoroughly before adding it.
Roll it thinner and let it dry on the plate.
quiz.question: The naan becomes leathery before puffing. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The dough is yeast and yogurt dough, stretched by hand into a teardrop and left thicker. It is laid wet side down on the plate so that it sticks and steams, and it is charred over the flame at the end and not puffed whole.

en: cook rice in a paella pan

comes_after.why: The broth and the base of a paella start from a sofrito.

cues.text: The bubbling gives way to a faint crackle as the last of the liquid goes and the bottom begins to toast.
A nutty, toasted smell. A burnt smell means the pan must come off the heat at once.
The rice lies in a thin, even layer with separate grains and no liquid standing.

technique/cook-a-paella.does: Cooks short-grain rice in a thin, even layer in a wide, shallow pan, in a well-flavoured broth, with no lid and no stirring, until the rice has taken the broth up and a thin toasted crust, the socarrat, forms on the bottom.
how: Bring the flavoured broth, which has already simmered with its meat and vegetables, to a lively boil in the paella pan. Taste it: it should taste a little strong, as the rice will soften it.
Scatter the rice evenly over the pan in one layer and stir once to spread it. Do not stir again.
Cook at a strong simmer, then turn the heat down once the rice has swollen. Turn the pan over the flame if it is bigger than the burner, so that all the rice cooks at one pace.
When the broth has almost gone and the rice is nearly tender, turn the heat up for a short while to toast the bottom.
Take the pan off the heat and let it rest, covered with a clean cloth, so that the rice finishes in its own steam.

intro.what: Rice absorbs broth in a wide shallow pan without stirring, with a toasted socarrat underneath.
intro.why: Leaving the grains undisturbed preserves a loose texture; the sound and aroma at the end help distinguish toasting from burning.

mistakes.fix: Spread it once and then leave it alone.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring the rice, which releases starch and makes it creamy like a risotto and not loose.

mistakes.fix: Measure the broth against the rice and keep the layer thin.
mistakes.mistake: Too much broth or too deep a layer, which leaves the rice soft, wet and uneven.

mistakes.fix: Listen for the crackle, smell the pan, and take it off the heat when it smells toasty.
mistakes.mistake: Toasting the bottom too long, so that the crust burns.

quiz.because: Repeated stirring releases starch, which changes the texture away from this paella method.
choices: To encourage a thick risotto-like sauce.
To keep all the rice above the broth.
To avoid making the rice creamy with released starch.
quiz.question: Why leave the rice unstirred after spreading it?

quiz.because: An even shallow layer helps the rice cook consistently across the broad pan.
choices: Spread evenly in a shallow layer.
Piled deeply in the centre.
Packed into separate tall mounds.
quiz.question: How should the rice sit in the pan?

quiz.because: The change reflects liquid disappearing and the base beginning to toast.
choices: A continuous loud splashing sound.
Bubbling changes to a faint crackle.
Silence while broth remains deep.
quiz.question: What sound signals the bottom beginning to toast?

quiz.because: Socarrat should be toasted; a burnt smell warns that the base has gone beyond that flavour.
choices: Keep toasting to make the crust darker.
Stir the burnt base through the rice.
Take the pan off the heat.
quiz.question: A burnt smell replaces the nutty aroma. What should happen?

variant_of.differs: The rice is cooked uncovered, in a thin layer in a wide pan and in a flavoured broth, with no stirring, and it is finished with a toasted crust on the bottom. Plain rice is cooked under a tight lid.

en: fry a paratha on the plate

comes_after.why: The layers are made by the folding, and the plate only sets them apart, so folding comes first.

cues.text: Golden brown spots spread over both faces and the layers lift a little at the edge.
The ghee sizzles softly at the edge of the bread and does not spit.
The bread is crisp at the surface, and the layers spring apart when it is pressed.

technique/cook-a-paratha.does: Cooks a folded and lightly rolled round of atta dough on a hot iron plate, spooning a little ghee over one face and then the other, until each face is golden in spots and the layers inside have set apart, flaky and soft. The bread stays on the plate from start to end.
how: Heat the iron plate until a sprinkle of flour dropped on it browns slowly.
Lay the bread on the plate and cook until the first face is dry in spots and the bread has turned pale and a little puffy.
Turn it, spoon ghee over the top and let it sink in at the edge.
Turn it again, spoon ghee on the other face and press the edges gently with the spatula, until both faces are golden brown in spots.
Lift it out and, while it is hot, crush it lightly between the palms so that the layers open.

intro.what: Folded atta dough cooks on a hot plate with ghee applied as its faces turn.
intro.why: Gentle pressure and fat preserve the layered structure, so the finished bread can separate into soft flaky layers.

mistakes.fix: Heat the plate first and spoon ghee on each face as it cooks.
mistakes.mistake: Using too little ghee or a plate that is not hot, so that the bread dries and turns leathery.

mistakes.fix: Press only gently at the edges, and crush it lightly after cooking.
mistakes.mistake: Pressing hard on the bread, which squeezes the layers together.

quiz.because: The folding and fat create layers that cooking should preserve.
choices: They should separate rather than compress into a dense sheet.
They should merge into a stiff solid centre.
They should remain coated in dry flour.
quiz.question: What texture should the folded layers retain?

quiz.because: Gentle edge pressure helps contact without squeezing the layers together.
choices: Hard across the whole centre.
Gently at the edges.
Firmly across both faces after every turn.
quiz.question: Where is pressure applied while the paratha cooks?

quiz.because: Lifting edges and separating layers match the intended flaky structure.
choices: The bread is flat and leathery with sealed edges.
The faces remain pale and wet.
They lift at the edges and spring apart when pressed.
quiz.question: Which cue shows the layers have remained distinct?

quiz.because: Heavy pressure compresses the structure the folded dough was meant to retain.
choices: Use gentler edge pressure.
Press harder across the centre.
Flatten the bread firmly after every turn.
quiz.question: The layers became dense after hard pressing. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: Ghee is spooned over each face as it cooks, so the bread browns in ghee and not on a dry or barely oiled plate, and the folded layers set apart inside.
The bread stays on the plate from start to end and is never lifted to puff on the open flame. A paratha is meant to be flaky and golden, and a chapati is meant to swell into a ball.

comes_after.why: The potato has to be soft before the egg goes round it, and it is cooked soft in oil first.
The cake is turned over in the same way as any food that must be turned while its top is still soft.

cues.text: The edge pulls from the pan and turns pale gold, and the top shrinks from wet to a soft, glossy skin.
The pan shakes freely and the cake slides on the oil.
A sweet, eggy smell. A sharp, burnt smell means the heat is too high.

technique/cook-a-tortilla.does: Sets a mix of beaten egg and soft cooked potato in a small pan into a thick, round cake, golden outside and tender or even creamy in the middle. It is turned over once with the help of a plate.
how: Heat a spoonful of the kept oil in a small non-stick pan over a medium heat, so that it coats the base and the sides.
Pour in the mix of egg and potato and press it level. It should hiss softly, not spit.
Cook gently. Shake the pan now and then and run a spatula round the edge to keep it neat and tucked in, until the underside is golden and the edge has set while the top is still wet.
Turn it over onto a flat plate and slide it back, as in the flip, then tuck the edges in and cook the other side briefly.
Slide it onto a plate and let it stand a while. The middle can be left soft or set firm, as the cook likes.

intro.what: Egg and softened potato form a thick Spanish tortilla that is turned with a plate.
intro.why: Gentle heat and a coherent underside let you manage a substantial egg cake without tearing it during the turn.

mistakes.fix: Cook it over a medium heat or lower, and give it time.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking it too hot, so that the outside burns before the egg in the middle has begun to set.

mistakes.fix: Wait until the edge is firm and the cake slides when the pan is shaken.
mistakes.mistake: Turning it before the underside has set, so that it tears and runs.

mistakes.fix: Use a small, deep pan, so that the cake is thick.
mistakes.mistake: Using a pan far too big, which leaves a thin, dry cake.

quiz.because: Pan size controls the depth and texture of the tortilla.
choices: To spread the mixture as thinly as possible.
To keep a thick cake rather than a thin dry layer.
To make the egg set as a very thin outer film.
quiz.question: Why use a suitably small pan for this tortilla?

quiz.because: A coherent moving cake is easier to turn without tearing.
choices: The underside is still loose and runs freely.
The cake is stuck firmly to the base.
The edge is firm and the cake slides when shaken.
quiz.question: What should you check before the plate-assisted turn?

quiz.because: Sliding shows that the cake can move as a joined shape before the turn.
choices: The cake slides freely when the pan is shaken.
The pan moves but the cake stays fixed.
Only loose egg moves around a stuck base.
quiz.question: What pan movement suggests the tortilla is released?

quiz.because: Gentler heat gives the thicker mixture time to change without burning the exterior.
choices: Raise the heat to darken the surface faster.
Lower the heat for gentler cooking.
Keep the heat high but turn the cake repeatedly.
quiz.question: The outside scorches before the centre starts setting. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The egg is a thick flat cake with soft potato inside it and is never rolled. It is cooked slowly, turned over with a plate, and served warm or at room temperature, with the middle left soft or firm to taste. A rolled omelette is thin, quick and creamy.

en: cook in garlic and chilli oil

comes_after.why: The garlic has to be sliced evenly, so that all of it turns pale gold at the same moment.

cues.text: A steady, lively sizzle when the food goes in, which dies down to a gentle bubbling.
Sweet garlic, with no sharp or bitter edge.
The garlic is pale gold and the shrimp are curled and opaque, with the oil bubbling round them.

technique/cook-al-ajillo.does: Cooks small pieces of shellfish or mushroom for a short time in a generous pool of olive oil scented with sliced garlic and a piece of hot pepper, in a shallow earthenware dish. The oil becomes the sauce, and the food reaches the table still sizzling in it.
how: Put the olive oil, the sliced garlic and the pieces of hot pepper in a cold earthenware dish and set it over a medium heat, so that the garlic warms along with the oil.
Let the oil heat until the garlic starts to bubble gently and turns pale gold. Do not let it brown.
Add the dry, salted shrimp or mushrooms in one layer and turn the heat up. Shake the dish now and then so that they cook evenly in the oil.
As soon as the shrimp turn opaque and curl, or the mushrooms soften, take the dish off the heat. The hot dish keeps the oil sizzling.
Scatter chopped parsley over and take the dish straight to the table, with bread to mop up the oil.

intro.what: Garlic and pepper scent olive oil before small pieces cook in the same shallow dish.
intro.why: The oil becomes the sauce, so managing the garlic colour controls the flavour of the whole dish.

mistakes.fix: Start it in cold oil, and add the food as soon as the garlic is pale gold.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the garlic brown, which turns the whole pool of oil bitter.

mistakes.fix: Take the dish off the heat the moment they turn opaque.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking the shrimp too long, so that they turn rubbery.

mistakes.fix: Pat them dry first.
mistakes.mistake: Adding wet shrimp, which spit and cool the oil.

quiz.because: Bitter garlic affects the whole pool of oil surrounding the food.
choices: The oil is discarded before serving.
Brown garlic gives the same mild flavour as pale gold garlic.
The garlic flavours all the oil that becomes the sauce.
quiz.question: Why does garlic colour matter especially here?

quiz.because: Warming garlic with the oil gives more control before it reaches pale gold.
choices: In cold oil that warms with it.
Thrown into already smoking oil.
Dry in the dish before oil is added.
quiz.question: How does the garlic begin cooking in this method?

quiz.because: Pale gold develops garlic flavour without the bitterness of excessive browning.
choices: Dark brown with a sharp bitter smell.
Pale gold with a sweet aroma.
Black edges and a smoking dish.
quiz.question: Which garlic cue is intended before adding the food?

quiz.because: Stopping the garlic at the intended colour prevents its burnt flavour spreading through the sauce.
choices: Keep browning the garlic before adding food.
Leave the garlic in smoking oil longer.
Add the food while the garlic is pale gold rather than brown.
quiz.question: The garlic made the oil bitter. What should change next time?

variant_of.differs: The food lies in a deep pool of oil and not in a thin film, the garlic and the pepper are warmed in the oil first, and the dish goes to the table as it was cooked, oil and all. A sauté keeps small pieces moving in a hot pan with a little fat.

comes_after.why: The onion is softened in the fat before the grain goes in.

cues.text: Small steam holes show in the surface and no liquid is left in the pan.
The grains are plump and tender with a slight bite, and they fall apart when fluffed.
A nutty, savoury taste with the sweetness of the onion and paste.

technique/cook-bulgur-pilaf.does: Fries coarse bulgur in fat with softened onion and a spoon of paste until every grain is coated, then covers it with hot liquid and leaves it under a lid, without stirring, until the grains have swollen, drunk the liquid and stand apart.
how: Soften the onion in the fat, then stir in the pepper or tomato paste and fry it until the colour deepens.
Add the bulgur and stir for a short while until each grain is coated and smells toasty.
Pour in hot water or stock, a little more than the volume of the bulgur, and add salt. Bring it to a boil.
Cover and turn the heat to its lowest. Do not stir.
When the liquid has gone, take the pan off the heat, lay a cloth under the lid and leave it to stand.
Fluff the grains with a fork before serving.

intro.what: Coated bulgur grains absorb hot liquid under a lid, then rest before being fluffed.
intro.why: Coating, undisturbed absorption and resting each support separate plump grains instead of a sticky porridge.

mistakes.fix: Stir only when the grains are coated, and fluff at the end.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring while it cooks, which breaks the grains and turns them sticky.

mistakes.fix: Measure the liquid and use only a little more than the bulgur.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in too much liquid, which leaves a wet porridge.

mistakes.fix: Let it stand under a cloth and lid first.
mistakes.mistake: Serving it straight from the heat, so that it is wet and clumped.

quiz.because: Stirring during absorption can damage the grains and make them cling together.
choices: To limit broken grains and stickiness.
To turn the grains into a thick paste.
To keep the seasoning only at the surface.
quiz.question: Why avoid stirring while the bulgur absorbs liquid?

quiz.because: Resting precedes the gentle final separation with a fork.
choices: Continuously while liquid is absorbed.
After cooking and a covered rest.
Before the hot liquid enters the pan.
quiz.question: When are the grains fluffed?

quiz.because: The aim is tender but distinct grains, rather than porridge or unabsorbed liquid.
choices: A wet paste without distinct grains.
Dry hard grains floating in excess stock.
Plump grains with a slight bite that separate when fluffed.
quiz.question: Which texture describes the intended bulgur?

quiz.because: Resting lets the moisture settle before the grains are separated.
choices: Include the covered resting stage before fluffing.
Stir vigorously while serving it straight away.
Add more liquid immediately before serving.
quiz.question: The pilaf is wet and clumped when served directly from the heat. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The grain is coarse bulgur, which is already steamed and dried, so it needs no washing or soaking and takes less liquid and less time than rice. A spoon of pepper or tomato paste goes in with the onion for colour and body.

comes_after.why: A tagine starts on a bed of softened onion, so a cook has to know how to soften onion in fat without colour.

cues.text: Only a few small bubbles stir at the edge of the sauce, and a little steam rises from the top of the cone.
The meat gives way to the side of a spoon without a pull.
The scent of the spices turns round and warm, with no sharp note of scorching.

technique/cook-in-a-tagine.does: Cooks meat or poultry slowly over low heat in a shallow earthenware dish under a tall cone lid, on a bed of sliced onion, fat and spices, with only a little water. The steam rises into the cone, cools and runs back down, so the food stews in its own juices and the sauce stays short and strong.
how: Spread sliced onion over the base of the dish with the fat and the spices, and pour in a little water, only enough to wet the base.
Lay the meat on top and season it. Do not brown it first.
Put on the lid and set the dish over the lowest heat, with a diffuser under it if the flame is fierce. Leave it alone and lift the lid as seldom as you can.
When the meat is tender, spread over it whatever finishes the dish, such as dried fruit, olives or vegetables, and cover again.
Cook on until the sauce has shrunk to a rich coat and the fat shines on top.

intro.what: A cone-lidded earthenware tagine cooks gently with restrained added water.
intro.why: The lid returns condensed steam to the dish. Keeping that cycle intact develops a concentrated sauce without treating the pot as a deep stew.

mistakes.fix: Start on the lowest heat, use a diffuser, and bring the heat up slowly.
mistakes.mistake: Setting the dish on a fierce heat, which scorches the base and can crack the clay.

mistakes.fix: Start with only a little. The lid sends the steam back down.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in water to cover, which makes a thin soup and washes out the taste of the spices.

mistakes.fix: Leave it covered and check only near the end.
mistakes.mistake: Lifting the lid again and again, which lets the steam escape.

quiz.because: Steam cools against the lid and runs back toward the food.
choices: Dry oven air that browns the meat.
Moisture condensed from rising steam.
Oil splashed upward from the pot base.
quiz.question: What does the cone lid return to the dish?

quiz.because: Gradual gentle heating protects the base and supports the restrained bubbling of this method.
choices: Over fierce direct heat from the start.
With the empty clay dish heated until smoking.
Over low heat, with a diffuser if needed.
quiz.question: How should this tagine begin on the stove?

quiz.because: Quiet bubbling fits the low-heat cooking and concentrated sauce.
choices: Occasional small bubbles near the sauce edge.
A violent rolling boil across the dish.
Dry smoking patches around the base.
quiz.question: What bubbling pattern belongs to this cooking style?

quiz.because: The tagine returns moisture, so excessive added water dilutes the intended sauce.
choices: Add more water whenever steam reaches the lid.
Begin with less water and rely on the covered moisture cycle.
Leave the lid open throughout to release all steam.
quiz.question: The sauce became thin after covering the food in water. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: Braising browns the food first and cooks it in a measured amount of liquid. A tagine skips the browning, lays the meat on a bed of onion and spices and adds only a little water, because the cone lid sends the steam back down.

comes_after.why: The gravy is made on a masala base cooked until its fat parts, so the base comes first.

cues.text: The gravy is thick and glossy and clings to the pieces, with a little fat shining at the edge.
The pieces give easily under a spoon and are tender throughout.
The scent is round and full, with no raw spice in it.

technique/cook-in-masala-gravy.does: Simmers pieces of meat, bird or firm cheese in a gravy made from a fried masala base, with a little water or cream, until they are tender and the gravy has thickened and clings to them.
how: Start from a masala base cooked until its fat has parted.
Add the pieces, raw or already roasted or fried, and stir them into the base for a moment so that they are coated.
Add hot water or cream a little at a time, and bring the pan to a gentle simmer. Cover it partly.
Stir now and then and scrape the bottom. Add a little more liquid if the gravy dries out before the pieces are tender.
Stop when the pieces are tender and the gravy is thick enough to coat them, with a shine of fat on top.
Stir in the finishing touches, such as cream, dried fenugreek leaf or garam masala, off the heat or just before.

intro.what: Pieces simmer gently in a fried masala base loosened into a coating gravy.
intro.why: The balance between added liquid and reduced sauce controls whether the masala clings while the pieces soften.

mistakes.fix: Add hot water, a little at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in cold water, which stops the cooking and thins the flavour.

mistakes.fix: Keep a gentle simmer and stir now and then.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling hard, so that the gravy splits and the pieces turn tough.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat for a moment, or lower the heat, before the cream goes in.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the cream or yogurt to a boiling pan, so that it splits.

quiz.because: The sauce should surround and coat rather than remain watery or catch on the base.
choices: A clear broth that leaves the pieces bare.
A dry burnt paste fixed to the pan.
Thick enough to cling to the pieces.
quiz.question: What consistency is this gravy intended to reach?

quiz.because: Gradual hot additions give control over the gravy while maintaining the cooking.
choices: Hot and gradually, followed by gentle simmering.
Cold in a large sudden addition, then hard boiling.
Only after the base has scorched dry.
quiz.question: How is liquid added to the fried masala base?

quiz.because: A glossy coating is the visual texture cue for the finished gravy.
choices: Watery with uncombined raw spice floating above it.
Thick and glossy with fat shining at the edge.
Dry black patches beneath a separated liquid.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches the intended gravy?

quiz.because: Reducing the heat before the finishing cream avoids the harsh boiling associated with splitting.
choices: Add cream while increasing the boil.
Keep boiling harder until the separation disappears.
Lower the heat or take the pan off it before adding cream.
quiz.question: The gravy split when cream met a hard boil. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The pieces are not browned first and there is no wine or stock. The liquid is water or cream added to a fried masala base, and the sauce is thick and clings to the pieces. It is cooked on the stove, covered only in part.

comes_after.why: The rice is soaked before it is cooked in the seasoned stock.

cues.text: A sweet, savoury steam rises from the pot.
The rice is evenly tinted by the seasoning, and the pieces are scattered on top.

technique/cook-mixed-rice.does: Cooks washed, soaked rice together with a seasoned stock and small pieces of vegetables, mushrooms or tofu, so that the taste cooks into every grain.
how: Put the washed, soaked, drained rice in the pot or the rice cooker and level it.
Pour in the seasoned stock, in place of plain water, up to the usual level. Stir once, then leave it still.
Scatter the cut pieces evenly over the top without stirring them in, and shut the lid.
Cook the rice as usual, then leave it to rest, covered.
Fold the pieces through the rice at the end.

intro.what: Rice absorbs seasoned stock beneath scattered vegetables, mushrooms or tofu.
intro.why: Layering the additions above the rice lets the grains cook evenly before a final fold distributes the pieces.

mistakes.fix: Lay the pieces on top and fold them in afterwards.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring the pieces into the rice before cooking, which makes some of the rice cook unevenly.

mistakes.fix: Use the same amount of liquid as for plain rice, counting the seasonings as part of it.
mistakes.mistake: Adding too much stock and seasoning, so that the rice is soft and salty.

quiz.because: Seasoned stock replaces plain water so its flavour enters the rice during absorption.
choices: From the seasoned cooking stock.
Only from toppings added after cooking.
From rinsing after the grains are cooked.
quiz.question: Where does the rice take up its seasoning in this method?

quiz.because: The method leaves the additions above the rice until the final fold.
choices: Stirred repeatedly through the rice as it cooks.
Scattered on top of the levelled rice.
Packed below the rice in a dense layer.
quiz.question: Where should the cut additions go before cooking?

quiz.because: Even tinting is the appearance expected from cooking the rice in seasoned liquid.
choices: Only dry topping pieces have colour.
Pale grain clumps sit in dark liquid.
The grains are evenly tinted.
quiz.question: What shows the stock has coloured the rice?

quiz.because: Delaying the mixing preserves the level rice bed during absorption.
choices: Leave the additions on top and fold them through after resting.
Stir the additions through more often during cooking.
Compress the additions firmly into the uncooked grains.
quiz.question: Rice cooked unevenly after the pieces were mixed in early. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The rice cooks in seasoned stock together with its pieces of vegetable and tofu, and not in plain water, so the whole pot is flavoured.

comes_after.why: The dough has to be folded into layers before it is cooked.

cues.text: Both faces are golden and speckled, and the edges look layered.
The fat sizzles gently under the dough.
The bread is crisp on the outside and soft inside, and pulls apart in thin sheets.

technique/cook-msemen.does: Stretches a folded square of layered dough out thin again with oiled fingertips, lays it on a hot, lightly oiled griddle and cooks both faces until it is golden in speckles and its layers have set apart, so that it comes away in flaky sheets.
how: Heat a flat griddle or a wide pan over a medium heat and oil it lightly.
Press the folded square out with oiled fingertips, to a flat square that is still in layers.
Lay it on the griddle and cook until the underside is gold and speckled.
Turn it over once and cook the other side the same way.
Lift it out, clap it between the hands so that the layers open, and serve it hot.

intro.what: A folded square of msemen dough is stretched gently and cooked on an oiled griddle.
intro.why: The folds need room to remain distinct: fingertip shaping and moderate heat preserve flaky sheets beneath the crisp surface.

mistakes.fix: Press it out with oiled fingertips.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling the square flat with a pin, which crushes the layers together.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat moderate.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking on too high a heat, so that the outside burns and the layers inside stay doughy.

quiz.because: Msemen is shaped in layers, so cooking should leave those layers distinguishable.
choices: A dense dough slab without layers.
Thin layers that pull apart in sheets.
A brittle crumb throughout the bread.
quiz.question: What structure should this cooking method preserve?

quiz.because: Fingertips spread the square without crushing the folded layers together.
choices: Rolled forcefully with a pin.
Pressed until all the seams disappear.
With oiled fingertips.
quiz.question: How is the folded square flattened before cooking?

quiz.because: Spotted browning and visible layers match the intended griddle texture.
choices: Speckled golden faces with layered edges.
Black faces around a dense wet centre.
Pale faces sealed into a smooth solid slab.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches the cooked bread?

quiz.because: Moderating the heat gives the inner layers time to change before the surface burns.
choices: Increase the griddle heat further.
Use more moderate heat.
Press the bread harder to fuse the layers.
quiz.question: The outside burns while inner layers stay doughy. What should change?

variant_of.differs: Griddling cooks flat breads that are already shaped. Here the dough is a folded square of many layers of fat and dough, pressed out thin by hand on the pan itself, turned once, and clapped open at the end.

cues.text: After the dips the arms curl into tight spirals and the purple skin is still on.
A knife slides into the thickest part of an arm as into a ripe pear, with no pull.
The cut rounds are glossy and keep their curl, with the skin still on the edge.

technique/cook-octopus.does: Cooks a whole octopus in plenty of water, first dipping it in and out of the boil several times so that the arms curl and the skin stays on, then lets it bubble steadily until the thickest part of an arm is tender. It is rested, then snipped into rounds with scissors.
how: Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Hold the octopus by the head with tongs and dip it in and out of the water, a few times, for a moment each time. The arms curl up.
Lower it in completely. When the water comes back to a boil, turn the heat down to a steady bubbling.
Cook until a knife slips into the thickest part of an arm with no pull. The time depends on the size of the animal, so test it often towards the end.
Lift it out onto a board, cover it with a cloth and let it rest while the potatoes cook in the same water. It goes on softening as it stands.
Snip the arms into rounds about as thick as a thumb with kitchen scissors, straight onto the serving dish. Cut the head into strips if it is used.

intro.what: Octopus is dipped into boiling water, simmered gently and cut into rounds with scissors.
intro.why: This method pays attention to the curled shape, skin and tender texture rather than treating vigorous boiling as the goal.

mistakes.fix: Dip it in and out of the boil first, to set the skin.
mistakes.mistake: Lowering the octopus straight in, so that the arms stay limp and the skin comes away.

mistakes.fix: Turn the heat down to a steady bubbling once it is in.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling it hard for the whole time, which toughens the outside before the middle has softened.

mistakes.fix: Snip them with scissors straight onto the dish.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting the rounds with a knife on a board, which squashes them and loses the juices.

quiz.because: Snipping produces rounds without the pressure that can crush them under a knife.
choices: They stretch the arms into straighter portions.
They press the rounds firmly flat as they cut.
They avoid squashing the arms against a board.
quiz.question: Why use scissors for the final rounds here?

quiz.because: The method reduces the heat after immersion to avoid a harsh boil.
choices: With steady gentle bubbling.
At a fierce rolling boil throughout.
Without movement as soon as the octopus enters.
quiz.question: After the initial dips and immersion, how should the water move?

quiz.because: Curling arms with attached skin are the preparation cues described for the dipping stage.
choices: The arms remain limp while the skin loosens.
The arms curl and the skin remains attached.
The arms curl while the skin peels away.
quiz.question: What change is observed after the initial dips?

quiz.because: Scissors reduce the board pressure that can squash the rounds.
choices: Press the knife more firmly through the arms.
Flatten the arms before slicing.
Snip them directly with kitchen scissors.
quiz.question: Rounds became flattened when sliced on a board. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The food is one whole animal and not many small pieces. It is dipped in and out of the boil first, then cooked at a steady bubbling, rested out of the water, and cut with scissors. Boiling cooks small pieces fast and evenly in fast-bubbling water.

en: seal the pot and cook slowly

comes_after.why: The rice goes into the pot only nearly cooked, so a cook has to be able to stop it at that point first.
The meat goes into the pot already marinated, and cooks in the steam without being browned.

cues.text: A rich scent of spice, saffron and ghee seeps out from under the lid when the pot is nearly ready.
A faint, steady hiss comes from the pot, with no hard bubbling.
The grains of rice on top are long, dry and separate, and the meat below is tender and coated in a thick gravy.

technique/cook-on-dum.does: Layers marinated meat and nearly cooked rice in a heavy pot, closes the lid tightly, often with a rope of dough, and finishes the dish in its own steam over a very low heat. Nothing is stirred, and the pot is opened at the table.
how: Spread the marinated meat in an even layer on the bottom of a heavy pot, with a little ghee.
Pile the nearly cooked rice over the meat in loose layers, with herbs, crisp fried onions and ghee between them. Do not press it down.
Sprinkle saffron steeped in warm milk over the top.
Seal the gap between the lid and the pot with a rope of firm dough, pressing it in all round. A heavy cloth under the lid works too.
Set the pot on a flat plate of iron over a medium heat for a short spell to build up steam, then turn the heat to its lowest and leave it undisturbed.
Rest the sealed pot off the heat before it is broken open. Fold the rice and the meat together from the bottom with a flat spoon, so the layers are kept.

intro.what: Layered rice and marinated meat finish in a tightly sealed pot over restrained heat.
intro.why: Dum depends on contained steam and intact layers. Keeping the pot closed matters more than repeated checking or stirring.

mistakes.fix: Press the rope of dough into the join all round, and patch any gap at once.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the seal leak, so that the steam escapes and the rice on top stays hard.

mistakes.fix: Set the pot on a flat iron plate and turn the heat to its lowest once the steam builds.
mistakes.mistake: Keeping the heat too high, so that the bottom layer scorches.

mistakes.fix: Leave the pot shut until the end of the rest.
mistakes.mistake: Lifting the lid to look, which lets the steam out and breaks the slow cooking.

mistakes.fix: Dig down to the bottom with a flat spoon and lift the layers out whole.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring the layers together, so that the dish turns into a heap of mush.

quiz.because: The seal contains the moisture on which the undisturbed cooking depends.
choices: To retain the steam that finishes the layered dish.
To dry the upper rice with escaping steam.
To make stirring through the layers easier.
quiz.question: Why seal the lid closely for this dum method?

quiz.because: Loose layering preserves the structure rather than compressing or mixing the grains.
choices: Packed firmly into a dense block.
In loose layers without pressing it down.
Stirred into the meat before sealing.
quiz.question: How should rice be placed over the meat?

quiz.because: The quiet hiss accompanies the restrained heat used after steam builds.
choices: Hard bubbling and loud spitting.
A sharp crackle from a drying base.
A faint steady hiss.
quiz.question: What sound fits the intended gentle cooking?

quiz.because: The plate and lower heat moderate the heat reaching the bottom layer.
choices: Reduce the heat and use the iron plate beneath the pot.
Increase the direct flame under the base.
Press the layers tightly against the bottom.
quiz.question: The base scorches while the pot stays sealed. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The seal is for a pot on the stove, over a very low heat, and not for a long bake. The food is layered, half-cooked rice over marinated meat, and cooks in the steam and scent held in the pot, never stirred.
A pilaf cooks raw rice in a measured amount of stock. Here the rice is boiled nearly done first, laid over meat that has not been browned, and finished by steam alone.

comes_after.why: A pilaf begins by sweating onion.

cues.text: The grains are separate and dry, with small steam holes across the surface and no liquid left.

technique/cook-pilaf.does: Cooks rice by coating it in hot fat with sweated onion, then letting it absorb a measured amount of hot stock under a lid.
how: Sweat finely cut onion in butter without colour.
Stir in the rice until every grain is coated and turns glassy at the edges.
Pour in the hot stock all at once, add a bouquet garni and bring to a boil.
Cover closely with paper and a lid, and finish in the oven or over the lowest heat, without stirring.
Rest it off the heat, then fluff it with a fork and a little butter.

intro.what: Rice is coated in fat, then absorbs hot stock without stirring beneath a close lid.
intro.why: Coating and controlled absorption produce separate grains. Resting and gentle fluffing complete the texture without stirring it into creaminess.

mistakes.fix: Leave it shut until the time is up.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring or lifting the lid while it cooks, which breaks the grains and lets the steam out.

mistakes.fix: Measure the rice by volume and the stock against it. With too much, it turns to porridge.
mistakes.mistake: Guessing the liquid.

quiz.because: The method limits disturbance so the grains retain their separate shape.
choices: A smooth rice paste.
Distinct grains rather than a creamy mass.
Grains floating in leftover stock.
quiz.question: What texture is this pilaf method intended to produce?

quiz.because: Coating comes before covered absorption in this sequence.
choices: Before the onion has softened or rice is coated.
Only after the rice has finished resting.
After the rice is coated in fat.
quiz.question: When is the hot stock added?

quiz.because: Steam holes and absorbed liquid accompany the separate-grain texture.
choices: Steam holes and no remaining loose liquid.
A deep pool above the grains.
A stirred glossy paste without distinct grains.
quiz.question: Which surface appearance fits the intended result?

quiz.because: Controlling the liquid helps avoid more moisture than the rice can absorb into the intended texture.
choices: Add stock without regard to the rice.
Measure the liquid against the rice.
Stir continuously to distribute the extra liquid.
quiz.question: The pilaf became porridge after the stock was guessed. What would you change next time?

cues.text: The polenta pulls away from the side of the pot in a mass as it is stirred.
A taste is soft and sweet, with no gritty or raw-flour bite.

technique/cook-polenta.does: Rains coarse maize meal in a thin stream into boiling salted water, stirring all the while, then cooks it for a long time over the lowest heat, stirring often, until it swells into a thick, smooth porridge that comes away from the sides of the pot. It is eaten soft and creamy, or poured out to set firm.
how: Bring plenty of salted water to a boil in a heavy pot with a broad base.
Lower the heat so that the water is just bubbling. With one hand let the meal fall in a thin stream, and stir with the other, so that no lumps form.
Keep the heat very low. The porridge will pop and spit, so stir with a long wooden spoon and keep a hand clear of the pot.
Stir often, scraping the base and the corners, for a long time, adding hot water if it gets too stiff to stir, until it is thick and smooth and the grains are tender, with no raw taste.
Beat in butter and cheese off the heat if the dish asks for them. Serve it soft at once, or pour it onto a board and let it set.

intro.what: Maize meal is stirred gradually into hot water and cooked gently into a smooth porridge.
intro.why: Thickening happens before the grains necessarily lose their grittiness. Texture, stirring and gentle heat all matter.

mistakes.fix: Let it fall in a thin stream while stirring.
mistakes.mistake: Tipping the meal in all at once, which clumps into lumps that never soften.

mistakes.fix: Keep it at the lowest heat and stir often.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking it at a fierce heat, which scorches the base and leaves the grains hard.

mistakes.fix: Keep cooking and stirring until the grains are tender.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping as soon as it thickens, when the grains are still raw.

quiz.because: A thick mixture can still taste gritty, so thickness alone is not the texture goal.
choices: Thickness proves the grains need no further attention.
Further cooking should make the thick mixture gritty again.
The grains still need to soften beyond initial thickening.
quiz.question: Why continue cooking after the polenta first thickens?

quiz.because: Gradual scattering with stirring reduces clumps as the meal meets the water.
choices: In a thin stream while stirring.
As a compact heap without stirring.
As several large handfuls before stirring begins.
quiz.question: How should maize meal enter the water?

quiz.because: Softened grains lose the grittiness of the earlier stage.
choices: A smooth liquid surrounding hard grains.
Soft without a gritty flour-like bite.
Dry flour sticking between the teeth.
quiz.question: Which taste texture matches the intended polenta?

quiz.because: Gentler heat and stirring limit scorching while the grains continue softening.
choices: Increase the heat to thicken it faster.
Leave the base untouched until a crust forms.
Lower the heat and stir while scraping the base.
quiz.question: The base scorches while grains remain hard. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The meal is rained in a thin stream into boiling water and the porridge is stirred for a long time over a very low heat, until the grains are tender and the mass pulls away from the pot. A white sauce or a milk pudding is stirred only until it thickens.

comes_after.why: Washing takes off the loose starch that would make the rice gluey.

cues.text: The bubbling goes quiet and the pot starts to hiss softly once the water is used up.
Small steam holes show on the surface and no water is left at the edge.
The grains are plump and tender, and a short-grain rice clings in a mass.

technique/cook-rice.does: Cooks washed rice in a measured amount of water in a covered pot until all the water is taken up, then leaves it covered off the heat so that the grains finish plump, tender and separate, or lightly sticky for a short-grain kind.
how: Wash the rice in several changes of cold water, swirling it, until the water is much less cloudy. Drain it well.
Put it in a pot with a tight lid and add the measured water. A short-grain rice takes a little less water than a long-grain one.
Bring it to the boil uncovered or just covered, then turn the heat to its lowest and cover tightly.
Leave the lid on and do not stir, so that the steam stays in.
Take it off the heat when the water has gone, and let it stand covered. Then fluff it with a fork, or fold it with a paddle.

intro.what: Washed rice absorbs measured water under a tight lid, then rests covered off the heat.
intro.why: Steam retention and rice type shape the texture. Separate long grains and lightly clinging short grains need not look identical.

mistakes.fix: Leave the lid on from the moment the heat goes down until the rice has rested.
mistakes.mistake: Lifting the lid again and again, so that the steam escapes and the top stays hard.

mistakes.fix: Do not stir. Fluff it with a fork only at the end.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring, which releases starch and turns the rice gluey.

mistakes.fix: Measure the water against the rice, and use a little less for a short-grain kind.
mistakes.mistake: Using too much water, so that the rice turns soft and wet.

quiz.because: The covered absorption method depends on keeping steam within the pot.
choices: To evaporate water as freely as possible.
To retain steam around the rice.
To make frequent stirring easier.
quiz.question: Why leave the lid on during the low-heat stage?

quiz.because: Resting precedes gentle separation and is part of the texture-building sequence.
choices: Immediate vigorous stirring with the lid open.
Rinsing the hot grains before they rest.
A covered rest before fluffing or folding.
quiz.question: What follows removal from the heat?

quiz.because: Visible holes and disappearing water are the described absorption cues.
choices: Steam holes with no loose water at the edge.
Unchanged dry grains above a deep pool.
A constantly stirred paste spreading over the rim.
quiz.question: Which appearance can belong to the absorption stage ending?

quiz.because: Frequent opening loses the steam that should stay around the upper rice.
choices: Lift it more frequently to release steam.
Keep the lid closed through cooking and resting.
Remove the lid as soon as the heat is lowered.
quiz.question: The upper grains stay hard after repeated lid lifting. What should change?

comes_after.why: The lentils are simmered first, and the rice goes into their pot.
Washing takes off the loose starch that would make the pot gluey.

cues.text: The liquid is gone and small steam holes show in the surface.
Both the rice and the lentils are tender, whole and separate.
The bubbling quietens to a soft hiss as the last liquid is taken up.

technique/cook-rice-with-lentils.does: Cooks rice in the pot where lentils have been simmering, so that the rice takes up the lentil water and its flavour, and the rice and the lentils finish together under one lid as a dish of tender grains and whole lentils.
how: Simmer the lentils in plenty of water until they are tender outside but still firm at the centre.
Wash the rice until the water is much less cloudy, and drain it.
Stir the rice into the pot with the lentils and add salt. If the liquid does not stand above them by about the depth of a finger, add hot water.
Bring to a boil, then turn the heat to its lowest, cover tightly and leave without stirring.
Rest it covered off the heat, then fluff it gently with a fork.

intro.what: Rice finishes in the lentil cooking liquid after the lentils have begun softening.
