intro.why: The starting textures must be coordinated so the rice can absorb flavour while the lentils remain whole.

mistakes.fix: Take the lentils off when the centre is still firm. They finish with the rice.
mistakes.mistake: Simmering the lentils soft before the rice goes in, so that they fall apart.

mistakes.fix: Let the liquid stand only a finger above the grains.
mistakes.mistake: Adding too much water, so that the dish turns to porridge.

mistakes.fix: Stir once to settle the rice, then leave it alone.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring after the rice has gone in, which turns the starch gluey.

quiz.because: The rice absorbs the seasoned lentil liquid as the ingredients finish together.
choices: It carries lentil flavour into the rice.
It prevents lentil flavour reaching the rice.
It seasons only the outside after the rice has finished cooking.
quiz.question: Why use the lentil cooking liquid for the rice?

quiz.because: The lentils need room to soften further while the rice cooks.
choices: Completely collapsed into puree.
Softening outside but still firm at the centre.
Completely firm despite having started simmering.
quiz.question: What lentil texture is wanted when rice is added?

quiz.because: The intended result brings the textures together without dissolving the lentils.
choices: A sticky paste with no whole lentils.
Hard grains sitting in loose water.
Tender distinct rice grains and whole lentils.
quiz.question: What texture should the finished mixture retain?

quiz.because: Starting the shared stage earlier preserves the lentils while the rice absorbs liquid.
choices: Add the rice before the lentils become fully soft.
Simmer the lentils into puree before adding rice.
Stir harder to redistribute the broken lentils.
quiz.question: The lentils dissolved before the rice finished. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The rice goes into a pot of part-cooked lentils and takes up their liquid, so the rice and the lentils finish together. It is not cooked alone in measured water.

comes_after.why: The rice is first softened in water, as in plain rice cooking.

cues.text: The pudding is pale and creamy and coats the spoon, and the grains are swollen and soft.
The spoon drags a little on the base of the pan, and the pudding is looser than it should be when set.
Sweet and milky, with no hard centre in the grain.

technique/cook-sutlac.does: Simmers washed rice in water until it is soft, then in plenty of milk with sugar, stirring often, until the grains are very tender and the milk has thickened to a loose, creamy pudding that sets a little as it cools.
how: Wash the rice and simmer it in water until it is soft and has drunk most of the water.
Pour in the milk and stir in the sugar. Bring it back to a gentle simmer.
Stir often, scraping the base of the pan, until the rice is very soft and the milk has begun to thicken.
Stir in a smooth slurry of rice flour if the pudding needs more body, and simmer for a short while longer.
Pour the pudding into bowls while it is still runny, because it thickens as it cools.

intro.what: Rice first softens in water, then simmers in milk into a loose creamy sütlaç.
intro.why: The pudding continues thickening as it cools, so the texture in the pan should be looser than the final bowl.

mistakes.fix: Stir often and keep the heat gentle.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it unstirred, so that the milk catches on the base of the pan and scorches.

mistakes.fix: Pour it into the bowls while it is still loose.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking it until it is stiff in the pan, so that it sets like glue when cool.

mistakes.fix: Soften the rice in water first.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the milk to hard rice, so that the grains stay firm in the thick milk.

quiz.because: Allowing for the cooling change prevents an overly stiff final pudding.
choices: Cooling loosens it again, so stiffness in the pan is needed.
The pudding should stop thickening once poured.
It thickens further as it cools.
quiz.question: Why pour the pudding while it is still loose?

quiz.because: This sequence softens the grains before the milk thickens around them.
choices: The rice softens in water.
The rice is soaked briefly but left hard.
Dry rice enters the milk before any softening.
quiz.question: What happens before the milk is added?

quiz.because: The pudding needs body without being cooked to its final cooled firmness.
choices: A rigid mass holding the spoon upright.
Creamy and spoon-coating but still loose.
Clear milk above hard dry grains.
quiz.question: What should the pudding look like before pouring?

quiz.because: Gentle heat and scraping reduce the milk sticking and scorching underneath.
choices: Leave it untouched over stronger heat.
Let a dark crust build before stirring.
Stir often over gentler heat, scraping the base.
quiz.question: Milk scorches against the pan base. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The rice is cooked in a large amount of milk and stirred often, to a soft, thick pudding. Plain rice is cooked in a measured amount of water, left alone and kept in separate grains.

cues.text: An even, unbroken wall of flesh and no hard core or seeds left inside.
The inside is smooth to the touch.

technique/core.does: Takes out the hard centre, the seeds or the pith of a fruit or vegetable, or hollows it out, so that the flesh is left as an even wall that cooks evenly or holds a filling.
how: Cut off the top, or push the corer in from the stem end, keeping the wall of the flesh even.
Twist the corer, or run the tip of a small knife round the inside, and lift out the core and seeds.
Scoop out any pith or hard bits that are left, taking care not to cut through the wall.
Keep the scooped flesh if it is wanted for the filling.

intro.idea: A hollow centre with intact walls
intro.what: The hard centre, seeds or pith are removed while an intact wall of flesh remains.
intro.why: When the food will hold a filling, the wall is part of the structure: careless hollowing can create leaks or collapse.

mistakes.fix: Work slowly and keep the corer in the middle.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting through the wall, so that a filling leaks.

mistakes.fix: Scrape the inside clean with a spoon.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving pith or seeds behind, which turn bitter or hard.

mistakes.fix: Leave a wall of about the width of a finger.
mistakes.mistake: Scooping out too much flesh, so that the wall collapses as it cooks.

quiz.because: The remaining flesh forms the container for the filling.
choices: It holds the filling without leaking.
It lets the filling drain through the sides.
It lets the filling spread through a deliberately thin broken shell.
quiz.question: Why preserve an even unbroken wall when coring for a filling?

quiz.because: A centred path removes the hard middle without puncturing the surrounding flesh.
choices: Against the outer wall until it cuts through.
Through the centre while keeping the wall intact.
Across the exterior without reaching the core.
quiz.question: Where should the corer be guided?

quiz.because: The hollow should be cleared without sacrificing the structure around it.
choices: A hard seed-filled centre under torn sides.
A paper-thin broken shell of flesh.
A clean hollow with an even intact wall.
quiz.question: What should remain after coring?

quiz.because: Keeping sufficient flesh preserves the hollowed food structure.
choices: Remove less surrounding flesh.
Scrape the wall thinner before filling.
Cut openings through the base.
quiz.question: The wall collapsed after excessive scooping. What would you change next time?

cues.text: Bubbles rise around the edge of the lid and the liquid reaches the top of the pieces.
The pieces keep their shape, and the liquid slowly turns glossy.

technique/cover-with-a-drop-lid.does: Lays a lid that is smaller than the pot straight on the food, so that the simmering liquid is pushed up and over every piece. The pieces cook evenly in a small amount of liquid and stay still.
how: Arrange the food in a single layer in a wide pot and add just enough liquid to come part of the way up.
Bring the liquid to a simmer.
Lay the drop lid on the food, inside the pot. Wet it first, so that nothing sticks to it.
Keep the liquid at a gentle simmer, so that it bubbles up around the edge of the lid.
Take the lid off for the last stretch if the liquid should reduce to a glaze.

intro.idea: A lid resting on the food
intro.what: A drop lid rests directly on food inside the pot while liquid simmers around it.
intro.why: Its position helps liquid wash over the pieces without rough stirring, supporting an even finish and intact shapes.

mistakes.fix: Use a drop lid, or a round of baking paper cut to fit with a small hole in the middle.
mistakes.mistake: Using a plain lid that sits on the rim of the pot, so that the top pieces stay dry and uncooked.

mistakes.fix: Turn the heat down until it only bubbles gently.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the liquid boil hard under the lid, which knocks the pieces about.

quiz.because: The smaller lid channels the bubbling liquid around and over the food.
choices: To keep all liquid away from the top pieces.
To help simmering liquid reach over the pieces.
To prevent liquid from reaching the sides of the pieces.
quiz.question: Why place a drop lid directly on the food?

quiz.because: Contact with the food distinguishes a drop lid from an ordinary pot lid.
choices: Above the food on the pot rim.
Below the food against the pot base.
Inside the pot, on the food.
quiz.question: Where should the lid sit?

quiz.because: Quiet liquid movement reaches the pieces without knocking them around.
choices: Gentle bubbles bringing liquid up around its edge.
Violent boiling throwing pieces against the lid.
A dry base with no moving liquid.
quiz.question: What should be visible around the drop lid?

quiz.because: Gentler bubbling preserves the shapes the lid is meant to protect.
choices: Raise the boil to move the lid faster.
Turn the heat down to a gentle simmer.
Stir hard around the lid.
quiz.question: The pieces are knocked apart beneath the lid. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The lid lies on the food itself, and not on the rim of the pot, so the liquid is held against every piece and little liquid is needed.

cues.text: A soft, steady hiss comes from under the lid.
Drops of steam gather on the inside of the lid and run back down.

technique/cover-with-a-lid.does: Puts a lid over a pot or a dish, so that steam and heat stay in and the food cooks gently in its own moisture.
how: Choose a lid that fits the pot or the dish well.
Put it on once the food is heated and the liquid is in.
Leave it on while the food cooks. Every time it is lifted, heat and steam escape.
Lift the lid away from you, so that the steam does not scald.

intro.what: A well-fitting lid keeps steam and heat around food in the pot.
intro.why: Covering changes moisture loss, so repeatedly opening the pot interrupts the cooking environment you are trying to maintain.

mistakes.fix: Leave it shut and trust the sound.
mistakes.mistake: Lifting the lid again and again to look, which lets the heat out.

mistakes.fix: Use a lid that sits snugly, or cover the dish tightly with foil.
mistakes.mistake: Using a lid that does not fit, so that the steam escapes.

quiz.because: The lid limits moisture and heat escaping from the pot.
choices: Dry outside air circulating across the surface.
The same evaporation as an open pot, without retaining steam.
Steam and heat.
quiz.question: What does a close-fitting lid mainly retain?

quiz.because: A snug fit supports the enclosed cooking environment.
choices: Snugly against the pot or dish.
With a wide gap around the rim.
Loosely tilted so steam escapes freely.
quiz.question: How should the lid fit?

quiz.because: Steam cools on the lid and gathers into drops.
choices: A completely dry inner surface throughout steaming.
Condensed drops that run back down.
Drops gathering only on the outside while the inside stays dry.
quiz.question: What can appear on the inside of a working lid?

quiz.because: Opening the lid repeatedly releases the heat and steam that covering was meant to retain.
choices: Lift it more often to equalize the air.
Set it aside while expecting the same moisture retention.
Leave the lid closed during the covered stage.
quiz.question: Frequent checking keeps releasing steam. What should change?

cues.text: The garlic turns from pieces to a pale, glossy, wet paste.
A sharp, raw scent rises as soon as it breaks, and fades into the dressing.

technique/crush.does: Presses a clove of garlic flat under the blade of a knife, or under a pestle, and works it with salt into a damp, rough paste that melts into a dressing or a sauce.
how: Peel the clove and set it on a board with a little salt. The salt grips it and wears it down.
Lay the flat of a broad knife on the clove and press down with the heel of the hand until it splits.
Drag the blade over the pieces with the flat tilted, again and again, until the garlic is a damp paste with no lumps.
Scrape the paste into the dressing or the sauce and stir it in at once.

intro.what: Garlic is pressed and worked with salt into a damp paste for a dressing or sauce.
intro.why: Changing pieces into paste lets the garlic disperse rather than remain as distinct chopped fragments.

mistakes.fix: Add a little salt first, so that it grips.
mistakes.mistake: Crushing without salt, so that the garlic slides about under the blade and stays in pieces.

mistakes.fix: Stir it into the acid or the oil soon after it is done.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the paste on the board to turn bitter and harsh.

quiz.because: A damp paste combines with the liquid more readily than intact pieces.
choices: So it stays in firm separate cubes.
So it disperses into the dressing or sauce.
So the cloves keep their whole shape.
quiz.question: Why make garlic into paste for this method?

quiz.because: Salt provides grip and abrasion while the garlic is worked down.
choices: It keeps the garlic sliding freely.
It keeps the garlic pieces firm while only the juices spread.
It helps grip and abrade the garlic.
quiz.question: What role does salt play during crushing here?

quiz.because: The visible pieces should have been worked into a cohesive wet paste.
choices: A pale damp paste without lumps.
Dry intact cloves with split skins.
Large firm cubes on a wet board.
quiz.question: Which appearance shows the intended result?

quiz.because: Salt helps prevent sliding while the garlic is worn into paste.
choices: Polish the board with oil first.
Work it with salt as this method describes.
Keep pressing intact cloves without working them.
quiz.question: Garlic slides around and remains in pieces. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The garlic is pressed and dragged flat under a blade or a pestle for a few moments into a damp, rough paste, and not worked long in a mortar until it is smooth.

en: thicken a bean soup with its own beans

comes_after.why: The beans must be simmered tender before any of them can be crushed.

cues.text: The broth turns cloudy and creamy and a spoon leaves a trail in it.
Some beans still hold their shape when pressed, while others melt into the broth.

technique/crush-some-of-the-beans.does: Presses a few spoonfuls of cooked, tender beans or other pulses against the side of the pot, or lifts out a ladle of them with a little broth and crushes them, then stirs the paste back in, so that the soup turns creamy and thick without flour or cream while the rest of the beans stay whole.
how: Wait until the beans are completely tender, or they will not crush.
Lift a ladle of beans, with a little of their broth, into a bowl.
Crush them to a rough paste with the back of a spoon or a masher. Do not make them completely smooth.
Stir the paste back into the pot and let the soup bubble gently for a little while, until it has thickened.
Crush more if the soup is still thin. Thin it with hot water if it has grown too thick.

intro.what: Part of a pot of tender beans is crushed and stirred back into the broth.
intro.why: Using the beans themselves thickens the soup while leaving whole beans for contrast. The amount crushed changes that balance.

mistakes.fix: Cook them longer, until a bean crushes at a light touch.
mistakes.mistake: Crushing beans that are still firm, which leaves a gritty, thin soup.

mistakes.fix: Crush only a ladle or so and leave the rest whole.
mistakes.mistake: Crushing nearly all of them, so that the soup turns to paste.

quiz.because: Crushed beans add body while the uncrushed portion keeps its shape.
choices: To thicken the broth while keeping whole beans.
To leave the broth clear and thin.
To remove every distinct bean from the soup.
quiz.question: Why crush only part of the beans?

quiz.because: Tender beans form a paste that can blend into the broth.
choices: Firm at the centre and difficult to press.
Tender enough to yield easily.
Still resistant enough to snap into gritty pieces.
quiz.question: What texture do the beans need before crushing?

quiz.because: The dispersed crushed beans give the broth body.
choices: It becomes clear and watery.
It remains thin around separate hard bean fragments.
It becomes cloudy, creamy and more spoon-coating.
quiz.question: What change should appear in the broth?

quiz.because: Keeping more whole beans preserves the intended contrast and limits excessive thickening.
choices: Crush a smaller portion and keep more whole.
Mash every remaining bean until smooth.
Remove all the broth before crushing.
quiz.question: The soup became a paste after nearly all the beans were crushed. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: Only a few beans are crushed, with no butter or milk, and the rest are left whole. The crushed beans thicken the soup they were cooked in.

cues.text: The cubes have clean, sharp corners and smooth sides.
The blade glides through with almost no pressure.

technique/cube-tofu.does: Cuts a block of soft tofu into neat cubes with a wet blade and a slicing motion, without pressing, so that the cubes keep their corners and do not break.
how: Lift the block out of its water and let it drain for a short while on a board.
Wet a thin, sharp knife.
Cut the block in slabs, then in sticks, then in cubes, drawing the blade through in one slow motion and never pressing down.
Slide the cubes into the dish on the flat of the knife or on a spoon, and do not stir them roughly.

intro.what: Soft tofu is sliced with a wet blade into cubes that keep their smooth sides.
intro.why: A delicate ingredient needs a gliding cut rather than pressure. Gentle transfer preserves the shape after cutting too.

mistakes.fix: Draw the blade through in a slicing motion.
mistakes.mistake: Pressing down with the knife, which crushes the block into crumbs.

mistakes.fix: Wet the blade.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting with a dry knife, so that the tofu drags and tears.

quiz.because: Soft tofu yields easily, so pressure can break it into crumbs.
choices: It makes the cubes hold sharper corners.
It removes the need to wet the blade.
It crushes the block instead of leaving intact cubes.
quiz.question: Why avoid pressing down hard on soft tofu?

quiz.because: A wet gliding blade reduces dragging and crushing.
choices: Draw a wet blade through in a smooth slicing motion.
Push a dry blade straight down forcefully.
Saw repeatedly while compressing the block.
quiz.question: How should the knife pass through the tofu?

quiz.because: Clean sides and corners show the block was sliced without breaking.
choices: Crumbly with torn edges.
Smooth-sided with clean corners.
Compressed into flat ragged sheets.
quiz.question: What should the cubes look like?

quiz.because: Wetting the blade reduces the drag that tears the delicate tofu.
choices: Press harder with the same dry blade.
Use rougher sawing strokes.
Wet the blade before slicing.
quiz.question: Tofu drags against the knife and tears. What should change?

variant_of.differs: Soft tofu is too tender to be stacked and cut like a vegetable, so the block is cut slab by slab with a wet blade and no pressure, and the cubes are moved on a flat blade.

comes_after.why: Batons start as thick, even slices.

cues.text: Sticks with flat faces and square corners, all of one thickness, so that they cook in the same time.

technique/cut-into-batons.does: Cuts food into even, square-sided sticks.
how: Peel the vegetable and trim its sides flat to make a block.
Slice the block into slabs as thick as the sticks you want.
Stack a few slabs and cut them lengthwise into sticks as wide as the slabs are thick.
Keep the trimmings for a soup or a mash.

intro.what: Food is cut into even square-sided sticks from a squared block.
intro.why: The shape begins before the final cut: matching slab thickness and stick width makes the pieces cook at a similar pace.

mistakes.fix: Trim the sides flat before you slice.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting from a round vegetable without squaring it first, so that the sticks come out as wedges.

mistakes.fix: Hold the knife straight and take the same width at every cut.
mistakes.mistake: Slabs of uneven thickness, so that thin sticks burn while thick ones stay raw.

quiz.because: Even thickness avoids large differences in cooking between the sticks.
choices: The sticks cook at a similar pace.
Uneven sticks should soften at deliberately different rates.
The shape matters but differences in thickness do not affect cooking.
quiz.question: Why aim for matching baton thickness?

quiz.because: A squared starting block gives the sticks flat faces rather than tapered sides.
choices: Leave the vegetable round and cut wedges.
Trim the sides to create a flat-sided block.
Slice slabs while leaving the curved outer sides in place.
quiz.question: What is done before cutting slabs?

quiz.because: The square-sided stick shape distinguishes batons from wedges or chopped pieces.
choices: Tapered wedges of different widths.
Small irregular crumbs.
Straight sticks with flat faces and square corners.
quiz.question: What should batons look like?

quiz.because: Flat starting faces remove the curve that causes wedge-shaped pieces.
choices: Square the vegetable before slicing.
Keep its rounded sides for the next batch.
Angle every slab differently.
quiz.question: The sticks came out as wedges. What should change?

cues.text: The pieces are blocky and about the same size.

technique/cut-into-chunks.does: Cuts a firm food into large, bite-sized pieces of about the same size, bigger and less exact than dice, so that they stay whole through a long simmer.
how: Peel the food if it needs peeling, and cut it in half or in long strips to get a flat base.
Cut across into thick pieces that fit one mouthful.
Keep the pieces about equal in size, so that they cook in the same time.
For a hard squash, rest the cut side down on the board so that it cannot slip.

intro.what: Firm food is cut into substantial roughly equal pieces rather than precise small dice.
intro.why: Similar size helps the pieces soften together, while their larger shape suits a longer simmer without disappearing.

mistakes.fix: Cut by eye to a single size.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting some pieces much smaller, so that they dissolve while the others are hard.

mistakes.fix: Cut it in halves on a steady board first.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting a hard squash held in the air, which slips.

quiz.because: Larger pieces suit cooking where small fragments might break down too soon.
choices: They dissolve before smaller pieces.
They retain their shape better than tiny pieces.
They remove the need to consider size.
quiz.question: Why use larger chunks for a long simmer?

quiz.because: A stable cut face keeps the squash from moving while it is divided.
choices: Held above the board while cutting.
Balanced on its rounded skin.
On a stable cut face on the board.
quiz.question: How should hard squash rest while being cut?

quiz.because: The pieces need not be precise dice, but their scale should remain consistent.
choices: Blocky pieces of roughly similar size.
Fine shreds mixed with large wedges.
Perfect thin ribbons.
quiz.question: What should the pile of chunks look like?

quiz.because: Similar size reduces the difference in how quickly the pieces soften.
choices: Add more tiny fragments among the large pieces.
Keep the chunks closer in size.
Make the size differences more pronounced.
quiz.question: Small pieces dissolved while large pieces stayed firm. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The pieces are large and not cut to an exact cube, because they are meant to be eaten as chunks after a long simmer.

cues.text: The pieces are small and similar in size, and can be scattered with a spoon.

technique/cut-into-small-pieces.does: Cuts food into small, loose pieces, not exact cubes, so that they spread through rice, a filling or a sauce.
how: Trim the food, take out any bone or tough stem, and slice it first if it is wide.
Cut the slices across into small, rough pieces.
Try to keep the pieces about the same size, so that they cook together.
Gather the pieces in a bowl as you go.

intro.what: Food is cut into small rough pieces that can be scattered through a mixture.
intro.why: The cut supports even distribution without requiring exact cubes. A clear board and a sharp blade help soft ingredients keep their texture.

mistakes.fix: Cut them about as small as a grain of rice.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting the pieces large, so that they cannot spread evenly through the rice.

mistakes.fix: Use a sharp knife and a clear board.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting soft food on a crowded board, so that it is squashed.

quiz.because: Small loose pieces can spread among the other ingredients.
choices: So it stays as a large central lump.
So every piece must have a perfect square outline.
So it distributes through the mixture.
quiz.question: Why cut food small for rice or a filling?

quiz.because: Clear space and a clean cutting stroke limit crushing of soft food.
choices: A sharp knife and a clear board.
A crowded board and heavy pressure.
A blunt blade dragged across a pile.
quiz.question: What helps keep soft food from being squashed while cutting?

Cut them smaller before mixing.

technique/cut-pasta.does: Cuts a thin sheet of rolled pasta dough into ribbons, strips or squares of even size, so that they cook at the same speed.

intro.why: The surface needs to be dry enough to release, yet flexible enough to fold. Consistent cuts help the pieces cook at a similar pace.

Wet the tray before laying the strips down.

technique/deep-fry.does: Cooks food under hot oil, so that its surface dries to a crisp shell while the inside steams.

Fill a deep, heavy pan no more than a third full of oil and heat it.
Lower in a small batch, so that the oil keeps its heat and the pieces do not stick together.
Lift the food out when it is crisp and golden, drain it on a rack and salt it at once.

intro.why: Oil heat and crowding affect the crust. Managing batches helps the surface crisp instead of becoming heavy and greasy.

mistakes.fix: Fry in small batches and let the oil come back to heat between them.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat at once and let it cool.
mistakes.mistake: Oil that smokes. It tastes acrid and is close to catching fire.

quiz.because: The drying surface becomes the crust while moisture within the food produces steam.
choices: The surface absorbs water until it swells.
The food surface loses moisture in the hot oil.
The surface stays wet beneath a cool oil film.
quiz.question: What produces the crisp shell during deep-frying?

Keep adding food as the bubbling slows.
Divide it into smaller batches and let the oil recover between them.

choices: A lively even crackle around the food.
Complete silence around a newly added batch.
Violent spitting from a wet surface.

choices: Crowd the pan more tightly next time.
Fry smaller batches with recovery between them.
Keep lowering the heat while adding more food.

cues.text: A sharp hiss and a burst of steam when the liquid hits the pan.

The raw smell of the wine goes as it boils.

technique/deglaze.does: Dissolves the browned layer stuck to a hot pan with a splash of liquid, turning it into the base of a sauce.
how: Pour off the fat, and keep everything brown that sticks to the pan.
Soften a little shallot or garlic in the pan first, if the sauce calls for it.
Take the pan off the flame to add wine or spirits, then put it back.
Scrape the bottom with a wooden spoon as the liquid boils, until the pan is clean and the liquid has turned brown.

intro.why: It shows how the brown traces left by cooking can become the base of a sauce.

mistakes.fix: Taste a scrap of the fond first. If it is bitter, wipe the pan out and build the sauce without it.

quiz.because: Liquid dissolves the browned layer, or fond, and carries it into the sauce base.

Only the fat floating in the pan.
Blackened residue from any burnt pan.
quiz.question: What does deglazing turn into a sauce base?

Pour it off while keeping the browned bits.
Wipe out the browned bits and keep the fat.

Clear fat collects around an untouched layer.
The pan comes clean under the spoon and the liquid darkens.

Wipe it out and build the sauce without it.
Scrape harder to include the black layer.

comes_after.why: The loose salt on the surface is rinsed off before the long soak.

cues.text: A flake from the thickest part tastes lightly salted, like seasoned fish and not like brine.

technique/desalt.does: Draws most of the salt out of salt cod by leaving it in cold water that is changed again and again, so that the fish tastes of cod and not only of salt, and can be cooked on its own.
how: Rinse the surface salt off the pieces under cold water.
Lay the pieces skin side up in a deep dish and cover them with plenty of cold water. Keep the dish in the fridge.
Change the water several times, and leave thick pieces longer than thin ones.
Taste a small flake from the thickest part. Stop when it tastes lightly seasoned, and go on if it still tastes of brine.
Drain the pieces and pat them dry before they are cooked.

intro.what: Salt cod soaks in repeatedly refreshed cold water to reduce its strong saltiness before cooking.
intro.why: Salt removal is uneven through a thick piece. Understanding the changing water and remaining seasoning helps prevent an oversalted finished dish.

mistakes.fix: Soak it in the fridge and change the water often.
mistakes.mistake: Soaking at room temperature, where the fish spoils and turns slimy before it loses its salt.

mistakes.fix: Taste a flake from the thickest part.

mistakes.fix: Taste the fish and the sauce before adding any salt.
mistakes.mistake: Salting the dish as usual afterwards, so that it ends up far too salty.

quiz.because: Fresh water replaces the salt-laden soaking liquid so salt can continue leaving the fish.
choices: To preserve the original brine strength around the fish.
To firm the outside while leaving its salt unchanged.
To replace water that has taken up salt.
quiz.question: Why change the soaking water repeatedly?

In a cool part of the kitchen without refrigeration.
At room temperature beneath a tight cover.

The centre stays as rigid as before while only the outside softens.

comes_after.why: A dice is a slice cut again, lengthwise and across, so an even slice comes first.

cues.text: The cubes are all one size, with square edges.

technique/dice.does: Cuts food into even cubes, so that every piece cooks at the same speed.
how: Trim the piece so that it has a flat side and sits still on the board.
Cut it into slabs as thick as the cube you want.

Turn the sticks and cut across them into cubes.

technique/drain.does: Lets water or oil run off food after it has been boiled, soaked, salted or fried, so that it is not watery or greasy when it meets the next step.
