quiz.because: Removing surface water lets the next heating stage act on the food without first steaming off that wet layer.
choices: To limit surface steaming that interferes with browning.
To retain moisture on the surface as a browning glaze.
To let the food steam before its surface begins browning.
quiz.question: Why dry a surface before browning it?

quiz.because: Gentle pot heat lets the remaining surface water steam away.
choices: Leave them resting in a little of their cooking water.
Return them to the empty warm pot over very low heat and shake gently.
Pile them on a cold plate and cover to retain their steam.
quiz.question: How are boiled pieces dried in this method?

quiz.because: A matt surface shows that the visible water film has gone.
choices: Glossy with running droplets.
Submerged in a fresh puddle.
Matt rather than shining with water.
quiz.question: Which appearance suggests the surface is drying?

quiz.because: The warm pot helps moisture leave instead of settling back onto the food.
choices: Use the empty warm pot to let surface moisture escape.
Cover the cold plate to collect steam.
Return the food to cold water.
quiz.question: Boiled food stays damp on a cold plate. What should change?

comes_after.why: An emulsion is whisked the whole time, so a steady whisking hand comes first.

cues.text: The sauce is smooth, opaque and glossy, and thickens as more fat goes in.
The whisk meets more resistance with every addition.

technique/emulsify.does: Makes fat and a water-based liquid hold together as one smooth sauce, by breaking one into droplets too small to find each other again.
how: Start with the water-based part and whatever helps it hold: egg yolk, mustard, or a liquid boiled down until syrupy.
Add the fat very slowly at first, drop by drop, whisking all the time.
Once the sauce has thickened and holds, add the fat in a thin stream.
Thin it with a few drops of water or acid if it turns stiff and looks oily at the edges.

intro.what: This whisked emulsion method brings fat and a water-based liquid together into a smooth sauce.
intro.why: It teaches you to add fat gradually and notice whether the sauce is holding together.

mistakes.fix: Stop. Start again with a fresh yolk or a spoonful of mustard, and whisk the broken sauce into it drop by drop.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the fat too fast at the start, so that the sauce stays thin and then separates into oil and liquid.

mistakes.fix: Let the egg, the mustard and the oil come to room temperature first.
mistakes.mistake: Ingredients at very different temperatures, which makes a cold emulsion refuse to take.

quiz.because: An emulsion holds fat and a water-based liquid together in a smooth sauce instead of separate layers.
choices: A separate layer of oil over liquid.
Visible pools of fat in a watery sauce.
Fat and a water-based liquid held together as a smooth sauce.
quiz.question: What is the aim of this emulsion method?

quiz.because: Adding fat too quickly can make the sauce separate. Begin very slowly while whisking continuously.
choices: Very slowly while whisking continuously.
All at once before any whisking.
In large additions with long pauses.
quiz.question: How do you add fat at the start of this whisked emulsion method?

quiz.because: A smooth, glossy sauce that thickens as fat goes in is holding together instead of separating into oil and liquid.
choices: Clear oil floating over a thin liquid.
A smooth, glossy sauce that thickens as fat is added.
An oily edge growing around a watery centre.
quiz.question: Which appearance suggests the sauce is holding together?

quiz.because: A fresh yolk or mustard provides a new starting base. Whisk the broken sauce into it slowly to rebuild this emulsion.
choices: Keep whisking the same mixture and pour in the remaining fat steadily.
Add a large splash of oil and whisk faster.
Start with fresh yolk or mustard and whisk the broken sauce in slowly.
quiz.question: Fat was added too quickly and the sauce separated. How would you restart this emulsion?

en: make a cream with pasta water

comes_after.why: The starchy water that binds the sauce comes from cooking the pasta.

cues.text: A smooth, glossy cream that coats the back of a spoon, with no lumps of cooked egg and no puddle of oil.
It flows like thin cream and clings to the pasta as it is tossed.
The pan has stopped sizzling before the egg goes in.

technique/emulsify-off-the-heat.does: Binds fat, egg and a hard cheese into one glossy cream with hot starchy water, off the heat. No fat is whisked in drop by drop: the starch in the water and the warmth of the pasta hold it together, and it splits or scrambles if the heat comes back.
how: Have everything ready before the pasta is done: the fat in the pan, the egg and cheese mixed in a bowl, and a mug of hot starchy cooking water.
Take the pan off the heat. Heat is what splits this kind of sauce.
Loosen the egg and cheese with a splash of the hot water, stirring, until it is a smooth pourable cream with no streaks.
Bring it together with the fat and the pasta, adding more water a splash at a time and tossing, until it turns glossy and clings.
Serve at once. It is at its best straight away and sets as it cools.

intro.what: Egg, cheese, fat and hot starchy pasta water are brought into a glossy sauce off the heat.
intro.why: This method uses retained warmth and gradual water additions rather than returning the pan to the burner. Texture guides the balance between thick and watery.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat before the egg goes in, and keep it off.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the pan on the heat, so that the egg scrambles into flecks.

mistakes.fix: Use hot water from the pasta pot, and add it a splash at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Using water that has gone cool or has no starch, so that the sauce stays thin and slides off.

mistakes.fix: Add it a splash at a time and stop when it is glossy.
mistakes.mistake: Adding all the water at once, so that the sauce turns watery.

quiz.because: The components should combine into a coating cream rather than remain separated.
choices: Separate oil floating around firm egg flecks.
A glossy cream that clings to the pasta.
A watery broth that leaves the pasta bare.
quiz.question: What is the intended result of this off-heat method?

quiz.because: Removing direct heat limits the scrambling and splitting described for this sauce.
choices: It stays over moderate heat as the egg mixture is added.
It returns to the burner before the egg is mixed through.
It comes off the heat and stops sizzling.
quiz.question: What happens to the pan before the egg mixture goes in?

quiz.because: A continuous glossy coating shows the intended combined texture.
choices: Smooth gloss without egg lumps or oil puddles.
Firm egg flecks suspended in loose oil.
A clear watery pool beneath bare pasta.
quiz.question: Which appearance suggests the sauce has come together?

quiz.because: Gradual additions let the cook control loosening before the sauce becomes too thin.
choices: Pour in all the available water immediately.
Add the hot starchy water gradually and stop at a coating texture.
Replace the pasta water with cold plain water.
quiz.question: The sauce became watery after a large water addition. What should change next time?

variant_of.differs: No fat is added drop by drop. The sauce is bound with hot starchy water, off the heat, and it splits or scrambles if the heat returns.

cues.text: A whole fillet with smooth edges, and a skeleton with almost no flesh left on it.
The blade rides on the bones the whole way.

technique/fillet.does: Cuts the flesh of a fish away from its bones in whole, clean pieces.
how: Lay the fish flat. Cut behind the head and the fin, down to the backbone.
Turn the blade flat and run it along the backbone toward the tail in long strokes, keeping it against the bones.
Lift the fillet away, turn the fish over and do the same on the other side.
Run a finger down each fillet and pull out the small bones it finds.
Keep the bones and the head for a stock.

intro.idea: Let the bones guide the blade
intro.what: Fish flesh is separated from the skeleton in whole pieces by following the bones.
intro.why: The skeleton guides the knife. Long controlled strokes retain more flesh and reduce the tearing caused by sawing.

mistakes.fix: Use a sharp, flexible blade and long, light strokes.
mistakes.mistake: Sawing with a dull or stiff knife, which tears the flesh.

mistakes.fix: Keep the flat of the blade pressed against the backbone.
mistakes.mistake: Lifting the blade away from the bones, which leaves flesh behind.

quiz.because: Following the bones keeps the separation near the skeleton rather than deep in the flesh.
choices: To cut more flesh away with the skeleton.
To remove the skin before separating the flesh from the ribs.
To separate the flesh without leaving much on the skeleton.
quiz.question: Why keep the blade close to the backbone?

quiz.because: Long light strokes follow the bones without tearing the fillet.
choices: Long light strokes with a sharp flexible blade.
Short sawing strokes that push through the flesh.
Cuts made while lifting the blade away from the backbone.
quiz.question: What kind of stroke is used along the backbone?

quiz.because: The result should preserve the fillet while limiting flesh left behind.
choices: A ragged fillet beside thick flesh on the skeleton.
A whole smooth-edged fillet and little flesh left on the skeleton.
Many torn fragments still attached to the bones.
quiz.question: Which appearance suggests economical filleting?

quiz.because: Moving away from the skeleton leaves more flesh attached to it.
choices: Angle the blade farther into the flesh.
Pull the fillet away before completing the cut.
Keep the blade closer against the bones.
quiz.question: A thick strip of flesh remained on the backbone. What would you change on the next fillet?

cues.text: Blue flames that rise, then sink and go out within moments.
The sharp smell of raw spirit gives way to a warm, sweet one.

technique/flambe.does: Sets light to a spirit poured over hot food. The flame burns away its harshness and leaves its flavour. Some of the alcohol stays in the dish.
how: Take the pan off the heat and clear the space above it.
Pour in the spirit from a ladle or a small glass, never from the bottle.
Put the pan back on the heat, lean back, and touch a long match to its edge.
Shake the pan gently until the flames die on their own.

intro.what: A spirit is ignited over hot food as an aromatic finishing technique.
intro.why: Flambé connects a changing aroma with a visible flame. Careful preparation and controlled pouring belong to the method, not just the dramatic appearance.

mistakes.fix: Measure the spirit into a ladle or a glass first.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring from the bottle, so that the flame can run up the stream.

mistakes.fix: Have the pan hot, and warm the spirit if need be.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the spirit to a pan that is too cool, so that it will not light and the dish tastes of raw alcohol.

mistakes.fix: Clear the space above the pan before you light it.
mistakes.mistake: Lighting it under a low shelf or a running fan.

quiz.because: The technique uses the spirit for its contribution to the finished flavour and aroma.
choices: It contributes an aromatic finish to the food.
To brown a dry crust over the food surface.
To reduce the sauce until it becomes spoon-coating.
quiz.question: What culinary role does the spirit have in flambé?

quiz.because: Preparing a separate vessel avoids pouring from the bottle near the pan flame.
choices: Directly from the bottle into the heated pan.
From a separate ladle or small glass while the pan is off the heat.
From an open bottle held over an existing flame.
quiz.question: How is the spirit introduced in this method?

quiz.because: The rising and subsiding blue flame is the visible change used to observe this stage.
choices: Tall flames stay at the same height throughout.
Flames keep growing as the pan is shaken.
Blue flames rise and then subside.
quiz.question: What visible flame movement is described?

quiz.because: Separating the pouring vessel from the bottle avoids the flame path described in this method.
choices: Set the bottle aside and use a separate vessel as described.
Move the bottle closer to the hot pan.
Begin pouring before taking the pan off the heat.
quiz.question: You are about to pour spirit straight from the bottle. What should change?

comes_after.why: Sinew and skin are cut away first, or they shrink and curl when the meat is beaten flat.

cues.text: The slice is an even sheet with no thick middle and no holes.
Under the pan the meat gives evenly and no longer springs back.

technique/flatten.does: Beats a slice of meat to an even, thin sheet between layers of paper, so that it cooks in moments and stays tender.
how: Trim away any sinew or skin from the slice, and nick the edge in a few places so that it does not curl.
Lay the slice between sheets of parchment paper.
Beat it from the middle outwards with the flat of a heavy pan, in even blows, turning it as you go.
Stop when the sheet is the same thickness from edge to edge, before it tears.

intro.what: A meat slice is gently beaten between paper into an even sheet without tears.
intro.why: The aim is consistent thickness rather than maximum thinness. Working from the middle prevents a thick centre surrounded by fragile edges.

mistakes.fix: Use the flat of the pan, with steady, even weight.
mistakes.mistake: Beating with hard, sharp blows that tear the meat into holes.

mistakes.fix: Start in the middle and work outwards.
mistakes.mistake: Beating the edges thin and leaving the middle thick, so that it cooks unevenly.

quiz.because: Consistent thickness reduces the contrast between the centre and edges during cooking.
choices: To keep a thicker centre that supports the thinner edges.
To avoid a thick centre cooking differently from thin edges.
To roughen the surface without changing its thickness.
quiz.question: Why aim for even thickness across the slice?

quiz.because: Starting centrally addresses the thick part before working toward the edges.
choices: At the edges until they become very thin.
Only at a corner of the slice.
In the middle, working outward.
quiz.question: Where should the flattening strokes begin?

quiz.because: An unbroken even sheet shows that the pressure has spread rather than torn the meat.
choices: An even sheet without holes.
Torn edges around a thick centre.
A narrow strip with punctures throughout.
quiz.question: What should the flattened slice look like?

quiz.because: Broad controlled pressure spreads the meat without concentrating the impact into tears.
choices: Use sharper impacts on the torn areas.
Use the flat of the pan with steady even pressure.
Keep striking the thinnest edges hardest.
quiz.question: Sharp hard blows tore holes in the meat. What would you change on the next slice?

comes_after.why: Turning at the right moment depends on reading the underside of food in a pan, which pan-frying teaches.

cues.text: The edges are set and dry, and the underside is a rich brown when the corner is lifted.
The food slides when the pan is shaken, and does not cling.

technique/flip.does: Turns food over in the pan or on the griddle at the right moment, so that its other side cooks and browns while the first side has set enough to hold together.
how: Wait until the underside has set and browned, and the food moves freely when the pan is shaken.
Slide a wide spatula fully under the food, so that none of it hangs over the edge.
Lift and turn in one quick, confident motion, close to the pan.
For a large, soft cake, slide it onto a plate, set the pan upside down over it and turn both over together, then slide it back.
Press gently to settle it, and cook the other side.

intro.what: Food is turned after its underside has formed enough structure to move as a whole.
intro.why: A successful turn starts before lifting: release, support and a controlled motion help preserve the shape while exposing the other face to the pan.

mistakes.fix: Wait until the edges are set and it moves freely.
mistakes.mistake: Flipping too early, so that the food is still soft and breaks.

mistakes.fix: Use a wide spatula, or slide the food onto a plate first.
mistakes.mistake: Using a narrow spatula, so that the food folds as it is lifted.

mistakes.fix: Turn it in one quick motion, close to the pan.
mistakes.mistake: Hesitating in mid-air, which tears or splashes.

quiz.because: A formed underside provides structure that soft food lacks earlier in cooking.
choices: So the upper side becomes the only side that browns.
So the food stays firmly attached to the pan.
So the food can hold together during the turn.
quiz.question: Why wait until the underside has set before flipping?

quiz.because: Full support limits folding or tearing as the food leaves the pan.
choices: Fully underneath it with a suitably wide blade.
Under a narrow corner with most of it hanging over.
Pressing down on top while pulling the pan away.
quiz.question: How should the spatula support the food?

quiz.because: Free movement shows the underside is no longer gripping the pan.
choices: Its centre stays fixed while the edges stretch.
It slides when the pan is shaken.
The whole piece clings tightly to the base.
quiz.question: What suggests the food has released enough to turn?

quiz.because: Broader support carries the soft food as a shape instead of bending it around a narrow edge.
choices: Lift it higher with the same narrow support.
Let more of the piece hang beyond the blade.
Use a wider spatula or a plate-assisted turn.
quiz.question: The food folds around a narrow spatula. What should change?

comes_after.why: Couscous is fluffed once it has drunk its liquid, so a cook has to be able to bring the grains to that point first.
Rice is fluffed once it has taken up its water, so a cook has to be able to cook it to that point first.

cues.text: The grains lie loose, each with its own outline, and the heap holds no wet patches.
The fork meets no resistance and the grains fall away from it.

technique/fluff.does: Loosens cooked grains with a fork or the fingertips, lifting and separating them, so that the steam escapes and each grain stands apart instead of sitting in a block.
how: Wait until the grains have taken up their liquid and the steam is no longer heavy.
Add a little butter or a trickle of oil, so that the grains stay loose.
Run a fork, or the fingertips, lightly through the grains, lifting from the bottom and letting them fall. Do not press and do not stir.
Rub any lumps between the fingertips to break them.
Cover with a cloth until it is time to serve, so that the grains stay warm without drying.

intro.what: Cooked grains are lifted and allowed to fall apart gently with a fork or fingertips.
intro.why: Separating is different from stirring or pressing. Gentle lifting releases steam and loosens clumps without smearing the grains into paste.

mistakes.fix: Lift and let fall, with light strokes.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring hard, which breaks the grains and turns them to paste.

mistakes.fix: Leave them covered until the liquid has gone.
mistakes.mistake: Fluffing while the grains are still wet, which smears them.

mistakes.fix: Fluff them once more just before serving.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the grains in a heap without airing them, so that they set into a block.

quiz.because: Lifting separates the grains and lets trapped steam escape.
choices: Loosen grains so they stand apart.
Pack the grains together so they keep their heat.
Stir the grains into a creamy mixture.
quiz.question: What is fluffing intended to do?

quiz.because: Lifting separates without the crushing associated with heavy stirring.
choices: Hard circular stirring against the pot.
Light lifting from below, letting the grains fall.
Firm pressing with the back of a spoon.
quiz.question: What movement is used when fluffing?

quiz.because: Loose outlines and easy movement show separation rather than compression.
choices: A solid block that resists the fork.
A smeared paste around intact dry lumps.
Distinct grain outlines with no wet clumps.
quiz.question: Which result matches properly loosened grains?

quiz.because: Wet grains are easily smeared; absorption should precede the separating movement.
choices: Wait until the liquid has been taken up before gentle lifting.
Press the wet grains harder with the fork.
Stir faster while loose liquid remains.
quiz.question: Wet grains smeared while being fluffed. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: There is nothing to fold until something has been whipped.

cues.text: An even, light mixture that still stands in soft mounds and has lost little of its volume.

technique/fold.does: Combines a light, airy mixture with a heavier one while keeping as much of the air as possible.
how: Stir a small part of the whipped mixture into the heavy one to loosen it.
Tip the rest on top.
Cut down through the middle with a spatula, sweep along the bottom, and bring it up and over.
Turn the bowl a little and repeat, stopping when only a few streaks remain.

intro.what: Folding brings an airy mixture into a heavier mixture while preserving its volume.
intro.why: It teaches you to lift and turn gently, stopping before repeated mixing knocks the air out.

mistakes.fix: Cut, lift and turn. Stop early: a few streaks do less harm than more folding.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring in circles, which knocks the air out and leaves a flat batter.

quiz.because: The aim is to combine the mixtures while keeping the volume provided by the air.
choices: To retain as much of its air as possible.
To make the foam denser before combining it.
To remove large bubbles through vigorous mixing.
quiz.question: Why fold rather than stir an airy mixture vigorously?

quiz.because: Cutting, lifting and turning combines the mixture without the flattening effect of circular stirring.
choices: Stir quickly around the bowl in circles.
Cut down, sweep across the bottom and lift over.
Press the mixtures firmly against the bowl sides.
quiz.question: What movement combines the mixtures gently?

quiz.because: Soft mounds and retained volume show the mixture has stayed light as it combined.
choices: A flat batter that has lost much of its volume.
Separate heavy lumps beneath untouched foam.
A light mixture that still stands in soft mounds.
quiz.question: What appearance suggests successful folding?

quiz.because: Overworking knocks air out; a few remaining streaks do less harm than excessive folding.
choices: Use lifting folds and stop before overmixing.
Stir faster until the volume returns.
Continue stirring until every tiny streak disappears.
quiz.question: Repeated stirring has flattened the batter. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: The dough must be rolled thin and even before it can be folded over a filling.

cues.text: The parcel is a flat half moon with an even bump of filling and a neat, thin rim.
The rim is pressed thin and sticks to itself, with no gap.

technique/fold-a-gozleme.does: Scatters a filling over one half of a thin round of dough, folds the other half over it and presses the edges shut, so that the filling is held in a flat parcel that cooks on a dry griddle.
how: Roll the dough out into a thin, even round and brush off the loose flour.
Scatter a thin layer of filling over one half, leaving a clear rim at the edge.
Lift the clear half over the filling and press the rim with the fingertips until it is sealed all the way round.
Carry the parcel to the hot griddle without letting it stretch.

intro.idea: A filling that leaves room to seal
intro.what: Thin dough is folded over a spread filling and sealed into a flat gözleme parcel.
intro.why: The filling and rim have different jobs: a restrained filling keeps the parcel flat, while a clean rim lets the dough adhere.

mistakes.fix: Spread the filling in a thin layer.
mistakes.mistake: Overfilling, so that the parcel bursts on the griddle.

mistakes.fix: Squeeze or drain a wet filling first.
mistakes.mistake: Using a wet filling, which soaks the dough and makes it soggy.

mistakes.fix: Brush the rim clean before pressing it shut.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving flour on the rim, so that it will not stick.

quiz.because: A restrained filling allows the dough to close without excessive pressure from inside.
choices: To fill the sealing rim as fully as the centre.
To keep the flat parcel from bursting.
To stretch the dough tightly around a raised mound.
quiz.question: Why spread the filling thinly rather than pile it high?

quiz.because: A clear rim provides dough-to-dough contact for the seal.
choices: A bare centre surrounded by a thick ring of filling.
Only the surface that will touch the griddle.
The sealing rim around the edge.
quiz.question: What should remain clear when spreading the filling?

quiz.because: A continuous joined rim keeps the filling within the parcel.
choices: Thinly pressed and joined without gaps.
Floury and loose with open sections.
Thick with filling separating the dough.
quiz.question: What should the sealed rim feel like?

quiz.because: Loose flour separates the dough surfaces instead of helping them adhere.
choices: Add a heavier flour layer between the edges.
Brush away loose flour before pressing it together.
Push more filling into the opening.
quiz.question: The floured rim will not stick shut. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The dough is folded once over a filling to make a flat sealed parcel, with no layers built up. Folding dough in the layered way stacks sheets over fat.

comes_after.why: The folds start from a round of dough that is rolled even, so a cook has to be able to roll one first.

cues.text: The cut edge of the folded triangle shows thin stripes of dough and ghee.
The triangle rolls out smoothly and the layers do not slide apart.

technique/fold-a-paratha.does: Brushes a rolled round of atta dough with ghee, dusts it with a little flour, and folds it over on itself into a half-moon and then a triangle, so that the dough is stacked in thin layers with ghee between them. The folded piece is then rolled out again, lightly.
how: Brush the whole rolled round with soft ghee and dust it with a little dry flour.
Fold the round in half to a half-moon, brush the top with ghee again and dust it lightly.
Fold the half-moon in half once more, into a triangle with its layers stacked inside.
Press the edges gently so that the layers stay together, and roll the triangle out lightly with even strokes.

intro.what: Ghee-brushed atta dough is folded into a triangle and rolled lightly to preserve layers.
intro.why: The fat between folds keeps the sheets distinct. Heavy rolling can undo the structure by forcing the fat out and pressing dough together.

mistakes.fix: Roll lightly and evenly, and stop as soon as the triangle is the size of the plate.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling hard after folding, so that the ghee is pressed out and the layers fuse into one.

mistakes.fix: Brush every fold with ghee, right to the edges.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the dough dry between the folds, so that the finished bread is tough and not flaky.

quiz.because: The fat separates the folded surfaces and supports the flaky structure.
choices: To make the folded surfaces adhere into a firmer sheet.
To season only the outside after the dough is cooked.
To keep the stacked dough layers distinct.
quiz.question: Why brush ghee between the folds?

quiz.because: Gentle rolling spreads the dough while retaining the fat between its layers.
choices: Lightly with even strokes.
Forcefully until ghee squeezes from the edges.
Only by pressing hard into the centre.
quiz.question: How should the folded triangle be rolled?

quiz.because: Visible stripes show that the folded surfaces remain separated.
choices: A solid dough block with no visible layers.
Fine stripes of dough and ghee.
Dry broken crumbs around an empty centre.
quiz.question: What should a cut edge show?

quiz.because: Reducing pressure protects the separating fat and the folded structure.
choices: Press harder until no fat remains inside.
Leave the dough dry between every fold.
Roll with less pressure after folding.
quiz.question: The layers fused after ghee was squeezed out. What would you change on the next piece?

variant_of.differs: The dough is a soft atta dough that is not rested between folds, the fat is ghee brushed on by hand, and it is folded once or twice into a half-moon or triangle and rolled out again lightly. It is not a pastry that is turned and rolled many times.

cues.text: Each pastry is a neat triangle with no filling showing at the corners.
The sealed flap holds without sticking and the triangle is firm and flat.

technique/fold-briouats.does: Cuts sheets of warqa into long strips, puts a spoonful of filling at one end of each strip and folds the end over it again and again, corner to corner, into a small neat triangle, with the loose end sealed down with a dab of fat.
how: Keep the warqa under a damp cloth. Cut a sheet into strips as wide as a hand, and brush each strip lightly with melted butter.
Put a small spoonful of filling at one end, a little in from the corner.
Fold the corner over the filling to make a triangle, then fold the triangle over on itself along the strip, again and again, as one folds a flag.
Seal the last flap with a dab of butter and tuck it under.
Lay the triangles on a tray and cover them until they are fried.

intro.what: Warqa strips wrap a filling in repeated corner-to-corner folds that make a neat triangle.
intro.why: Keeping the pastry supple and the filling restrained lets the thin sheet close without cracks or exposed corners.

mistakes.fix: Use only a small spoonful.
mistakes.mistake: Overfilling, which splits the thin sheet and leaks in the oil.

mistakes.fix: Cut only a few at a time and keep the rest under a damp cloth.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the strips dry out, so that they crack when folded.

quiz.because: Supple warqa can fold around the filling without snapping.
choices: To prevent drying that causes cracks during folding.
To dry the surfaces so the folds hold their corners.
To make the pastry soak up extra filling moisture.
quiz.question: Why keep unused warqa strips under a damp cloth?

quiz.because: The repeated diagonal folds enclose the filling within the triangular shape.
choices: Roll the strip into an open cylinder.
Fold it corner to corner repeatedly along the strip.
Gather the strip into loose pleats above the filling.
quiz.question: How is the triangle carried along the strip?

quiz.because: Enclosed corners and a secured flap show the wrapper has closed around the filling.
choices: A loose strip with filling exposed at each end.
A split parcel with a thick mound pushing through.
A neat triangle with filling enclosed at the corners.
quiz.question: What should the finished briouat look like?

quiz.because: Reducing the filling relieves pressure on the thin wrapper.
choices: Use less filling so the folds can close.
Pack more filling against the split.
Stretch the dry strip harder across the mound.
quiz.question: The warqa split around an overfilled centre. What would you change on the next parcel?

variant_of.differs: Wrapping encloses a filling in a leaf, caul fat or a thin omelette. Here the wrapper is a paper-thin sheet cut in strips, and the filling is folded up in a series of triangle folds along the strip.

comes_after.why: A dough is rolled or stretched into an even sheet before it is folded.

cues.text: The layers show along a cut edge as fine, even lines.
The dough is supple and springs back slowly, and tears only when it is pulled hard.

technique/fold-dough.does: Folds a sheet or a round of dough over itself, from the sides and into a square or a letter, so that it stacks into layers or gains strength, and so that any fat or oil brushed between the layers stays shut in them.
how: Rest the dough first, so that it relaxes and does not spring back.
Stretch or roll it into an even sheet on a lightly oiled or floured surface.
Brush or sprinkle the surface with the fat or the dusting the dish asks for, right to the edges.
Lift one edge and fold it over towards the middle, then bring the opposite edge over it, as when folding a letter. For a square, fold the other sides in as well.
Press the folded shape lightly, turn it, and rest it before it is rolled or stretched again.

intro.what: Rested dough is spread into a sheet and folded over itself in the shape the dish requires.
intro.why: Folding can build structure and stack layers. When the dish uses fat between folds, complete coverage and gentle handling preserve that separation.

mistakes.fix: Let it rest until it relaxes.
mistakes.mistake: Folding dough that is still tense, which tears and shrinks back.

mistakes.fix: Brush the fat right to the edges.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the corners and edges bare, so that the layers weld together there.

quiz.because: Folding stacks the dough surfaces; separating fat keeps those surfaces from simply joining.
choices: A thicker sheet with the layers pressed firmly together.
Stacked sheets with the prescribed fat between them.
A tightly rolled strand with no sheet-like layers.
quiz.question: What can folding create in a layered dough?

quiz.because: Resting reduces the resistance that makes tense dough shrink or tear.
choices: Pull harder while it springs back.
Fold it tightly without spreading it.
Let it rest until it relaxes.
quiz.question: What should happen before stretching tense dough?

quiz.because: Lines along the edge reveal the stacked sheets inside the dough.
choices: Fine even lines along a cut edge.
A solid fused edge without lines.
A ragged dry edge filled with holes.
quiz.question: What can show that a layered fold has remained distinct?

quiz.because: Fat coverage at the corners helps maintain separation there as well as at the centre.
choices: Leave a wider dry border around every fold.
Carry the prescribed fat to the edges before folding.
Press the dry corners together harder.
quiz.question: The layers welded together at dry corners. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: The crust must be on the meat before it goes into the oil.

cues.text: A steady, lively sizzle that softens as the cutlet browns.
An even, deep gold crust, with the bubbles around it slowing down.

technique/fry-a-cutlet.does: Fries a crumbed cutlet whole in deep oil, turning it once, until the crust is deep gold. It is then stood upright to drain, rested a little and cut across in strips, so that the crust stays crisp.
how: Heat deep oil in a heavy pan to a moderate heat, enough to cover the cutlet.
Test it with a few flakes of panko, which should sink briefly and then rise in a stream of fine bubbles.
Lower in one cutlet at a time, so that the oil keeps its heat, and leave it alone until the crust has set.
Turn it once and fry until the crust is deep gold on both sides.
Lift it out and stand it upright against a rack, so that the oil drains from the crust instead of pooling under it.
Rest it for a short while, then cut across in strips with a sharp knife, sawing lightly so that the crust does not shatter.

intro.what: This crumbed-cutlet method deep-fries the cutlet whole, then drains it upright before slicing.
intro.why: It teaches you to protect a crisp crust through moderate frying heat, draining and gentle cutting.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat moderate and test with a few flakes of panko.
mistakes.mistake: Frying in oil that is too hot, so that the crust browns before the meat is ready.

mistakes.fix: Stand it upright against a rack.
mistakes.mistake: Laying the fried cutlet flat on a plate, where it steams and the crust goes soft.

mistakes.fix: Let it rest for a short while first.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting at once, so that the juice runs out and the crust goes limp.

quiz.because: A flat cutlet can steam in pooled oil; upright draining helps its crust stay crisp.
choices: So the crust sits in its draining oil.
So oil runs off instead of pooling under the crust.
So the underside softens before slicing.
quiz.question: Why stand the fried cutlet upright to drain?

quiz.because: The brief sinking and rising test matches the moderate frying heat used here.
choices: Panko stays pale at the bottom without bubbling.
Panko turns dark immediately on contact.
Panko sinks briefly then rises with fine bubbles.
quiz.question: How do you check the oil before adding the cutlet?

quiz.because: Even gold is the intended crust colour, rather than rapid overbrowning or a greasy pale coating.
choices: Even deep gold on both sides.
A black crust with pale patches.
A pale coating that looks saturated with oil.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches the intended crust?

quiz.because: Resting and gentle sawing avoid crushing the brittle crust while cutting strips.
choices: Press straight down hard with a blunt knife.
Use a sharp knife with a light sawing motion after resting.
Tear the cutlet apart before draining.
quiz.question: The crust shatters when sliced. What would you change?

variant_of.differs: One thick, crumbed piece of meat is fried whole at a moderate heat and turned once, then stood upright to drain, rested and cut across, where deep-frying works on small pieces and is salted at once.

en: fry in ghee and soak in syrup

comes_after.why: The balls are made from khoya dough, so the dough comes first.

cues.text: The balls swell, rise and turn an even, deep reddish brown, with no pale patches.
A soaked ball is soft and spongy, and gives under the spoon without breaking.

technique/fry-and-soak-in-syrup.does: Fries balls of dough slowly in ghee over a gentle heat until they are deep brown and cooked to the middle, then drops them into warm sugar syrup, which they drink up until they are soft, swollen and sweet to the centre.
how: Make the syrup first and keep it warm. It should be thin and sticky, not thick.
Heat the ghee or oil gently. A test ball should rise slowly, with a few bubbles, and not brown at once.
Slide in a few balls and shake the pan so that they turn. Keep the heat low, so that they swell and colour slowly.
Fry until they are deep, even brown all over. Lift them out with a slotted spoon and let the extra fat drip off.
Drop the hot balls into the warm syrup and leave them to soak, turning once, until they swell and are soft all the way through.

intro.what: This sweet-making method gently fries dough balls, then lets them absorb warm, thin syrup.
intro.why: It teaches you to match gradual browning with a syrup consistency that soaks in rather than coating only the surface.

mistakes.fix: Test with one ball and keep the heat low.
mistakes.mistake: Frying in fat that is too hot, so that the outside darkens while the middle stays raw and dense.

mistakes.fix: Keep the syrup warm and thin.
mistakes.mistake: Putting the balls into cold or boiling syrup, so that they stay hard or fall apart.

mistakes.fix: Boil it just until it turns sticky.
mistakes.mistake: Making the syrup too thick, so that it sits on the surface and does not soak in.

quiz.because: Thick syrup sits on the surface rather than being absorbed into the sweet.
choices: So it forms a hard shell without soaking.
So it holds the balls above the liquid.
So it soaks into the balls instead of staying outside.
quiz.question: Why keep the soaking syrup thin rather than thick?

quiz.because: A gradual rise and slow colouring match the gentle frying used for these sweets.
choices: Rise slowly with a few bubbles, without browning at once.
Turn dark immediately as soon as it enters.
Stay at the bottom without any bubbling.
quiz.question: How should a test ball behave in the frying fat?

quiz.because: Absorption makes the balls swell and soften while keeping their shape.
choices: A hard dry shell with no swelling.
Soft and spongy, giving under a spoon without breaking.
A disintegrating mass falling apart in the syrup.
quiz.question: What texture should the soaked ball have?

quiz.because: A warm, thin syrup can be absorbed; excessive thickness prevents the intended soaking.
choices: Boil it into a thicker glaze.
Use a cold dense syrup straight from storage.
Stop thickening it while it is still thin and sticky.
quiz.question: The syrup stays on the surface instead of soaking in. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The fat is held low and gentle, so that the balls swell and colour slowly and the middle cooks. It is not a hot fry meant to crisp a thin crust, and the fried balls are not drained dry, they go into syrup.
The soaking is done in warm sugar syrup, straight after frying, so that the fried balls drink it up as they cool.

comes_after.why: The pastries must be folded and sealed before they go into the oil.

cues.text: The pastry is a deep, even gold and the layers show a fine blister.
The oil sizzles quietly and steadily, with no spitting.
The honey coat is thin and glossy, and the pastry still crackles under it.

technique/fry-briouats.does: Fries small folded pastries in a good depth of hot oil, turning them until they are golden and crisp, then dips them while hot in warm honey scented with orange blossom water and scatters them with toasted sesame seeds.
how: Warm the honey gently with a spoonful of water and the orange blossom water, and keep it at the side of the stove.
Heat the oil in a wide pan to about a finger deep, until a scrap of warqa sizzles at once.
Fry the pastries a few at a time, turning them, until they are golden on every side.
Lift them out and let the oil run off for a moment.
Dip each one into the warm honey, turn it over, lift it out and set it on a rack. Scatter with toasted sesame seeds.

intro.what: This briouat method fries folded pastries until crisp, then dips them briefly in warm scented honey.
intro.why: It teaches you to add a glossy sweet coat without losing the crackling pastry beneath it.

mistakes.fix: Test the oil with a scrap of warqa first.
mistakes.mistake: Frying in oil that is too cool, which leaves the pastry greasy and pale.

mistakes.fix: Dip them for a moment only and set them on a rack.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the pastries in the honey, which turns them soggy.

mistakes.fix: Warm it gently and keep it just hot.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the honey boil, which makes it bitter and hard.

quiz.because: Brief dipping adds sweetness and shine while preserving the crisp pastry.
choices: A thin glossy coating over pastry that still crackles.
Pastry softened completely by a long honey soak.
A thick hard honey shell hiding the pastry.
quiz.question: What finish are you aiming for after the honey dip?

quiz.because: Draining excess frying oil comes before the warm honey coating.
choices: Dip them into honey while they still carry pooled frying oil.
Let the excess oil run off briefly.
Leave them flat in the collected frying oil before dipping.
quiz.question: What should happen between frying and the honey dip?

quiz.because: Golden blistered layers are the intended fried texture before coating.
choices: Pale sheets heavy with oil.
Black edges around a wet pale centre.
Even gold with fine blisters in the layers.
quiz.question: Which pastry appearance matches the frying stage?

quiz.because: A prolonged honey soak softens the pastry; a brief dip and rack preserve more crispness.
choices: Dip briefly and move them onto a rack.
Leave them in honey until fully saturated.
Pile them in the honey while still draining oil.
quiz.question: The honey-coated pastries have become soggy. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: Pan-frying cooks a flat piece in a thin layer of fat and turns it once. Here small filled triangles fry in oil about a finger deep, are turned until gold on every side, and are then dipped hot into warm honey.

comes_after.why: There is nothing to fry until the croquetas are shaped and coated.

cues.text: A sharp, steady sizzle when they go in, which quietens as the shell sets.
The shell is an even deep gold, with no cracks.
The croquetas are light for their size and the shell feels firm when pressed.

technique/fry-croquetas.does: Fries coated croquetas in a few at a time in hot oil deep enough to cover them, turning them until the shell is deep golden all round and the paste inside has melted soft.
how: Heat plenty of oil in a deep, heavy pan. A crumb dropped in should sizzle at once and rise.
Lower a few croquetas in with a slotted spoon. Do not crowd the pan, or the oil cools and the shells go greasy.
Turn them gently until they are deep golden all round.
Lift them out onto a rack and let the oil run off. Serve at once, while the shell is crisp and the middle is soft.

intro.what: Frying croquetas turns their coating into a crisp golden shell around a soft paste.
intro.why: It teaches you to keep frying heat steady and turn a delicate shell without piercing it.

mistakes.fix: Wait until a crumb sizzles at once, and fry only a few at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Frying in oil that is not hot enough, so that the shell soaks up oil and the paste leaks out.

mistakes.fix: Fry in small batches and let the oil heat up again between them.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, which cools the oil.

mistakes.fix: Turn them with a slotted spoon.
mistakes.mistake: Piercing the shell with a fork while turning.

quiz.because: Crowding lowers the oil heat, which can make the shell absorb oil and leak.
choices: To keep the coating pale and soft.
To avoid cooling the oil and making the shells greasy.
To let the shells press tightly against each other.
quiz.question: Why fry croquetas in small batches?

quiz.because: A slotted spoon turns the croqueta without puncturing its coating.
choices: By piercing the shell with a fork.
By squeezing the middle firmly with a fork.
Gently with a slotted spoon.
quiz.question: How should you turn them?

quiz.because: An evenly coloured intact shell is the intended result of gentle frying and turning.
choices: Even deep gold without cracks.
A pale shell with paste leaking through cracks.
Dark patches around a wet coating.
quiz.question: Which shell appearance is the aim?

quiz.because: Smaller batches and reheating address the drop in oil heat caused by crowding.
choices: Add the next batch before the oil recovers.
Fry fewer and let the oil heat up again.
Keep the pan tightly packed to stop movement.
quiz.question: The oil cools when a large batch goes in. What would you change for the next batch?

variant_of.differs: The food is a soft paste in a fragile shell that has to set in the first moments, so the oil must be hot at once and only a few go in each time. A firm food such as a potato is fried to cook it and then fried again to crisp it.

cues.text: A lively crackle as the egg goes in, which settles to a steady sizzle.
The white is set and frilled, golden and lacy at the edge, and the yolk is still glossy and wobbly.

technique/fry-eggs.does: Cooks eggs in a generous depth of hot olive oil, so that the whites puff, bubble and turn lacy and crisp at the edges while the yolks stay soft.
how: Heat a good depth of olive oil in a small, deep frying pan until a breadcrumb dropped in sizzles at once.
Break each egg into a small bowl first, so that a broken yolk or a shell is found before the pan.
Slide the egg in from close to the oil at the side of the pan, so that the white curls round the yolk.
Tilt the pan and spoon hot oil over the white until it is set and frilled, while the yolk stays soft.
Lift the egg out with a slotted spoon, drain it on paper and salt it at the end.

intro.what: This olive-oil method fries eggs with puffed whites and lacy, crisp edges.
intro.why: It teaches you to direct hot oil onto the white and manage browning without breaking the yolk.

mistakes.fix: Heat the oil until a breadcrumb sizzles at once.
mistakes.mistake: The oil is too cool, so that the egg spreads thin and greasy with a pale, limp white.

mistakes.fix: Lower the heat a little and spoon the oil over the white.
mistakes.mistake: The oil is too hot, so that the white turns brown and leathery before the yolk is warm.

mistakes.fix: Break the egg into a small bowl first and slide it in low.
mistakes.mistake: Breaking the yolk as the egg goes in.

quiz.because: Hot oil makes the white puff and frill into crisp edges.
choices: Lacy and crisp.
Pale and limp.
Smooth and firm without bubbles.
quiz.question: What texture does this egg-frying method aim for at the edge?

quiz.because: A bowl lets you spot broken yolks or shell before sliding the egg in low.
choices: Crack it directly high above the pan.
Slide it from a small bowl close to the oil.
Pour it rapidly into the centre from above.
quiz.question: How do you add the egg without breaking the yolk?

quiz.because: Cool oil lets the egg spread into a greasy, limp white rather than puffing its edges.
choices: A lively crackle as the egg enters.
Golden, lacy edges around the white.
A pale, limp white spread thin and greasy.
quiz.question: What suggests the oil was too cool?

quiz.because: Excess heat darkens the white too quickly; lower it and direct the oil over the white.
choices: Lower the heat and spoon oil over the white.
Increase the heat to warm the yolk faster.
Leave the same heat and stop spooning oil.
quiz.question: The white is turning brown and leathery too quickly. What would you change?

variant_of.differs: The egg swims in a generous depth of hot olive oil and not in a thin film of fat, so the white frills and crisps at the edge. Nothing is turned, and the oil is spooned over the white.

cues.text: A steady, lively sizzle. A roar means the oil is too hot, and silence means it is too cool.
The edges turn lacy and golden before the middle sets.

technique/fry-fritters.does: Drops spoonfuls of a thick mixture of grated vegetable, egg, cheese and a little flour into hot oil, flattens them lightly and turns them once, so that each fritter is crisp and golden outside and soft inside.
how: Make the mixture thick enough to sit on a spoon. If it runs, stir in a little more flour. If it is stiff and dry, loosen it with a spoonful of water.
Warm a shallow layer of oil in a wide pan until a crumb of the mixture sizzles at once.
Drop in spoonfuls with room between them, and press each to a flat round with the back of the spoon.
Leave them alone until the underside is deep golden and the edges look set, then turn each once.
Lift them onto a rack or paper to drain. Fry the rest in lots, and wipe the pan if bits of the mixture scorch.

intro.what: Frying these vegetable fritters makes flattened spoonfuls crisp outside and soft within.
intro.why: It connects mixture thickness, space in the pan and patient turning with a fritter that holds together.

mistakes.fix: Wait for the sizzle before the first spoonful goes in.
mistakes.mistake: Frying in oil that is too cool, so that the fritters soak it up and turn greasy.

mistakes.fix: Fry a few at a time, with room between them.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, so that the fritters steam and join together.

mistakes.fix: Wait until the underside is golden and the edges are set.
mistakes.mistake: Turning too soon, so that the fritter tears.

quiz.because: The spoonfuls are pressed into separate flat rounds rather than left as tall lumps.
choices: To spread them into a joined sheet.
To form flat rounds for frying.
To squeeze their liquid into the oil.
quiz.question: Why flatten the spoonfuls lightly in this method?

quiz.because: A mixture that sits on a spoon can be dropped and flattened into separate fritters.
choices: Thin enough to pour in a stream.
Dry enough to crumble apart.
Thick enough to sit on a spoon.
quiz.question: How thick should the mixture be before frying?

quiz.because: Waiting for colour and set edges helps the fritter hold together as it turns.
choices: A golden underside and edges that look set.
A pale underside with loose edges.
The first bubbles before the underside colours.
quiz.question: Which cue suggests a fritter can be turned?

quiz.because: Space between fritters prevents crowding that makes them steam and merge.
choices: Press them closer to share the heat.
Fry fewer at a time with space between them.
Add more mixture to fill the spaces.
quiz.question: The fritters steamed and joined together. What would you change for the next batch?

variant_of.differs: A fritter mixture has no shape of its own, so it is dropped in by the spoonful and flattened, in more oil than a cut of meat or fish would be fried in, and it is turned only once it has set.

comes_after.why: The base is built on a paste of ginger, garlic and spices, so a cook has to be able to make one first.

cues.text: The paste turns a deeper colour and shiny fat parts from it and gathers at the edge of the pan.
The raw sharp smell of garlic and spice is gone, replaced by a rounded, roasted scent.
The spoon leaves a clean track across the paste on the pan.

technique/fry-masala-base.does: Cooks onion, ginger and garlic, ground spices and tomato in fat over a medium heat, stirring often and sprinkling a little water when the pan dries, until the water of the vegetables is gone and the fat parts from the paste and shines on its edge. This is the base of a gravy.
how: Heat the fat and cook the sliced or chopped onion until it is soft and golden.
Add the ginger and garlic paste or the spice paste and stir until the raw smell goes.
Add the ground spices and stir for a few moments. Sprinkle in a little water if they catch.
Add the tomato, mash it down with the spoon and cook, stirring, until it has collapsed into a thick paste.
Go on until the fat separates from the paste and gathers in a bright pool at the edge. Add a spoonful of water and scrape the pan whenever the paste sticks.

intro.what: This masala base cooks onion, aromatics, spices and tomato in fat into a concentrated paste.
intro.why: It teaches you to develop the base before adding gravy liquid, watching for the fat to shine at the edges.

mistakes.fix: Wait until the fat shines at the edge of the paste.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the liquid too soon, before the fat has parted, so that the gravy tastes raw and thin.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat moderate, sprinkle in a little water when the pan dries, and add the tomato soon after the spices.
mistakes.mistake: Burning the ground spices by frying them in dry, hot fat.

mistakes.fix: Keep a medium heat and be patient. The wait is the point.
mistakes.mistake: Rushing it over a high heat, which scorches the paste.

quiz.because: Adding liquid before the paste develops can leave the gravy tasting raw and thin.
choices: To keep the tomato pieces firm and separate.
To preserve the sharp raw smell of garlic.
To develop it beyond a raw, thin-tasting base.
quiz.question: Why cook the masala paste before adding gravy liquid?

quiz.because: A little water and moderate heat help keep the ground spices from scorching.
choices: Sprinkle in a little water and keep the heat moderate.
Raise the heat to finish them quickly.
Leave them dry until the tomato is ready.
quiz.question: What do you do when the spices begin catching in a dry pan?

quiz.because: Separated shiny fat and a deeper colour accompany a thick paste with a rounded roasted scent.
choices: Tomato floats in a loose watery mixture.
Shiny fat gathers at the edge of a deeper-coloured paste.
The garlic still smells sharply raw.
quiz.question: What indicates the paste has developed in this method?

quiz.because: Moderate heat and loosening stuck paste with water let the base develop without scorching.
choices: Keep high heat and add gravy liquid immediately.
Stop stirring so a crust forms underneath.
Use medium heat and scrape with a little water when it sticks.
quiz.question: The paste starts sticking as the pan dries. What would you change?

variant_of.differs: A sofrito is cooked slowly in olive oil to a sweet, jammy paste. Here ground spices and a spice paste go in as well, with a splash of water whenever the pan dries, and the cook stops when the fat parts from the paste.

comes_after.why: The noodles must be pulled apart before they go into the pan.

cues.text: The sauce smells sweet and tangy as it hits the hot pan.
The strands are evenly brown, separate, and there is no wet pool in the pan.

technique/fry-noodles-in-sauce.does: Tosses loosened noodles in a very hot pan with meat and vegetables that are already cooked, and pours a sweet, tangy sauce round the edge of the pan, until the noodles are coated, lightly browned in places and still separate.
how: Have the noodles loosened, the sauce mixed and everything else cut and at hand.
Cook the meat and the firmest vegetables first in a hot pan with a little oil, then add the leaves and sprouts for a short time.
Add the noodles and toss them with tongs, lifting from the bottom, until they are hot.
Pour the sauce round the edge of the pan, so that it sizzles on the metal before it is tossed in.
Toss until the sauce is taken up, and serve at once, before the noodles soften.

intro.what: This method tosses loosened noodles with cooked additions and sauce in a hot pan.
intro.why: It teaches you to coat strands while keeping them separate, rather than letting them stew in sauce.

mistakes.fix: Loosen them first.
mistakes.mistake: Adding noodles that are still in a clump, so that they tear and cook unevenly.

mistakes.fix: Pour it round the edge of the hot pan.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring the sauce on top of the noodles, so that they stew and turn soft.

mistakes.fix: Use a wide pan, or cook in batches.
mistakes.mistake: Packing too much into the pan, so that the food steams.

quiz.because: The sauce should be taken up around separate strands, with no wet pool remaining.
choices: Coated strands that stay separate.
Soft strands sitting in a wet pool.
A compact noodle cake with a firm crust.
quiz.question: What result are you aiming for when frying these noodles in sauce?

quiz.because: Sauce sizzles on the metal at the pan edge before being tossed through the noodles.
choices: Onto the centre of the noodle pile.
Around the edge of the hot pan.
Into the noodles before the pan is heated.
quiz.question: Where do you pour the sauce?

quiz.because: Separate coated strands and no wet pool show the sauce has been taken up.
choices: Pale clumps floating in excess sauce.
Torn strands in a soft, wet mass.
Evenly brown, separate strands without pooled sauce.
quiz.question: What appearance matches the intended finish?

quiz.because: Loosening noodles first avoids tearing them while trying to break up a clump in the pan.
choices: Loosen them before adding them to the pan.
Pull the clump apart forcefully as it fries.
Add extra sauce to stew the clump apart.
quiz.question: The noodles tore while you broke up a clump in the pan. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The main food is noodles and not rice or vegetables. They are loosened first and added late, and the sauce is poured round the edge of the pan so that it sizzles before it coats them.

comes_after.why: Even slices brown at one pace, so a cook who can slice evenly fries better onions.

cues.text: A deep, even brown with a few darker tips, and no black.
A loud bubbling at the start that calms to a quiet sizzle as the water leaves the onions.
A piece lifted out and cooled snaps when it is pressed.

technique/fry-onions-dark.does: Fries thinly sliced onions in a generous layer of hot oil until they turn deep brown and crisp at the edges, then lifts them out to drain. They bring a bittersweet crunch to rice and lentils, and the oil they leave behind is full of their flavour.
how: Slice the onions thin and evenly, so that they brown at one pace.
Heat a good depth of oil in a wide, heavy pan until a slice sizzles the moment it goes in.
Add the onions in a loose layer, in batches if need be. Stir often at first, then less often as they darken.
Lower the heat once the edges go dark, and keep frying until the onions are a deep brown. They crisp further as they cool.
Lift them out with a slotted spoon onto a rack or paper, and salt them lightly. Keep the oil.

intro.what: This method fries thin onions until deeply browned, then drains them for a bittersweet crunch.
intro.why: It teaches you to control the last stage of browning and judge crispness after cooling.

mistakes.fix: Fry in batches, in the widest pan you have.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, so that the onions steam, turn limp and never crisp.

mistakes.fix: Stay by the pan and lift them out as soon as they are deep brown.
mistakes.mistake: Looking away at the end, when the onions go from brown to bitter black in moments.

mistakes.fix: Wait until a slice sizzles at once.
mistakes.mistake: Starting in cool oil, which soaks into the onions and leaves them greasy.

quiz.because: Deep browning and draining produce a crisp topping rather than a soft onion base.
choices: A pale, soft layer with no browning.
A bittersweet crunch.
A wet onion sauce.
quiz.question: What do these fried onions add to rice and lentils?

quiz.because: A loose layer avoids crowding that makes the onions steam and stay limp.
choices: Packed tightly into a deep mound.
Pressed together under a lid.
In a loose layer, using batches if needed.
quiz.question: How should the slices sit in the pan?

quiz.because: The onions crisp further as they cool; a cooled piece should snap.
choices: Let it cool and see whether it snaps.
Judge only by softness while it is still hot.
Look for black edges before testing it.
quiz.question: How can you judge crispness after lifting out a piece?

quiz.because: Starting in properly heated oil avoids the greasy result of a cool start.
choices: Add all the onions before heating the oil.
Wait until an onion slice sizzles immediately.
Use a tighter pile to retain the heat.
quiz.question: The onions are becoming greasy from a cool start. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The onions are cut thin and fried in plenty of hot oil until dark and crisp at the edges, and not coaxed slowly in a little fat until soft and sweet.

comes_after.why: Slices of an even width brown together, so the cook has to be able to slice onions evenly first.

cues.text: The slices pass from limp and pale to amber and then deep brown, with the edges darkest.
The sizzle is loud while the onions are wet and fades to a quiet crackle as the water goes.
A slice lifted out and left to cool snaps between the fingers.

technique/fry-onions-deep-brown.does: Fries thinly sliced onions in a generous amount of fat until their water has gone and they turn deep brown and crisp, then lifts them out to drain. They are crushed into a marinade, layered into rice, scattered on top, or stirred into a gravy.
how: Slice the onions thin and even, so that they brown together. Spread them out to dry a little if they are wet.
Heat plenty of fat in a wide pan until a slice sizzles at once, then add the onions in a loose layer.
Stir often at a steady medium heat. They go limp, then pale gold, then amber.
Lower the heat as the colour deepens. The last stage takes only moments, so stay at the pan.
Lift them out with a slotted spoon the moment they are deep brown, and spread them on paper to drain. They crisp as they cool.

intro.what: This method fries thin onions deep brown and drains them so they crisp as they cool.
intro.why: It teaches you to anticipate continued darkening and lift onions out before the final colour goes too far.

mistakes.fix: Fry in a wide pan, in a thin layer, or in batches.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, so that the onions steam and stay limp and pale.

mistakes.fix: Lift them out while they are a shade lighter than wanted. They go on darkening in the fat they carry.
mistakes.mistake: Walking away at the end, when the onions turn from brown to bitter black in moments.

mistakes.fix: Lift them out and spread them on paper at once.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving them in the hot fat to cool, so that they go soft and greasy.

quiz.because: Onions left cooling in hot fat can become soft and greasy; draining lets them crisp.
choices: So they stop developing any crispness.
So they retain a coating of pooled fat.
So they drain and crisp instead of becoming soft and greasy.
quiz.question: Why lift the onions out of the fat to cool?

quiz.because: The final darkening happens quickly, so lower heat and close attention matter.
choices: Lower it and stay beside the pan.
Raise it to speed the final browning.
Keep it high and leave them unattended.
quiz.question: How should you adjust heat as their colour deepens?

quiz.because: Less water remains as frying progresses, and the loud sizzle fades.
choices: A quiet start grows into a constant roar.
A loud sizzle fades to a quiet crackle.
The sound stays unchanged throughout.
quiz.question: What happens to the sound as water leaves the onions?

quiz.because: The fat carried on the onions continues darkening them after lifting, so anticipate that change.
choices: Wait for darker edges before draining.
Leave them in the fat until cool.
Lift them a shade lighter because they continue darkening.
quiz.question: The onions kept darkening into bitterness after lifting. What would you change for the next batch?

variant_of.differs: Caramelising keeps the onions soft and sticky, in little fat and over a low heat. Here the slices swim in a generous amount of fat at a steady medium heat until they dry out, turn deep brown and crisp, and are lifted out and drained, to be used as a topping, a layer or a flavouring.

comes_after.why: There is nothing to fry until the balls are shaped, coated and chilled.

cues.text: A sharp, steady sizzle as they go in, which quietens as the shell sets.
An even deep gold all round, with no cracks in the shell.
A ball is light for its size and the shell feels firm and dry when pressed.

technique/fry-rice-balls.does: Fries coated, filled rice balls a few at a time in hot oil deep enough to cover them, turning them until the shell is deep golden all round and the filling inside is hot and soft.
how: Heat plenty of oil in a deep, heavy pan and hold it steady. A crumb dropped in should sizzle at once and rise.
Lower a few balls in with a slotted spoon. Do not crowd the pan, or the oil cools and the shells go greasy.
Turn them gently until they are deep golden all round. Keep the heat moderate, so that the warmth reaches the filling before the shell gets too dark.
Lift them out onto a rack and let the oil run off. Rest them briefly before serving, because the middle stays very hot.

intro.what: This method deep-fries coated, filled rice balls to an evenly golden shell.
intro.why: It teaches you to balance shell colour with moderate heat and avoid cooling the oil through crowding.

mistakes.fix: Keep the oil at a steady, moderate heat and use a thermometer.
mistakes.mistake: Frying in oil that is too hot, so that the shell turns dark while the filling is still cold.

mistakes.fix: Wait until a crumb sizzles at once, and fry only a few at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Frying in oil that is not hot enough, so that the shell soaks up oil and splits.

mistakes.fix: Fry in small batches and let the oil heat up again between them.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, which cools the oil.

quiz.because: Very hot oil can darken the shell while the filling remains cold.
choices: To let warmth reach the filling before the shell becomes too dark.
To darken the shell as quickly as possible.
To keep the coating pale and soft.
quiz.question: Why use steady, moderate heat for these filled rice balls?

quiz.because: A small batch avoids cooling the oil and making the shells greasy.
choices: Fill the pan tightly to keep them from turning.
Lower in only a few balls without crowding.
Add the full batch before heating the oil.
quiz.question: How should you arrange the frying batch?

quiz.because: Gentle turning and steady heat aim for even colour around an intact shell.
choices: Dark patches around a pale shell.
A pale, greasy shell splitting open.
Even deep gold without cracks.
quiz.question: Which shell matches the intended appearance?

quiz.because: Crowding cools the oil; smaller batches and reheating address that drop.
choices: Fry smaller batches and let the oil reheat between them.
Keep adding balls to use the same oil.
Press the balls together so they support each other.
quiz.question: The oil cools as a large batch goes in. What would you change?

variant_of.differs: The food is a filled ball of rice in a crumb shell, and the filling has to be hot all through when the shell is done, so the oil is held steady and moderate and only a few go in each time.
The balls are larger and hold a filling in a firm rice wall, and not a soft paste, so they stay in the oil a little longer at a slightly gentler heat for the middle to warm.

comes_after.why: The dough must have risen until it is light and full of gas before it goes into the oil.

cues.text: The ring floats, swells and turns an even gold on both sides.
The oil sizzles steadily and not wildly.
A finished ring is light for its size and springs back when pressed.

technique/fry-sfenj.does: Shapes lumps of very soft, risen dough into rings with a wet hand and drops them into hot oil, turning them once, until they puff up golden with a thin crisp crust and a light, chewy crumb. They are lifted out at once, drained and tossed in sugar.
how: Heat the oil until a scrap of dough dropped in sizzles and rises at once.
Wet one hand and a plate. Pull off a lump of dough, flatten it, and poke a hole through the middle with a wet thumb.
Slide the ring into the oil and fry only a few at a time, so that the oil stays hot.
Turn each ring once with a skewer or the handle of a spoon when it has puffed and coloured underneath.
Lift the rings out when golden on both sides, drain them well and toss them in sugar while they are warm.

intro.what: Frying sfenj turns rings of very soft risen dough into golden, light, chewy fritters.
intro.why: It teaches you to handle sticky dough gently and keep frying heat steady through small batches.

mistakes.fix: Test the oil with a scrap of dough first.
mistakes.mistake: Frying in oil that is too cool, which makes greasy, heavy rings.

mistakes.fix: Fry a few at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Putting in too many at once, which cools the oil.

mistakes.fix: Wet the hand each time.
mistakes.mistake: Handling the dough with dry hands, which sticks and tears it.

quiz.because: Hot oil makes the soft risen dough puff into a light ring with a thin crust.
choices: A dense ring with a thick hard shell.
A thin crisp crust with a light, chewy crumb.
A pale ring heavy with oil.
quiz.question: What texture is the aim for sfenj?

quiz.because: A wet hand helps shape the sticky dough without tearing it.
choices: Work with dry hands and pull harder.
Keep adding dry flour to the shaping hand.
Wet your hand each time.
quiz.question: How do you keep the soft dough from sticking as you shape it?

quiz.because: Puffing and even gold on both sides are the visible cues for this method.
choices: They float, swell and turn evenly golden.
They stay flat and pale in quiet oil.
They darken on one side without swelling.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches the frying rings?

quiz.because: A scrap should sizzle and rise immediately, helping avoid the cool start that makes heavy rings.
choices: Add a full batch to bring the oil up gradually.
Test the oil with a scrap of dough before frying.
Leave the rings in the oil longer without changing the heat.
quiz.question: The rings were heavy and greasy from cool oil. What would you change before frying the next batch?

variant_of.differs: Deep-frying cooks food that is firm or coated. Here the food is a sticky raw dough that is shaped in the hand moments before it goes in, and the oil is what makes it puff.

cues.text: The garnish sits on top of the food, in a light scatter.
A fresh scent rises as the garnish meets the heat.

technique/garnish.does: Adds a small, fresh or crisp finishing touch just before serving, such as a herb, a seed, a flake or a shaving, for scent, colour or crunch.
how: Keep the garnish ready at the side, cut or measured.
Add it as the last step, when the food is hot or just plated.
Scatter or place a little where it will be seen, and do not cover the food.
Add the delicate ones at the table.

intro.what: Garnishing adds a small finishing touch for scent, colour or crunch just before serving.
intro.why: It teaches you to preserve delicate finishes and use enough to complement the food without hiding it.

mistakes.fix: Add it at the last moment.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the garnish too early, so that it wilts or sinks.

mistakes.fix: Use only a small amount.
mistakes.mistake: Using too much, so that it hides the food.

quiz.because: A garnish finishes the dish lightly rather than replacing or covering it.
choices: A thick covering that hides the whole dish.
A base cooked into the food from the start.
A small finishing touch for scent, colour or crunch.
quiz.question: What is the role of a garnish in this method?

quiz.because: Late addition keeps delicate garnishes from wilting or sinking.
choices: At the last moment, or at the table.
Before the dish begins cooking.
Before reheating the plated dish.
quiz.question: When should delicate garnishes be added?

quiz.because: A small visible scatter adds a finish without concealing the dish.
choices: A dense blanket hiding the main food.
A light scatter visible on top.
Pieces submerged beneath the sauce.
quiz.question: What should the garnish look like on the food?

quiz.because: Adding a delicate garnish too early lets it wilt or sink.
choices: Add a thicker layer earlier.
Stir it into the dish before cooking.
Add it later, just before serving.
quiz.question: The garnish wilted and sank. What would you change next time?

cues.text: No liquid is left: a shiny film coats each piece and the pan.
The bubbling turns to a sizzle as the last of the water goes.

technique/glaze.does: Cooks small vegetables in a little water, butter and sugar until the water has gone and they are left tender and coated in a shiny syrup.
how: Put the vegetables in a wide pan in a single layer.
Add water to come half way up them, with butter, a little sugar and salt.
Cover with a round of paper and simmer until the vegetables are nearly tender.
Take the paper off and boil away the last of the liquid, rolling the vegetables in the syrup as it forms.
Stop there for a pale glaze, or go on a moment for a golden one.

intro.what: This vegetable glaze reduces water, butter and sugar into a shiny coating around small vegetables.
intro.why: It connects tenderness with evaporation, so you can form a glaze without continuing to soften the vegetables too far.

mistakes.fix: Use less, and pour some off if they are tender before the glaze forms.
mistakes.mistake: Too much water, so that the vegetables are overcooked before it has gone.

mistakes.fix: Stay, and keep them rolling.
mistakes.mistake: Walking away at the end, when the syrup burns.

quiz.because: As water leaves, the remaining syrup becomes a shiny film around the pieces.
choices: Evaporating the water until a shiny syrup coats the vegetables.
Keeping plenty of watery liquid around them.
Adding flour to make an opaque sauce.
quiz.question: What turns the cooking liquid into a glaze?

choices: Leave them still against the pan.
Roll the vegetables in the forming syrup.
Cover them again to trap the steam.
quiz.question: What do you do as the last liquid boils away?

choices: A sizzle becomes a quiet simmer.
The pan stays full of gently bubbling water.
Bubbling changes to a sizzle.
quiz.question: What sound marks the last of the water leaving?

choices: Pour some liquid off rather than waiting for all of it to boil away.
Keep simmering until the vegetables break down.
Add more water to delay glazing.
quiz.question: The vegetables are tender but too much liquid remains. What would you do?

cues.text: Loose, separate shreds that do not clump.

technique/grate.does: Rubs firm food against a rough surface to turn it into fine shreds.
how: Chill a soft cheese first, so that it shreds and does not smear.
Hold the grater steady on the board or over a bowl.
Push the food down the grater in long strokes with the flat of your hand.
Stop while there is still enough left to hold.

intro.what: Grating rubs firm food against a rough surface to make fine shreds.
intro.why: It teaches you to control texture and stop before the remaining piece becomes difficult to hold.

mistakes.fix: Stop early and chop the end with a knife.
mistakes.mistake: Grating the last small piece and catching a knuckle.

quiz.because: The rough grating surface breaks firm food into fine shreds.
choices: A smooth smeared paste.
Thick slices with flat faces.
Fine, loose shreds.
quiz.question: What should grating produce?

choices: Chill it before grating.
Warm it until very soft.
Press it harder as it smears.
quiz.question: How can you help soft cheese grate cleanly?

quiz.because: Separate shreds show the food is cutting against the grater rather than smearing.
choices: Smears clinging in a paste.
Loose, separate shreds.
A compressed clump without visible shreds.
quiz.question: Which appearance suggests clean grating?

quiz.because: Stop while enough remains to hold; chop the end instead of chasing it down the grater.
choices: Keep grating with fingertips against the teeth.
Press the last piece harder with your knuckles.
Stop grating and chop the end with a knife.
quiz.question: Only a small hard-to-hold end remains. What would you do?

cues.text: The grated daikon is a soft, wet, white mound.

technique/grate-daikon.does: Grates a daikon on a fine grater into a wet, light, snowy mound, which is eaten raw beside rich or grilled food to freshen the mouth.
how: Peel the daikon, or leave the skin on if it is tender, and cut it into a piece that is easy to hold.
Grate it with firm, even strokes on the finest side of the grater, in one direction.
Let the juice drain away a little in a sieve, but do not press it dry.
Shape the mound with a spoon and serve it straight away.

intro.what: This method finely grates daikon into a light, juicy mound for serving alongside rich food.
intro.why: It teaches you to preserve a fresh texture by draining lightly and grating close to serving.

mistakes.fix: Grate it just before serving.
mistakes.mistake: Grating long ahead, so that it turns bitter and watery.

mistakes.fix: Drain it lightly only.
mistakes.mistake: Squeezing it dry, which leaves it harsh.

quiz.because: Light draining preserves the wet, light texture of finely grated daikon.
choices: A tightly squeezed dry mass.
A soft, juicy mound.
Long, coarse dry shreds.
quiz.question: What texture should this grated daikon retain?

quiz.because: Gentle draining removes a little juice while keeping the mound fresh and juicy.
choices: Twist it hard in a cloth until dry.
Leave it soaking in its juice for a long time.
Let some juice run through a sieve without pressing it dry.
quiz.question: How should you drain it?

quiz.because: Fine grating produces a soft snowy mound, rather than coarse ribbons.
choices: A soft, wet, white mound.
A compact dry block.
Broad ribbons that keep their shape.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches this preparation?

quiz.because: Grating long ahead can spoil the fresh taste and texture; prepare it close to serving.
choices: Grate it further ahead to drain longer.
Grate it just before serving.
Squeeze it completely dry before storing.
