variant_of.differs: It is grated very fine and wet, kept juicy and loose and served as a raw mound, not dried or used to flavour a dish.

cues.text: A blistered, golden-brown crust that bubbles at the rim.
Toasted cheese. A sharp, bitter smell means it has gone too far.

technique/gratinate.does: Browns the top of a dish under strong heat from above, until it forms a golden crust.

Set it on a high shelf, under a grill that is already hot.
Stay beside it. The crust goes from pale to burnt very fast.
Turn the dish for an even colour, and take it out when it is golden and bubbling at the edges.

intro.what: Gratinating browns the top of a dish under strong heat from above.
intro.why: It separates making a golden crust from warming the dish beneath it, and teaches close attention to fast browning.

mistakes.fix: Watch it the whole time, with the oven door ajar.
mistakes.mistake: Walking away from the grill.

mistakes.fix: Warm the dish in the oven first, then brown the top.
mistakes.mistake: Grilling a dish that is cold in the middle, so that the top burns before the inside is hot.

quiz.because: Strong heat from above browns the topping into a crust.
choices: A golden crust on top.
A pale, wet topping.
A crust on the bottom alone.
quiz.question: What is gratinating intended to create?

quiz.because: An already hot grill supplies the strong heat from above that browns the topping.
choices: On a low shelf in a cold oven.
On a high shelf beneath an already hot grill.
Under a tight lid away from top heat.
quiz.question: How does this method position the dish for browning?

quiz.because: A blistered golden-brown crust is the aim. A sharp, bitter smell suggests the topping has gone too far.
choices: A pale topping without any colour.
A black surface with a bitter smell.
A blistered, golden-brown top bubbling at the rim.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches the intended crust?

quiz.because: The top can burn before a cold middle warms. Warm the dish first, then use the grill to brown its surface.
choices: Warm the dish in the oven, then brown the top.
Move the cold dish closer to the grill to heat the middle faster.
Add the topping and grill the cold dish straight away.

cues.text: Brown speckles on the underside, and bubbles or puffing on the top.
A toasty, bready smell, and not a burnt one.

technique/griddle.does: Cooks flat foods on a wide, flat, heavy surface that is dry or only lightly oiled, so that they brown in speckles and spots on each face and stay soft within, without being fried in a pool of fat.

Wipe it with a thin film of oil, or leave it dry for a dough that holds its own fat.
Lay the food down flat and leave it still until the underside is spotted brown and it lifts easily.
Turn it and cook the other face, pressing lightly if it puffs.
Stack the finished pieces in a cloth so that they stay soft.

intro.why: It teaches you to distinguish spotted browning from frying in fat and to keep finished flatbreads soft.

mistakes.fix: Preheat it until it is evenly hot.

mistakes.fix: Wipe on only a thin film.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving the finished food open to the air, where it dries and stiffens.

A deep layer of oil around each piece.

As soon as the top puffs, even if the underside still clings.

choices: A wet pale underside with no spots.
An even coating of deep frying oil.
Brown speckles underneath and puffing or bubbles on top.

choices: Stack them in a cloth.
Spread them uncovered to cool completely.
Leave them on the hot griddle between servings.
quiz.question: Finished pieces are drying and becoming stiff. What would you change?

variant_of.differs: The food lies on a flat surface that is dry or barely oiled and browns in speckles, where pan-frying cooks in a film of fat.

cues.text: An evenly browned or blistered surface, with no black, bitter patches.
A smell of toasting, not of burning.

technique/grill.does: Cooks food close to fierce, direct heat, so that its surface colours and chars lightly while the inside stays moist.
how: Heat the grill until it is very hot before the food goes near it.
Dry the food, oil it lightly and season it.
Set it close to the heat and leave it until the surface has coloured, then turn it once.
Move a thick piece further from the heat once it has coloured, so that the inside can catch up.

mistakes.fix: Let it lose its chill first.

A raw scent with little toasted aroma.

Keep it close and turn it more rapidly.
Move it farther from the heat.

cues.text: The meat is browned and speckled with dark spots on every side, with no black patch.
A smoky, meaty scent rises from the coals.
The meat springs back when pressed, instead of giving way.

technique/grill-over-charcoal.does: Cooks skewered minced meat over glowing coals, turning it often, so that the outside takes a smoky crust while the inside stays juicy.

Press the meat down onto the grate.

comes_after.why: Spices and nuts are toasted first so that they grind to a finer, more fragrant powder.

mistakes.mistake: Adding too much liquid to a paste, which turns it to soup.

quiz.because: Grinding can produce different textures; stop at the texture needed rather than always making a smooth paste.
choices: The longest time the machine can run.
A completely smooth result for every food.
The powder, meal or paste texture the dish needs.
quiz.question: What determines when to stop grinding?

quiz.because: Small batches and short bursts limit heating and help the grind stay even.
choices: In short bursts with small batches.
Continuously with the bowl packed full.
Until the bowl feels warm, then add more food.
quiz.question: How should you run a grinder for these foods?

quiz.because: Whole pieces among dust show that some food has ground much faster than the rest.
choices: An even powder without whole pieces.
Dust mixed with pieces still left whole.
A paste that holds together when pressed.
quiz.question: What suggests an uneven grind?

quiz.because: Only enough liquid to keep the blades moving is needed; excess turns the paste into soup.
choices: Pour all the liquid in before starting.
Keep adding liquid after the paste moves freely.
Add liquid gradually and stop when the blades turn.
quiz.question: The paste has become too thin after adding liquid. What would you change next time?

cues.text: The paste is moist and coarse, with a slow ribbon when it falls from the spoon.
Fresh, mild and sweet from the coconut, with a sharp warmth from the chilli and a clean finish.

technique/grind-a-chutney.does: Grinds fresh coconut or fresh herbs with green chilli, ginger, salt and a little cold water in a blender or on a stone into a coarse, moist paste, which is served raw as a fresh relish.
how: Put the coconut or the herbs in the blender with the green chilli, the ginger, the salt and any thickener, such as roasted split chickpeas.
Add a little cold water to start. Pulse and scrape down the sides.
Add more water a spoonful at a time, until the blades catch and the paste turns over and over.
Stop when the paste is coarse and moist, thick enough to hold on a spoon, and not a smooth purée.
Taste and adjust the salt and the chilli. It is served the same day, often with a hot tempering poured over it.

intro.what: This fresh chutney method grinds coconut or herbs with chilli and ginger into a moist, coarse relish.
intro.why: It teaches you to use just enough cold water to move the blades while keeping texture and fresh flavour.

mistakes.fix: Add the water a spoonful at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Adding all the water at once, so that the chutney is thin and bland.

mistakes.fix: Pulse in short bursts and stop while it is still coarse.
mistakes.mistake: Grinding too long, so that the paste turns warm and pasty.

mistakes.fix: Use cold water.
mistakes.mistake: Using warm water, which turns the herbs dark and the coconut sour sooner.

quiz.because: A little texture and enough body to sit on a spoon distinguish this chutney from a thin purée.
choices: A moist, coarse paste that holds on a spoon.
A thin liquid that pours freely.
A warm, completely smooth purée.
quiz.question: What texture is the aim of this fresh chutney method?

quiz.because: Gradual additions help the blades move without thinning and diluting the chutney.
choices: All at once before checking the texture.
Gradually, only until the blades catch and the paste turns.
Keep pouring after the mixture turns freely.
quiz.question: How should you add water during grinding?

quiz.because: A moist paste should move slowly from the spoon while retaining its coarse texture.
choices: A watery stream without body.
A stiff, dry mass stuck above the blades.
A coarse paste falling in a slow ribbon.
quiz.question: Which appearance suggests the desired consistency?

quiz.because: Long grinding warms the paste; short pulses preserve the intended coarse texture.
choices: Pulse briefly and stop while it is still coarse.
Keep the motor running to smooth it further.
Use warm water to help the blades.
quiz.question: The chutney became warm and pasty during grinding. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The food is ground fresh and wet to a coarse, moist paste and served raw, not dried and ground to a powder. A little cold water is added slowly so that the blades catch.

cues.text: A deep, nutty, warm scent rises from the bowl.
The mixture turns into a damp, oily paste with some seeds left whole.

technique/grind-sesame.does: Toasts sesame seeds until they are fragrant, then grinds them in a ridged bowl to a rough, oily paste with some seeds left half whole, ready to coat vegetables or to thicken a dressing.
how: Toast the seeds in a dry pan, shaking them, until they smell nutty and begin to pop.
Tip them into the ridged bowl while they are still warm.
Grind them with a circular motion, pressing against the ridges, until they are half crushed and oily.
Stir in the other seasonings and use the paste right away, as its scent fades.

intro.what: This method toasts sesame and grinds it into a rough, oily paste for dressings and vegetables.
intro.why: It shows how to develop a nutty scent while retaining some seed texture instead of making a greasy paste.

mistakes.fix: Toast them first.
mistakes.mistake: Grinding raw seeds, which gives a pale, flat taste.

mistakes.fix: Stop while the seeds are still half whole.
mistakes.mistake: Grinding too long, which turns the paste greasy and pasty.

quiz.because: Toasting brings out the nutty scent missing from raw ground seeds.
choices: To keep the seeds pale and raw-tasting.
To develop a nutty scent and fuller taste.
To dry out all the oil in the seeds.
quiz.question: Why toast sesame before grinding it here?

quiz.because: Pressing against the ridges breaks the toasted seeds into a rough paste.
choices: Tap lightly without pressing against the ridges.
Wait until cold and stir without crushing.
Press and grind in circles while they are still warm.
quiz.question: How do you work the seeds in the ridged bowl?

quiz.because: This method stops with a rough texture and some visible seeds, rather than grinding everything smooth.
choices: A damp, oily paste with some seeds still partly whole.
A completely smooth, greasy paste.
Loose dry seeds without any crushed paste.
quiz.question: Which texture should remain in the ground sesame?

quiz.because: Overgrinding loses the intended rough seed texture and makes the paste greasy.
choices: Grind longer to absorb the oil.
Stop grinding while some seeds remain partly whole.
Skip toasting and grind until smooth.
quiz.question: The paste has become greasy and pasty. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The seeds are ground only until half crushed, in a ridged bowl, so that the paste stays rough and oily instead of becoming fine powder.

comes_after.why: A fish is scaled first, so that loose scales do not stick to the flesh when the belly is opened.

cues.text: The cavity is pale and clean, with no dark blood left along the backbone.
A clean fish smells of the sea and of nothing sour or sharp.

technique/gut-a-fish.does: Opens the belly of a whole fish and takes out the guts and the gills, then rinses the cavity, so that the fish can be cooked whole or filleted without a bitter taste.
how: Lay the fish on a board with the belly towards you.
Slide the tip of the knife in at the vent near the tail and slit the belly up to the gills, shallow, with the blade pointing up so that the guts are not pierced.
Reach in, loosen the guts at the throat and pull them out in one piece.
Lift the gill cover and cut the gills away at both ends. They taste bitter if they are left in.
Rinse the cavity under cold running water, rubbing away the dark blood along the backbone, and pat the fish dry.

intro.what: Gutting opens a whole fish to remove the guts and gills and clean the cavity.
intro.why: It teaches precise shallow cutting and careful removal so bitter contents do not taint the flesh.

mistakes.fix: Cut shallow, with the tip of the knife pointing up.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting too deep and piercing the guts, which taints the flesh with bitterness.

mistakes.fix: Cut them out at both ends and rinse the cavity.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the gills in, which turn a stock or a sauce bitter.

quiz.because: A shallow cut protects the guts from being pierced and spilling bitter contents.
choices: Their contents can taint the flesh with bitterness.
It keeps the flesh connected along the backbone.
It keeps the opening narrow for whole-fish presentation.
quiz.question: Why avoid piercing the guts while opening the fish?

quiz.because: A shallow upward-pointing cut opens the belly without cutting into the guts.
choices: Deeply towards the backbone.
Shallowly, with the blade tip pointing up.
By sawing firmly through the contents.
quiz.question: How should you make the belly slit?

quiz.because: Rubbing away the dark blood and rinsing leaves the cavity visibly clear.
choices: Gills still attached inside the opening.
A dark strip of blood left along the backbone.
A pale cavity without dark blood along the backbone.
quiz.question: What should you see after rinsing the cavity?

quiz.because: This preparation removes the gills rather than carrying their bitter taste into the sauce.
choices: Cut them away at both ends and rinse the cavity.
Rinse only the outside of the fish.
Leave them attached and use more sauce liquid.
quiz.question: A sauce became bitter after the gills were left in. What would you change in the preparation next time?

cues.text: The liquid smells clearly of the flavouring when you bend over the pan.
Saffron turns the liquid a deep gold, and the threads go pale.

technique/infuse.does: Lets a flavouring steep in a warm liquid until the liquid has taken on its scent, colour and taste, and then lifts or strains the flavouring out. It is the reverse of soaking, where the food takes up the liquid.
how: Warm the liquid until it steams. Do not let it boil hard, which dulls a delicate scent and makes milk climb the pan.
Add the flavouring, such as strips of peel, a stick of cinnamon, a split vanilla pod, threads of saffron or herbs, and take the pan off the heat.
Cover and leave it to steep until the liquid smells strongly of the flavouring.
Strain, or lift the flavouring out, before the liquid is used. Press it gently to give up the last of its taste.

intro.what: Infusing steeps a flavouring in warm liquid, then removes it once the liquid has taken up its taste and scent.
intro.why: It teaches you to draw flavour into liquid gently and judge the result rather than relying only on waiting.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat before the flavouring goes in.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling the liquid with the flavouring in it, which turns peel and saffron harsh and bitter.

mistakes.fix: Taste it, and leave it longer if it is weak.
mistakes.mistake: Straining too soon, so that the liquid is only faintly flavoured.

quiz.because: Infusion flavours the liquid, unlike soaking aimed at letting a solid take up liquid.
choices: Only the solid flavouring itself.
The liquid around the flavouring.
A dry pan beneath the flavouring.
quiz.question: What takes up flavour during an infusion?

quiz.because: Gentle steeping preserves delicate scent; hard boiling can make peel or saffron harsh.
choices: Keep the liquid at a hard boil throughout.
Begin in a dry hot pan without liquid.
Warm the liquid, then steep away from strong heat.
quiz.question: How do you manage heat for delicate flavourings?

quiz.because: Judge the liquid itself for the flavour and scent it has taken up.
choices: It smells clearly of the flavouring.
It still has only a faint trace of scent.
Only the removed solids smell strongly.
quiz.question: What suggests the liquid has infused well?

quiz.because: More steeping can strengthen a weak infusion without using harsh boiling.
choices: Strain sooner to preserve the faint scent.
Let it steep longer and taste again before straining.
Boil it hard with the flavouring still in.
quiz.question: The liquid tasted weak after straining. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: A julienne starts as thin, even slices.

cues.text: Fine strips of one length that bend without snapping and fall apart from each other.

technique/julienne.does: Cuts food into fine, even strips the length of a matchstick.
how: Cut the vegetable into lengths as long as the strips you want.
Slice each length into thin, flat sheets.
Stack a few sheets and slice them lengthwise into strips as wide as the sheets are thick.
For a leek, split a length open, lay the layers flat and slice along the grain.

intro.what: Julienne cuts vegetables into fine, even strips.
intro.why: It teaches you to build a precise cut from flat sheets and keep the strips consistent.

mistakes.fix: Stack only a few sheets at a time and keep the pile flat.
mistakes.mistake: Stacking too many sheets, so the pile slides and the strips come out as wedges.

quiz.because: Julienne means fine strips of an even length and width, rather than cubes or wedges.
choices: Tiny cubes.
Fine, even strips.
Large, uneven wedges.
quiz.question: Which shape is the aim of julienne?

quiz.because: Slicing lengthwise keeps the intended strip length. Match the width of each strip to the thickness of the sheets.
choices: Slice the stack across its width into short pieces.
Cut across them into cubes immediately.
Slice the stacked sheets lengthwise.
quiz.question: How do the flat sheets become strips?

quiz.because: Fine, even strips that separate from each other show a consistent julienne cut.
choices: Fine strips of a similar length that fall apart from each other.
A wet mash of tiny pieces.
Broad wedges with different thicknesses.
quiz.question: Which pile most closely matches julienne?

quiz.because: A tall stack can slide and turn the cuts into wedges. Keep the stack small and flat.
choices: Stack more sheets to make it heavier.
Use fewer sheets and keep the pile flat.
Press the loose pile into a tall heap.
quiz.question: The stack slides and your strips become wedges. What would you change?

cues.text: A piece lifted out is still steaming hot, with no steam rushing off.
The liquid barely moves.

technique/keep-warm.does: Holds finished food at a gentle heat, below a simmer, so that it stays hot and goes on taking up flavour until it is served.
how: Take the pot off the strong heat and turn the flame as low as it goes, or move the food to a warm place.
Keep the food covered so that it does not dry or skin over.
Stir or turn it now and then, so that the bottom does not catch.
Serve from the pot. Do not leave it for a very long time.

intro.what: This finishing method reduces heat after cooking and covers the food while it waits to be served.
intro.why: It teaches you to protect texture from continued simmering, drying and skin formation.

mistakes.fix: Lower the heat until the liquid is still.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the food on a simmer, which cooks it past tender.

mistakes.fix: Cover it.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it uncovered, so that a skin forms or it dries.

quiz.because: Continued simmering can soften food beyond the intended tenderness.
choices: To keep the food boiling until serving.
To reduce the sauce as quickly as possible.
To avoid continuing to cook it past the intended texture.
quiz.question: Why reduce the heat after finishing the dish?

quiz.because: A cover reduces drying and skin formation on the finished dish.
choices: Keep it covered.
Leave it uncovered over the same heat.
Stir only the surface and leave the lid off.
quiz.question: How do you protect the surface from drying while it waits?

quiz.because: The aim is to avoid continued simmering, rather than keep cooking strongly.
choices: A steady rolling boil.
Barely any movement.
Constant bubbles across the whole surface.
quiz.question: What liquid movement matches this gentle finishing method?

quiz.because: An uncovered surface can dry and form a skin; covering addresses that texture problem.
choices: Raise the heat beneath the uncovered pot.
Leave it exposed and stir only before serving.
Cover it.
quiz.question: A skin forms while the food waits uncovered. What would you change?

cues.text: A dough turns from rough and tacky to smooth and elastic, and springs back slowly when it is pressed.
A kneaded mince or bulgur mixture holds together when pressed into a ball and does not crumble.
The surface of a kneaded dough is smooth and satiny, with no dry patches.

technique/knead.does: Works a dough, or a loose mixture such as minced meat or soaked bulgur, with the heels of the hands, pressing and turning it until it comes together and holds its shape. In a dough this builds the stretch that gives bread its chew. In a mixture it binds the pieces so that they do not fall apart in the pan.
how: Bring the mixture together in a wide bowl or on a clean surface, with just enough liquid to make it hold.
Press a dough away from you with the heel of the hand, fold it back over itself, give it a quarter turn and press again.
Keep a steady rhythm. Dust a dough that sticks with a little flour, and wet one that cracks with a little water.
Work minced meat or bulgur with wet hands, squeezing and pressing, until it turns sticky and holds when pressed into a ball.
Stop when a dough is smooth and springs back, or when a mixture sticks to itself and not to the bowl, then let it rest.

intro.what: Kneading presses and turns dough or a binding mixture until it holds together.
intro.why: It teaches you to distinguish elastic dough from a mixture that needs only enough working to bind.

mistakes.fix: Keep the dough a little tacky, and dust the surface only as needed.
mistakes.mistake: Working in too much flour, so that the dough turns dry and heavy.

mistakes.fix: Keep going until it is smooth and springs back when pressed.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping early, so that the dough tears when it is stretched and bakes dense.

mistakes.fix: Keep the meat cold, and stop as soon as the mixture turns sticky.
mistakes.mistake: Working minced meat for long with warm hands, so that the fat smears.

quiz.because: Working dough builds the stretch that contributes to bread's chew.
choices: Stretch and chew.
A deliberately crumbly texture.
Separate dry pieces that do not join.
quiz.question: What does kneading build in bread dough?

quiz.because: Pressing, folding and turning works the dough evenly as it comes together.
choices: Work only the top without folding.
Press away with the heel, fold back and turn before repeating.
Stir the surface while leaving dry patches untouched.
quiz.question: How do you knead a dough with your hands?

quiz.because: A smooth, elastic dough that springs back differs from rough, underworked dough.
choices: It stays rough and tears immediately.
It becomes drier with every addition of flour.
It becomes smooth and elastic and springs back.
quiz.question: Which change suggests the dough has been worked sufficiently?

quiz.because: Excess flour makes the dough dry and heavy; a little tackiness is expected here.
choices: Keep it slightly tacky and dust only as needed.
Add more flour until no tackiness remains.
Rub dry flour into every fold.
quiz.question: The dough became dry and heavy after extra flour. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: Laminating starts with a dough rolled out thin and even.
Laminating is folding a dough over fat again and again.

cues.text: A cut edge shows fine, even layers, each one shining with fat.
The cooked dough pulls apart in thin, crisp sheets.

technique/laminate.does: Builds a dough into many thin layers with fat between them, by rolling or stretching it out, spreading it with fat, folding it over and repeating, so that in the heat each layer cooks apart from the next and the finished bread or pastry comes away in flaky sheets.
how: Start from a smooth dough that has rested and is soft enough to stretch thin.
Roll or stretch it out as thin as it will go without tearing.
Brush the whole sheet with melted fat or oil, or lay a slab of cold butter on it. For some breads, sprinkle fine semolina over the fat, so that the layers do not weld.
Fold the sheet over the fat, as a letter or into a square, so that the fat is sealed inside.
Rest the dough between folds: cold for a dough with butter, covered at room warmth for an oiled one.
Repeat the rolling and folding until the dough has as many layers as the dish needs, then shape it and cook it.

intro.what: Laminating repeatedly folds dough with fat between the layers to make flaky sheets.
intro.why: It teaches you to preserve distinct layers through gentle rolling and rests matched to the fat being used.

mistakes.fix: Chill the dough between folds and keep the butter cold.
mistakes.mistake: Letting butter warm and melt into the dough, so that the bread is not flaky.

mistakes.fix: Roll with an even, light pressure and rest the dough when it fights back.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling so hard that the fat tears through the layers.

quiz.because: Layers separated by fat can cook apart instead of welding into a single mass.
choices: Fat fully mixed through an unlayered dough.
Thin dough layers separated by fat.
A thick outer coating of flour.
quiz.question: What creates the flaky sheets in laminated dough?

quiz.because: Chilling preserves butter between the layers instead of letting it melt into the dough.
choices: Uncovered in a warm place until the butter melts.
Over gentle heat to soften the fat into the dough.
Chilled, keeping the butter cold.
quiz.question: How should a butter-laminated dough rest between folds?

quiz.because: Visible fine layers show the dough and fat remain distinct.
choices: Fine, even layers with fat between them.
An even solid mass without layers.
Large tears where fat has broken through.
quiz.question: What should a cut edge reveal before cooking?

quiz.because: Gentle pressure and resting reduce tearing while preserving the layers.
choices: Press harder to force it flat.
Use light, even pressure and rest dough that resists.
Skip the rests and roll faster.
quiz.question: Hard rolling is making fat tear through the dough. What would you change?

cues.text: A level top, and layers of the same thickness when the dish is cut.

technique/layer.does: Builds a dish in even layers, so that it cooks evenly and holds together when it is served.
how: Have every part ready and within reach before you start.
Spread each layer to the edges, in one even thickness.
Season lightly between the layers, not only on top.
Finish with the layer that should brown.

intro.what: Layering builds a dish in even sheets of its different parts.
intro.why: It helps you distribute thickness and seasoning throughout a dish rather than concentrating them on top.

mistakes.fix: Take a moment to level each layer.
mistakes.mistake: Thick and thin patches, which cook at different speeds.

mistakes.fix: Season lightly as you go.
mistakes.mistake: Seasoning only the top, which leaves the inside bland.

quiz.because: Thick and thin patches cook at different speeds. Even layers help the dish cook evenly.
choices: To make stirring during cooking unnecessary in every layered dish.
To keep the flavours of the layers from mixing at all.
To help the dish cook evenly.
quiz.question: Why make each layer an even thickness?

quiz.because: Spread each layer to the edges at an even thickness, rather than leaving a mound in the centre.
choices: To the edges in an even thickness.
In a tall mound at the centre.
In thin patches with gaps between them.
quiz.question: How should each layer be spread?

quiz.because: A level top and layers of similar thickness show that the filling has been spread evenly.
choices: A steep mound with thin edges.
A level top and evenly thick layers in a cut portion.
Thick and thin patches throughout.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches the intended result?

quiz.because: Seasoning only the top leaves the inside bland. Season lightly between layers as you build.
choices: Season only the final layer more heavily.
Season only the bottom before adding the other layers.
Season lightly between the layers as you build.
quiz.question: The inside tastes bland although the top is seasoned. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: The biscuits must be dipped before they are laid down, or they stay dry.
The cream goes between the layers, so it is made first.

cues.text: The layers are flat and even, and show as stripes where a square is cut out.
A knife cuts through without the cream running, and the biscuits are soft right through.

technique/layer-a-cold-dessert.does: Builds a dessert without baking it, from dipped biscuits and a soft cream laid in even layers in a dish, dusts the top and chills it for long enough that the layers soften into each other and the whole can be cut in squares.
how: Have the dipped biscuits and the cream within reach before the first layer goes down.
Lay a single layer of biscuits side by side in the dish, close together with no gaps.
Spread half the cream over them in an even layer, right to the corners, and smooth it with a spatula.
Lay a second layer of biscuits, then spread the rest of the cream and smooth the top.
Sift cocoa over the top just before serving, so that it stays dry and dark.
Cover the dish and chill it until the layers have melded and the cream is firm enough to cut cleanly.

intro.what: This chilled dessert method alternates dipped biscuits and soft cream in even layers.
intro.why: It teaches you to connect resting texture with neat slices and delay a dry cocoa finish until serving.

mistakes.fix: Leave it to chill until it is firm, ideally overnight.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting the dessert after only a short chill, so that the cream runs and the layers slide.

mistakes.fix: Dust it on just before serving.
mistakes.mistake: Dusting the cocoa on before chilling, so that it dissolves into a damp, patchy top.

quiz.because: Chilling lets biscuits soften into the cream while the dessert firms enough for clean portions.
choices: To keep the biscuits hard and separate from the cream.
To make the cream run between the layers.
To let the layers meld and the cream become firm enough to slice.
quiz.question: Why chill the assembled dessert before cutting?

quiz.because: A late dusting stays dry and dark rather than dissolving into a damp top.
choices: Just before serving.
Before the assembled dessert begins chilling.
Before adding the first cream layer.
quiz.question: When should cocoa be sifted over the top?

quiz.because: A clean cut depends on firm cream and softened biscuits working together.
choices: The cream flows out as the biscuit layers slide.
The knife cuts without cream running and the biscuits are soft.
Hard biscuits drag through loose cream.
quiz.question: What shows the dessert has the intended slicing texture?

quiz.because: A short chill leaves the cream too loose to support the layers.
choices: Cut sooner while the cream is looser.
Add cocoa to hide the slipping layers.
Chill it longer until the cream is firm.
quiz.question: The layers slide and cream runs when cut. What would you change?

variant_of.differs: Nothing is baked. The layers are built cold and soften together as they chill, so the dessert needs a long rest before it is cut.

cues.text: Every sheet shines evenly with fat, and none is left dry at the edges.
The baked pie crackles under the knife and the top breaks into fine flakes.

technique/layer-phyllo.does: Builds a pie from paper-thin sheets of phyllo laid one on another, each brushed with oil or melted butter, so that the baked pie is made of many crisp, flaky layers around its filling.
how: Keep the stack of sheets under a barely damp cloth and lift out only the sheet in hand, because open sheets dry and crack within moments.
Brush the dish lightly with fat. Lay a sheet in, let the edges hang over the sides, and brush the whole sheet with fat right to the edges.
Add the next sheet at a slight turn, so that the hanging edges reach all round the dish, and brush it in the same way. Go on until the base is thick enough to hold the filling.
Spread the filling in an even layer and fold the hanging edges back over it.
Lay the top sheets one at a time, brushing each with fat. Tuck the edges down inside the dish and brush the top.
Cut through the top layers into portions before the pie goes in the oven. A baked crust shatters under the knife.

intro.what: Layering phyllo stacks thin sheets brushed with fat around a filling to make a crisp flaky pie.
intro.why: It teaches you to manage fragile sheets, even fat coverage and filling moisture.

mistakes.fix: Keep them under a barely damp cloth and take out one sheet at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the stack uncovered, so that the sheets dry out, crack and crumble.

mistakes.fix: Brush a thin, even coat on every sheet, right to the edges.
mistakes.mistake: Brushing too lightly, so that the sheets stick together and bake leathery, or too heavily, so that the pie turns greasy.

mistakes.fix: Drain the filling well and let it cool before it goes in.
mistakes.mistake: Putting a wet filling on the base sheets, which turns them soggy.

mistakes.fix: Cut through the top layers before baking.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting the pie only after it is baked, so that the crust shatters.

quiz.because: A thin, even coat helps layers bake flaky rather than sticking together.
choices: To create separate crisp, flaky layers.
To make the sheets stick into a dense leathery layer.
To soak the base with the filling liquid.
quiz.question: Why brush fat between the phyllo sheets?

quiz.because: Exposed sheets dry and crack quickly; a barely damp covering protects them.
choices: Spread uncovered beside the dish.
Under a barely damp cloth, lifting out a sheet as needed.
Immersed in water until needed.
quiz.question: How should you keep sheets not yet in use?

quiz.because: An even thin coat covers edges without leaving the pie greasy.
choices: Shiny only in the middle with dry edges.
Pools of fat collecting in folds.
Evenly shiny, including the edges.
quiz.question: What should a sheet look like after brushing?

quiz.because: Excess filling moisture soaks the delicate base; draining and cooling address that problem.
choices: Drain the filling well and let it cool before adding.
Add the wet filling immediately while hot.
Brush only the centre of the bottom sheet.
quiz.question: A wet filling made the base sheets soggy. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The layers are the dough itself, paper-thin sheets each brushed with fat so that they bake crisp and stay apart, and the filling is closed between them. A plain layer stacks cooked food in turn with its sauce.

cues.text: The strands are separate and glossy.
The strands slide apart with no tearing.

technique/loosen-noodles.does: Pulls apart a clump of steamed, oiled noodles, with a splash of water or a short warming in the pan, until each strand is free and ready to be stir-fried.
how: Put the clump in a hot pan or in a bowl, and add a splash of water.
Cover for a very short time to steam, so that the strands relax.
Pull the strands apart with chopsticks or tongs, working gently from the edge to the middle.
Drain off any water and use the noodles at once.

intro.what: Loosening separates a clump of steamed, oiled noodles before stir-frying.
intro.why: It teaches you to relax the strands gently with a little warmth and water rather than tearing them apart cold.

mistakes.fix: Warm it first so that it relaxes.
mistakes.mistake: Tearing the clump while it is cold, which breaks the strands.

mistakes.fix: Use only a splash.
mistakes.mistake: Adding too much water, so that the noodles are soggy.

quiz.because: Separate strands are ready for stir-frying instead of being pulled forcefully from a cold clump.
choices: To soften them into a single thick mass.
To separate strands without tearing them in the pan.
To wash away every trace of surface oil.
quiz.question: Why loosen noodles before stir-frying?

quiz.because: Brief warmth relaxes the strands, and gentle work from the edge avoids tearing.
choices: Pull hard through the cold centre first.
Cover it completely with water and leave it soaking.
Warm it briefly, then separate gently from the edge inward.
quiz.question: How should you work through the clump?

quiz.because: Freely separating strands show the clump has relaxed enough to handle gently.
choices: Strands slide apart without tearing.
The clump resists and strands snap.
The noodles have become soggy and swollen.
quiz.question: Which feel suggests the noodles have loosened?

quiz.because: Too much water makes the noodles soggy instead of simply loosening them.
choices: Add more water to separate them further.
Use only a little water and drain it off.
Leave them sitting in the water before frying.
quiz.question: The noodles became soggy while loosening. What would you change for the next batch?

comes_after.why: The yolks are first whisked over gentle heat to a ribbon, as in a sabayon, before the butter goes in.

cues.text: The yolks leave a ribbon on the surface, and the finished sauce is glossy and thick enough to coat a spoon.
Sharp at first, then rounded by the butter, with a clear note of tarragon.

technique/make-a-bearnaise.does: Makes a warm sauce of egg yolk and butter, as a hollandaise is made, but sharpened with a strong reduction of vinegar, white wine, shallot and tarragon in place of lemon juice, and finished with chopped tarragon.
how: Put the vinegar, the wine, the chopped shallot and part of the tarragon in a small pan and boil them down until only a few spoonfuls of strong, sharp liquid are left.
Strain the reduction and let it cool a little.
Melt the butter gently and keep it warm.
Whisk the yolks with the reduction in a bowl over a pan of barely trembling water until they are pale, thick and leave a ribbon. Lift the bowl away from the heat as soon as it gets too hot to touch.
Off the heat, whisk in the warm butter, a drop at a time at first and then in a thin stream, leaving the milky part in the pan.
Season, stir in the rest of the tarragon, chopped, and keep the sauce warm, never hot, until it is served.

intro.what: Béarnaise combines yolk and butter with a sharp vinegar, wine, shallot and tarragon reduction.
intro.why: It teaches you to balance a concentrated flavour base with gentle heat and gradual butter additions.

mistakes.fix: Lift the bowl off the heat often and keep whisking.
mistakes.mistake: Heating the yolks too long or too hot, so that they scramble.

mistakes.fix: Start a drop at a time. If it splits, whisk the split sauce into a fresh yolk slowly.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the butter too fast, so that the sauce splits.

mistakes.fix: Stop when a few spoonfuls of syrupy liquid are left.
mistakes.mistake: Reducing the vinegar too little, so that the sauce is sour and thin, or too far, so that it is harsh.

mistakes.fix: Keep it in a warm bowl, away from direct heat.
mistakes.mistake: Keeping the sauce too hot while it waits, so that it separates.

quiz.because: The reduction supplies the sharp base, and chopped tarragon finishes the sauce.
choices: Lemon juice alone added after the butter.
Raw flour cooked in the butter.
A reduction of vinegar, wine, shallot and tarragon.
quiz.question: What gives this butter sauce its distinctive sharp tarragon flavour?

quiz.because: Gradual butter additions help the yolk mixture hold the sauce rather than split.
choices: Very slowly at first, whisked in away from the heat.
All at once over direct high heat.
Before the reduction is strained or the yolks thickened.
quiz.question: How should butter enter the thickened yolks?

quiz.because: A ribbon shows a thickened yolk mixture; grains suggest excess heat.
choices: They stay as thin as the starting liquid.
They fall in a ribbon.
They form firm grains at the bowl edge.
quiz.question: Which cue indicates the yolks have thickened before butter is added?

quiz.because: Excess holding heat can separate this sauce, so keep it away from direct heat.
choices: Return it to a stronger flame.
Keep heating until the separated fat boils.
Keep it warm away from direct heat.
quiz.question: The sauce separated while waiting in a hot place. What would you change about holding it next time?

variant_of.differs: A hollandaise takes its sharpness from lemon juice. A béarnaise starts with a strong reduction of vinegar, wine, shallot and tarragon, which is strained into the yolks, and ends with fresh tarragon.

comes_after.why: A béchamel begins with a pale roux, so a cook has to be able to cook flour in fat without lumps or colour.

cues.text: The sauce is smooth and ivory, and runs off the spoon in a slow, even ribbon.
The smell of raw flour has gone and a gentle smell of milk and nutmeg remains.

technique/make-a-bechamel.does: Cooks a pale roux, whisks warm milk into it a little at a time and simmers it to a smooth white sauce seasoned with nutmeg. Thin, it coats food. Thick, it holds a baked dish together.
how: Warm the milk in a second pan until it is hot but not boiling.
Melt the butter in a saucepan, stir in an equal weight of flour and cook it, stirring, only until it smells like biscuit and has taken no colour.
Take the pan off the heat and whisk in a ladle of milk until the paste is smooth. Add the rest a ladle at a time, whisking each one smooth.
Set the pan back on a low heat and simmer gently, stirring into the corners, until the raw taste of flour has gone and the sauce coats a spoon.
Season with salt and a grating of nutmeg. For a baked dish, cook it thicker. For coating, leave it looser.
If it must wait, press a piece of buttered paper onto its surface so that no skin forms.

intro.what: Béchamel joins milk to a pale roux and simmers it into a smooth white sauce.
intro.why: It teaches you to add liquid gradually and choose thickness for coating food or binding a baked dish.

mistakes.fix: Add it a ladle at a time and whisk each one smooth. A lumpy sauce can be rescued through a sieve.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in all the milk at once, which leaves lumps.

mistakes.fix: Stir into the corners all the while and keep the heat low.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the sauce unstirred on the heat, so that it catches on the base of the pan.

mistakes.fix: Simmer it gently until it tastes of milk and not of flour.
mistakes.mistake: Serving it before the flour is cooked out, so that it tastes pasty.

quiz.because: Thickness serves the job: a coating sauce can be looser than a sauce that binds a dish.
choices: Looser for coating, thicker for holding a baked dish together.
Always equally thick regardless of use.
Thinner for binding a baked dish than for coating.
quiz.question: How does the desired use affect the sauce thickness?

quiz.because: Gradual additions help the paste join the milk smoothly instead of forming lumps.
choices: All at once before beginning to whisk.
Gradually, whisking each addition smooth.
Only after browning the roux dark.
quiz.question: How do you add milk to the pale roux?

quiz.because: A smooth ivory ribbon shows the milk and pale roux have combined.
choices: Brown sauce with floating flour lumps.
Thin milk separated from a grainy paste.
Ivory sauce flowing in a slow, even ribbon.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches a smooth béchamel?

quiz.because: Gentle heat and stirring across the base and corners reduce catching.
choices: Keep the heat low and stir into the corners.
Raise the heat and stir only the surface.
Leave it still until a skin forms.
quiz.question: The sauce is starting to stick at the base. What would you change?

cues.text: A clear, deep amber, like dark honey. Smoke means it has gone too far.
Toasted sugar. An acrid smell means a bitter caramel.

technique/make-a-caramel.does: Cooks sugar until it melts and browns to an amber syrup with a bittersweet taste.
how: Put the sugar in a clean, heavy, pale pan with just enough water to wet it.
Heat it without stirring. Swirl the pan if it colours unevenly.
Watch as it turns from clear to straw to amber.
Stop it the moment it is the colour of dark honey, by adding the liquid the recipe calls for, standing well back.
For a sweet and sour base, stop it with vinegar and boil until syrupy.

intro.what: Making caramel heats sugar until it melts and turns into an amber, bittersweet syrup.
intro.why: It teaches close attention to colour and smell as sugar moves quickly from browning to burning.

mistakes.fix: Leave it alone and swirl the pan.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring the sugar as it melts, which makes it seize into crystals.

mistakes.fix: Stay with it, and have the liquid ready beside the stove.
mistakes.mistake: Walking away. Caramel goes from amber to burnt in moments.

quiz.because: Caramel develops amber colour and bittersweet flavour as the sugar browns.
choices: It stays clear while water is added repeatedly.
It melts and browns to amber.
It forms pale dry crystals.
quiz.question: What change makes the sugar into caramel?

quiz.because: Stirring can encourage crystals in this method; swirling moves the sugar without stirring it.
choices: Stir continuously with a spoon.
Scrape the melting sugar into a pile.
Swirl the pan rather than stirring the sugar.
quiz.question: How do you even out the colour while the sugar melts?

quiz.because: Deep amber is the target; smoke and an acrid smell mean it has gone too far.
choices: Deep amber like dark honey.
Colourless syrup.
Black syrup giving off smoke.
quiz.question: Which colour is the intended stopping cue?

quiz.because: The change from amber to burnt is fast, so prepare the finishing liquid before that stage.
choices: Use higher heat to shorten the wait.
Have the liquid ready and stay beside the pan.
Start checking only after smoke appears.
quiz.question: The caramel burned while you fetched the finishing liquid. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: The yolks and the sugar are whisked first.

cues.text: It coats the back of the spoon, and a finger drawn through the coating leaves a clear line that does not close.
The spoon moves through something a little heavier than milk.

technique/make-a-custard.does: Thickens sweetened milk with egg yolks over gentle heat, stirring until it coats a spoon and before the yolks scramble.
how: Whisk the yolks with the sugar until pale.
Heat the milk with the vanilla until it steams, and pour it slowly onto the yolks while whisking.
Return it to the pan over low heat and stir without stopping, sweeping the whole bottom and the corners.
Take it off the heat the moment it coats the back of the spoon, and strain it at once into a cold bowl.

intro.what: This stirred custard thickens sweetened milk with egg yolks over gentle heat.
intro.why: It teaches you to use the spoon coating as a texture cue while preventing the yolks from turning grainy.

mistakes.fix: Take it off early and strain it straight into a bowl set in iced water. If it has only just started to grain, blending can rescue it.
mistakes.mistake: Letting it get too hot, so that the yolks scramble into grains.

mistakes.fix: Trust the line on the spoon, not the clock.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping too soon for fear of scrambling, which leaves a thin sauce.

quiz.because: Gentle heat lets the yolks thicken the milk into a smooth coating sauce.
choices: Firm scrambled grains in milk.
A thin liquid unchanged from the milk.
A smooth sauce that coats a spoon.
quiz.question: What texture is the aim of this stirred custard?

quiz.because: Slow pouring and whisking combine the hot milk with the yolks before gentle cooking.
choices: Pour it slowly while whisking.
Pour it all at once without stirring.
Add the yolks directly to strongly boiling milk.
quiz.question: How should hot milk meet the yolks?

quiz.because: A clear line that does not close shows the custard has thickened enough to coat the spoon.
choices: The coating runs back immediately without a line.
A line through the coating stays clear.
Dry grains collect on the spoon.
quiz.question: Which spoon cue shows the intended thickness?

quiz.because: Removing heat and transferring promptly limits further scrambling of the yolks.
choices: Increase the heat until it thickens further.
Leave it in the hot pan and stop stirring.
Remove it and strain into a cold bowl promptly.
quiz.question: The custard is beginning to turn grainy from excess heat. What would you do?

comes_after.why: The mushrooms must be minced very fine before they are cooked down.

cues.text: The paste is dark and dry, and holds a line when a spoon is drawn through it.
A deep, roasted mushroom smell.

technique/make-a-duxelles.does: Cooks finely minced mushrooms and shallot in butter until all their water has gone, to a dark, dry paste that is spread or stuffed for its deep flavour.
how: Wipe the mushrooms clean with a cloth. Do not soak them.
Mince the mushrooms and the shallot very fine, with a knife.
Cook them in butter in a wide pan over a medium heat, stirring often, until the water has cooked off and the paste starts to brown.
Season with salt, then let the paste cool before it is used.

intro.what: Duxelles cooks finely minced mushrooms and shallot into a dry, deeply flavoured paste.
intro.why: It teaches you to remove mushroom moisture before using the paste as a filling or spread.

mistakes.fix: Keep cooking until the pan is dry.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping while the paste is still wet, so that it steams grey and makes a filling soggy.

mistakes.fix: Mince them very fine.
mistakes.mistake: Chopping the mushrooms coarse, so that the filling falls apart.

quiz.because: A wet paste can steam and make the surrounding filling soggy.
choices: To concentrate it without making a filling soggy.
To keep loose mushroom liquid in the filling.
To preserve large separate mushroom pieces.
quiz.question: Why cook duxelles until dry?

quiz.because: Fine mincing helps the finished filling hold together instead of falling apart.
choices: Into large uneven chunks.
Very finely with a knife.
Into broad slices left separate.
quiz.question: How finely should you cut the mushrooms and shallot?

quiz.because: A lasting spoon line and a dry pan show the mushroom water has cooked off.
choices: Grey pieces floating in watery liquid.
A loose paste whose spoon track fills immediately.
A dark, dry paste that holds a spoon line.
quiz.question: What appearance suggests the intended consistency?

quiz.because: Continue removing the water before using the paste, rather than trapping it in the filling.
choices: Continue cooking until the pan is dry.
Stop and add it straight to the filling.
Cover the pan tightly to trap the moisture.
quiz.question: The paste is still wet and would soak the filling. What would you do?

comes_after.why: The parsley is chopped small and even, and a cook has to be able to chop first.

cues.text: Bright lemon and green parsley, with a sharp edge of garlic.
The mix is fine and even and still bright green.

technique/make-a-gremolata.does: Chops parsley very fine with lemon zest and a little raw garlic, to be scattered over a rich, slow-cooked dish at the very end, where its sharp freshness cuts through the fat. Nothing is cooked.
how: Pick the parsley leaves from the stalks and dry them well.
Grate the zest of the lemon in fine strips, taking only the yellow.
Peel the garlic and chop it fine with the parsley, then chop in the zest, until everything is small and even.
Make it just before serving and scatter it over the dish at the table, and not into the pot.

intro.what: Gremolata finely chops parsley, lemon zest and raw garlic into a fresh finish.
intro.why: It teaches you to add contrast to a rich dish without cooking away the bright scent of the garnish.

mistakes.fix: Take only the yellow of the peel.
mistakes.mistake: Grating in the white pith, which tastes bitter.

mistakes.fix: Scatter it over the dish at the very end.
mistakes.mistake: Mixing it into the pot early, so that it loses its freshness and turns dull.

mistakes.fix: Dry the leaves first.
mistakes.mistake: Chopping wet parsley, which turns to a paste.

quiz.because: Fresh parsley, lemon and garlic finish the dish with a bright contrast.
choices: A long-cooked vegetable base.
A sharp, fresh contrast at the end.
A thick sauce cooked into the pot.
quiz.question: What does gremolata bring to a rich dish?

quiz.because: The yellow zest supplies the lemon scent without the bitter white pith.
choices: The white pith beneath the zest.
A thick shaving containing all the pith.
The yellow zest without the white pith.
quiz.question: Which part of the lemon peel should you grate?

quiz.because: Dry leaves and fine chopping preserve a bright, even finishing mixture.
choices: Fine, even pieces that are still bright green.
A dull green paste dissolved into the sauce.
Large wet parsley clumps with white pith.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches freshly made gremolata?

quiz.because: Early cooking dulls the fresh finish; add it at serving instead.
choices: Add it before the slow cooking begins.
Scatter it over the dish at the very end.
Cook it separately until the parsley darkens.
quiz.question: The gremolata loses freshness after cooking in the pot. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: The onion and garlic are softened in oil before the meat goes in.

cues.text: Warm cinnamon and allspice over sweet tomato, with no sharp smell of raw wine.
The sauce is thick, and a spoon drawn across the pan leaves a track that closes slowly.

technique/make-a-kima.does: Cooks minced meat with softened onion, tomato and a little red wine, scented with cinnamon, allspice and a bay leaf, until it is a thick, moist, mildly sweet sauce that sits under a white sauce in a baked dish or is spooned over pasta.
how: Soften the onion and garlic in olive oil first, and keep the pan wide so that the meat browns and does not stew.
Add the minced meat in small lots and break it up with a spoon. Let it take colour before more goes in.
Pour in the wine and let it bubble away almost completely.
Stir in the tomato paste, then the tomatoes, the cinnamon, the allspice and the bay leaf.
Simmer gently with the lid ajar, stirring now and then, until the meat is tender and the sauce is thick enough to hold a track.
Take out the bay leaf, season, and stir in the parsley. A kima for baking is cooked drier than one for pasta, so that it does not flood the dish.

intro.what: This kima simmers browned mince with tomato, wine and warm spices into a thick sauce.
intro.why: It teaches you to brown meat in stages and adjust the finished moisture for pasta or a baked dish.

mistakes.fix: Add them with the tomato, once the wine has gone.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the spices to a pan that is too hot, so that they scorch and taste bitter.

mistakes.fix: Cook it until a spoon leaves a track.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the sauce loose, so that it floods the dish it is baked in.

mistakes.fix: Add it in small lots and let each take colour.
mistakes.mistake: Tipping all the meat in at once, so that it steams grey.

quiz.because: A loose meat sauce can flood a baked dish, so its intended use guides the reduction.
choices: So the spice flavour disappears.
So it pours more freely between layers.
So it does not flood the baked dish.
quiz.question: Why make kima for a baked dish drier than kima for pasta?

quiz.because: Small lots in a wide pan help the meat brown instead of steaming grey.
choices: In small lots, letting each take colour.
As a packed pile added all at once.
After all the tomato liquid has been added.
quiz.question: How should you add the minced meat?

quiz.because: A slowly closing track shows a thick, moist sauce rather than a loose liquid.
choices: The track fills immediately with watery liquid.
A spoon track closes slowly.
Dry separate crumbs without any sauce.
quiz.question: What consistency shows the sauce has thickened?

quiz.because: Adding the spices with tomato avoids the excessively hot dry pan that scorches them.
choices: Fry them longer in the hottest part of the dry pan.
Add them before softening the onion.
Add them with tomato after the wine has bubbled away.
quiz.question: The spices scorch and taste bitter. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: A kima is spiced with cinnamon, allspice and a bay leaf, and is built on onion and tomato paste, where a ragu starts from a soffritto of onion, carrot and celery and is finished with milk. It is cooked drier, so that it can sit under a white sauce without flooding it.

comes_after.why: The cream is made with the sweet yolk foam, which must be whisked and cooled first.

cues.text: The cream is smooth and glossy, with no grains and no streaks.
It holds a soft peak on the spatula and does not run.

technique/make-a-mascarpone-cream.does: Loosens soft mascarpone with a cooled, sweet egg-yolk foam into a smooth, thick cream that holds its shape in a spoon. It is the cream of tiramisu and of other cold layered desserts.
how: Cool the egg-yolk foam completely. A warm foam melts the cheese into a loose soup.
Put the mascarpone into a wide bowl and stir it with a spatula only until it is smooth. Never beat it hard.
Stir in a spoonful of the foam to loosen the cheese, then fold in the rest in small lots.
Stop as soon as the cream is smooth and even, with no streaks. Use it at once or keep it cold.

intro.what: This dessert cream gently folds cooled sweet yolk foam into mascarpone.
intro.why: It teaches you to preserve a thick, smooth texture by cooling the foam and avoiding hard beating.

mistakes.fix: Stir it gently with a spatula, only until smooth.
mistakes.mistake: Beating the mascarpone hard, so that it turns grainy and then oily.

mistakes.fix: Let the foam cool first.
mistakes.mistake: Mixing in a foam that is still warm, which thins the cheese.

quiz.because: The cream must hold its shape for a layered dessert rather than run or split.
choices: Thick and smooth enough to hold a soft peak.
Thin enough to run from the spatula.
Grainy with visible pools of oil.
quiz.question: What texture should the mascarpone cream have?

quiz.because: Warm foam thins the mascarpone into a loose mixture.
choices: Fold it in while still warm.
Cool it completely.
Warm it again before every addition.
quiz.question: How should the yolk foam be prepared before mixing?

quiz.because: Stop when the cream is smooth and even rather than continuing to beat it.
choices: Visible foam streaks among cheese lumps.
An oily, grainy mixture.
Smooth, glossy cream without streaks or grains.
quiz.question: Which appearance indicates mixing can stop?

quiz.because: Hard beating can spoil the texture; gentle stirring and folding avoid overworking the cheese.
choices: Stir gently only until smooth, then fold in the foam.
Beat faster to remove the grains.
Keep beating after all streaks disappear.
quiz.question: Hard beating makes the mascarpone grainy and oily. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: Nothing is whipped to hold air. A dense, soft cheese is loosened with a foam and combined with a spatula until smooth, and beating it hard would spoil it.

comes_after.why: A pesto starts as a pounded paste, and a cook has to be able to grind food in a mortar without bruising it.

cues.text: The paste is bright green and thick, with the oil bound into it and not floating on top.
It smells of fresh basil, with no trace of bitterness.

technique/make-a-pesto.does: Crushes fresh basil leaves with a little coarse salt and garlic in a mortar, then pine nuts, then grated hard cheese, and works in olive oil last, into a thick, green, raw sauce. It is the sauce of Genoa and the coast of Liguria, and it is never cooked.
how: Pick the basil leaves and dry them. Wet leaves make a dull, watery sauce.
Pound the garlic with coarse salt in a stone mortar until it is a paste.
Add the pine nuts and pound them in, then the basil a handful at a time, grinding each lot against the wall in circles until it is a rough green paste.
Work in the grated cheese, then pour in the olive oil in a thin stream, stirring, until the sauce is thick and glossy.
Keep it raw. Stir it into hot pasta off the heat, loosened with a spoonful of the cooking water.

intro.what: This Ligurian-style pesto crushes basil, garlic, pine nuts and cheese, then incorporates olive oil.
intro.why: It teaches you to preserve a fresh herb sauce and bind the oil without heating the basil.

mistakes.fix: Pound it in a mortar, or pulse it briefly with chilled things.
mistakes.mistake: Chopping the basil in a fast blade, which warms it and turns it dark and bitter.

mistakes.fix: Stir it into the pasta off the heat.
mistakes.mistake: Heating the pesto in the pan, which dulls the basil and splits the oil.

mistakes.fix: Add it in a thin stream, stirring.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in all the oil at once, so that the sauce does not bind.

quiz.because: Heating pesto in the pan dulls the basil and can separate the oil.
choices: To cook the basil until its colour darkens.
To preserve the basil and avoid splitting the oil.
To reduce it into a dry coating.
quiz.question: Why mix this pesto into pasta off the heat?

quiz.because: Gradual oil additions help it bind into the thick paste rather than float separately.
choices: All at once before crushing the leaves.
After boiling the paste until dry.
In a thin stream while stirring.
quiz.question: How do you incorporate olive oil into the paste?

quiz.because: The intended sauce keeps a bright colour and holds its oil rather than separating.
choices: Bright green and thick, with oil held in the paste.
Dark leaves beneath a separate pool of oil.
A pale watery paste with wet leaf clumps.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches the intended pesto?

quiz.because: Gentle grinding or brief cool processing avoids warming and dulling the basil.
choices: Run the blade longer until the paste is very warm.
Use a mortar or brief pulses with chilled ingredients.
Heat the leaves before blending.
quiz.question: The basil warms and darkens during fast blade processing. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The ingredients go in a fixed order, from the hardest to the softest, and the oil and cheese are worked in at the end. The sauce is never heated, and it is a finished sauce and not just a paste.

comes_after.why: A ragu is built on a soffritto that has been cooked until it is soft and golden.

cues.text: The fat gathers in a glossy red ring at the edge, and the sauce is thick enough to hold the trail of a spoon.
Rich and sweet, with the raw smell of tomato gone.

technique/make-a-ragu.does: Cooks minced meat very slowly with a soffritto, wine and tomato until it turns into a thick, rich sauce that clings to pasta or fills a rice ball. Every region has its own ragu, and this card holds the common method.
how: Make a soffritto in a wide, heavy pot and cook it until it is soft and golden.
Add the minced meat in small lots and break it up with a spoon. Let it brown before moving on, and stir so that it cooks in fine crumbs.
Pour in the wine and let it bubble away almost completely.
Add the tomato and a little stock or milk, then turn the heat low and leave it to simmer with the lid ajar, stirring now and then, until the meat is very tender and the fat shows at the edge.
Season at the end.

intro.what: This minced-meat ragù method slowly cooks browned meat with soffritto, wine and tomato.
intro.why: It teaches you to build a fine-textured sauce that clings, rather than a thin sauce around meat lumps.

mistakes.fix: Add the meat in small lots and let each brown.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, so that the meat steams grey and does not brown.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat low and give it time to cook down.
mistakes.mistake: Rushing it, so that the sauce is thin and tastes raw.

mistakes.fix: Break it up as it browns.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the meat in lumps, which makes a coarse sauce that does not cling.

quiz.because: Large meat lumps make a coarse sauce that does not cling well.
choices: To keep large lumps separate from the sauce.
To prevent any surface browning.
To make fine crumbs in a sauce that clings.
quiz.question: Why break the minced meat up as it browns?

quiz.because: Small lots avoid crowding that steams the meat instead of browning it.
choices: In small lots that can brown before more is added.
All at once in a packed mound.
Only after filling the pot with liquid.
quiz.question: How should the meat enter the soffritto pan?

quiz.because: A held spoon trail and fat showing at the edge accompany the intended thick sauce.
choices: Watery liquid immediately filling every trail.
A thick spoon trail and glossy fat at the edge.
Firm raw-looking tomato pieces in thin liquid.
quiz.question: What shows the sauce has cooked down?

quiz.because: Slow gentle cooking develops this sauce beyond a thin, raw-tasting mixture.
choices: Raise the heat sharply and stop stirring.
Add more liquid and serve immediately.
Continue gently over low heat as it cooks down.
quiz.question: The sauce is thin and still tastes raw from rushing. What would you do?

variant_of.differs: The meat is minced and browned loose in crumbs and not left in pieces, and the pot is left with the lid ajar so that the sauce thickens and does not stay a thin liquid.

cues.text: The smell changes from raw flour to biscuit, then to toasted nuts as it darkens.
A smooth paste that froths like wet sand and pulls away from the pan.

technique/make-a-roux.does: Cooks flour in melted butter to a paste that thickens a liquid without lumps or a raw taste.
how: Melt the butter over medium-low heat until it foams.
Tip in an equal weight of flour, all at once, and stir until smooth.
Keep stirring as the paste bubbles, until the raw smell of flour is gone.
Go on to the colour the sauce needs: pale for a white sauce, sandy for a blond one, nut-brown for a brown one.
Add the liquid cold to a hot roux, or hot to a cold one, a little at a time, whisking each addition smooth.

intro.what: A roux is flour cooked in butter to make a paste for thickening liquid.
intro.why: It teaches you to cook the flour, choose the colour and add liquid gradually for a smooth sauce.

mistakes.fix: Give the roux time, until it smells of biscuit.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the liquid before the flour has cooked, which leaves a pasty taste that no simmering removes.

mistakes.fix: Add it in stages and whisk each one smooth. A lumpy sauce can be rescued through a sieve.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in all the liquid at once, which makes lumps.

quiz.because: The cooked flour paste thickens the liquid added to it.
choices: Thicken a liquid.
Separate fat from liquid.
Form a crisp coating on top of a finished sauce.
quiz.question: What job does the roux do in this method?

quiz.because: Adding liquid in stages and whisking each addition smooth helps prevent lumps.
choices: All at once without stirring.
In stages, whisking each addition smooth.
Pour it in quickly and whisk only after all of it is added.
quiz.question: How do you add liquid to the roux in this method?

quiz.because: As the roux cooks, its smell changes from raw flour towards biscuit, then toasted nuts as it darkens.
choices: It smells of browned butter before any flour smell changes.
It stays raw and dusty throughout.
From raw flour towards biscuit and toasted nuts.
quiz.question: How does the smell change as the roux cooks and darkens?

quiz.because: Cook and stir the flour paste before adding liquid. The change from raw flour towards a biscuit smell gives you a cue.
choices: Cooking and stirring the roux until its smell changes towards biscuit.
Adding the liquid all at once before stirring.
Leaving the raw flour untouched in the melted butter.
quiz.question: You added liquid while the paste still smelled of raw flour. What step did you skip?

en: cook the yolks to a ribbon

cues.text: Pale, thick and foamy. The whisk draws lines that hold for a moment, and the mixture falls from it in a ribbon.
The bowl is warm to the hand, never hot.

technique/make-a-sabayon.does: Whisks egg yolks with a little liquid over gentle heat until they are thick, pale and foamy, ready to take butter.
how: Put the yolks and a spoonful of water for each in a round-bottomed bowl.
Set it over a pan of barely simmering water, or over the lowest heat.
Whisk without stopping, and lift the bowl off the heat whenever it feels hot to the hand.
Stop when the whisk leaves a trail that shows the bottom of the bowl.

intro.what: This sabayon method whisks egg yolks with liquid over gentle heat into a pale foam before butter is added.
intro.why: It teaches you to balance whisking and gentle heat while watching the mixture thicken.

mistakes.fix: Lift the bowl off the heat and keep whisking. If grains have formed, start again.
mistakes.mistake: Too much heat, which scrambles the yolks at the edge of the bowl.

mistakes.fix: Whisk until the trail holds.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping early, so that the sauce stays thin however much butter goes in.

quiz.because: For this sauce method, yolks and liquid are whisked into a thick, pale foam before butter is added.
choices: A thin liquid with separated fat.
A thick, pale, foamy yolk mixture.
Firm scrambled pieces of yolk.
quiz.question: What is this sabayon method preparing before butter is added?

quiz.because: Too much heat can scramble the yolks. Keep whisking and lift the bowl away whenever it feels hot.
choices: Leave it over a rolling boil without stirring.
Stop whisking whenever it begins to thicken.
Whisk continuously and lift it away when it feels hot.
quiz.question: How do you control the bowl and whisking as the sabayon heats?

quiz.because: A trail that holds briefly shows the yolk mixture has thickened, rather than staying thin.
choices: The whisk leaves a trail that holds briefly.
The mixture stays thin with no visible trail.
Grains of set yolk appear around the edge.
quiz.question: Which cue shows the texture this method aims for?

quiz.because: Adding butter too early can leave this sauce thin. Keep whisking gently until the trail holds.
choices: Add the butter now so it supplies the missing thickness.
Continue whisking gently until the trail holds.
Raise the heat sharply so the mixture thickens faster.
quiz.question: The mixture stays thin because you stopped whisking early. What would you do?

variant_of.differs: The whisking is done over gentle heat, which cooks the yolks as it fills them with air.

comes_after.why: A sauce is brought to its body at a simmer.

cues.text: It coats the back of a spoon, and a finger drawn through the coat leaves a clear line.
Round and clean, with neither a raw floury taste nor a raw sharpness of spice.

technique/make-a-sauce.does: Builds a sauce from a flavouring base cooked in fat, a liquid and a short simmer, until it coats a spoon. It is seasoned at the end, and strained or blended if it should be smooth.
how: Cook the flavouring base in the fat first: a roux, tomato, or a spice such as paprika stirred into oil off the heat.
Add the liquid a little at a time, whisking, until the sauce is smooth.
Simmer gently, stirring now and then, until the sauce coats the back of a spoon.
Blend or strain it if it should be smooth.
Taste and season last, because a sauce grows saltier as it thickens.

intro.what: This sauce method combines a flavouring base cooked in fat with gradually added liquid.
intro.why: It teaches you to build smoothness and spoon-coating body before making the final seasoning adjustment.

mistakes.fix: Season at the end.
mistakes.mistake: Salting early and then boiling the sauce down, so that it ends up too salty.

mistakes.fix: Add it a little at a time and whisk.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring all the liquid in at once, which makes lumps.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat first.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring a spice into hot oil, where it burns and turns the sauce bitter.

quiz.because: Concentration can make early seasoning too salty, so judge the sauce after thickening.
choices: Reduction can make the salt already present taste stronger.
Early salt stops the sauce thickening as liquid leaves.
Early salt prevents lumps when the liquid meets the base.
quiz.question: Why judge final seasoning after this sauce has simmered down?

quiz.because: Gradual additions and whisking help prevent lumps as the sauce comes together.
choices: Pour it all in before starting to mix.
Add it gradually while whisking.
Add the liquid only after the base has finished simmering.
quiz.question: How do you join the liquid to the cooked base?

quiz.because: A spoon coating with a clear line shows a smooth thickened sauce.
choices: A bare spoon without a coating.
Large dry lumps clinging to the spoon.
A coating that holds a clear line drawn through it.
quiz.question: What spoon cue indicates the intended body?

quiz.because: Moving the pan off the heat avoids burning the delicate spice into bitterness.
choices: Take the pan off the heat before stirring it in.
Leave the oil on high heat for longer.
Add the paprika before heating the empty pan.
quiz.question: Paprika scorched when added to hot oil. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: A soffritto is only as good as its cut, and the pieces must be small and even to melt.

cues.text: Sweet and rounded, with the raw sharpness of the onion gone.
The pieces have melted into a soft golden mass, and the oil is lightly tinted.

technique/make-a-soffritto.does: Cooks very finely chopped onion, carrot and celery slowly in olive oil, until they melt together into a soft, sweet, golden base on which the rest of the dish is built.
how: Chop the onion, carrot and celery very fine and as even as you can, so that they melt into the dish and do not show as pieces.
Warm olive oil in a wide, heavy pan over low heat, then add the vegetables with a little salt.
Stir now and then and keep the heat gentle. The vegetables first give up their water, then slowly turn soft and pale gold.
Take it as far as the dish needs: pale and sweet for a delicate soup, deeper gold for a sauce or a ragu. Stop before it turns dark or bitter.

intro.what: This soffritto slowly softens finely chopped onion, carrot and celery in olive oil.
intro.why: It teaches you to build a sweet base whose vegetables blend into the dish rather than remain hard pieces.

mistakes.fix: Lower the heat and add a spoonful of water to hold back the colour.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking it over high heat, so that it browns before it softens and tastes bitter.

mistakes.fix: Chop them small and even.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting the vegetables in different sizes, so that some burn while others stay hard.

mistakes.fix: Give it the time it needs.
mistakes.mistake: Going on to the next ingredient too soon, before the vegetables have melted, so that the base tastes raw.

quiz.because: Even small pieces develop together instead of leaving a mixture of burnt and hard vegetables.
choices: So they brown before their centres soften.
So they soften together and blend into the dish.
So they remain distinct pieces in the finished sauce.
quiz.question: Why chop the soffritto vegetables finely and evenly?

quiz.because: Gentle heat allows softening and sweetness before the base becomes dark or bitter.
choices: Use high heat to brown before softening.
Keep the vegetables still over strong heat.
Keep it gentle and stir now and then.
quiz.question: How should you control the heat?

quiz.because: The vegetables should soften together into a golden base rather than keep hard centres.
choices: A soft golden mass with lightly tinted oil.
Hard bright pieces in clear oil.
Dark edges around firm centres.
quiz.question: What appearance matches a developed soffritto?

quiz.because: Lower heat and a little water slow browning while the vegetables soften.
choices: Increase the heat to soften the centres faster.
Lower the heat and add a little water to hold back colour.
Move on immediately to the next ingredient.
quiz.question: The vegetables brown before they soften. What would you do?

variant_of.differs: It uses olive oil and not butter, the vegetables are chopped much finer, and it is cooked longer, until it turns gold, where a sweat stops before any colour. A French mirepoix is cut larger and is often strained out of the dish. A soffritto stays in.

comes_after.why: Small, even pieces melt into the paste together.

cues.text: The oil seeps out at the edges of the paste, which has darkened from bright red to deep brick.
Sweet and rich, like jam. The sharp smell of raw tomato and raw garlic has gone.
Sweet and deep, with no raw sourness.

technique/make-a-sofrito.does: Cooks onion, garlic and ripe tomato slowly in a generous amount of olive oil until their water has gone and what is left is a dark, sweet, jammy paste. It is the base of rice dishes, stews and sauces.
how: Chop the onion and the garlic fine, if they are used. Grate or chop the tomato and keep its juice.
Warm a generous amount of olive oil in a wide pan over a low to medium heat.
Cook the onion with a little salt, stirring now and then, until it is soft and pale gold. Add the garlic for the last moments.
Add the tomato and keep cooking, stirring now and then, as it gives up its water and the mixture thickens.
Go on until the oil seeps out at the edges and the paste is dark, sweet and jammy. Do not hurry it with a high heat.
If paprika is wanted, take the pan off the heat and stir it in, because it turns bitter in hot oil.

intro.idea: From watery tomato to jammy paste
intro.what: This tomato-based sofrito slowly cooks onion, garlic and tomato in olive oil to a jammy paste.
intro.why: It teaches you to wait for moisture to leave and sweetness to develop without scorching the base.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat low, and add a splash of water if it starts to catch.
mistakes.mistake: Turning up the heat to hurry it, so that the garlic and the paste scorch and turn bitter.

mistakes.fix: Keep going until the oil seeps out at the edges.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping while the tomato is still wet and sharp, which leaves a thin, sour base.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat first.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring the paprika into hot oil, where it burns within moments.

quiz.because: Slow cooking removes water and develops the sweet concentrated base.
choices: Firm tomato pieces suspended in water.
Raw garlic remaining sharply scented.
A dark, sweet, jammy paste rather than wet sharp tomato.
quiz.question: What distinguishes the developed sofrito from its starting mixture?

quiz.because: Rushing over high heat scorches the garlic and paste instead of developing it gently.
choices: Keep it low to moderate rather than hurrying it.
Use the strongest heat until the garlic darkens.
Cover tightly so all tomato water stays in.
quiz.question: How should you handle the heat as tomato cooks down?

quiz.because: Oil at the edges and a dark jammy texture show the tomato has cooked down.
choices: Bright wet tomato with a sharp raw smell.
