Add more grated cheese without loosening it.
quiz.question: The finished risotto is too stiff. What would you change?

variant_of.differs: French mounting whisks butter into a reduced liquid, to thicken a sauce. Here butter and grated cheese are beaten into rice, and it is the starch of the rice, not a reduced liquid, that holds the fat in a creamy sauce.

cues.text: Meat from a wine marinade is stained on the outside. The colour does not reach far inside.
The meat smells of the wine and the herbs.

technique/marinate.does: Steeps food in a seasoned liquid before it is cooked, so that its surface takes on the flavour.
how: Mix the wine or the acid with the aromatics and a little oil.
Turn the food in it until it is coated, in a bowl that acid does not attack.
Cover it and keep it in the fridge, turning it once or twice.
Lift the food out and dry it well before browning it. Keep the marinade for the pot.

intro.what: Marinating coats food in a seasoned liquid before cooking so the surface takes on flavour.
intro.why: It teaches you to separate surface flavouring from the later dry browning step.

mistakes.fix: Drain it and pat it dry first.
mistakes.mistake: Browning meat straight from the marinade, wet, so that it steams and will not colour.

mistakes.fix: It flavours the surface. Only long, gentle cooking makes a tough cut tender.
mistakes.mistake: Expecting a marinade to make a tough cut tender.

quiz.because: The visible staining and scent concentrate at the surface rather than reaching far inside.
choices: Every part equally far into a thick piece.
Only the liquid, leaving the food unchanged.
The surface of the food.
quiz.question: What does this marinade primarily flavour?

quiz.because: Turning gives the surfaces contact with the seasoned liquid before the covered rest.
choices: Turn the food until coated, then cover and refrigerate.
Leave part of the food dry above the liquid throughout.
Dry the food before its first contact with the marinade.
quiz.question: How do you distribute the seasoned liquid?

quiz.because: Wine can stain the outside, illustrating the surface-focused effect of marinating.
choices: Identical deep colour through the whole piece.
Surface staining that does not reach far inside.
A browned crust already formed by the marinade.
quiz.question: What might you see on meat lifted from a wine marinade?

quiz.because: Removing surface moisture lets the browning step proceed instead of steaming the wet meat.
choices: Pour extra marinade into the browning pan.
Cover the pan to retain the surface moisture.
Drain and pat it dry before browning.
quiz.question: Wet marinated meat steams instead of browning. What would you change next time?

cues.text: Bright lemon and dried oregano, with garlic underneath.
Every piece is coated in a glossy film of oil and none sits in a pool.

technique/marinate-in-oil-and-lemon.does: Turns small pieces of meat in olive oil, lemon juice, oregano and garlic for a short while before they are grilled, so that the surface takes up the flavour and the oil keeps the meat from drying on the fire.
how: Cut the meat into even pieces so that they take the marinade and cook at the same pace.
Mix the oil, the lemon juice, the oregano, the crushed garlic and a little salt in a bowl.
Turn the meat in it until every piece shines, then cover the bowl and keep it in the cold.
Keep the time short. Lemon juice dries meat the longer it sits, and the surface turns chalky.
Lift the meat out and let the extra drip off before it goes on the skewers or the grill. Do not spoon used marinade over food that has been cooked.

intro.what: This marinade coats small meat pieces with olive oil, lemon, oregano and garlic before grilling.
intro.why: It teaches you to flavour the surface without a prolonged acidic soak or excess liquid dripping onto the fire.

mistakes.fix: Keep the time short.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the meat in lemon juice for a long time, so that it turns dry and chalky.

mistakes.fix: Let the extra marinade drip away first.
mistakes.mistake: Putting the meat on the fire dripping wet, so that it flares and scorches.

mistakes.fix: Use a little salt and season again at the end.
mistakes.mistake: Salting heavily in the marinade, which draws out juice.

quiz.because: The coating gives the surface its lemon, oregano and garlic flavour before grilling.
choices: Seasoning the interior as strongly as the surface.
Making every tough cut tender regardless of cooking.
Seasoning the surface with lemon, herbs and garlic.
quiz.question: What is the main flavouring role of this marinade?

quiz.because: Excess dripping marinade can flare and scorch, so drain the pieces before grilling.
choices: Lift them out and let excess marinade drip off.
Pour all the marinade over the fire with the pieces.
Leave them dripping in a deep coating.
quiz.question: What should happen before the coated pieces go onto the grill?

quiz.because: Turning distributes a thin glossy coat instead of leaving uneven dry and pooled patches.
choices: Some pieces are dry while others sit in a pool.
Every piece shines with a glossy film.
A chalky surface replaces the glossy coating.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches evenly coated pieces?

quiz.because: This lemon marinade is intended as a short surface-flavouring step, not a prolonged soak.
choices: Leave it longer to reverse the chalkiness.
Add more lemon and extend the wait.
Keep the marinating period short.
quiz.question: A prolonged lemon soak leaves the surface chalky and dry. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The liquid is olive oil and lemon juice with oregano and garlic, with no wine, and the time is short, because lemon juice dries meat. The oil carries the flavour and protects the meat on the fire, where a wine marinade is made for a long braise.

cues.text: The pieces are stained an even brown and glisten, with only a little liquid left in the bowl.
The bowl smells strongly of ginger and garlic.

technique/marinate-in-soy-sauce.does: Steeps pieces of poultry for a short while in soy sauce and sake with ginger and garlic, so that the flavour sinks in and the surface is seasoned. The salty liquid is let drip off before frying and is not kept for the pot.
how: Cut the meat into even, bite-sized pieces, so that each takes up the same amount of flavour.
In a bowl, mix the soy sauce and the sake with finely grated ginger and garlic.
Add the meat and work the liquid in with your hands until every piece is wet.
Leave it for a short while, turning the pieces once. Soy is salty, and a long steep turns the meat firm and dry.
Lift the pieces out and let the extra liquid drip off before they are coated.

intro.what: This method briefly coats poultry pieces in soy sauce, sake, ginger and garlic before frying.
intro.why: It teaches you to distribute a salty marinade evenly and drain it before applying a dry coating.

mistakes.fix: Steep it for a short while only.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the meat in the soy for too long, so that it turns salty and firm.

mistakes.fix: Let the extra liquid drip off first.
mistakes.mistake: Coating the pieces while they are still dripping, which turns a dry coat to paste.

quiz.because: Soy supplies strong saltiness, and a prolonged steep can make the pieces firm and overly salty.
choices: A long steep can make the pieces salty and firm.
More time removes the salt from the surface.
A longer steep keeps the saltiness from increasing.
quiz.question: Why keep this soy marinade brief?

quiz.because: Extra liquid turns a dry coating into paste, so drain the pieces first.
choices: Coat the pieces while they are dripping.
Let excess marinade drip off.
Pour the remaining marinade into the dry coating.
quiz.question: What do you do before applying the coating?

quiz.because: Even staining and gloss show the pieces have been turned through the marinade.
choices: Dry pale patches among heavily stained pieces.
A dry coating already hiding all the marinade.
Even brown staining and a glistening surface.
quiz.question: What appearance suggests the marinade has coated evenly?

quiz.because: Draining removes the extra liquid that changes the intended dry coat into paste.
choices: Drain the excess marinade before coating.
Add more marinade while coating.
Keep the pieces submerged until the flour is added.
quiz.question: The dry coating becomes a paste on wet pieces. What would you change for the next batch?

variant_of.differs: The liquid is salty soy sauce and sake with ginger, not wine or acid, and the steeping is brief, since soy firms the meat if it sits long. The meat is let drip and not dried, because a little soy stays on for the coat to cling to.

comes_after.why: The marinade is built on a paste of garlic, ginger, chilli and ground spices, so the paste has to be made first.

cues.text: The marinade sits on the food as an even, thick coat that does not slide off.
Thick pieces of meat feel a little softer under the finger after the wait.

technique/marinate-in-yogurt.does: Steeps meat or firm cheese in yogurt that has been mixed with a spice paste and salt, so that the mild acid of the yogurt softens the surface and the spices are carried right into it. The coat browns and chars in strong heat.
how: Make the spice paste first, with garlic, ginger, fresh chilli, ground spices, salt and a little lemon juice.
Whisk the paste into thick yogurt. Hang the yogurt in a cloth first if it is thin, so that the marinade clings and does not run off.
Cut a few slashes into thick pieces of meat so that the marinade can get in.
Turn the food in the marinade until every surface is coated, cover the bowl and keep it in the fridge. Tough cuts want a long wait. Tender pieces and paneer want a short one.
Lift the food out and let the extra drip away before it meets the heat. Thick yogurt left on it will steam and not char.

intro.what: This yogurt marinade mixes spice paste into thick yogurt to coat meat or firm cheese.
intro.why: It teaches you to control coating thickness and draining so the food browns rather than steaming under excess yogurt.

mistakes.fix: Give them a short wait only, and give the long wait to tough cuts.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving paneer or tender pieces in the yogurt for too long, so that they turn mushy and sour.

mistakes.fix: Hang the yogurt in a cloth to drain, or strain it, before the paste goes in.
mistakes.mistake: Using thin, watery yogurt, so that the marinade runs off and the food steams in the pan.

mistakes.fix: Use a glass, china or steel bowl that does not take on a metallic taste.
mistakes.mistake: Using a metal bowl that reacts with the acid.

quiz.because: Drained thick yogurt holds the spice paste on the food instead of releasing a watery coating.
choices: So the food sits in a loose pool for cooking.
So the spice coating clings instead of running off.
So no surface coating remains.
quiz.question: Why use thick rather than watery yogurt?

quiz.because: Straining removes excess liquid before the marinade is mixed.
choices: Add it with all its watery liquid.
Heat the finished marinade until it reduces.
Drain it in a cloth before adding the spice paste.
quiz.question: How should you prepare yogurt that is too thin?

quiz.because: An even clinging coat shows the yogurt and paste have combined at the intended thickness.
choices: An even coat that stays on the surface.
A watery pool beneath mostly bare pieces.
Dry spice streaks above separate yogurt liquid.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches the intended marinade on the food?

quiz.because: Excess yogurt left on the food steams; draining it back leaves a coating more suited to browning.
choices: Spoon more yogurt over it as it cooks.
Let excess marinade drip away before heating.
Pack the coated pieces closely together.
quiz.question: A heavy yogurt coating makes the food steam instead of char. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The liquid is thick yogurt and not wine or vinegar, and it carries a spice paste into the food. Its lactic acid is gentle, so it tenderises without turning the surface chalky, and the coat is meant to stay on and char in hot, dry heat.

comes_after.why: The potatoes are boiled first.

cues.text: A smooth, glossy purée that falls slowly from the spoon and holds a soft peak.
No lumps under the spoon, and nothing gluey or stretchy.

technique/mash.does: Crushes boiled potatoes while they are hot and dry, then beats in butter and hot milk to make a smooth purée.
how: Boil floury potatoes in their skins or in large pieces, starting in cold salted water.
Drain them and let them steam dry for a moment.
Push them through a ricer or a food mill while they are still hot.
Beat in cold butter first, then hot milk little by little, until the purée is smooth and soft.

intro.what: This potato mash crushes hot, steam-dried potatoes, then incorporates butter and hot milk.
intro.why: It teaches you to choose gentle tools and control moisture for a soft purée without gluey stretch.

mistakes.fix: Use a ricer, a food mill or a masher, and stop when it is smooth.
mistakes.mistake: Using a blender or a food processor, which turns potato to glue.

mistakes.fix: Mash them hot, straight after they have steamed dry.
mistakes.mistake: Mashing potatoes that are cold or waterlogged.

quiz.because: The intended purée is smooth and glossy, with neither lumps nor gluey elasticity.
choices: Elastic and sticky like a stretched paste.
Smooth and soft without gluey stretch.
Wet liquid around firm potato lumps.
quiz.question: What texture should this potato mash have?

quiz.because: Hot, steam-dried potatoes mash more readily than cold or waterlogged ones.
choices: Once cold and still soaked in cooking water.
Before draining any water from the pot.
While hot, after draining and briefly steaming dry.
quiz.question: When should you rice or mill the potatoes?

quiz.because: A smooth soft peak shows the intended body without the gluey texture of overprocessing.
choices: A soft peak without lumps or stretchiness.
Long sticky strings when the spoon lifts.
Firm lumps surrounded by loose milk.
quiz.question: Which spoon cue matches the intended texture?

quiz.because: The blender can turn potatoes gluey; gentler mashing tools preserve the intended texture.
choices: Run the blender longer to break the gluey texture.
Use a ricer, mill or masher and stop when smooth.
Add cold potatoes to the processor and beat harder.
quiz.question: Blade processing has made the potatoes gluey. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: The flesh is soft and smoky from the flame before it is mashed.

cues.text: Rough strands and small soft lumps, not a smooth paste.
No firm bits left under the fork.

technique/mash-with-a-fork.does: Breaks soft, cooked flesh into a rough, stringy mash with a fork, so that some texture is left and the smoky taste of the food is not lost to a machine.
how: Make sure the flesh is completely soft, and let any bitter juice drain off.
Put the flesh in a bowl and press and drag a fork through it until it falls into strands and small soft lumps.
Stir in the dressing a little at a time as you go, so that the flesh takes up the seasoning.
Stop while some texture is left.

intro.what: Fork mashing breaks soft cooked flesh into rough strands and small lumps.
intro.why: It teaches you to preserve a deliberate texture instead of processing every mash into a smooth purée.

mistakes.fix: Use a fork, and stop while strands are still showing.
mistakes.mistake: Blending it to a smooth paste, so that the texture is lost.

mistakes.fix: Keep it on the heat until it has collapsed completely.
mistakes.mistake: Mashing flesh that is not soft all the way, which leaves hard bits.

quiz.because: The rough fork-made texture is intentional rather than a failure to blend smoothly.
choices: To keep strands and small soft lumps.
To make the smoothest possible liquid purée.
To leave firm uncooked chunks for crunch.
quiz.question: Why use a fork for this mash?

quiz.because: Pressing and dragging breaks soft flesh into strands without turning it into a smooth paste.
choices: Run a blender until completely uniform.
Press and drag the fork through it.
Chop firm flesh finely before it softens.
quiz.question: How do you work the soft flesh?

quiz.because: Stop with some soft texture still showing rather than blending it away.
choices: A completely smooth paste without strands.
Large firm pieces that resist the fork.
Rough strands and small soft lumps.
quiz.question: What should remain visible?

quiz.because: The flesh must be soft before fork mashing; extra pressing alone leaves hard bits.
choices: Soften the flesh further with heat before mashing.
Blend the firm pieces hard into the rest.
Add more dressing without softening them.
quiz.question: Firm bits remain under the fork. What would you change?

variant_of.differs: The flesh is broken into a rough, stringy mass by hand and not beaten smooth, and no butter or milk goes in.

cues.text: Smooth and glossy, with no lumps and no grainy streaks.
Barely warm to the touch, never hot.

technique/melt.does: Turns chocolate or a solid fat liquid over gentle heat, without letting it colour, scorch or seize.
how: Chop chocolate into small, even pieces, and cut butter into cubes.
Set a bowl over a pan of barely simmering water, with the bottom of the bowl clear of the water.
Stir now and then, and take the bowl off while a few small lumps are left. They melt as you stir.
Butter on its own can be melted in a small pan over low heat.

intro.what: Melting gently turns chocolate or solid fat into a smooth liquid without browning it.
intro.why: It teaches you to use gentle heat and residual warmth rather than overheating the last solid pieces.

mistakes.fix: Keep the bowl and the spoon dry, and the water at a bare simmer.
mistakes.mistake: Letting steam or a drop of water into chocolate, which makes it seize into a stiff, grainy paste.

mistakes.fix: Melt it over water, and off the heat for the last lumps.
mistakes.mistake: Heating chocolate straight on the flame or too fast, so that it scorches and turns thick and bitter.

quiz.because: Melting aims for a smooth liquid while keeping browning and scorching out of the process.
choices: The solids develop a deep nut-brown colour.
The surface chars before the centre softens.
The solid becomes liquid without colouring or scorching.
quiz.question: What distinguishes gentle melting from browning?

quiz.because: Residual warmth melts the last small lumps without unnecessary additional heat.
choices: While small lumps remain, then stir them in.
Only after heating the smooth liquid strongly.
After the chocolate becomes thick and smoky.
quiz.question: When should you take melting chocolate off the warm water?

quiz.because: A smooth glossy liquid shows melting without seizing or scorching.
choices: A stiff grainy paste.
Smooth and glossy without grainy streaks.
Dark scorched patches in a thick mass.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches melted chocolate?

quiz.because: Water entering chocolate can cause seizing; dry tools and gentle indirect heat avoid that mistake.
choices: Let more steam condense into the bowl.
Use a stronger flame directly under the chocolate.
Keep bowl and spoon dry and the water at a bare simmer.
quiz.question: A little water has made the chocolate seize. What would you change next time?

cues.text: A fine, moist pile with no piece larger than a grain.
Garlic smells sharp and strong the moment it is cut this fine.

technique/mince.does: Cuts food so fine that it melts into a dish and leaves no piece to bite on.
how: Slice the food thinly, then cut across the slices.
Rock the knife over the pile, scraping it together now and then, until no piece stands out.
For garlic, crush the clove under the flat of the blade first, so that the skin slips off and the flesh breaks open.

intro.what: Mincing cuts food very finely so distinct pieces do not stand out in the dish.
intro.why: It teaches you to recognise an even fine cut and prepare strong aromatics close to when they are needed.

mistakes.fix: Mince it last, just before it goes into the pan.
mistakes.mistake: Mincing garlic long before it is needed, so that it turns harsh.

quiz.because: Very fine cutting lets the food blend in rather than remain as noticeable chunks.
choices: So it blends into the dish without large pieces to bite on.
So a few bites contain most of the aromatic.
So every piece stays large and distinct.
quiz.question: Why mince an aromatic rather than leave large pieces?

quiz.because: Gathering the pile lets repeated rocking cuts reach the remaining larger pieces.
choices: Spread the pieces widely and stop gathering them.
Rock the knife and scrape the pile together as needed.
Press once with the blade and leave the pieces coarse.
quiz.question: How do you keep the pile together as you mince?

quiz.because: An even fine pile shows the larger pieces have been cut down consistently.
choices: Long strips mixed with large chunks.
A few whole cloves beside finely cut pieces.
Fine and even with no piece standing out.
quiz.question: What should the finished pile look like?

quiz.because: Preparing minced garlic close to use avoids the harshness described after a long wait.
choices: Mince it just before it goes into the pan.
Mince it earlier and leave it exposed longer.
Crush it into finer pieces far in advance.
quiz.question: Garlic tastes harsh after being minced long ahead. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: It goes on much longer, until the pieces are almost a paste and vanish into the dish.

comes_after.why: Butter can only be mounted into a liquid that has been boiled down first.

cues.text: The sauce turns opaque, glossy and creamy, with no beads of clear fat at the edge.
It coats a spoon lightly, like thin cream.

technique/mount-with-butter.does: Whisks cold butter into a hot liquid off the boil, so that it melts into a smooth, glossy, lightly thickened sauce and not into a layer of fat.
how: Boil the liquid down first, until only a few syrupy, strong spoonfuls are left in the pan.
Take the pan off the heat, or turn the heat to its lowest.
Add cold butter in small cubes, a few at a time, and whisk or swirl the pan until each lot has vanished before the next goes in.
Stop when the sauce is glossy and coats a spoon. Season it and serve it at once: it can be neither boiled nor kept.

intro.what: Mounting with butter brings cold butter into a reduced hot liquid away from the boil.
intro.why: It teaches you to build gloss and light thickness while keeping the butter from separating into oil.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat. If the sauce splits, whisk in a spoonful of cold water or cream off the heat.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the butter over high heat, or letting the sauce boil afterwards, which melts the butter to oil and leaves the sauce greasy.

mistakes.fix: Use butter cold from the fridge, cut small.
mistakes.mistake: Using soft or melted butter, which goes straight to oil.

mistakes.fix: Reduce further before the butter goes in.
mistakes.mistake: Too much liquid left in the pan, so that the butter cannot thicken it.

quiz.because: Butter held in the sauce gives a smooth, glossy finish. Separate pools of fat mean it has split.
choices: A clear layer of fat on top.
A thinner sauce with visible pools of butter.
A smooth, glossy, lightly thickened finish.
quiz.question: What finish is this method intended to give a sauce?

quiz.because: Small additions of cold butter, whisked in away from the boil, help it join the sauce rather than melt into a separate layer.
choices: Cold and in small additions, whisking or swirling each in.
Melted and poured in all at once over high heat.
Soft and left unstirred on a rolling boil.
quiz.question: How is the butter added in this method?

quiz.because: An opaque, glossy sauce without clear fat at the edge shows the finish this method aims for.
choices: Clear fat beads around a thin centre.
An opaque, glossy sauce without clear fat at the edge.
A separate pool of melted butter.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches the intended sauce?

quiz.because: Excess heat can split the sauce. Take it off the heat; whisking in a little cold water or cream may help bring it together.
choices: Boil harder to drive off the fat.
Add more melted butter over high heat.
Take it off the heat and whisk in a little cold water or cream.
quiz.question: The sauce splits after getting too hot. What could help bring it together?

variant_of.differs: The fat is cold butter, the liquid is hot, and nothing but the butter's own milk solids holds the sauce together.

cues.text: The pan shines lightly, with no pool of oil.
Egg poured in gives a soft hiss.

technique/oil-the-pan.does: Wipes a thin film of oil over the pan with a folded paper towel, to keep thin layers of batter or egg from sticking, with no pool of oil left to fry them.
how: Warm the pan over a medium heat.
Fold a paper towel, dip the corner in oil and wipe it over the whole surface of the pan, including the sides.
Wipe the pan again between layers, so that every layer meets a fresh, thin film.
Keep the towel to hand on a small dish.

intro.idea: A film rather than a pool
intro.what: This method wipes a thin film of oil across a warm pan for thin batter or egg layers.
intro.why: It teaches you to prevent sticking without leaving enough pooled oil to fry and pit delicate layers.

mistakes.fix: Wipe on a thin film only.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring oil straight in, so that the layers fry and turn pitted.

mistakes.fix: Oil again each time.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the oil between layers, so that later layers stick.

quiz.because: A thin film prevents sticking while excess pooled oil fries and pits the layers.
choices: To immerse the batter in oil.
To leave a thin film without a frying pool.
To create a deep crisp crust on each layer.
quiz.question: Why wipe on oil instead of pouring it in?

quiz.because: A fresh thin film helps each layer release rather than letting later layers stick.
choices: Oil only before the first layer.
Add a deep pool after the first layer.
Wipe again between layers.
quiz.question: How often should you refresh the oil when making successive layers?

quiz.because: A light shine shows the intended film without excess frying oil.
choices: Lightly shiny without pooled oil.
Dry and matte with no oil anywhere.
A deep pool gathering at the edge.
quiz.question: What should the oiled pan look like?

quiz.because: Repeated thin wiping restores the coating that later layers need without creating a pool.
choices: Keep using the dry pan without oil.
Refresh the thin film before each layer.
Pour in enough oil to surround the next layer.
quiz.question: Later layers begin sticking after you skip wiping. What would you change?

cues.text: An even, golden underside.
A steady, gentle sizzle. Spitting means the heat is too high or the food is wet.

technique/pan-fry.does: Cooks a flat piece of food in a thin layer of hot fat, turning it once.
how: Heat a film of fat in the pan over medium heat.
Lay the food in, away from you, and leave it alone.
Turn it once, when the underside is golden and it lifts without sticking.
For an egg, keep the heat gentle and spoon hot fat over the white until it is set.

intro.what: Pan-frying cooks a flat piece in a thin layer of hot fat.
intro.why: It teaches you to leave the surface in contact with the pan long enough to develop colour before turning.

mistakes.fix: Turn it once. If it sticks, it is not ready to turn.
mistakes.mistake: Turning the food again and again, so that it never browns.

quiz.because: Steady pan contact lets the underside develop colour before it is turned.
choices: To give the underside time to brown.
To keep the underside pale.
To let the underside absorb as much fat as possible.
quiz.question: Why leave a flat piece undisturbed at first when pan-frying?

quiz.because: A film of hot fat supports shallow surface cooking rather than deep-frying.
choices: Fill it deeply enough to submerge the food.
Heat a thin film of fat over medium heat.
Start with a dry cold pan and no fat.
quiz.question: How is the pan prepared for this method?

quiz.because: A gentle sizzle fits the intended moderate heat; spitting can point to excess heat or surface water.
choices: Loud irregular spitting.
Complete silence around wet food.
A steady gentle sizzle.
quiz.question: Which sound suits gentle pan-frying?

quiz.because: Giving the surface uninterrupted pan contact allows colour to develop instead of repeatedly disturbing it.
choices: Let the underside colour before turning.
Turn even more frequently.
Keep lifting and pressing the piece.
quiz.question: Repeated turning is interrupting browning. What should change?

variant_of.differs: Larger, flat pieces that lie still and are turned once, over gentler heat.

comes_after.why: Rice for layering must lose its loose starch first or it clumps, so rinsing comes before boiling.

cues.text: A grain bends but then snaps, and the core is firm and chalky white.
The grains have grown long and are still separate, with no mush in the water.

technique/parboil-rice.does: Boils rinsed and soaked rice in a large pot of well-salted water, with whole spices if the dish asks for them, only until each grain is nearly tender with a firm core, then drains it at once. The grains finish later, in steam, in a layered dish.
how: Rinse the rice in several changes of cold water until the water is nearly clear, then leave it to soak in cold water for a good while and drain it.
Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil with plenty of salt, and the whole spices if there are any. The water should taste of the sea.
Slide in the rice, bring the water back to the boil and stir once, gently, to stop the grains sticking.
Test a grain often. It is ready when it snaps cleanly and shows a white, firm core when pressed between the fingers.
Drain it at once into a colander and spread it out. Do not rinse it. It must not be left to sit and go on cooking.

intro.what: This layered-rice method boils soaked grains only partway before draining for a later steaming stage.
intro.why: It teaches you to plan texture across successive cooking steps rather than finish the rice during the first boil.

mistakes.fix: Drain it while the core is still firm. It has a long steam still to come.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling the rice until it is soft, so that it turns to paste during the final steaming.

mistakes.fix: Rinse until the water is nearly clear, then soak before boiling.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the rinse and the soak, so that the grains clump and break.

mistakes.fix: Salt the water boldly. Most of it goes down the drain.
mistakes.mistake: Salting the water too lightly, so that the finished dish tastes flat.

quiz.because: The first boil is deliberately incomplete because the layered dish still has a steaming stage.
choices: It will be served immediately without further cooking.
It will soften further during the later steaming.
Its centre should remain dry in the finished dish.
quiz.question: Why drain this rice while its core is still firm?

quiz.because: Prompt draining limits further softening before the planned final steam.
choices: Leave them sitting in the hot water.
Continue boiling until they collapse.
Drain promptly and spread them out.
quiz.question: What should happen when the grains reach the intended firm-core stage?

quiz.because: The outside has softened while a firm core leaves room for the later cooking step.
choices: A grain bends then snaps with a firm chalky core.
A grain crushes into a completely soft paste.
A grain is unchanged and dry throughout.
quiz.question: Which texture fits rice at the end of parboiling?

quiz.because: Fully softening rice before steaming gives it more cooking than the intended texture can tolerate.
choices: Boil it fully soft before layering.
Stop the first boil while the core remains firm.
Leave drained rice in the hot cooking water.
quiz.question: Rice turns pasty during the final steam. What should change next time?

variant_of.differs: The rice is boiled in a great deal of water, as pasta is, and drained while a firm core remains. It is not cooked in a measured amount of water until all the water is gone. The last of the cooking is done later in steam.
The food is rice, boiled in a large pot of well-salted water only until nearly tender, to be finished later by steaming.

cues.text: Smooth flesh, with no skin left and no deep gouges.

technique/peel.does: Takes off the skin or the shell, and as little as possible of what lies under it.
how: Wash the vegetable first, so that dirt does not travel from the skin to the flesh.
Draw a peeler along its length in long strokes, turning it as you go.
Use a knife for a thick or knobbly skin: cut a flat base, then follow the curve from top to bottom.
For a boiled egg, crack the shell all over and peel from the wide end under a thin stream of water.
For a cooked lobster or crab, crack the shell and ease the flesh out in whole pieces.

intro.what: Peeling removes skin or shell while keeping as much of the food beneath as possible.
intro.why: It teaches you to follow a curved surface rather than cut away useful flesh with the covering.

mistakes.fix: Peel just before use, or hold the pieces under water with a little lemon juice.
mistakes.mistake: Peeling long before cooking, so that potato and celeriac turn brown.

quiz.because: Controlled shallow removal keeps more useful flesh while leaving a clean surface.
choices: Cut away a thick layer with every stroke.
Leave deep grooves to show where the skin was.
Remove the skin with minimal loss beneath it.
quiz.question: What is the aim when peeling a vegetable?

quiz.because: A flat base steadies the vegetable while the blade follows its natural contour.
choices: Cut a flat base and follow its curve downward.
Balance it on its rounded end and cut straight slabs.
Cut deeply across the middle before removing skin.
quiz.question: How should a thick knobbly vegetable be prepared for knife peeling?

quiz.because: A clean smooth surface shows the covering removed without needless loss of flesh.
choices: Deep cuts beside remaining strips of skin.
Smooth flesh without skin patches or deep gouges.
Ragged flesh under an intact outer shell.
quiz.question: Which surface suggests careful peeling?

quiz.because: Limiting exposure or protecting the cut surface reduces browning after peeling.
choices: Leave it exposed for longer before cooking.
Dry the cut pieces in warm air.
Peel near use or hold it in water with a little lemon.
quiz.question: Peeled celeriac browned while waiting. What would you change next time?

cues.text: A clean rim, and each part easy to tell from the others.
A plate for hot food is warm to the hand.

technique/plate.does: Arranges the finished parts on a plate, so that each reaches the table at its best.
how: Warm the plates for hot food and chill them for cold.
Have every part ready before the first one is plated.
Set the main part down first, then build around it without crowding the rim.
Sauce last, beside or under anything crisp, and wipe the rim clean.

intro.what: Plating arranges finished components so their temperature and textures last to the table.
intro.why: It teaches you to coordinate readiness and place sauces without softening a crisp surface.

mistakes.fix: Warm the plates in a low oven or under hot water.
mistakes.mistake: Plating hot food on cold plates, so that a sauce sets and eggs cool before they reach the table.

mistakes.fix: Put the sauce beside it or under it.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring sauce over crisp skin or crust, which softens it at once.

quiz.because: Coordinated readiness reduces the time finished components wait on the plate.
choices: To assemble without leaving early portions waiting.
To let the first plated food cool while the rest cooks.
To replace checking the final arrangement.
quiz.question: Why have every component ready before plating begins?

quiz.because: Keeping sauce off the crisp surface helps preserve its texture.
choices: Directly over the crisp surface.
Beside it or underneath it.
Pooled over every exposed edge.
quiz.question: Where should sauce go beside a crisp skin or crust?

quiz.because: Separation and a clean rim make each finished part easy to recognise.
choices: Components hidden beneath an overflowing sauce.
Food crowded across a smeared rim.
Distinct components and a clean rim.
quiz.question: Which appearance suggests a clear plate arrangement?

quiz.because: A warm plate takes less heat from the food during assembly and service.
choices: Use warmed plates for the hot dish.
Use colder plates to set the sauce faster.
Plate the sauce well before the other components.
quiz.question: A hot sauce cooled and set before reaching the table. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: Poaching sits just under a simmer, so a cook has to be able to find a simmer first.

cues.text: The surface shivers and steams, and nothing rolls.
A poached egg feels like a soft cushion when pressed: the white is set and the yolk is loose inside.

technique/poach.does: Cooks delicate food gently in liquid that is hot but never boils.
how: Heat the liquid until it trembles, with small bubbles on the bottom of the pan and almost none rising.
Slide the food in gently.
Hold the heat there. Turn it down the moment bubbles start to break the surface.
Lift the food out with a slotted spoon and drain it well.
For an egg, add a little vinegar to the water, crack the egg into a small bowl first, and tip it in at the surface.
For dumplings of choux paste, drop spoonfuls into salted water at a tremble, and lift them out with a slotted spoon once they float and feel firm.

intro.what: Poaching cooks delicate food in gently heated liquid without a rolling boil.
intro.why: It teaches you to control liquid movement so that delicate food is not knocked about.

mistakes.fix: Turn the heat down, or add a splash of cold liquid.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the liquid boil, which tears an egg apart and toughens fish and chicken.

mistakes.fix: Use the freshest eggs you have, and drain off the watery part of the white through a sieve.
mistakes.mistake: Using an old egg, whose thin white spreads into rags.

quiz.because: Boiling can tear delicate food apart. Gentle liquid movement treats it more softly.
choices: To treat delicate food gently.
To use movement in the water to keep the food from breaking.
To stop the liquid from losing any volume.
quiz.question: Why does this method keep the liquid from boiling?

quiz.because: Slide the food gently into the liquid instead of splashing it into a rolling boil.
choices: Tip the food in with a quick splash to separate the pieces.
Slide it in gently.
Stir it rapidly into a rolling boil.
quiz.question: How do you add food to the poaching liquid?

quiz.because: A shivering, steaming surface without rolling bubbles shows the gentle liquid movement used here.
choices: A rolling surface with large breaking bubbles.
A still, cold surface without steam.
A shivering, steaming surface that does not roll.
quiz.question: Which surface matches the gentle liquid heat used for poaching?

quiz.because: Lowering the heat or adding a splash of cold liquid brings the liquid back away from a boil.
choices: Turn the heat down or add a splash of cold liquid.
Turn the heat up to maintain the rolling boil.
Stir harder to keep the bubbles moving.
quiz.question: The liquid starts boiling after the food goes in. What should you change?

cues.text: A thick, glossy paste with no whole pieces of leaf.
The scent of garlic and basil rises sharply as they break down.

technique/pound.does: Crushes food in a mortar until it becomes a paste.
how: Start with the hardest thing: garlic, with a little coarse salt to grip it.
Pound straight down to break it, then grind in circles against the wall of the mortar.
Add soft leaves a few at a time, and grind each lot to a paste before the next.
Work in oil or cheese last, a little at a time.

intro.what: Pounding uses a mortar and pestle to turn firm aromatics and leaves into a paste.
intro.why: It teaches you to combine crushing and grinding while adding ingredients in manageable stages.

mistakes.fix: Add a few leaves at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Filling the mortar with leaves, which slide about and bruise without breaking down.

quiz.because: Breaking and grinding the ingredients brings them together instead of only bruising intact leaves.
choices: Large leaves merely coated in oil.
A cohesive paste without whole leaf pieces.
Dry chopped pieces that remain separate.
quiz.question: What is the aim when pounding garlic and leaves for a paste?

quiz.because: Grinding against the wall continues breaking the ingredients after the initial downward crushing.
choices: Tap only the loose top leaves.
Stir without pressing against the surface.
Grind in circles against the mortar wall.
quiz.question: How should the pestle move after firm ingredients have been broken down?

quiz.because: Breaking the aromatics releases their scent into the mortar and surrounding air.
choices: Their scent rises sharply as they break down.
Their aroma disappears as soon as they are crushed.
Their aroma stays faint until oil is added.
quiz.question: Which smell change accompanies breaking garlic and basil?

quiz.because: Smaller additions keep the pestle in contact with the leaves instead of letting an overfilled pile slide.
choices: Add all remaining leaves and press only on top.
Add leaves in smaller batches and grind each before adding more.
Pour in all the oil before breaking the leaves.
quiz.question: A full mortar of leaves slides around without becoming paste. What should change?

cues.text: The surface oil, which floated as a sheen, has run off with the water.
The smell of oil or of the making is gone.

technique/pour-boiling-water-over.does: Pours boiling water over a ready-made food, to wash off the surface oil or the smell from the making before it goes into a pot or a dish. The food is not cooked, only scalded.
how: Put the food in a colander or a heatproof bowl.
Pour boiling water over it, slowly and evenly, so that every surface is touched.
Drain it, and press it gently with a clean cloth or paper if it will be fried or stuffed.
Cut or use it right away.

intro.what: This preparation scalds a ready-made food by pouring boiling water across its surface.
intro.why: It teaches you to remove surface oil without immersing the food in a prolonged boil.

mistakes.fix: Only scald it by pouring.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling the food in the pot, which makes it soft and waterlogged.

mistakes.fix: Scald it first, every time.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the scald before simmering, so that the broth turns greasy.

quiz.because: A brief surface rinse can remove oil without the prolonged immersion that waterlogs the food.
choices: To hydrate the food deeply before further cooking.
To soften the whole piece before it reaches the pan.
To carry off surface oil before further preparation.
quiz.question: What is the purpose of this pouring step?

quiz.because: Even pouring treats the surface while keeping this a scalding step rather than a long boil.
choices: Pour slowly and evenly across all surfaces.
Leave the food submerged at a rolling boil.
Wet only the centre and leave the edges untouched.
quiz.question: How should the water contact the food?

quiz.because: Oil carried away in the runoff leaves less free oil on the surface.
choices: The sheen remains on the surface after draining.
The oily sheen runs off with the water.
Water gathers without carrying a visible sheen.
quiz.question: Which visible change suggests surface oil has been washed away?

quiz.because: Limiting water contact preserves structure while removing the surface residue.
choices: Boil it longer to even out the texture.
Leave it soaking after the pour.
Pour the water over and drain instead of boiling it in the pot.
quiz.question: The food became soft and waterlogged. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: The food is laid out in the dish first, and the liquid goes over it last.

cues.text: The liquid stands at one level all round, and the tops of the pieces show above it.

technique/pour-over.does: Pours a liquid or a loose sauce onto food laid in a dish, slowly and from the side, so that it settles into the gaps without washing off the top.
how: Lay the food out in the dish first, in the way it is to be served.
Pour from low down near the rim, in a thin steady stream, and not straight onto the middle.
Stop when the liquid has reached the level the dish asks for. Leave the top of the food showing if it is to brown.
Tap the dish gently so that the liquid settles into every gap.

intro.what: Pouring over adds liquid to arranged food gently from the side of its dish.
intro.why: It teaches you to fill gaps without dislodging seasoning, toppings or the arrangement.

mistakes.fix: Pour low, from the side, in a thin stream.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring from high up, which splashes and washes off the seasoning or the topping.

mistakes.fix: Leave a gap below the rim.
mistakes.mistake: Filling the dish to the brim, so that it spills in the oven.

quiz.because: A gentle side stream reaches the gaps with less force against the exposed surface.
choices: To let liquid settle without washing off the top.
To push the topping away from the centre.
To leave the gaps beneath the food completely dry.
quiz.question: Why pour near the side rather than onto the middle?

quiz.because: Gentle tapping settles the liquid without dismantling the arrangement.
choices: Shake the dish hard enough to move the pieces.
Tap the dish gently.
Press the topping down into the liquid.
quiz.question: What helps liquid settle into the gaps after pouring?

quiz.because: Exposed tops can brown while liquid surrounds the lower parts.
choices: All tops submerged beneath a full dish.
Liquid overflowing a crowded rim.
An even liquid level with the tops still exposed.
quiz.question: Which appearance suits a dish whose tops should brown?

quiz.because: Reducing the height and force of the stream protects the surface arrangement.
choices: Pour from low near the rim in a thin stream.
Pour faster from higher above the centre.
Direct the stream onto the topping’s highest point.
quiz.question: Pouring washed the topping off. What would you change next time?

cues.text: The cloth is wet and the block has become a little thinner.
The tofu is firm and springs back.

technique/press-tofu.does: Presses water out of a block of firm tofu under a light weight, so that it is firmer, absorbs a sauce and browns instead of steaming.
how: Wrap the block in a clean cloth or paper towels.
Set it on a tray or a board, put a plate and a light weight on top and tilt the tray so the water runs off.
Leave it until the water has stopped running out.
Unwrap, pat dry and cut.

intro.what: Pressing removes free water from firm tofu under a light weight.
intro.why: It teaches you to control surface moisture before seeking a browned exterior.

mistakes.fix: Use a plate or a light bowl only.
mistakes.mistake: Pressing with a heavy weight, which cracks the block.

mistakes.fix: Pat it dry.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the drying, so that the tofu spits in the pan.

quiz.because: Reducing excess water helps the surface brown rather than spend its early pan contact shedding moisture.
choices: To keep more free water on its surface.
To remove water that would encourage steaming instead of browning.
To break it into a soft puree.
quiz.question: Why press firm tofu before pan cooking?

quiz.because: Drainage separates the tofu from the moisture being pressed out.
choices: Leave the block sitting in pooled water.
Pour collected water back over the cloth.
Let it run away from the wrapped block on a tilted tray.
quiz.question: How should released water be handled during pressing?

quiz.because: Water transferred to the cloth and a little compression show moisture leaving the block.
choices: A wet cloth and a slightly thinner block.
A dry cloth around a swollen block.
A cracked block beneath a very heavy weight.
quiz.question: Which appearance is consistent with pressing?

quiz.because: Firm tofu needs gentle pressure; excessive force damages its structure.
choices: Add more weight to flatten the cracks.
Use a lighter weight.
Press harder before wrapping it.
quiz.question: The tofu cracked under a heavy weight. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: Rinsing washes off dust and loose skins that would foam up and clog the valve.
Large hard pulses are soaked first so that they cook evenly in the pot.

cues.text: A steady hiss or a regular whistle from the valve. Wild spitting means the heat is too high.
A cooked pulse crushes easily between the fingers, with no hard core.
Split pulses have fallen apart into a thick, creamy mass when stirred.

technique/pressure-cook.does: Cooks pulses in a sealed pot that holds steam in, so that the liquid gets hotter than in an open pot and hard dried seeds soften and fall apart in a fraction of the usual time.
how: Rinse the pulses. Soak the large hard kinds such as kidney beans, if the recipe asks.
Put them in the pot with plenty of water and a little turmeric. Fill the pot no more than half, as pulses swell and foam.
Close the lid, seat the valve or weight and heat on high until the steam starts to hiss or whistle steadily.
Turn the heat down so that the hiss stays steady, and cook for the time the pulse needs.
Take the pot off the heat and let the pressure fall on its own before opening it. Open the lid away from you.
Stir. Mash the soft pulses against the side of the pot if the dish should be smooth.

intro.what: This pulse-cooking method uses a sealed pressure pot to soften dried seeds more quickly.
intro.why: It teaches you to distinguish pressure cooking from open-pot simmering and to judge the texture sought for the dish.

mistakes.fix: Fill the pot no more than half and add a spoonful of oil or ghee to calm the foam.
mistakes.mistake: Filling the pot too full, so that foam rises and clogs the valve.

mistakes.fix: Let the pressure fall by itself first.
mistakes.mistake: Opening the lid before the pressure has dropped, which sprays hot steam and liquid.

mistakes.fix: Cover them with plenty of water. Add more if the dish is too thick.
mistakes.mistake: Using too little water, so that the pulses scorch at the bottom.

quiz.because: A pressure pot retains steam and operates differently from an open pot, allowing hotter liquid.
choices: Retained pressure allows the liquid to become hotter.
The sealed pot works mainly by evaporating water faster.
The sealed pot softens pulses mainly by drying their surfaces.
quiz.question: How does pressure cooking differ from an open simmer?

quiz.because: Once pressure is established, the described method reduces heat rather than continuing to increase it.
choices: Lower the heat to maintain steady activity.
Keep increasing heat until the valve spits wildly.
Remove it from the heat so the hiss stops for the whole cooking stage.
quiz.question: In this stovetop method, what follows a steady hiss or whistle?

quiz.because: Softened split pulses can lose their individual shape and give body to the liquid; this is a texture cue only.
choices: They retain hard dry centres.
They break down into a thick creamy mixture when stirred.
They remain rigid and separate despite stirring.
quiz.question: Which texture is sought for split pulses intended for a creamy dish?

quiz.because: Pulses absorb liquid, so an inadequate initial supply can leave the base dry and catching.
choices: Begin with less water to concentrate the flavour faster.
Keep the same dry setup and increase the heat.
Begin with ample water appropriate to the pot and method.
quiz.question: The pulses scorch because the pot began with too little water. What should change next time?

variant_of.differs: The pot is sealed, so the liquid gets hotter than a simmer and the pulses cook in a fraction of the time. The cook cannot lift the lid to check, and the pressure must fall before the pot is opened.

cues.text: A neat spread of small holes all over, none of them a tear.

technique/prick.does: Makes small holes in a skin or a crust with the tip of a knife or a fork, so that steam can leave and the skin does not split or the crust puff.
how: Dry the surface, so that the tip does not slip.
Prick evenly all over with the point, a little way in, about as far apart as the width of a fork.
On a sausage, turn it and prick on every side. On pastry, prick the base and the sides.
Cook it soon after, before the holes close.

intro.what: Pricking makes small shallow holes in a skin or pastry crust.
intro.why: It teaches you to create steam outlets without turning a delicate surface into tears or deep cuts.

mistakes.fix: Prick only just through the skin.
mistakes.mistake: Stabbing deep into a sausage, which lets the juices run out and dries it.

mistakes.fix: Prick evenly, all over.
mistakes.mistake: Pricking unevenly, which leaves a patch that still splits or puffs.

quiz.because: Small openings release steam that could otherwise lift or split the surface.
choices: Steam to escape instead of forcing a surface to puff or split.
The entire filling to drain out freely.
A thick solid crust to become completely sealed.
quiz.question: What do the small holes made by pricking allow?

quiz.because: Even coverage avoids untreated patches where steam can still push the surface upward.
choices: Only in a dense cluster at an edge.
Evenly across the relevant surface.
As deep long slashes through the food.
quiz.question: How should the holes be distributed?

quiz.because: The aim is controlled small openings rather than structural damage.
choices: Long ragged splits across the surface.
Deep channels reaching the filling.
Small neat holes without tears.
quiz.question: Which appearance fits careful pricking?

quiz.because: An unpricked patch can still trap steam even when neighbouring areas have outlets.
choices: Prick the surface more evenly, including missed areas.
Make every existing hole much deeper.
Leave more of the base unpricked.
quiz.question: A pastry patch puffed while the rest stayed flat. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: Scoring cuts shallow lines. Pricking makes only small holes and takes nothing away, so that steam leaves without the skin or the crust splitting or puffing.

comes_after.why: A dough rises evenly only once it has been worked smooth.

cues.text: The dough has swelled and looks puffy and domed, with small bubbles under the skin.
A fingertip leaves a dent that fills back slowly.
A mild, yeasty, slightly sweet smell, and not a sharp sour one.

technique/proof.does: Leaves shaped yeast dough in a warm, still place to rise, so that the yeast fills it with gas and it swells and turns light, airy and ready to bake or fry.
how: Shape the dough and set it in a lightly oiled bowl, or on a tray, with room to swell.
Cover it with a damp cloth or oiled film, so that its skin does not dry out.
Leave it somewhere warm and free of draughts until it has roughly doubled, or puffed as the shape asks.
Press a fingertip lightly into it: it is ready when the dent fills back slowly.
Bake or fry it at once, and handle it gently so that the air stays in.

intro.what: Proofing lets shaped yeast dough swell before baking or frying.
intro.why: It teaches you to judge dough by its response to touch rather than by waiting alone.

mistakes.fix: Choose a gently warm place and give it more time.
mistakes.mistake: Proofing in a spot that is too hot, so that the dough turns sour and loose.

mistakes.fix: Wait until the dent fills back slowly.
mistakes.mistake: Baking too soon, so that the bread is dense and tight.

mistakes.fix: Check it often and bake it as soon as it is ready.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it too long, so that it collapses when it is touched or baked.

quiz.because: Yeast produces gas that expands the dough; gentle handling preserves that airy structure.
choices: To let gas make it light and airy.
To dry its outer skin.
To tighten its shape by pressing out gas.
quiz.question: Why proof shaped yeast dough?

quiz.because: A cover protects the surface from drying while the dough expands.
choices: With a dry cloth pressed into its surface.
With a damp cloth or oiled film.
With no cover so a skin forms.
quiz.question: How should the dough be covered while it rises?

quiz.because: A slowly returning dent distinguishes puffy dough from a tight dough or a collapsing one.
choices: The dent springs back immediately.
The dough collapses under the touch.
The dent fills back slowly.
quiz.question: Which response to a light fingertip press suggests the dough has risen enough?

quiz.because: Gentle warmth allows a steadier rise without the loose texture associated with excess heat.
choices: Use a gently warm place and allow more time.
Use a hotter place for a shorter wait.
Remove the cover to dry the dough.
quiz.question: Dough becomes loose in a very hot proofing spot. What should change next time?

comes_after.why: Food is simmered soft before it is pureed.

cues.text: It falls from the spoon in a smooth ribbon, with no grains or strings.
Nothing gritty between finger and thumb.

technique/puree.does: Breaks cooked food down until it is smooth, in a blender or through a sieve.
how: Cook the food until it is completely soft. Nothing firm will blend smooth.
Blend with only part of the cooking liquid at first.
Add more liquid little by little until the texture is right.
Pass it through a fine sieve for a truly smooth finish.

intro.what: Pureeing breaks softened food into a smooth mixture.
intro.why: It teaches you to control texture through softness, added liquid and sieving.

mistakes.fix: Fill it less than half way, hold the lid down with a cloth and start slowly.
mistakes.mistake: Filling a blender to the top with hot soup, so that the steam blows the lid off.

mistakes.fix: Hold liquid back. It is easy to thin a puree and hard to thicken one.
mistakes.mistake: Adding all the liquid at once and ending with a thin soup.

mistakes.fix: Blend a potato soup only briefly, or push it through a sieve.
mistakes.mistake: Blending potatoes hard, which turns them to glue.

quiz.because: Soft food can be broken down into a continuous mixture rather than separate pieces.
choices: Small separate pieces suspended in broth.
A smooth texture without grains or strings.
A coarse mixture with a firm bite.
quiz.question: What is the aim of pureeing cooked food?

quiz.because: Gradual additions let you stop at the desired thickness instead of making the puree too thin.
choices: Pour it all in before blending.
Discard it all before checking texture.
Hold some back and add it gradually.
quiz.question: How should the cooking liquid be added?

quiz.because: Grit and strings interrupt a smooth texture; a fine sieve can remove remaining pieces.
choices: Grit or strings remain in its texture.
It falls smoothly from the spoon.
It has an even appearance when stirred.
quiz.question: What would suggest a puree needs more smoothing?

quiz.because: Prolonged hard blending makes potato mixtures gluey; gentler processing avoids that change.
choices: Blend harder until it looks glossy.
Blend briefly or push it through a sieve.
Keep blending while adding more potatoes.
quiz.question: Blended potato soup has become gluey. What would you change next time?

cues.text: Sand and grit gather on the bottom of the bowl, and the clams show their siphons a little.

technique/purge-clams.does: Leaves live clams in cold, well-salted water, like the sea, so that they open a little, breathe and spit out the sand they hold, before they are cooked.
how: Look over the clams. Throw away any that are broken, or that stay open when they are tapped on the counter.
Stir plenty of salt into cold water until it tastes like the sea, in a bowl wide enough to hold the clams in a single layer.
Lay in the clams without crowding and leave them in a cool, dim place, so that they spit out their sand.
Lift them out of the water with your hands or a slotted spoon, leaving the grit on the bottom of the bowl. Do not tip them into a colander, which pours the sand back over them.

intro.what: Purging gives clams a cold salty-water bath to release sand before cooking.
intro.why: It teaches you to separate grit from food without pouring that grit back over it.

mistakes.fix: Make the water as salty as the sea.
mistakes.mistake: Using fresh water, which makes the clams shut or kills them.

mistakes.fix: Lift them out by hand and leave the grit behind.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring the clams into a colander, so that the sand falls back over them.

mistakes.fix: Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding them in a warm place, so that they do not open.

quiz.because: Clams release sand into the water; lifting them out separates them from the settled grit.
choices: Only loose dirt on the outside of the shells.
The water trapped between the shells.
Sand and grit held inside them.
quiz.question: What is purging intended to remove from clams?

quiz.because: Grit settles beneath the clams, so lifting them avoids carrying that sediment back over them.
choices: Lift them out and leave the water behind.
Pour the bowl through a colander.
Stir up the bottom before draining.
quiz.question: How should clams be removed from the purging bowl?

quiz.because: Settled sand shows grit has left the clams and collected below them.
choices: The water remains clear with no sediment.
Grit gathers on the bottom of the bowl.
The shells become polished on the outside.
quiz.question: Which observation shows that sand has been released?

quiz.because: Pouring carries settled sand with the water; lifting leaves the grit behind.
choices: Rinse them with the same settled water.
Shake the bowl before pouring.
Lift the clams instead of tipping out the bowl.
quiz.question: Sand coats the clams again when you pour out the bowl. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The water is cold and as salty as the sea, not fresh. The aim is not to soften the food but to make live shellfish spit out their sand, and they are lifted out and not drained.

comes_after.why: A pan sauce is deglazed first and reduced second.
A cook who can hold a simmer can judge a boil that must not scorch.

cues.text: The bubbles grow larger and slower, and a finger drawn across the back of a coated spoon leaves a clear path.
The boil deepens from a rattle to a slow, thick plop.

technique/reduce.does: Boils a liquid down, so that its water leaves as steam and what remains is thicker and stronger.
how: Use a wide pan. The wider the surface, the faster the water leaves.
Boil steadily, uncovered.
Watch the level against the side of the pan, and the size of the bubbles.
Stop when it coats the back of a spoon, and season only then.

intro.what: Reducing boils liquid uncovered so that water leaves as steam and the liquid grows thicker and stronger.
intro.why: It teaches you to connect evaporation with flavour and texture, and to season after concentrating a sauce.

mistakes.fix: Season at the end.
mistakes.mistake: Salting before reducing, so that the salt is concentrated with everything else.

mistakes.fix: Stay with it once it starts to thicken, and pull it off the heat early.
mistakes.mistake: Walking away near the end, when a sauce goes from syrup to scorched in moments.

quiz.because: Water leaves as steam, so the remaining liquid becomes more concentrated and thicker.
choices: It becomes more diluted.
It becomes thicker and stronger as water leaves.
It keeps the same strength while its colour changes.
quiz.question: What happens to a liquid as it reduces?

quiz.because: A wide surface lets water leave faster. Keeping the pan uncovered lets the steam escape.
choices: A tightly covered narrow pot.
A wide pan under a tight lid.
A wide pan, boiling steadily without a lid.
quiz.question: Which pan setup helps liquid reduce?

quiz.because: A coating that holds a clear path across the spoon shows the sauce has thickened.
choices: A finger leaves a clear path across the back of a coated spoon.
The liquid looks exactly as thin as at the start.
The spoon emerges without any coating.
quiz.question: What spoon test helps you judge whether the sauce has thickened?

quiz.because: Salt concentrates along with the sauce. Season after reducing so you judge the concentrated liquid.
choices: Season to the final taste before starting to boil.
Season at the end of the reduction.
Cover the pan to keep all the water in.
quiz.question: A reduced sauce tastes too salty. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: Refreshing is how boiling or blanching ends.

cues.text: A piece is cold to the middle when it is squeezed.
The colour stays as bright as it was in the pot.

technique/refresh.does: Stops the cooking at once by plunging hot food into iced water, which keeps green vegetables bright and firm.
how: Have a large bowl of water and ice ready before the food is cooked.
Lift the food straight from the pot into the iced water.
Leave it only until it is cold to the middle.
Drain it well, so that it does not soak.

intro.what: Refreshing plunges hot food into iced water to halt further softening.
intro.why: It teaches you to manage the heat that food retains after leaving the pan.

mistakes.fix: Take it out as soon as it is cold and drain it on a cloth.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving food to soak in the water, which washes out its taste.

quiz.because: Rapid cooling checks the continued softening caused by heat remaining in the vegetables.
choices: To stop further cooking and retain firmness.
To keep softening them slowly.
To draw out as much flavour as possible.
quiz.question: Why refresh green vegetables after cooking?

quiz.because: Having the cooling bath ready allows an immediate transfer rather than continued cooking while you prepare it.
choices: After the food has cooled on a plate.
Before the food leaves the cooking pot.
After draining the vegetables for serving.
quiz.question: When should the iced-water bowl be prepared?

quiz.because: Cooling the centre removes lingering heat; further soaking adds no benefit to this step.
choices: Only the outside feels cool.
The piece has become waterlogged.
The piece feels cold to the middle.
quiz.question: Which texture check guides removal from the bath?

quiz.because: Prolonged soaking washes out flavour, so cooling and draining should be separate steps.
choices: Drain them as soon as they are cold.
Leave them soaking until service.
Replace the bath repeatedly while they wait.
quiz.question: The refreshed vegetables taste washed out. What should change?

comes_after.why: Food is warmed again at a gentle simmer, so a cook has to be able to hold one.

cues.text: Small, steady bubbles break at the surface in the middle of the pan as well as at the edge.
The spoon moves freely along the bottom, with nothing stuck.

technique/reheat.does: Brings food that was cooked earlier back to a hot, bubbling state, gently enough that it neither dries out nor catches on the pan. Beans and soups often taste better for the rest, and the Tuscan ribollita is made for exactly that: a soup that is boiled again.
how: Take the food from the fridge a little ahead of time if it is thick and dense.
Put it in a heavy pan with a splash of stock or water, to loosen it and stop it catching.
Warm it over low heat, stirring up from the bottom now and then, until it bubbles gently at the centre as well as at the edge.
Taste and adjust the salt, which can flatten as the food rests.

intro.what: This pan method warms previously cooked soups, beans or stews gently while stirring.
intro.why: It teaches you to balance heat and moisture so a thick mixture warms without sticking or breaking apart.

mistakes.fix: Use low heat and stir up from the bottom.
mistakes.mistake: Reheating over high heat, so that the bottom catches while the top is still cold.

mistakes.fix: Add a splash of stock or water first.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving a thick soup or stew with no extra liquid, so that it dries and sticks.

mistakes.fix: Keep it at a gentle bubble.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling hard, so that beans break and fall apart.

quiz.because: Gentle heat gives warmth time to spread while limiting sticking and damage to the beans.
choices: To reduce it as fast as possible.
To warm it without catching or breaking the beans.
To brown the bottom before stirring.
quiz.question: Why use gentle heat for a thick bean soup?

quiz.because: Extra liquid loosens a dense mixture and stirring redistributes heat from the pan base.
choices: Heating it without stirring until the edges boil.
Pouring off its remaining liquid first.
A splash of stock or water and stirring from the bottom.
quiz.question: What helps a thick soup move freely in the pan?

quiz.because: A freely moving spoon shows the mixture is not sticking to the base of the pan.
choices: The spoon moves freely along the bottom.
The spoon drags over a stuck layer.
The spoon meets dry patches at the base.
quiz.question: Which spoon movement suggests the base is not catching?

quiz.because: Hard boiling agitates tender beans; a gentler bubble limits that movement.
choices: Maintain a vigorous boil but stir less.
Keep the mixture at a gentle bubble.
Reduce the liquid so it heats faster.
quiz.question: Beans are breaking apart during reheating. What should change?

cues.text: No liquid pools at the bottom of the bowl, and the grains have swollen to about double their size.
The grains are tender with at most a little bite, and fall apart when they are pressed lightly between the fingers.

technique/rehydrate-couscous.does: Swells precooked, dried couscous grains in hot liquid poured over them off the heat, and lets them stand covered until the liquid is taken up, so that no steaming is needed.
how: Put the grains in a wide bowl with a little salt and a spoonful of oil or butter, and rub until every grain is coated, so that they do not clump when the liquid arrives.
Bring the liquid, plain water or a well-flavoured stock, to a boil. Measure it by volume against the grains: about the same amount, a little more for a softer grain.
Pour the boiling liquid over the grains all at once, stir once, and cover the bowl tightly with a plate or a lid.
Leave it off the heat until the liquid has gone and the grains have swollen. Then uncover and fluff.

intro.what: Precooked dried couscous swells in hot liquid while standing covered off the heat.
intro.why: It teaches you how absorption and trapped steam can soften grains without boiling them in a pan.

mistakes.fix: Measure the liquid against the grains. If it is already wet, spread the grains on a tray and let the steam go.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring on too much liquid, which leaves a wet, gluey mass.

mistakes.fix: Bring the liquid to a boil first.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring on liquid that is not hot, so that the centres of the grains stay hard.

mistakes.fix: Cover it tightly while the grains drink.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the bowl uncovered, so that the steam escapes and the top layer stays dry.

mistakes.fix: Coat the dry grains with oil or butter before the liquid goes on.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the oil, so that the grains stick in clumps.

quiz.because: Precooked dried grains can absorb hot liquid off the heat; traditional steaming is a different method.
choices: Raw couscous needing repeated steaming.
Couscous already softened in a sauce.
Precooked dried couscous.
quiz.question: Which couscous is this covered-bowl method intended for?

quiz.because: A tight cover retains steam while the grains absorb the liquid.
choices: Cover the bowl tightly and leave it off the heat.
Leave the bowl open and stir continuously.
Keep the grains boiling in the bowl.
quiz.question: What should happen after hot liquid is poured over the grains?

quiz.because: The grains take liquid into their structure rather than leaving it free at the bottom.
choices: Dry grains sitting above a puddle.
Swollen grains with no liquid pooling beneath them.
A firm dry surface with liquid below.
quiz.question: Which observation suggests absorption has taken place?

quiz.because: Escaping steam can leave the upper grains dry; covering retains moisture around them.
choices: Leave it uncovered to release more steam.
Stir the uncovered grains continuously while they stand.
Keep the bowl tightly covered during absorption.
quiz.question: The top layer stayed dry while the grains beneath softened. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The grains are precooked and dried, so they only need to drink hot liquid. There is no couscoussier, no steam over a stew, and no rounds of sprinkling and raking: the grain is ready in the time it takes to stand covered. The result is a little denser and less airy than grain steamed by hand, and it tastes of its liquid alone and not of the stew's steam.

cues.text: The seaweed has opened out and turned a glossy dark green.
It is soft and slippery, with no hard, dry centre.

technique/rehydrate-seaweed.does: Soaks dried seaweed in cold water until it swells and turns soft, silky and bright green, then squeezes out the water and cuts away any hard rib.
how: Put a small handful of dried seaweed in a large bowl, as it swells to many times its size.
Cover it with cold water and leave it until it is soft and glossy.
Lift it out, drain it and squeeze it lightly.
Cut away any hard rib and cut the rest into bite-sized pieces.

intro.what: This method softens dried seaweed in cold water before draining and trimming it.
intro.why: It teaches you to allow for swelling and stop soaking when the desired bite remains.

mistakes.fix: Start with a small handful.
mistakes.mistake: Using too much, so that the bowl overflows with swollen seaweed.

mistakes.fix: Lift it out as soon as it is soft.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it in the water for too long, so that it turns slimy and loses its bite.

quiz.because: Water opens and expands the dried seaweed, so a small dry portion can occupy much more room.
choices: It expands considerably as it absorbs water.
It must be kept pressed against the bowl.
It shrinks as it softens.
quiz.question: Why give dried seaweed plenty of room in the bowl?

quiz.because: Light squeezing removes excess water while trimming removes tough parts that soaking has not softened.
choices: Leave the hard rib attached to keep it chewy.
Squeeze lightly and cut away any hard rib.
Return it to the water until it breaks down.
quiz.question: What comes after soaking and draining in this method?

quiz.because: The dry centre should soften while the seaweed still retains some texture.
choices: Soft outside with a brittle centre.
Slimy and losing all its bite.
Soft and slippery without a hard dry centre.
quiz.question: Which feel suggests the seaweed has softened?

quiz.because: Prolonged soaking can damage the desired texture; checking softness prevents unnecessary waiting.
choices: Lift it out as soon as it softens.
Keep soaking until its colour fades.
Use a longer soak in more water.
quiz.question: The seaweed became slimy and lost its bite. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: Dried seaweed swells very fast and to many times its size in cold water, so it is soaked for a short while only, then squeezed, and any hard rib is cut away.

cues.text: A slow sizzle that grows as the fat pools.
Clear fat in the pan, and pieces that have shrunk and turned golden at the edges.

technique/render.does: Melts the fat out of bacon or skin over gentle heat, leaving the meat crisp and the fat clear for cooking.
how: Start with a cold pan and no added fat.
Lay the pieces in a single layer and set the pan over medium-low heat.
Let the fat run slowly, stirring now and then.
Turn the heat up at the end to crisp the pieces, then lift them out and keep the fat.

intro.what: Rendering releases fat from bacon or skin over gentle heat before crisping the pieces.
intro.why: It teaches you to distinguish slowly melting fat from quickly browning a surface.

mistakes.fix: Start cold and take your time.
mistakes.mistake: Starting in a hot pan, which browns the outside before the fat has melted, so that the pieces stay chewy.

quiz.because: Gentle heat melts fat out of the food so it can pool separately in the pan.
choices: Only water released by the pieces.
Clear fat from the pieces.
Fat poured in separately at the start.
quiz.question: What does rendering release for further cooking?

quiz.because: Starting cold gives fat time to run before the exterior browns too quickly.
choices: In a very hot pan with plenty of oil.
In a warm pan with added fat before the pieces go in.
In a cold pan without added fat.
quiz.question: How does this pan-rendering method begin?

quiz.because: As fat leaves the food, the pieces shrink and clear melted fat gathers around them.
choices: Clear fat pools as the pieces shrink.
A dry crust forms while no fat appears.
The pieces swell in a cloudy liquid.
quiz.question: Which appearance suggests fat is rendering?

quiz.because: Rapid browning can outpace fat release; a slower start allows rendering before final crisping.
choices: Start hotter to form a faster crust.
Start cold and let the fat run slowly.
Add the pieces only when oil is smoking.
quiz.question: The outside browns but the pieces remain chewy. What should change next time?

comes_after.why: Resting is how a sear ends.

cues.text: Little juice runs out when it is sliced, and the cut face is evenly coloured.
The meat has relaxed and gives a little under a finger.

technique/rest.does: Leaves cooked meat alone off the heat for a while, so that its juices settle and stay in when it is cut.
how: Lift the meat out of the pan onto a rack or a warm plate.
Leave it uncovered, or loosely tented, somewhere warm.
Wait about as long as it took to sear a steak, and much longer for a large roast.
Pour the juices it gives up back into the sauce.

intro.what: Resting leaves meat off the heat before it is carved.
intro.why: It asks you to plan a pause before slicing and to notice the effect on the juices and crust.

mistakes.fix: Wait. The meat stays hot inside for longer than you think.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting it straight away, so that the juice floods the board and the meat eats dry.

mistakes.fix: Leave it open, or tent the foil loosely.
mistakes.mistake: Wrapping it tightly in foil, which steams the crust soft.

quiz.because: Resting gives juices time to settle, helping more stay in the meat when it is sliced.
choices: To keep browning the meat in the cooking pan.
To trap steam tightly against the crust.
To let juices settle before slicing.
quiz.question: Why rest meat before slicing it?

quiz.because: Lift the meat out of the hot pan onto a rack or warm plate for its pause off the heat.
choices: Onto a rack or warm plate, away from the pan heat.
Back into the hot frying pan.
Into a tightly sealed foil parcel every time.
quiz.question: Where does the meat go to rest in this method?

quiz.because: Less juice running onto the board is the result this resting method aims for.
choices: Juice floods the board immediately.
Little juice runs out when the meat is sliced.
A crisp crust turns wet beneath tight foil.
quiz.question: Which observation is consistent with the intended result?

quiz.because: Tight foil traps steam against the crust. A loose tent or no cover avoids steaming it soft.
choices: Seal the foil around the edges to retain more warmth.
Leave it tightly wrapped until the crust dries again.
Leave it uncovered or tent the foil loosely.
quiz.question: Tight foil has steamed the crust soft. What would you change?

comes_after.why: Rice rests only after it has been cooked.
