cues.text: The surface of the rice is dry and shiny, with no wet patches.
The grains are plump, separate and slightly sticky.

technique/rest-and-fluff.does: Leaves cooked rice covered off the heat for a while, so that the steam spreads evenly through the grains, then cuts through it with a paddle to let the steam out and loosen the grains.
how: As soon as the rice is cooked, take it off the heat and keep the lid on.
Leave it to rest, undisturbed, so that the grains finish steaming.
Wet a rice paddle, and cut through the rice in a slicing motion, turning it over from the bottom.
Cover it again until it is served.

intro.what: Resting covered rice redistributes steam before a paddle loosens the grains.
intro.why: It teaches you to finish rice texture with retained steam and gentle movement rather than more stirring.

mistakes.fix: Keep it shut until the rest is over.
mistakes.mistake: Lifting the lid during the rest, so that the steam escapes.

mistakes.fix: Cut and fold with a wet paddle.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring the rice, which crushes the grains and makes it pasty.

quiz.because: The covered rest holds steam around the rice while its moisture becomes more even.
choices: To dry it immediately in moving air.
To build a crust on the pan base.
To let retained steam spread through the grains.
quiz.question: Why leave cooked rice covered off the heat?

quiz.because: Cutting and folding loosens grains while limiting crushing and sticking to the paddle.
choices: Cut and fold with a wet paddle.
Stir hard in circles.
Press the grains firmly against the pot.
quiz.question: How should the paddle move when fluffing rice?

quiz.because: An even surface without wet patches is consistent with moisture spreading through the rice.
choices: A wet puddle covering the surface.
Dry and shiny without wet patches.
A broken, pasty surface.
quiz.question: Which surface matches rice after this rest?

quiz.because: Stirring crushes grains; a paddle used to cut and fold keeps more of their structure.
choices: Stir more quickly to separate the paste.
Mash the rice before turning it over.
Use a slicing and folding motion instead of stirring.
quiz.question: Fluffing turned the rice pasty. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The rice rests in its own steam under a lid and is then cut through with a wet paddle to loosen it.

comes_after.why: The batter must be mixed before it can rest.

cues.text: A few bubbles have risen to the surface and the batter has thickened slightly.
The batter is smoother when stirred than just after mixing.

technique/rest-batter.does: Leaves a mixed batter to stand, so that the flour takes up its liquid and the batter turns smooth and thickens a little. Cooked after resting, it spreads evenly and comes out tender.
how: Cover the bowl of batter.
Leave it to stand in a cool place, or in the fridge if it will wait for long.
Stir it gently once before it is used.
If it has thickened too much, loosen it with a splash of liquid.

intro.what: Resting gives mixed batter time to become smoother as flour absorbs liquid.
intro.why: It teaches you to distinguish hydration from extra mixing when adjusting batter texture.

mistakes.fix: Let it stand first.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking the batter right away, so that the pancakes are tough and uneven.

mistakes.fix: Give it only one gentle stir.
mistakes.mistake: Beating it again after it has rested, which knocks out the bubbles.

quiz.because: Absorption continues after mixing, making the batter smoother and slightly thicker.
choices: To let flour absorb liquid and the batter smooth out.
To dry the surface into a skin.
To separate the flour from the liquid.
quiz.question: Why rest a flour batter before cooking?

quiz.because: A gentle stir evens the mixture without undoing the texture gained during the rest.
choices: Beat vigorously until very foamy.
Stir gently rather than beating it again.
Scrape off the thick surface without mixing.
quiz.question: How should rested batter be mixed before use?

quiz.because: Flour taking up liquid accounts for the slight thickening and smoother feel.
choices: Dry flour remaining separate at the surface.
A thinner mixture with more obvious grit.
A smoother batter that has thickened slightly.
quiz.question: What change would you expect after resting?

quiz.because: Liquid adjusts an over-thick batter directly; extra flour would thicken it further.
choices: Loosen it with a splash of liquid.
Beat it harder without adding liquid.
Add more dry flour before cooking.
quiz.question: The rested batter is too thick to spread. What should you do?

variant_of.differs: The food that rests is a batter, left covered so that its flour swells, and not a piece of cooked meat.

cues.text: The last water stays as clear as it went in.
Brined food tastes pleasantly salty and no longer harsh.

technique/rinse.does: Washes food in cold water, to carry off grit, loose starch, or the salt and brine it was kept in.
how: Put the food in a colander, or in a large bowl of cold water.
Run cold water over it, or move it about in the bowl with your hands.
Change the water until it stays clear. Lift leaves out of the water, so that the grit stays behind.
Drain it well, and dry whatever will be fried or dressed.

intro.what: Rinsing uses cold water to remove loose grit, starch or excess brine.
intro.why: It teaches you to remove unwanted residue while keeping the flavour and texture you want.

mistakes.fix: Lift the leaves out and leave the grit at the bottom.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring washed leaves and their water out together, so that the grit lands back on them.

mistakes.fix: Taste as you go, and stop while they still have bite.
mistakes.mistake: Rinsing sauerkraut or capers until none of their sharpness is left.

quiz.because: Cold water carries away loose material or excess brine, depending on the food.
choices: Only dirt visible on the outside.
Loose grit, starch or excess brine.
All salt and flavour throughout the food.
quiz.question: What can rinsing remove from food?

quiz.because: Lifting separates the leaves from grit that has settled beneath them.
choices: Tip leaves and water through a sieve together.
Stir the grit back up before draining.
Lift them out before emptying the bowl.
quiz.question: How should washed leaves leave a bowl of water?

quiz.because: Rinsing should moderate excess brine without washing away the food’s intended character.
choices: It remains pleasantly salty without harsh brine.
It loses every trace of sharpness.
It tastes exactly as harsh as before.
quiz.question: What tasting cue guides rinsing brined food?

quiz.because: Checking flavour prevents excessive rinsing from removing the sharpness that makes the ingredient useful.
choices: Rinse longer to equalise their flavour.
Taste as you rinse and stop while they retain bite.
Soak them in fresh water until bland.
quiz.question: Rinsed capers lost their sharpness. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: Roasting is searing done by an oven: the same dry surface and the same patience, on a larger piece.

cues.text: A deep golden-brown surface, and browned juices stuck to the tin.
A rich roasting smell fills the kitchen well before the food is done.
A steady sizzle from the tin.

technique/roast.does: Cooks food uncovered in the dry heat of a hot oven, so that the outside browns while the inside cooks in its own juices.
how: Dry the surface of the food well.
Season it, and rub it with a little fat.
Set it in a tin that fits it without crowding, in an oven that is fully hot.
Turn it or baste it now and then, so that it browns evenly.
Rest it before carving, and make a jus from what is left in the tin.

intro.what: Roasting uses the dry heat of an oven to brown food in an uncovered tin.
intro.why: It connects surface dryness and space in the tin with browning and the juices left for a sauce.

mistakes.fix: Leave space around every piece, or use a second tin.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the tin, so that the food steams and stays pale.

mistakes.fix: Rest it first, loosely covered.
mistakes.mistake: Carving a roast straight from the oven.

quiz.because: Uncovered dry oven heat browns the outside of the food.
choices: A browned surface.
A deliberately pale, steamed surface.
A surface submerged in stock.
quiz.question: What does the uncovered dry heat of roasting help develop?

quiz.because: Start with a dry surface before seasoning and adding a little fat.
choices: Soak the surface and leave it wet.
Dry the surface well.
Wrap the food tightly in foil.
quiz.question: What do you do to the surface before seasoning and adding fat?

quiz.because: A golden-brown surface and browned juices in the tin show the browning this method develops.
choices: A pale surface in pooled water.
A wet, pale surface with little colour in the tin.
A golden-brown surface and browned juices in the tin.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches the browning described here?

quiz.because: Crowded pieces steam and stay pale. More space, or another tin, gives them room to brown.
choices: Leave room around the pieces or use another tin.
Pack more food into the same tin.
Cover the tin tightly to trap steam.
quiz.question: Food in a crowded tin is steaming and staying pale. What would you change?

cues.text: A deep, warm scent fills the kitchen. A sharp, bitter smell means they are scorched.
The spices turn a shade darker and the seeds begin to smoke very lightly.

technique/roast-spices.does: Roasts whole spices in a dry, heavy pan over a low heat until they darken a shade and smell strong, then cools them, so that they can be ground into a blend or a powder that keeps its scent.
how: Set a heavy dry pan over a low heat and let it warm.
Add the spices that take the longest first, such as coriander seed and cumin, and the softer ones a little later. Roast each at its own pace if they differ.
Stir or shake all the while so that nothing sits and scorches.
Tip the spices out onto a cold plate the moment they smell strong and have darkened a shade.
Let them cool completely before grinding, so that the powder does not turn damp or gummy.

intro.what: Roasting whole spices in a dry pan deepens their aroma before grinding.
intro.why: It teaches you to judge fragrant warmth, avoid scorching and account for spices that heat at different rates.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat low and take your time.
mistakes.mistake: Roasting on a high heat, so that the outsides scorch while the insides stay raw.

mistakes.fix: Roast the hard ones first, or roast each kind in turn.
mistakes.mistake: Roasting all the spices together when they take different times.

mistakes.fix: Cool them completely first.
mistakes.mistake: Grinding the spices while they are still hot, so that the powder clumps.

quiz.because: Gentle dry heat develops the scent before the spices are cooled and ground.
choices: To make them absorb cooking fat.
To leave their aroma unchanged.
To develop a deeper warm aroma.
quiz.question: Why dry-roast whole spices before grinding?

quiz.because: Different spices can scorch at different rates, so staggered or separate roasting allows closer control.
choices: Start slower ones first or roast kinds separately.
Add them together and wait for the hardest to darken.
Add the softest first and leave them longest.
quiz.question: How should spices with different roasting speeds be handled?

quiz.because: A bitter sharp smell signals scorching rather than the warm aroma sought from roasting.
choices: A deep warm scent.
A sharp bitter smell.
A strengthening fragrant aroma.
quiz.question: Which smell suggests spices have scorched?

quiz.because: Grinding hot spices can leave a damp or gummy powder; cooling first helps it stay loose.
choices: Grind them while still hot.
Keep them covered in the warm pan.
Cool the spices completely before grinding.
quiz.question: Freshly ground roasted spices clumped. What would you change before grinding the next batch?

variant_of.differs: Toasting browns one food for a short while. Here a mix of whole spices is roasted slowly, each at its own pace, as the first step of making a blend, and then cooled and ground, and nothing is left whole to garnish.

comes_after.why: Rolling is wrapping with a flat wrapper, so a cook who can close a wrapper snugly rolls neater.

cues.text: The roll is even in width, with the ends tucked in and the seam underneath.
A finished roll is firm and gives slightly when pressed.

technique/roll.does: Rolls a flat wrapper, such as a leaf, a sheet of dough or a thin pancake, up around a line of filling into a neat cylinder, with the ends folded in so that nothing can fall out.
how: Soften the wrapper if it is stiff, by blanching a leaf or covering a sheet of dough with a damp cloth.
Lay it flat with the side that should show on the outside facing down, and set a line of filling near the edge closest to you.
Fold that edge over the filling and fold the sides in towards the middle.
Roll away from you, firm but not tight, and set the roll down with its seam underneath.

intro.what: Rolling encloses filling in a leaf, dough sheet or thin pancake.
intro.why: It teaches you to balance filling, wrapper flexibility and firm shaping without stretching the wrapper.

mistakes.fix: Use a thin line of filling and leave room at the ends.
mistakes.mistake: Overfilling, so that the roll splits when the filling swells.

mistakes.fix: Roll firmly, keep the seam underneath and pack the rolls snugly in the pot.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling loosely, so that the roll unwinds as it cooks.

mistakes.fix: Soften it first with a quick blanch or a damp cloth.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling a brittle leaf or sheet that cracks.

quiz.because: Tucked sides close the ends as the wrapper forms a cylinder.
choices: To keep filling enclosed at the ends.
To make the wrapper narrower than its filling.
To leave openings for filling to expand through.
quiz.question: Why fold in the sides before rolling?

quiz.because: The weight of the roll helps hold an underside seam closed.
choices: Facing upward.
Underneath the roll.
Along an unsupported outer edge.
quiz.question: Where should the finished seam sit?

quiz.because: A little give allows a firm enclosure without straining the wrapper.
choices: Loose enough to unwind.
Stretched taut around the filling.
Firm with a little give.
quiz.question: How should a shaped roll feel?

quiz.because: A softened leaf or sheet bends around filling more readily than a brittle one.
choices: Soften it with the method suited to the wrapper.
Add more filling to support it.
Roll it more tightly while dry.
quiz.question: A brittle wrapper cracks while rolling. What comes first?

variant_of.differs: The wrapper is a flat sheet that is rolled up round the filling into a cylinder with its ends folded in, and not folded into a parcel.

comes_after.why: The first half of an omelette is a fast scramble. A cook who can stop a scramble in time can stop an omelette in time.

cues.text: A pale yellow, smooth skin with no brown. The top still glistens when you start to roll.
The omelette slides freely when the pan is shaken.

technique/roll-an-omelette.does: Sets beaten eggs into a thin, tender sheet with a creamy middle, and rolls it into a smooth, pale cylinder.
how: Heat butter in a pan over medium heat until it foams and the foam starts to fall.
Pour in the beaten eggs and stir fast in small circles while shaking the pan.
Stop stirring when the eggs are mostly set but still wet on top, and let the bottom firm for a moment.
Scatter any filling down the middle.
Tilt the pan, fold the near edge over, and roll the omelette to the far lip.
Turn it out onto the plate, seam side down.

intro.what: This French-style omelette method forms beaten eggs into a pale sheet and rolls it into a smooth cylinder.
intro.why: It teaches you to coordinate stirring, pan movement and folding while controlling surface colour.

mistakes.fix: Lift the pan off the heat while you stir, and turn the heat down.
mistakes.mistake: The pan is too hot, so the skin browns and turns leathery.

mistakes.fix: Roll while the top is still wet. The heat inside finishes it.
mistakes.mistake: Waiting for the top to dry before rolling, which leaves the middle firm and dull.

quiz.because: This French-style omelette is rolled into a smooth cylinder with a pale surface, rather than browned or broken into curds.
choices: A deeply browned flat round.
A smooth, pale cylinder.
Loose browned curds.
quiz.question: Which shape and surface does this omelette method aim for?

quiz.because: Stirring in small circles while shaking the pan helps form the thin sheet that you will roll.
choices: Leave the pan still and never stir.
Wait for the bottom to brown before moving the eggs.
Stir in small circles while shaking the pan.
quiz.question: After pouring in the eggs, how do you move the eggs and pan?

quiz.because: An omelette that slides freely is not stuck to the pan, so you can begin folding and rolling it.
choices: It slides freely when the pan is shaken.
It stays firmly stuck despite shaking.
Its skin becomes brown and leathery.
quiz.question: Which pan movement suggests the omelette is free enough to roll?

quiz.because: Excess heat browns and toughens the skin. Lift the pan away while stirring and lower the heat.
choices: Raise the heat to speed up the rolling.
Lift the pan off the heat while stirring and turn the heat down.
Press the eggs into the hot pan without moving them.
quiz.question: The skin is browning and becoming leathery. What should you change?

cues.text: Each layer is thin, and the finished block shows many thin spirals.
The block is springy and tender, and holds together when lifted.

technique/roll-in-layers.does: Cooks a thin layer of egg in a pan, rolls it up while it is still soft, then pours more egg into the room left behind, cooks it and rolls again, so that the block grows layer upon layer.
how: Oil the pan and heat it. Pour in a thin layer of beaten egg and tilt it to cover the pan.
When the egg is almost set but still wet on top, roll it up toward the far side with chopsticks or a spatula.
Push the roll to the far side, oil the empty part and pour in more egg, lifting the roll so that the egg runs under it.
When it is nearly set, roll the block back toward you around the first one.
Repeat until the egg is used up, and turn out the finished block.

intro.what: This Japanese-style egg method rolls successive thin layers into a tender block.
intro.why: It teaches you to coordinate setting and rolling so each new layer joins the previous roll.

mistakes.fix: Pour in just enough to coat the pan thinly.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in too much egg, so that the layers are thick and hard to roll.

mistakes.fix: Roll while the top is still wet.
mistakes.mistake: Waiting until the egg is fully set before rolling, so that the layers will not join.

quiz.because: Rolling each thin layer around the earlier roll builds the layered structure.
choices: Successive thin egg layers rolled around the earlier roll.
A thick egg sheet folded only after cooling.
Loose curds pressed together at the end.
quiz.question: What builds the layered egg block?

quiz.because: Fresh egg beneath the roll helps the new layer join the block as it cooks.
choices: To let the roll dry before joining.
To let fresh egg run underneath it.
To remove the roll until the new sheet is firm.
quiz.question: Why lift the existing roll when adding more egg?

quiz.because: Thin layers wrapped successively remain visible as spirals through the block.
choices: A dense centre without visible layers.
Separate egg sheets that slide apart.
Many thin spirals in the finished block.
quiz.question: Which appearance shows the intended layered structure?

quiz.because: A still-moist surface allows neighbouring layers to bond instead of remaining separate sheets.
choices: Roll while the new layer is still wet on top.
Wait until each layer is completely dry.
Cool each sheet before rolling it.
quiz.question: The egg layers are not joining. What would you change for the next layer?

variant_of.differs: The egg is cooked and rolled in several thin layers, each one added while the roll is still moist, so the result is a firm, layered block and not one creamy cylinder.

comes_after.why: A dough has to be smooth and rested before it rolls out evenly without tearing.

cues.text: The sheet is even, with no thick middle or thin rim and no tears.
The dough slides freely on the surface when it is nudged.

technique/roll-out.does: Flattens a dough with a rolling pin into an even sheet of the thickness the dish asks for, whether thin enough to see through, for a filled pastry, or thick enough to stay soft, for a flat bread.
how: Rest the dough first, or it will spring back. Shape it into a flat round or square before the pin touches it.
Dust the surface and the pin lightly with flour, so that the dough slides and does not stick.
Roll from the middle outwards in one steady push, lift and give the dough a quarter turn, and roll again.
Turn the dough over now and then and dust again only where it sticks.
Stop when the sheet is even from edge to edge. Let it rest and spring back before it is cut or filled.

intro.what: Rolling out flattens rested dough into an even sheet with a pin.
intro.why: It teaches you to balance dough relaxation, light flouring and controlled pressure.

mistakes.fix: Cover it and let it rest, then roll again.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling a tense dough that keeps shrinking back.

mistakes.fix: Use only as much as it takes to stop it sticking, and brush off the extra.
mistakes.mistake: Dusting with too much flour, which dries the dough and leaves white streaks.

mistakes.fix: Roll from the middle outwards and stop short of the edge.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling over the edges, which leaves them thin and the middle thick.

quiz.because: Even thickness makes the sheet behave consistently when cut, filled or cooked.
choices: A thin rim surrounding a thick centre.
As much surface flour as the dough can take.
Even thickness suited to the dish.
quiz.question: What is the main aim when rolling out a dough sheet?

quiz.because: Working outward and turning spreads the dough while avoiding a persistently thick middle.
choices: In the middle, working outward while turning the dough.
At the rim, pressing toward the centre.
Across the edges repeatedly without turning.
quiz.question: Where should each rolling stroke begin?

quiz.because: A sheet that slides can be turned without pulling and tearing attached patches.
choices: It stretches while its base stays fixed.
It slides freely when nudged.
It tears whenever it is lifted.
quiz.question: Which feel suggests the sheet is not sticking?

quiz.because: Resting lets a tense dough relax; more force or flour does not address that resistance.
choices: Press harder until it stops resisting.
Keep adding flour while forcing it wider.
Cover it and let it rest before rolling again.
quiz.question: The dough keeps shrinking back under the pin. What should you do?

comes_after.why: The rounds are rolled from a rested atta dough, so the dough comes first.

cues.text: The round is even in thickness and has a smooth edge with no cracks.
It peels from the board without sticking and does not tear.

technique/roll-out-a-chapati.does: Rolls a ball of atta dough into a thin, even round, a little at a time, turning it often, so that it is the same thickness all over and puffs evenly when it is cooked.
how: Flatten a ball of dough in a dish of dry flour, coating both faces lightly.
Roll from the centre outwards with short, firm strokes. Give the dough a small turn after each stroke, so that it grows into a round.
Use just enough flour to stop it sticking. Shake off the extra, because burnt flour makes a bitter smell on the hot plate.
Stop when the round is thin and even from the middle to the edge, with no thick patches or tears.
Cook it at once. A rolled round that waits dries at the edge and tears when lifted.

intro.what: Rolling chapati turns atta dough into a thin even round for the hot plate.
intro.why: It teaches you how an even thickness and light dusting influence puffing and surface flavour.

mistakes.fix: Roll from the centre outwards and turn the dough after every stroke.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling thick in the middle and thin at the edge, so that it cooks unevenly and does not puff.

mistakes.fix: Dust lightly and shake off what is not needed.
mistakes.mistake: Using too much dry flour, which burns on the hot plate.

mistakes.fix: Cook each one as it is rolled.
mistakes.mistake: Stacking rolled rounds without flour, so that they stick.

quiz.because: An even round avoids thick patches that lag behind the rest during cooking.
choices: To keep the edge crisp while the middle stays thick.
To help it cook and puff evenly.
To make extra dusting flour unnecessary in every case.
quiz.question: Why aim for the same thickness across a chapati?

quiz.because: Turning distributes the rolling strokes around the dough and helps maintain a round shape.
choices: Leave it fixed and roll across the same line.
Stretch only its outer edge by hand.
Turn it a little while rolling from the centre outward.
quiz.question: How should the dough move between rolling strokes?

quiz.because: A consistent sheet without tears is easier to lift and cooks more evenly.
choices: Even thickness and a smooth edge without cracks.
A thick centre and translucent rim.
A cracked edge around a sticky middle.
quiz.question: Which sign suggests a well-rolled chapati round?

quiz.because: Dusting should prevent sticking; excess flour left on the surface can burn and taste bitter.
choices: Add a thicker flour coating before cooking.
Dust lightly and shake off excess before cooking.
Leave loose flour beneath each round.
quiz.question: Loose flour burns on the hot plate. What should change?

variant_of.differs: Each round is rolled alone, from a small ball, and cooked at once. The dough is soft and unrested between rolls. The aim is a thin, even disc that will puff, and not a sheet that holds its shape and is cut.

cues.text: Liquid has collected under the colander, and the pieces have gone limp and glossy.
A piece bends without snapping.

technique/salt-and-drain.does: Draws water out of a watery vegetable with salt before it is cooked or dressed, so that it keeps its bite and does not flood the dish.
how: Slice or dice the vegetable and toss it with fine salt.
Leave it in a colander over a bowl until it has given up its water.
Rinse off the salt if the dish will be salted again, and press or pat the pieces dry.

intro.what: Salting and draining draws excess water from watery vegetables before dressing or cooking.
intro.why: It teaches you to control the liquid a vegetable contributes to the finished dish.

mistakes.fix: Press it gently in a cloth before you use it.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the drying, so that the vegetable goes into the pan or the dressing still wet.

mistakes.fix: Taste before you add any more salt.
mistakes.mistake: Salting the dish as usual afterwards, so that it ends up far too salty.

quiz.because: Removing released water beforehand limits dilution of the pan or dressing.
choices: To retain all its water beneath the dressing.
To keep released water from flooding the dish.
To replace drying after rinsing.
quiz.question: Why salt and drain a watery vegetable?

quiz.because: A colander separates the vegetable from water as it is released.
choices: In their collected liquid.
In a sealed bowl without drainage.
In a colander over a bowl.
quiz.question: Where should salted vegetables drain?

quiz.because: Collected liquid and more flexible pieces show moisture leaving the vegetable.
choices: Liquid below the colander and limp glossy pieces.
Dry rigid pieces and no collected liquid.
Wet pieces sitting in their own liquid without drainage.
quiz.question: Which change shows water has been drawn out?

quiz.because: The vegetable already carries salt, so later seasoning needs adjustment.
choices: Salt the dressing as heavily as usual.
Taste before adding further salt.
Add more salt to finish drying the pieces.
quiz.question: The finished dish was too salty after this step. What would you change next time?

cues.text: The slices have gone limp and flexible.
The bitterness is softer.

technique/salt-and-squeeze.does: Rubs thin slices of a watery or bitter vegetable with salt, leaves them to wilt a little, and squeezes them by hand to wring out the bitter liquid. They keep a firm bite and a milder taste.
how: Slice the vegetable thin and put it in a bowl.
Sprinkle on salt and rub it in lightly with your hands.
Leave it for a short while until it has softened and given up water.
Squeeze the slices in a handful and pour off the liquid. Rinse and squeeze again if they are still harsh.

intro.what: Salting and squeezing wilts thin vegetable slices before pressing out liquid.
intro.why: It teaches you to soften harshness while preserving a firm bite instead of crushing the vegetable.

mistakes.fix: Sprinkle evenly and rub lightly.
mistakes.mistake: Adding salt in a heap, which makes the slices too salty.

mistakes.fix: Squeeze firmly but not to a pulp.
mistakes.mistake: Squeezing too hard, which bruises them.

quiz.because: Released liquid carries away some harshness while gentle squeezing preserves the slices.
choices: A stronger salty taste with the liquid retained.
Drier slices without changing their harshness.
A milder taste while retaining some bite.
quiz.question: What is the aim of salting and squeezing these slices?

quiz.because: Even distribution avoids intensely salty patches and helps the slices wilt consistently.
choices: Sprinkle evenly and rub it in lightly.
Leave it in a heap on top.
Add it only after squeezing the dry slices.
quiz.question: How should salt be applied?

quiz.because: Wilting makes thin slices bend and release liquid without needing to be pulped.
choices: Rigid and snapping.
Limp and flexible.
Crushed into a paste.
quiz.question: Which feel shows the slices are ready to squeeze?

quiz.because: The aim is to expel liquid while preserving a recognisable vegetable texture.
choices: Twist them harder to remove every trace of water.
Chop them more finely after squeezing.
Squeeze firmly but with less crushing pressure.
quiz.question: The slices became bruised and pulpy. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The slices are rubbed with salt and squeezed by hand to wring out the liquid, instead of being left to drain in a colander.

cues.text: Beads of water form on the skin, and the flesh looks firmer.
The fishy smell is less sharp.

technique/salt-fish.does: Sprinkles fresh fish with a little salt and leaves it for a short while before grilling or frying, to season it, firm the flesh and draw out the surface water and smell. It is not the long curing of salt cod.
how: Pat the fish dry.
Sprinkle salt evenly over both sides, and a little more on the tail and fins if the fish is whole.
Leave it at room temperature for a short while, until beads of water show on the skin.
Wipe the water off with paper and cook the fish at once.

intro.what: This brief salting method seasons fresh fish and draws water to its surface before cooking.
intro.why: It teaches you to manage surface moisture and distinguish brief seasoning from a long salt cure.

mistakes.fix: Salt lightly and evenly.
mistakes.mistake: Using too much salt, which makes the fish too salty.

mistakes.fix: Wipe it dry as soon as water shows and cook it.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it too long, so that it turns dry and hard.

quiz.because: The purpose is seasoning and surface moisture control, not preservation.
choices: It is brief surface seasoning before cooking.
It is a long drying cure.
It preserves fish for storage in salt.
quiz.question: How does this method differ from curing salt cod?

quiz.because: Wiping removes the surface water drawn out by the salt.
choices: Leave it pooled under the fish.
Wipe it away before cooking.
Rub it back in with more salt.
quiz.question: What should happen to the water that appears on the skin?

quiz.because: Surface droplets show that water has been drawn out and can now be wiped away.
choices: The fish becomes hard and dry.
A thick salt crust forms.
Beads of water appear on the skin.
quiz.question: Which visible change guides the end of this brief salting step?

quiz.because: A light even coating seasons the surface without excessive salt accumulation.
choices: Apply salt lightly and evenly.
Use a thicker salt coating in fewer places.
Leave the same heavy coating on longer.
quiz.question: The fish becomes too salty. What should change next time?

cues.text: The palms are damp and a little gritty with salt, and the rice no longer clings.
The outside of the shaped rice is lightly salty.

technique/salt-hands.does: Wets the hands and rubs salt over the palms before shaping warm rice, so that the rice does not stick and is lightly seasoned from the outside.
how: Keep a bowl of cold water and a small dish of salt beside the board.
Dip your fingers in the water and shake off the excess.
Rub a little salt over the palms and fingers.
Wet and salt your hands again for each portion.

intro.what: Dampening and lightly salting the hands helps shape warm rice without sticking.
intro.why: It teaches you how a small change at the contact surface controls handling and outside seasoning.

mistakes.fix: Rub on only a light dusting.
mistakes.mistake: Using too much salt, so that the rice is too salty.

mistakes.fix: Use cold water.
mistakes.mistake: Using hot water, which burns the hands and makes the rice stick.

quiz.because: Damp hands release the rice more easily while the salt contacts its outer surface.
choices: To make the rice release all its moisture.
To reduce sticking and lightly season the outside.
To season every grain equally throughout.
quiz.question: Why dampen and salt hands before shaping rice?

quiz.because: Light dampness helps release the rice without soaking its surface.
choices: Leave water dripping from the palms.
Dry the hands completely before shaping.
Shake off excess before rubbing on salt.
quiz.question: What should you do after dipping fingers in cold water?

quiz.because: A light salt dusting on damp hands aids handling without a heavy coating.
choices: Damp, lightly gritty, with rice releasing readily.
Dry and tacky with rice clinging.
Dripping wet with thick salt deposits.
quiz.question: Which feel matches prepared hands?

quiz.because: Surface seasoning comes from the hands, so reducing that dusting directly reduces salt on the rice.
choices: Rub on more salt before each portion.
Use a lighter dusting of salt on the hands.
Keep the heavy salt layer but shape harder.
quiz.question: The outside of the shaped rice tasted too salty. What would you change for the next portion?

cues.text: The filling shows evenly at the edge and does not squeeze out.
The pieces stick lightly to the filling.

technique/sandwich.does: Places a filling between flat pieces of soft bread or pancake, so that it holds together and is eaten in one hand.
how: Lay out the bottom pieces in a row.
Spoon or spread the filling on each, leaving a narrow edge clear.
Cover with the top pieces and press gently so that the filling spreads without spilling.
Pat the edges together, then serve.

intro.what: Sandwiching holds filling between flat pieces of bread or pancake.
intro.why: It teaches you to distribute filling so the layers hold together without spilling.

mistakes.fix: Spread a thin even layer and leave an edge.
mistakes.mistake: Overfilling, so that the filling is squeezed out.

mistakes.fix: Let them cool a little first.
mistakes.mistake: Using pieces that are too hot, which melts the filling.

quiz.because: Evenly distributed filling supports contact without being forced out at the edge.
choices: A mound of filling concentrated at the rim.
A top pressed hard against an overflowing filling.
An even filling layer that lightly joins the pieces.
quiz.question: What helps a filled sandwich hold together?

quiz.because: A clear edge gives filling room to spread under gentle pressure.
choices: Evenly, leaving a narrow clear edge.
Right over every edge.
As a tall central pile without spreading.
quiz.question: How should filling be spread before adding the top?

quiz.because: Even contact keeps the layers aligned and the filling contained.
choices: It bulges from a single side.
It shows evenly at the edge without squeezing out.
The top slides over an uneven mound.
quiz.question: Which appearance suggests the filling is well distributed?

quiz.because: Reducing heat transferred from the outer pieces helps the filling retain its intended texture.
choices: Press the top down harder while hot.
Add more filling to the hot pieces.
Let overly hot bread or pancake pieces cool a little.
quiz.question: The filling melted when the pieces were assembled. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: Sweating teaches how a pan sounds and looks on low heat. Sautéing asks for the same watchfulness at speed.

cues.text: A lively sizzle from the moment the food goes in. If it falls silent, the pan is too full or too cool.
Golden-brown edges, and a dry pan with no liquid pooling in it.

technique/saute.does: Cooks small pieces fast in a hot pan with a little fat, moving them so that they brown on all sides.
how: Heat the pan first, then the fat, until the fat shimmers.
Add the food in a single layer, with room between the pieces.
Leave it a moment to take colour, then toss or stir.
Keep the heat high and the food moving until it is browned outside and just tender inside.

intro.what: Sautéing cooks small pieces quickly in a hot pan with a little fat.
intro.why: It teaches you to use space, movement and the sound of the pan to encourage browning.

mistakes.fix: Cook in batches, and let the pan heat up again between them.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, so the food steams and turns grey.

mistakes.fix: Salt mushrooms, courgette and aubergine near the end.
mistakes.mistake: Salting watery vegetables at the start, which draws their water into the pan.

quiz.because: Crowding makes food steam instead of brown. Space between the pieces helps them colour.
choices: To make them steam in pooled liquid.
To keep the pan cool.
To help them brown instead of steaming.
quiz.question: Why leave room between the pieces when sautéing?

quiz.because: Heat the pan first, then the fat, and add the food when the fat shimmers.
choices: The pan, then the fat.
The food in a cold pan.
The fat in a separate pan before transferring it.
quiz.question: What is heated first in this method?

quiz.because: Golden edges and no pooled liquid show browning rather than steaming in a wet pan.
choices: Grey pieces sitting in pooled liquid.
Golden edges with no liquid pooling in the pan.
Pale, wet pieces in a crowded heap.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches the intended result?

quiz.because: Smaller batches avoid crowding. Let the pan reheat between them so each batch starts in a hot pan.
choices: Raise the heat and keep the full batch in the pan.
Stir the full batch continuously without letting the pan reheat.
Cook smaller batches and reheat the pan between them.
quiz.question: The pan is crowded and the food is steaming. What should you change?

cues.text: The skin is smooth under a finger run from tail to head, with no rough edge.
A dry rasping sound as the scales lift. It goes quiet once the skin is bare.

technique/scale-a-fish.does: Scrapes the scales off the skin of a whole fish, so that none are left to catch in the mouth or to make the skin gritty.
how: Hold the fish firmly by the tail on a board that cannot slip. A deep sink or a large tray catches the flying scales.
With the back of a knife, scrape from the tail towards the head in short firm strokes, against the way the scales lie.
Turn the fish over and do the other side. Go carefully round the fins, the belly and the base of the head, where scales hide.
Rinse the fish under cold water and run a finger from tail to head to find any scale that is left.

intro.what: Scaling scrapes the overlapping scales from fish skin before further preparation.
intro.why: It teaches you to work against the direction of the scales while preserving the skin.

mistakes.fix: Scrape from the tail towards the head, against the scales.
mistakes.mistake: Scraping from the head towards the tail, which only presses the scales flat.

mistakes.fix: Use the back of the blade, in short firm strokes.
mistakes.mistake: Using the sharp edge of the knife, which cuts the skin.

quiz.because: Scaling cleans the skin surface while leaving the skin itself intact.
choices: To avoid rough gritty scales in the finished skin.
To cut the flesh into portions.
To remove the skin along with the scales.
quiz.question: Why remove scales from fish skin?

quiz.because: Working against their overlap lifts scales; the blunt back limits cutting into the skin.
choices: Long strokes with the sharp edge from head toward tail.
Short strokes with the back of the blade from tail toward head.
Smooth strokes along the direction the scales lie.
quiz.question: Which tool movement lifts scales?

quiz.because: Feeling against the scale direction catches edges that might otherwise lie flat.
choices: Feel only from head toward tail.
Look only at the centre of the side.
Run a finger from tail toward head for rough edges.
quiz.question: How can remaining scales be found after rinsing?

quiz.because: Changing direction works against the overlap and lifts the scales rather than smoothing them down.
choices: Work from tail toward head.
Continue from head toward tail with more force.
Switch to cutting through the skin.
quiz.question: Scraping presses scales flat instead of lifting them. What should change?

cues.text: A neat pattern of diamonds, with white fat in every cut and no red flesh showing.

technique/score.does: Cuts shallow lines through skin or fat, so that the fat can melt out and the skin crisps without curling.
how: Chill the piece so that the fat is firm.
Draw a sharp knife across the fat in parallel lines a finger apart, cutting through the fat but not into the flesh.
Turn the piece and cut across the first lines to make diamonds.

intro.what: Scoring makes shallow cuts through skin or fat without cutting into the flesh.
intro.why: It teaches you to control knife depth so fat can render and skin can crisp without unnecessary damage below.

mistakes.fix: Use the tip of the knife with a light hand, and stop when the colour changes.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting into the flesh, so that the meat loses juice and dries where it was cut.

quiz.because: Shallow openings allow fat to escape and reduce the pull that can curl skin.
choices: Deep cuts through the flesh for portioning.
Rendering and crisping without curling.
Keeping melted fat trapped under the skin.
quiz.question: What is scoring skin or fat intended to encourage?

quiz.because: Firm fat offers a more controlled surface for shallow knife work.
choices: Soft warm fat guides the knife more evenly.
Chilling makes deep flesh cuts necessary.
Firm fat is easier to cut precisely.
quiz.question: Why chill the piece before scoring?

quiz.because: The colour beneath each cut helps distinguish fat from flesh.
choices: White fat in the cuts without red flesh showing.
Red flesh visible along every line.
Deep gaps passing through the piece.
quiz.question: Which appearance suggests cuts stayed within the fat?

quiz.because: Light shallow cuts preserve the flesh while opening the fat layer.
choices: Press harder to keep all cuts equally deep.
Use a light hand and stop when the colour changes.
Warm the fat until it smears.
quiz.question: The knife keeps cutting into the meat. What should change?

comes_after.why: The eggs are whisked before they are scrambled.

cues.text: Small, glossy curds held in a thick, creamy sauce, with no dry or browned bits.
The spoon leaves a trail that closes slowly.

technique/scramble.does: Stirs beaten eggs over gentle heat until they set into small, soft, creamy curds.
how: Whisk the eggs with salt until no streaks of white are left.
Melt butter in a pan over low heat until it foams.
Pour in the eggs and stir without stopping, scraping the bottom and the corners.
Lift the pan off the heat whenever the curds form too fast, and keep stirring.
Stop while the eggs still look wet, and stir in a little cold butter or cream to halt the cooking.

intro.what: This gentle scramble method stirs beaten eggs into small, soft, creamy curds.
intro.why: It teaches you to respond to texture by stirring and moving the pan away from excess heat.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat low and take the pan off it often.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking over high heat, which gives large, dry, rubbery curds that weep water.

mistakes.fix: Take them off while they still look too wet. They go on setting on the way to the plate.
mistakes.mistake: Waiting until the eggs look done in the pan.

quiz.because: This gentle method aims for small, soft, creamy curds rather than large, dry ones.
choices: Small, soft, creamy curds.
Large, dry, rubbery curds.
A firm sheet for rolling.
quiz.question: Which texture is the aim of this scramble method?

quiz.because: Stir continuously and scrape the bottom and corners so you do not leave eggs sitting against the hot pan.
choices: Only across the surface, leaving the base untouched.
Continuously, scraping the bottom and corners.
Only after a browned layer has formed.
quiz.question: How do you stir the eggs for this gentle scramble?

quiz.because: A spoon trail that closes slowly matches the thick, creamy texture of this scramble.
choices: A dry gap that never closes.
No trail in a completely watery mixture.
A trail that closes slowly.
quiz.question: Which spoon trail matches the texture described here?

quiz.because: Fast-forming curds signal too much heat for this gentle method. Lift the pan away and keep stirring.
choices: Lift the pan off the heat and keep stirring.
Keep the pan on the heat and stir faster.
Reduce stirring so the curds have time to join together.
quiz.question: The curds are forming too fast. What would you do?

comes_after.why: The pot is filled in layers first, and sealed only when everything is in.

cues.text: An unbroken ring of paste all round the join, with no gap for steam to find.
The paste is pliable and does not crack when it is rolled.

technique/seal-with-dough.does: Closes the gap between a pot and its lid with a rope of plain flour paste, so that no steam leaves during a long, slow bake. The seal is broken open at the table.
how: Mix flour with just enough water to make a stiff paste that rolls between the hands and does not stick.
Fill the pot, then put the lid on.
Roll the paste into a rope long enough to go round the rim.
Press the rope into the join where the lid meets the pot, and smooth it into both sides with a wet finger. Leave no gap.
Bake without lifting the lid. Break the seal open when the pot is brought to the table.

intro.what: A flour-paste rope seals the join between a pot and its lid for a slow bake.
intro.why: It teaches you how retaining steam limits liquid loss from a covered dish.

mistakes.fix: Work in more flour until it is stiff.
mistakes.mistake: Making the paste too wet, so that it runs and does not hold.

mistakes.fix: Run a wet finger round the whole join before the pot goes in the oven.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving a gap in the ring, so that steam escapes and the liquid cooks away.

quiz.because: Closing the join helps retain moisture during the covered bake.
choices: The rate of browning on an uncovered surface.
The thickness of the food inside the pot.
Steam escaping through the lid join.
quiz.question: What does the dough ring control?

quiz.because: The seal works by closing the route where steam would otherwise leave.
choices: Into the join between the lid and pot.
On top of the lid without covering its join to the pot.
Around the pot below the join, leaving the gap open.
quiz.question: Where should the paste rope be pressed?

quiz.because: A continuous ring closes the join all around the pot.
choices: Separate pieces with openings between them.
An unbroken ring without gaps.
A rope that has slipped down the outside.
quiz.question: Which appearance suggests the join is sealed?

quiz.because: A stiff paste stays in the join instead of sliding away and exposing gaps.
choices: Add more water to make it easier to spread.
Leave a thinner wet coating around the rim.
Work in flour until it becomes stiff and pliable.
quiz.question: The paste runs instead of holding its shape. What should change?

comes_after.why: Sautéing teaches a hot pan and room between the pieces. Searing adds the hardest part: leaving the food alone.

cues.text: A loud, steady sizzle that does not fade. A weak hiss means the pan was not hot enough.
A deep brown crust, and a brown line climbing the side of the piece.
The piece lets go of the pan when it is ready to turn. If it sticks, it is not ready.

technique/sear.does: Browns the surface of meat or fish fast in a very hot pan, building a crust full of flavour while the inside stays underdone.
how: Dry the surface well. Wet food steams before it browns.
Salt it just before it goes in.
Heat a heavy pan until a thin film of oil shimmers and gives off its first wisp of smoke.
Lay the food in away from you and press it flat. Then leave it alone.
Turn it when it lifts off the pan by itself and the underside is deep brown.
Take it out to rest. The crust left on the pan is the fond for a sauce.

intro.what: Searing browns the surface of meat or fish quickly in a very hot pan.
intro.why: It teaches you to control surface moisture and pan contact to build a flavourful crust.

mistakes.fix: Leave it until it releases by itself.
mistakes.mistake: Moving the food before it has browned, which tears the crust and leaves it on the pan.

mistakes.fix: Sear in batches with space between the pieces, and let the pan heat up again.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, so that the pieces stew in their own juice and turn grey.

mistakes.fix: Pat it dry with paper on every side first.
mistakes.mistake: Putting food in the pan while its surface is wet.

quiz.because: Fast surface browning builds a crust full of flavour.
choices: To stew the food in its juices.
To build a browned, flavourful surface crust.
To keep the surface pale and wet.
quiz.question: What is the main aim of searing?

quiz.because: Wet food steams before it browns. Dry the surface well before it meets the pan.
choices: Leave the surface dripping wet.
Submerge it in stock.
Dry its surface well.
quiz.question: What does this method do before the food meets the pan?

quiz.because: In this method, a deep brown underside and release from the pan are cues to turn rather than pull at a stuck surface.
choices: It releases from the pan and has a deep brown underside.
It is still stuck and pale underneath.
Its surface is wet and the pan has fallen silent.
quiz.question: Which cue does this method use before turning a piece?

quiz.because: Crowding makes pieces stew in their juices. Use batches with space between pieces and let the pan reheat.
choices: Pack them closer to increase contact.
Sear in batches with room between pieces and reheat between them.
Cover the pan to trap more liquid.
quiz.question: Crowded pieces are stewing in their own juices. What would you change?

cues.text: The dish tastes more of itself and not of salt. It is bright, and nothing sticks out.

technique/season.does: Brings out the taste of a dish with salt, and balances it with pepper, acid or fat.
how: Salt in small steps as the dish cooks, not only at the end.
Taste before serving, from a clean spoon.
Add a little salt if the dish tastes flat, and a few drops of acid if it tastes dull or heavy.
Stir, wait a moment and taste again.

intro.what: Seasoning adjusts salt, acid, pepper or fat to balance a dish.
intro.why: It teaches you to taste, change a little and taste again rather than rely on a fixed addition.

mistakes.fix: Salt lightly anything that will reduce, and correct it at the end.
mistakes.mistake: Salting a liquid fully before it has boiled down, so that it ends up too salty.

mistakes.fix: Taste every time. No amount on paper replaces it.
mistakes.mistake: Seasoning without tasting.

quiz.because: Balance lets the ingredients taste more distinct without an addition overwhelming them.
choices: The flavour of the dish rather than a dominant salt taste.
The strongest possible salt taste.
The same sharpness in every dish.
quiz.question: What should successful seasoning bring forward?

quiz.because: Mixing distributes the addition so the next taste reflects the whole dish.
choices: Keep adding before mixing.
Stir, pause and taste again.
Judge the final dish from the dry seasoning alone.
quiz.question: What should follow a small seasoning addition?

quiz.because: Balanced seasoning supports the dish’s own flavours rather than replacing them.
choices: Salt dominates the other flavours.
Acid masks all the other ingredients.
Bright and clear, with nothing standing out harshly.
quiz.question: Which taste suggests seasoning is balanced?

quiz.because: Reduction concentrates salt with the liquid, so final adjustment should reflect its reduced state.
choices: Salt lightly before reducing and adjust at the end.
Add the full final seasoning before reduction.
Add more salt as the volume falls.
quiz.question: A reduced sauce ended up too salty. What would you change next time?

cues.text: The white is clear, with no streak of yellow in it, and the yolk is whole and round.

technique/separate-eggs.does: Parts the yolk of an egg from its white, so that each can be used alone: the yolks to enrich or thicken, the whites to whip.
how: Set out a small bowl to separate over, and a larger bowl for the whites that are clean.
Crack the egg on a flat surface, not on a rim, and open it over the small bowl with the yolk in one half of the shell.
Pass the yolk gently from one half of the shell to the other until the white has run into the bowl.
Tip the yolk into its own bowl, and move the white to the larger bowl only when it is clean.

intro.what: Separating eggs keeps yolks and whites apart for their different cooking roles.
intro.why: It teaches you to protect whites intended for whipping while reserving yolks for richness or thickening.

mistakes.fix: Separate each egg over a small bowl first, and lift out any speck with a piece of shell.
mistakes.mistake: Letting a speck of yolk fall into the whites, which then will not whip.

mistakes.fix: Crack it on a flat surface.
mistakes.mistake: Cracking the egg on the rim of a bowl, which pushes in shell and breaks the yolk.

quiz.because: Each part has useful properties that a recipe may need independently.
choices: To use the whites for richness and the yolks as the only whipping part.
Yolks enrich or thicken while whites can be whipped.
To whip both parts together after checking their colour.
quiz.question: Why separate eggs for different preparations?

quiz.because: An isolated egg can be checked without contaminating the whole bowl with yolk.
choices: To mix any broken yolk into all the whites immediately.
To avoid needing a separate place for yolks.
To check the white before adding it to the collected whites.
quiz.question: Why separate each egg over a small bowl first?

quiz.because: Yellow streaks indicate yolk contamination, which interferes with whipping the whites.
choices: Clear whites without yellow streaks.
Whites with a broken yolk mixed through.
A uniformly yellow liquid.
quiz.question: Which appearance suits whites intended for whipping?

quiz.because: A flat cracking surface reduces the rim pushing shell inward and damaging the yolk.
choices: Strike harder against the sharp rim.
Crack them on a flat surface.
Open each egg directly into the collected whites.
quiz.question: Cracking eggs on a bowl rim keeps breaking yolks. What should change?

cues.text: The surface loses its wet shine and the edge pulls cleanly from the tin.
A light press on the middle springs back, and a cut leaves a clean face.

technique/set.does: Leaves a hot, cooked mixture to cool undisturbed in its mould or tin until it firms enough to hold its shape and be cut.
how: Pour or spoon the mixture into the mould or tin while it is still hot. Press it into the corners and smooth the top.
Leave it somewhere cool and still. Do not stir it, shake it or cut it while it sets.
Let it cool right through before it is cut or turned out. Chill it only if the dish asks for it.
Cut with a thin knife dipped in hot water, or run the knife round the edge and turn it out onto a plate.

intro.what: Setting lets a cooked mixture cool undisturbed until it can hold a cut shape.
intro.why: It teaches you to distinguish a hot flowing texture from the structure that develops during cooling.

mistakes.fix: Wait until it has cooled right through.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting or turning it out while it is still warm, so that it slumps.

mistakes.fix: Leave it still in a cool place.
mistakes.mistake: Moving the tin while it sets, which cracks the surface.

mistakes.fix: Cook it longer next time, until it comes away from the sides of the pan before it is poured.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in a mixture that was cooked too little, so that it never firms.

quiz.because: The mixture gains structure as it cools, allowing cutting or unmoulding.
choices: To let it firm enough to hold its shape.
To keep it flowing for pouring.
To create a browned surface crust.
quiz.question: What is the purpose of setting a mixture in a mould?

quiz.because: Movement disturbs a developing set and can crack the surface.
choices: Stir repeatedly to keep the surface soft.
Leave it still rather than stirring or shaking.
Shake often to loosen its edges.
quiz.question: How should the mould be handled during setting?

quiz.because: A clean stable face indicates structure through the mixture rather than only at its surface.
choices: A loose centre flowing into the cut.
A warm mound that slumps after slicing.
A clean face that holds its shape.
quiz.question: Which cut suggests the mixture has set?

quiz.because: Cooling through the centre allows the interior to support the shape.
choices: Wait until it has cooled throughout.
Unmould earlier while it is more fluid.
Stir it repeatedly during cooling.
quiz.question: The shape slumped when turned out while still warm. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: Setting is chilling a liquid until it holds, so a cook has to be able to chill evenly first.

cues.text: The cooled jelly runs slowly off a spoon and leaves a thin coat.
A finished set trembles when the dish is shaken, and holds its shape when it is cut.

technique/set-in-aspic.does: Holds cooked food in a clear, savoury jelly, which sets as it cools and turns a loose mixture into a firm block that can be turned out and cut in slices.
how: Make the jelly from a clear, well-flavoured stock with enough gelatin to hold it. Soak the gelatin in cold water first, then melt it into the warm stock.
Let the jelly cool until it is syrupy and just starting to thicken, before it meets the food.
Pack the cooked food loosely into a deep dish, with herbs between the layers.
Pour the jelly over the food until it is covered, and press gently so that it runs into every gap.
Chill until it is firm throughout. To turn it out, dip the dish briefly in hot water and tip it over a plate.

intro.what: Aspic surrounds cooked food in a clear savoury jelly that firms as it cools.
intro.why: It teaches you to coordinate jelly thickness, filling distribution and chilling for a sliceable shape.

mistakes.fix: Use less, and aim for a gentle tremble.
mistakes.mistake: Using too much gelatin, so that the jelly turns stiff and rubbery.

mistakes.fix: Let it cool until it starts to thicken.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring the jelly on while it is still hot, so that the herbs turn dull and the pieces rise to the top.

mistakes.fix: Leave it to chill until it is firm all the way through.
mistakes.mistake: Turning the set out too early, while the centre is still loose.

quiz.because: The cooling jelly binds the arranged pieces into a shape that can be turned out and sliced.
choices: A hot sauce meant to stay fluid.
A dry crumb coating around separate pieces.
A savoury jelly that holds the food in a sliceable shape.
quiz.question: What does aspic contribute to the assembled dish?

quiz.because: Slight thickening helps suspend the pieces without the jelly being too firm to fill gaps.
choices: When cooled to a syrupy texture and beginning to thicken.
While still very hot and freely flowing.
Only after it has formed a solid block.
quiz.question: When should the jelly meet the food?

quiz.because: A gentle set supports the food without the rubbery texture of excessive gelatin.
choices: A stiff rubbery resistance.
A gentle tremble while holding its shape when cut.
A liquid centre that flows out on slicing.
quiz.question: Which feel suits a finished aspic set?

quiz.because: Too much gelatin makes a rigid texture; reducing it changes the strength of the set.
choices: Add more gelatin for stronger slices.
Chill the same overly firm mixture longer.
Use less gelatin and aim for a gentle tremble.
quiz.question: The jelly is stiff and rubbery. What should change next time?

cues.text: The sauce goes from clear and oily to pale and creamy.
The pan grows heavier to move as the sauce thickens.

technique/shake-the-pan.does: Moves fish that gives up its own gelatine in a pan by holding the handle and shaking the pan in small circles, with no spoon or whisk, so that delicate pieces stay whole while the oil and the juices slowly bind into a creamy sauce.
how: Use a wide pan, with the fish in a single layer in a little oil and a splash of liquid, over a low, steady heat.
Hold the handle and shake the pan back and forth in small circles, so that the sauce swirls round the pieces.
Keep it up as the juices and the oil turn pale and creamy. Lift the pan off the heat for a moment if it starts to catch.
Add a splash of water if the sauce gets too thick, and stop when it coats the fish like a thin cream.

intro.what: This fish method shakes the pan so cooking juices and oil form a creamy sauce without stirring the pieces.
intro.why: It teaches you to build an emulsion through gentle pan movement while protecting delicate fish.

mistakes.fix: Shake the pan and leave the pieces alone.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring with a spoon, which breaks the fish into flakes.

mistakes.fix: Keep the heat low, and lift the pan off it for a moment when the sauce gets hot.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking over too high a heat, so that the sauce splits into oil and water.

quiz.because: Pan movement circulates the sauce without a spoon breaking the fish.
choices: To break the fish into the sauce deliberately.
To bind the sauce while keeping delicate pieces whole.
To keep oil and juices permanently separate.
quiz.question: Why shake this fish pan instead of stirring with a spoon?

quiz.because: Small circular movements swirl the liquid around intact pieces while gentle heat limits splitting.
choices: With hard vertical jolts over high heat.
By scraping the pieces across the base.
In small circles over low steady heat.
quiz.question: How should the pan move?

quiz.because: A pale creamy appearance shows oil and juices joining rather than separating.
choices: Clear oily liquid turns pale and creamy.
Clear oil forms a widening layer on top.
The fish breaks into flakes in thin liquid.
quiz.question: Which change shows the sauce binding?

quiz.because: Excess heat can split the sauce; reducing heat addresses the cause without damaging the fish.
choices: Increase the heat and shake harder.
Lower the heat and lift the pan away briefly.
Stir the fish vigorously with a spoon.
quiz.question: The sauce separates as the pan gets too hot. What should change?

variant_of.differs: Nothing is whisked. The pan is shaken in circles so that the oil and the juices of the fish bind into a sauce while the pieces stay whole.

cues.text: Pieces of one size with smooth surfaces and no cracks.
The piece holds when it is lifted, and gives a little under a finger.

technique/shape.does: Forms a soft mixture into even pieces that hold together when they are cooked.
how: Chill the mixture first. A cold mixture holds its shape and does not stick.
For quenelles, dip a pair of spoons in hot water, scoop the mixture with the first, and pass it back and forth between them until its sides are smooth.
For patties and balls, wet your hands and press lightly, only until the piece holds.
Make every piece the same size, so that they cook in the same time.

intro.what: This shaping method forms chilled soft mixtures into smooth even portions.
intro.why: It teaches you to judge cohesion and use minimal handling for a lighter texture.

mistakes.fix: Handle it as little as you can.
mistakes.mistake: Working the mixture for too long or pressing it hard, which makes it dense and tough.

mistakes.fix: Chill it until it is firm before you start.
mistakes.mistake: Shaping a warm, loose mixture, which sticks to everything and falls apart in the pot.

quiz.because: Size consistency limits differences in how each portion responds to heat.
choices: To keep their cooking rates similar.
To make all mixtures equally firm.
To replace chilling a loose mixture.
quiz.question: Why make shaped portions similar in size?

quiz.because: Warm wet spoons release the mixture as it is passed between them to form smooth sides.
choices: Shape only with the edge of a single dry spoon.
Pass the mixture between spoons dipped in hot water.
Press the mixture onto the board with a dry spoon.
quiz.question: How are spoon-shaped quenelles smoothed?

quiz.because: A little give with sufficient cohesion avoids both slumping and excessive compaction.
choices: It runs off the spoon without a shape.
It is tightly packed and rigid.
It holds when lifted and gives a little when pressed.
quiz.question: Which feel suggests a portion is well shaped?

quiz.because: Chilling gives the mixture more body so it can hold its shape with gentler handling.
choices: Chill it until firm before shaping.
Press it harder while it stays warm.
Make larger portions from the same loose mixture.
quiz.question: A warm loose mixture sticks and falls apart. What should happen first?

comes_after.why: The mixture is kneaded until it holds before it is shaped.

cues.text: Each piece is an even oval with the print of the fingers along it.
The piece holds together when lifted and does not crumble.

technique/shape-a-finger-kofte.does: Squeezes a small lump of a soft, cool mixture in the closed fist, so that it takes the print of the fingers and comes out as a small ridged oval, with nothing cooked afterwards.
how: Keep a bowl of water beside the work and wet the hands lightly.
Take a small lump of the mixture and close the fist around it.
Squeeze, so that it presses into an oval along the fingers and takes their marks.
Set it on a platter and go on until the mixture is used.
Keep it cool and serve it cold.

intro.what: This köfte method squeezes a prepared soft mixture into ridged finger-shaped ovals.
intro.why: It teaches you to judge whether a mixture has enough cohesion to hold the marks made by your hand.

mistakes.fix: Wet the hands lightly and often.
mistakes.mistake: Working with dry hands, so that the mixture sticks and tears.

mistakes.fix: Leave it to swell longer, or knead in a little more fine bulgur.
mistakes.mistake: Shaping a mixture that is still loose, so that the pieces slump.

mistakes.fix: Take about the same amount each time.
mistakes.mistake: Making the pieces different sizes, which looks untidy on the plate.

quiz.because: The mixture takes the imprint of the fingers as the fist closes around it.
choices: Rolling each piece smooth on the board.
Flattening it with a rolling pin.
Squeezing the mixture along the fingers in a closed fist.
quiz.question: What gives these köfte their characteristic ridges?

quiz.because: Light moisture reduces sticking and helps the surface release without tearing.
choices: Keep them lightly wet while shaping.
Leave them dry so the mixture grips.
Coat them with a thick dry flour layer.
quiz.question: How should the hands be prepared?

quiz.because: A cohesive mixture retains its oval shape and finger marks during handling.
choices: It slumps flat on the platter.
An oval holds together when lifted.
It crumbles as soon as it is picked up.
quiz.question: Which result shows sufficient cohesion?

quiz.because: More absorption or fine bulgur can give a loose mixture the body needed to retain a shape.
choices: Wet the loose mixture more heavily.
Squeeze larger pieces with less pressure.
Let the mixture swell further or knead in fine bulgur.
quiz.question: The shaped pieces slump. What should happen before shaping again?

variant_of.differs: There is no meat and nothing is cooked afterwards. The piece is squeezed in the fist into a ridged oval and not rolled round between the palms, and it is served cold.

comes_after.why: The mixture is worked until it is sticky and holds together before it is shaped.

cues.text: Each piece is an even, smooth oval with a shallow dent and no cracks at the edge.
The piece holds together when it is lifted and springs back a little when it is pressed.

technique/shape-a-flat-kofte.does: Presses a portion of rested kofte mixture between wet palms into a short, flat oval with a shallow dent from the thumb, so that it holds together over the fire and cooks fast and evenly, and is cooked afterwards on a grill or in a pan.
how: Keep a bowl of water beside the work and wet the hands lightly, so the mixture does not stick.
Take a portion about the size of a walnut and roll it once between the palms to bring it together.
Press it into a short oval, a little longer than it is wide, and flatten it so that it is the same thickness from end to end.
Press the thumb along the middle for a shallow dent, which keeps the middle from puffing up as it cooks.
Set the pieces on a tray, close in size, and keep them cool until they go on the heat.

intro.what: This köfte method shapes rested mixture into flat ovals with a shallow thumb dent.
intro.why: It teaches you to control thickness and cohesion before the pieces meet the heat.

mistakes.fix: Knead it until sticky and let it rest in the cold before shaping.
mistakes.mistake: Shaping a mixture that was not worked or rested, so that the pieces crack and fall apart on the grill.

mistakes.fix: Flatten them to an even, modest thickness.
mistakes.mistake: Making the pieces thick and round, so that the outside burns before the middle is done.

mistakes.fix: Wet the hands lightly and often.
mistakes.mistake: Working with dry hands, so that the meat clings and tears.

quiz.because: Even thickness reduces differences between the centre and edges during cooking.
choices: To avoid a thick centre heating differently from the edges.
To make the centre deliberately thicker.
To remove the need to rest the mixture.
quiz.question: Why flatten the köfte evenly?

quiz.because: A shallow central dent helps the oval retain a flatter shape as it cooks.
choices: The amount of surface moisture.
The middle puffing up during cooking.
The mixture sticking to the hands.
quiz.question: What does the shallow thumb dent help control?

quiz.because: A smooth cohesive oval can be lifted while retaining its even thickness.
choices: Round balls with thick centres.
Ragged ovals that split when lifted.
Smooth even ovals without edge cracks.
quiz.question: Which shape suggests well-formed flat köfte?

quiz.because: Working and resting develops cohesion before individual pieces are formed.
choices: Work the mixture until sticky and let it rest cold.
Shape the loose mixture into larger portions.
Dry the hands and squeeze only the cracked edges.
quiz.question: Pieces crack and fall apart during shaping. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The piece is pressed into a flat oval with a thumb dent and not rolled into a ball, and the mixture takes soaked bread as its binder. It is made to be cooked fast over fierce heat.

en: shape rice balls round a filling

comes_after.why: There is no risotto to shape until it has been cooked, then cooled and chilled.
The beaten-in butter and cheese make the rice cling together when it is cold.

cues.text: Cold rice holds together when pressed and does not cling to wet hands.
Each ball is closed all round, with no filling showing and an even coat of crumbs.

technique/shape-a-stuffed-rice-ball.does: Presses cold, firm risotto round a small piece of filling into a ball, a cone or an oval, and coats it in flour, beaten egg and crumbs in turn, so that it fries with a crisp shell around a soft, savoury middle.
how: Cook the risotto a little firmer and thicker than for eating. Spread it out thin on a tray and let it cool right down, then chill it until it is stiff and holds together when pressed.
Have the filling cold and in small pieces. Set out shallow dishes in a row: flour, beaten egg and crumbs.
Wet the hands. Press a handful of rice into a hollow in the palm, set the filling in the middle, close the rice over it and turn it into the shape wanted, pressing out any crack or gap.
Roll it in the flour and shake off the extra, turn it through the egg, then roll it in the crumbs, pressing so that they cover it all round.
Lay them on a tray without touching and chill them for a short while before frying, so that the shell holds.

intro.what: This arancini-style method encloses filling in firm risotto and coats the shape in crumbs.
intro.why: It teaches you to manage a soft filling inside a continuous rice wall and an even outer shell.

mistakes.fix: Cook the risotto a little firmer, then cool it right down and chill it until it is stiff.
mistakes.mistake: Shaping risotto that is warm or loose, which sticks to the hands and bursts in the oil.

mistakes.fix: Close the rice all the way over the filling and press out any crack before the coat goes on.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving a gap over the filling, through which it leaks out in the hot oil.

mistakes.fix: Use a small piece of filling and enough rice to wrap it with a firm wall all round.
mistakes.mistake: Packing in too much filling, so that the rice wall is thin and splits.

names.en: Shape and crumb stuffed rice balls

quiz.because: A continuous rice enclosure supports the filling beneath the crumb shell.
choices: Leave a small opening for filling to escape.
Form a continuous wall without gaps.
Make a very thin patch only at the base.
quiz.question: What must the rice do around the filling?

quiz.because: Flour, egg and crumbs build the coating in stages so the shell covers the rice evenly.
choices: Crumbs, flour, then egg.
Egg, crumbs, then loose flour.
Flour, beaten egg, then crumbs.
quiz.question: What is the coating order?

quiz.because: Firm chilled rice holds a wall around the filling instead of clinging and slumping.
choices: Cold and firm enough to hold when pressed.
Warm and loose between the fingers.
Fluid enough to run from the palm.
quiz.question: Which feel suits rice before shaping?

quiz.because: Reducing the filling leaves enough rice to form an intact supporting wall.
choices: Stretch the same thin wall further.
Use less filling and enough rice to enclose it firmly.
Hide the exposed filling beneath loose crumbs.
quiz.question: The rice wall split around a large filling. What would you change when shaping the next ball?

variant_of.differs: The mixture is whole grains of cold risotto and not a smooth paste, and it is pressed round a piece of filling, which a croqueta does not have. The shell is the same flour, egg and crumbs.

The rice is risotto cooked in stock and chilled until stiff, and not plain warm rice, and it is wrapped round a filling and then coated in flour, egg and crumbs to be fried. Onigiri are plain rice pressed warm with salted hands and eaten as they are.

comes_after.why: There is nothing to shape until the paste has been made and chilled.

cues.text: The paste rolls clean between floured hands and does not stick.
Each croqueta is covered all round with an even coat of crumbs and no bare patch.

technique/shape-and-crumb-croquetas.does: Rolls cold, firm croqueta paste into small logs or balls and coats each one in flour, beaten egg and breadcrumbs in turn, so that it fries with a crisp shell and a soft, creamy middle.
how: Set out shallow dishes in a row: flour, beaten egg and breadcrumbs, in that order. Have a tray ready.
Scoop a spoonful of the chilled paste and roll it between floured hands into a short log or a ball. Keep them all one size.
Roll each one in the flour and shake off the extra, turn it through the egg, then roll it in the crumbs, pressing so that they cover it all round.
Lay them on the tray without touching. For a thicker shell, dip them in the egg and the crumbs a second time.
Chill them again for a short while before frying, so that the shell sets.

intro.what: Croquetas are formed from cold firm paste and coated in flour, egg and crumbs.
intro.why: It teaches you to handle a creamy centre while building a complete shell around it.

mistakes.fix: Turn each one through the egg and the crumbs until it is covered all round.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving a bare patch, through which the paste bursts out in the hot oil.

mistakes.fix: Chill the paste until it is firm, and flour your hands.
mistakes.mistake: Shaping warm paste, which squashes and sticks to the hands.

mistakes.fix: Keep one hand for the flour and the crumbs and the other for the egg.
mistakes.mistake: Using the same hand for the dry coats and for the egg, which builds up gluey lumps on the fingers.

quiz.because: The coating encloses the shaped paste and creates a contrasting crisp exterior.
choices: A loose dusting that falls away in the oil.
A replacement for firming the paste.
A crisp outside around a soft creamy middle.
quiz.question: What is the purpose of the crumb shell?

quiz.because: Separating wet and dry handling limits coating building up on the fingers.
choices: Keep a hand for dry coatings and the other for egg.
Use egg-coated fingers in the crumb bowl each time.
Mix flour, egg and crumbs into a paste first.
quiz.question: How can gluey lumps on the fingers be reduced?

quiz.because: Bare areas interrupt the shell and give soft filling a route out.
choices: Loose crumbs around an exposed paste centre.
An even crumb coat without bare patches.
A heavy coating only on the ends.
quiz.question: Which appearance matters before frying?

quiz.because: Cold firm paste is easier to handle without collapsing into the hands.
choices: Shape it warmer with more pressure.
Add the egg coating before forming a shape.
Chill it until firm and flour the hands.
quiz.question: The paste squashes and sticks during shaping. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The food is a soft paste that has to be rolled to shape first, and it takes flour, then egg, then crumbs, so that the shell holds the paste in when it is fried. The coat of a cutlet goes straight onto firm meat with egg or mustard and crumbs.

comes_after.why: Wet, salted hands come first.

cues.text: The rice holds together when lifted, and still feels light.
The shape has clean edges and a surface with no cracks.

technique/shape-by-hand.does: Presses a portion of warm cooked rice between wet, salted hands into a firm triangle, ball or barrel that holds together but is not packed hard.
how: Wet your hands in cold water, rub a little salt over the palms and shake off the excess.
Scoop up a portion of warm rice and press it lightly into a ball.
