Turn it in the hollow of one hand while pressing the other hand into a corner or an edge, to form the shape. Add a filling in the middle first if it is wanted.
Squeeze only enough to hold it together, so that air stays between the grains.

intro.what: Hand-shaping presses warm rice into a ball, triangle or barrel without packing it hard.
intro.why: It teaches you to find the light pressure that joins grains while preserving an airy feel.

mistakes.fix: Press just until it holds.
mistakes.mistake: Packing the rice hard, which turns it dense and heavy.

mistakes.fix: Wet and salt your hands each time.
mistakes.mistake: Shaping with dry hands, so that the rice sticks to them.

quiz.because: The rice needs enough contact to hold together without being compressed into a heavy mass.
choices: To keep the shape light rather than dense.
To ensure the grains remain completely loose.
To squeeze out every space between grains.
quiz.question: Why avoid packing the rice hard?

quiz.because: Turning lets gentle pressure define the outline without crushing the whole portion.
choices: Flatten it completely before cutting corners away.
Turn the rice in a cupped hand while the other presses an edge.
Keep it still and squeeze only the centre.
quiz.question: How are corners formed while shaping?

quiz.because: Light cohesion balances structural support with space between the grains.
choices: The shape is hard and tightly compacted.
The rice falls apart as soon as it is lifted.
The rice holds when lifted but still feels light.
quiz.question: Which feel suggests suitable shaping pressure?

quiz.because: Damp hands release the rice more readily, protecting the surface while shaping.
choices: Wet and lightly salt the hands again.
Press harder with dry palms.
Let a thicker layer of rice build up on the hands.
quiz.question: Rice sticks to dry hands and tears. What should change?

variant_of.differs: Warm cooked rice is shaped with wet, salted hands and kept light, so that the grains stay whole, not packed like a meat mixture.

comes_after.why: The mat shapes an egg block that has already been cooked in layers.

cues.text: The block has an even shape with square edges.
The block is firm and holds together when it is cut.

technique/shape-in-a-mat.does: Rolls a warm, soft food up in a bamboo mat and presses it, so that it sets into a firm, even block with square edges.
how: Lay the mat on the board with the bamboo sticks running side to side.
Place the warm food at the near edge and roll the mat over it tightly.
Press and squeeze along the whole length so that the sides are straight.
Leave it rolled in the mat for a short while to set, then unroll and cut.

intro.what: A bamboo mat shapes warm soft food into an even block as it firms.
intro.why: It teaches you to use distributed pressure and warmth to control shape without cracking.

mistakes.fix: Shape it while it is still warm.
mistakes.mistake: Rolling when the food is cold and stiff, so that it cracks.

mistakes.fix: Squeeze the whole length of the mat with both hands.
mistakes.mistake: Pressing unevenly, so that one end is thinner.

quiz.because: The rolled mat supports the food while pressure defines its sides and edges.
choices: Loose pieces separated by the bamboo.
An even block with straight sides.
A thin sheet stretched across the board.
quiz.question: What does pressing in the mat create?

quiz.because: Warm soft food can take the mat’s shape without the cracking caused by stiffness.
choices: Only after it is cold and stiff.
After slicing it into finished portions.
While still warm and pliable.
quiz.question: When should the food be shaped in the mat?

quiz.because: A firm coherent block shows that it has taken and retained its shape.
choices: Hold together with an even outline.
Slump into a loose mound.
Break along cracks from rolling.
quiz.question: What should the block do when cut?

quiz.because: Distributed pressure prevents local compression from narrowing parts of the block.
choices: Squeeze that thin end harder.
Press evenly along the whole mat with both hands.
Press only at the centre of the mat.
quiz.question: An end of the block became thinner than the rest. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The food is rolled and pressed in a bamboo mat, which gives straight, square edges that hand shaping cannot.

comes_after.why: Minced meat is kneaded with its seasoning so that it holds together before it is rolled.

cues.text: The balls are the same size, smooth and round, with no cracks.
Each ball holds together when it is lifted, and springs back a little under a finger.

technique/shape-meatballs.does: Rolls seasoned minced meat between wet palms into round balls of an even size, so that they hold together and cook at the same pace.
how: Knead the minced meat with its seasoning until it holds together, and chill it briefly so that it handles well.
Wet the hands, or rub them with a little oil, so that the meat does not stick.
Take up equal portions with a spoon, to keep the balls the same size.
Roll each portion between the palms with light pressure until it is round and smooth, with no cracks.
Set the balls on a tray, not touching, until they are cooked.

intro.what: Meatball shaping turns a cohesive mince mixture into lightly rolled portions of similar size.
intro.why: It teaches you to control portion size and handling pressure without making the mixture dense.

mistakes.fix: Roll with light pressure, only until they hold.
mistakes.mistake: Packing the balls hard, which makes them dense and dry.

mistakes.fix: Portion the meat with a spoon before rolling.
mistakes.mistake: Making balls of different sizes, so that some are done before others.

mistakes.fix: Wet or oil the hands often.
mistakes.mistake: Working with dry hands, so that the meat sticks and tears.

quiz.because: Similar portions produce similar-sized balls rather than pieces that respond differently to heat.
choices: So they can be packed more tightly when rolling.
So the surface needs no smoothing.
So their sizes do not cause different cooking rates.
quiz.question: Why portion meatballs consistently?

quiz.because: Portioning before shaping separates size control from the rolling motion.
choices: Measure them out with a spoon before rolling.
Judge each size only after cooking.
Pull off random amounts and press them equally hard.
quiz.question: How can the portions be kept consistent?

quiz.because: A smooth cohesive surface holds together during handling.
choices: A mix of large and small rough pieces.
Similar-sized smooth balls without cracks.
Deep seams left around each ball.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches well-shaped meatballs?

quiz.because: Excess pressure compacts the mixture; light rolling keeps it less dense.
choices: Pack them more firmly to remove all spaces.
Roll them repeatedly for a longer time.
Use light pressure only until each ball holds.
quiz.question: Rolled meatballs became dense and heavy. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: Shape forms a soft mixture into even pieces between spoons. Here the meat is firm enough to be rolled by hand into round balls, and the mixture must first be kneaded to bind.

cues.text: The slivers are thin, slightly curled and about the same length.
The water in the bowl turns brown, and clears when changed.

technique/shave.does: Whittles a long root into thin, curled slivers, turning it against the knife as a pencil is sharpened. The slivers cook fast and keep a crunch.
how: Scrub the root and scrape off the skin, but not too hard, as most of the taste lies just under it.
Hold the root at a slant and turn it against the knife, taking thin slivers as it turns.
Let the slivers fall straight into a bowl of cold water.
Change the water when it turns brown.

intro.what: This root-shaving method whittles thin curled slivers while turning the root.
intro.why: It teaches you to control thickness and protect freshly cut surfaces from browning.

mistakes.fix: Let them fall into water as they are cut.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the slivers in the air, where they brown at once.

mistakes.fix: Shave them thin.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting thick slivers, which stay hard.

quiz.because: Turning the angled root against the knife creates fine curled pieces.
choices: Thick square chunks.
Thin slightly curled slivers.
Wide flat slabs of uneven thickness.
quiz.question: What cut does this root-shaving method aim for?

quiz.because: Water limits the browning that develops on exposed cut surfaces.
choices: Onto a dry board to wait.
Into a tightly packed dry pile.
Into cold water.
quiz.question: Where should fresh slivers fall as they are cut?

quiz.because: Consistent thin slivers provide the quick-cooking texture sought from this cut.
choices: Thin curled slivers of similar length.
Thick wedges with broad ends.
Crushed fragments mixed with large pieces.
quiz.question: Which appearance suits the intended cut?

quiz.because: Thinner slivers respond to heat more readily than thick pieces.
choices: Cut thicker pieces for more weight.
Shave them more thinly.
Cut the same thick slivers into shorter lengths.
quiz.question: The slivers remain hard during cooking. What should change next time?

variant_of.differs: The root is turned against the blade and whittled to slivers, instead of being cut straight across.

cues.text: The threads are very fine and loose, and spring up when they are lifted.
The threads crunch when they are bitten.

technique/shred-cabbage.does: Cuts cabbage into very fine, long threads, which stay crisp and fresh. They are then often soaked briefly in cold water, so that they fluff and stiffen.
how: Cut the cabbage into wedges and cut out the hard core.
Stack a few leaves, roll them up tightly and slice them across as thin as paper.
Put the threads in cold water for a short while, so that they curl and crisp.
Drain them very well and dry them in a cloth, so that they do not water down the dish.

intro.what: Fine cabbage shredding makes long light threads for a crisp accompaniment.
intro.why: It teaches you how thin cutting and thorough drying influence both bite and the liquid on the plate.

mistakes.fix: Roll the leaves tightly and slice as thin as possible.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting thick shreds, which are tough.

mistakes.fix: Drain and dry them well.
mistakes.mistake: Serving them wet, so that the plate floods.

quiz.because: Very thin slicing creates a lighter accompaniment while retaining crunch.
choices: Thick tough strips with a firm core.
A crushed wet cabbage paste.
Fine loose strands with a crisp bite.
quiz.question: What texture is sought from these cabbage threads?

quiz.because: A compact roll steadies the leaves for consistent thin cuts.
choices: Roll them tightly and slice across the roll.
Leave them loosely piled and chop at random.
Slice through the hard core with the leaves.
quiz.question: How are stacked cabbage leaves prepared for fine slicing?

quiz.because: Fine separate threads lift lightly instead of forming a heavy mass.
choices: They fall as dense stiff wedges.
They spring up loosely when lifted.
They cling together in a wet paste.
quiz.question: Which movement suggests light fine shreds?

quiz.because: Removing free water keeps the cabbage from diluting the rest of the dish.
choices: Serve it directly from the soaking bowl.
Add dressing before draining the water.
Drain well and dry it in a cloth after soaking.
quiz.question: The cabbage watered down the plate. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The cut is as thin as thread and the shreds are crisped in cold water, to be eaten raw beside a rich fried dish.

comes_after.why: A simmer is found by coming down from a boil, so a cook has to know a boil first.

cues.text: A bubble or a small cluster of them rising every moment or so, and a surface that shivers.
Near silence. A pot that rolls and rattles is boiling.

technique/simmer.does: Cooks food in liquid that is kept just below a boil, so that it turns tender without being knocked about.
how: Bring the liquid up to a boil, then turn the heat down at once.
Find the setting where a few bubbles break the surface now and then.
Leave the lid off or ajar, so that the heat does not build back up to a boil.
Look in from time to time, and top the pot up if food shows above the liquid.

intro.what: Simmering keeps food in liquid that moves gently below a rolling boil.
intro.why: It teaches you to judge heat by the movement and sound of the liquid.

mistakes.fix: Turn the heat down, or move the pot half off the burner.
mistakes.mistake: Letting it boil, which toughens meat and turns a stock cloudy.

mistakes.fix: Leave the lid ajar.
mistakes.mistake: Covering the pot tightly, so that it climbs to a boil unseen.

quiz.because: Gentle liquid movement cooks the food without knocking it about as a rolling boil would.
choices: To cook as rapidly as a rolling boil with less noise.
To prevent any liquid from evaporating.
To cook gently without the movement of a rolling boil.
quiz.question: Why keep the liquid at a simmer in this method?

quiz.because: Once the liquid reaches a boil, turn the heat down to find a gentle simmer.
choices: Turn the heat down at once.
Cover tightly and increase the heat.
Keep the same rolling boil throughout.
quiz.question: After bringing the liquid to a boil, what comes next?

quiz.because: Occasional bubbles and a shivering surface show a simmer. A rolling, rattling pot is boiling.
choices: A rolling surface and a rattling pot.
A shivering surface with a few bubbles now and then.
An almost still surface with no bubbles rising at all.
quiz.question: Which description matches a simmer?

quiz.because: A tight lid can let heat build until the liquid boils. Leave the lid off or ajar and lower the heat.
choices: Keep it tightly covered and increase the heat.
Stir hard without changing the lid or heat.
Leave the lid off or ajar and lower the heat.
quiz.question: A tightly covered pot keeps returning to a boil. What would you change?

comes_after.why: The leaves are filled and rolled first, and a loose roll will not survive the pot.

cues.text: The rolls are plump and have kept their shape, and the liquid is mostly taken up and glossy with oil.
A leaf is tender and the rice inside is soft when a roll is pressed.

technique/simmer-rolled-leaves.does: Cooks filled, rolled leaves packed snugly seam down in a lined pot, weighed down with a plate, in a little oil, lemon juice and water. The leaves turn soft and tart and the rice inside swells and softens.
how: Line the base of a wide pot with slices of tomato or a few spare leaves, so that the rolls do not catch.
Pack the rolls tightly, seam down, in circles, layer on layer, so that none can unroll.
Pour in the olive oil and the lemon juice, add water to come part of the way up the rolls, and salt the liquid.
Set a plate that fits inside the pot upside down on the rolls, so that they stay put.
Cover, bring to a gentle simmer and cook on a low heat until the leaves are tender and the filling has swelled. Leave the rolls to cool in the pot.

intro.what: Filled leaves simmer gently while packed snugly in a lined pot.
intro.why: It teaches you to support delicate rolls and manage liquid as the filling swells.

mistakes.fix: Pack them tight and weigh them with a plate.
mistakes.mistake: Packing the rolls loosely, so that they float and unroll.

mistakes.fix: Add liquid only part of the way up.
mistakes.mistake: Covering the rolls completely with liquid, so that the filling washes out and the dish turns watery.

mistakes.fix: Keep the pot at a gentle simmer.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking on a high heat, which splits the leaves and breaks the rolls.

quiz.because: Support from neighbouring rolls and the plate helps the wrappers stay closed.
choices: To keep them from floating and unrolling.
To press the filling out into the liquid.
To expose each seam to stronger bubbling.
quiz.question: Why pack the rolls snugly and weigh them with a plate?

quiz.because: A lining separates delicate wrappers from the pot surface.
choices: To increase direct contact with the hot metal.
To keep the rolls from catching on the base.
To replace the liquid entirely.
quiz.question: Why line the pot base with spare leaves or tomato?

quiz.because: The filling swells while the supported wrappers retain their shapes.
choices: Split wrappers floating in a watery pot.
Loose filling washed out between leaves.
Plump intact rolls with mostly absorbed liquid.
quiz.question: Which appearance matches the intended result?

quiz.because: Gentler liquid movement reduces stress on the delicate leaves.
choices: Keep the liquid at a gentle simmer.
Maintain the boil and stir the rolls.
Remove the plate and increase bubbling.
quiz.question: The wrappers split during vigorous cooking. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The food is rolled leaves packed seam down and held under a plate, in liquid that comes only part of the way up, and it is left to cool in the pot.

comes_after.why: The butter is melted gently first, without letting it colour.

cues.text: The butter is a clear, bright red and the flakes are sizzling gently, not black.
A warm, sweet smell of dried pepper, with no scorched edge.

technique/sizzle-chilli-butter.does: Melts butter, takes it off the heat and stirs in dried chilli flakes or paprika, which sizzle for a moment and turn the butter bright red and fragrant. It is spooned over yogurt, eggs, dumplings or soup at the last moment.
how: Melt the butter in a small pan over a gentle heat until it foams, and stop before it browns.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the chilli flakes or the paprika.
Stir for a few moments while the flakes sizzle gently and the butter turns a deep red.
Spoon it over the food at once, while it is still bubbling.

intro.what: Chilli butter uses residual heat in melted butter to release dried pepper colour and aroma.
intro.why: It teaches you that delicate spices can bloom without staying over direct heat.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat before the chilli goes in.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the pan on the heat after the chilli goes in, so that it scorches and turns the butter bitter.

mistakes.fix: Melt the butter only until it foams.
mistakes.mistake: Browning the butter first, which gives a nutty taste and a dull colour in place of the clean red.

mistakes.fix: Make it as the dish is ready and spoon it over while it is hot.
mistakes.mistake: Making it long before it is needed, so that it turns thick and dull.

quiz.because: Brief gentle sizzling releases the pepper’s colour and aroma without scorching it.
choices: Dark brown with a bitter pepper taste.
Bright red and fragrant without a scorched edge.
Pale butter with dry unheated flakes.
quiz.question: What is the intended character of this chilli butter?

quiz.because: Residual heat is enough for the flakes, reducing the chance of burning them.
choices: Before heating the butter over a strong flame.
After browning the butter deeply.
After taking the foaming melted butter off the heat.
quiz.question: When should chilli or paprika be added?

quiz.because: A warm pepper scent indicates blooming rather than scorching.
choices: Warm sweet dried-pepper aroma.
A sharp scorched smell.
A bitter burnt-butter smell.
quiz.question: Which smell suggests the intended result?

quiz.because: Direct heat after the flakes are added can scorch them quickly.
choices: Keep the pan on the heat and stir faster.
Remove the butter from the heat before adding it.
Brown the butter further before adding more chilli.
quiz.question: The chilli turned black and bitter. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The fat is butter and not ghee or oil, the spice is ground or flaked red pepper and not whole seeds, and the pan is off the heat when the pepper goes in, so that the red does not scorch. The butter is spooned over finished food as a sauce.

cues.text: The pieces sit straight and snug, and are all about the same size.
The pieces do not spin on the skewer when it is turned.

technique/skewer.does: Threads pieces of food, or presses a mince round a flat skewer, so that they can be turned as one and cook evenly over fierce heat, with their juices held in.
how: Soak wooden skewers in water first, so that they do not scorch. Metal skewers need no soaking.
Cut the food into pieces of an even size, so that they cook at the same pace.
Thread the pieces on snugly, with a little room between them so that the heat reaches every face.
For mince, wet the hands and press it firmly round a flat skewer into a long shape, with no gaps.
Leave the ends of the skewer bare, to hold by.

intro.what: Skewering supports evenly cut pieces or shaped mince so they turn together over heat.
intro.why: It teaches you to balance firm attachment with enough space for heat to reach the food.

mistakes.fix: Leave a little room between pieces.
mistakes.mistake: Packing the pieces tight, so that the insides stay raw while the outsides burn.

mistakes.fix: Thread each kind on its own skewer.
mistakes.mistake: Mixing pieces that cook at different speeds on one skewer.

mistakes.fix: Chill the mince and press it firmly with wet hands.
mistakes.mistake: Pressing mince too loosely, so that it falls off in the heat.

quiz.because: Packed surfaces shield each other from heat; space improves exposure.
choices: To make them spin independently when turned.
To press their juices into adjacent pieces.
To allow heat to reach their surfaces.
quiz.question: Why leave space between skewered pieces?

quiz.because: Separate skewers allow different foods to be moved or removed independently.
choices: Put each kind on its own skewer.
Alternate them randomly on the same skewer.
Use larger fast-cooking pieces without checking sizes.
quiz.question: How should foods that cook at different rates be arranged?

quiz.because: Secure attachment lets the skewer control which faces meet the heat.
choices: The pieces hang loosely and rotate independently.
The pieces turn with the skewer instead of spinning.
Mince slides along the skewer when lifted.
quiz.question: Which handling cue suggests food is attached firmly?

quiz.because: A firm cohesive mixture in close contact with the skewer is less likely to detach.
choices: Leave gaps between mince and skewer.
Warm the mixture before lightly draping it on.
Chill it and press it firmly around a flat skewer with wet hands.
quiz.question: Mince falls off the skewer. What should change?

comes_after.why: Skimming only works on a pot held at a simmer.

cues.text: A clear surface with a few bright beads of fat and no grey foam.

technique/skim.does: Lifts off the foam and fat that rise to the top of a simmering liquid, so that it stays clear and tastes clean.
how: Bring the pot up slowly. The grey foam rises as it nears a simmer.
Hold a ladle flat, just under the surface, and let the foam flow into it.
Move the pot half off the heat, so that the foam gathers on the cooler side.
Skim often at the start, then now and then as fat collects.

intro.what: Skimming lifts foam and fat from the surface of a gently simmering liquid.
intro.why: It teaches you to remove what collects on top without stirring it back through a stock.

mistakes.fix: Keep it at a bare simmer and skim as soon as foam appears.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the pot boil before skimming, which churns the foam and fat back in and clouds the liquid for good.

mistakes.fix: Leave it still. Stirring spreads through the liquid what was rising to be skimmed.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring a stock.

quiz.because: Foam and fat rise to the surface, where you can lift them away from the liquid.
choices: Foam and fat that rise to the surface.
The clear liquid just beneath the foam.
Solids strained from the entire liquid through a sieve.
quiz.question: What do you remove when skimming a stock?

quiz.because: A flat ladle held just below the surface lets the foam flow into it.
choices: Deep in the bottom of the pot.
Flat, just under the surface.
Tilted deep into the liquid to scoop from below the foam.
quiz.question: How do you position the ladle to skim the surface?

quiz.because: A surface without grey foam shows the result of skimming. A few bright beads of fat may still remain.
choices: Grey foam covering the top.
Foam churned throughout a rolling boil.
A clear surface without grey foam.
quiz.question: Which surface shows the result you want after skimming?

quiz.because: Stirring spreads through the stock what was rising to the surface. Leave it still and skim gently.
choices: Leave it still and lift foam gently from the surface.
Continue stirring until the foam is too fine to see.
Bring it to a rolling boil before skimming.
quiz.question: Stirring is spreading the foam through the stock. What should you change?

cues.text: Slices of the same thickness from the first to the last.
A quiet stroke. A knock on the board at every cut means you are chopping down, not slicing forward.

technique/slice.does: Cuts food into flat pieces of one thickness.
how: Give the food a flat side to rest on.
Hold it with your fingertips tucked back and your knuckles against the side of the blade.
Push the knife forward and down in one stroke, and let its length do the cutting.
Move the guiding hand back by the thickness of a slice after each cut.

intro.what: Slicing cuts food into flat pieces of consistent thickness with a forward-and-down stroke.
intro.why: It teaches you to guide the blade smoothly instead of crushing food with downward pressure.

mistakes.fix: Slide the blade forward as it goes down. Sharpen it if it still crushes.
mistakes.mistake: Pressing straight down, which crushes soft food such as a tomato.

mistakes.fix: Slow down. Even matters more than fast.
mistakes.mistake: Slices that grow thicker as the hand tires.

quiz.because: Consistent cuts give the slices a predictable shape rather than an uneven chopped texture.
choices: Flat pieces of consistent thickness.
Chunks with varied thicknesses.
A finely crushed mixture.
quiz.question: What is the main aim of slicing evenly?

quiz.because: Using the length of the blade cuts more smoothly than forcing the edge straight downward.
choices: Straight down with repeated heavy pressure.
Forward and down in a smooth stroke.
Sideways against the guiding fingers.
quiz.question: How should the blade move through the food?

quiz.because: The sound can reveal a hard downward movement instead of a controlled sliding cut.
choices: The slices are necessarily even.
The blade is moving quietly forward through the food.
A downward chopping action rather than a smooth slicing stroke.
quiz.question: What might a repeated knock on the board suggest?

quiz.because: A sliding sharp edge cuts the skin and flesh with less crushing pressure.
choices: Slide forward as you cut and check blade sharpness.
Press harder directly downward.
Make faster downward blows.
quiz.question: Soft tomato is being crushed rather than sliced. What should change?

en: cook slowly in a sealed pot

comes_after.why: Slow cooking is a braise with less liquid and far more time, so a cook has to know how a braise behaves first.

cues.text: A fork slides in and the meat falls apart under light pressure.
The juices are glossy, with a layer of clear fat on top.
A deep, sweet smell rises when the pot is opened, and nothing smells scorched.

technique/slow-cook.does: Cooks a tough cut for a very long time at the lowest heat in a closed pot with only a little liquid, so that it softens in its own juices and fat until it falls apart, with its taste deep and little left to reduce.
how: Season the meat early, and rub it with the spices and the fat.
Pack it snugly into the pot with the aromatics, and add only a little liquid, well below the top of the meat.
Close the pot tightly: with its lid, with parchment tied over the mouth, or with a rope of dough around the lid.
Cook in a low oven, or on the lowest heat, and keep the pot shut for most of the time.
Open it near the end, and check that the meat falls apart under a fork and that the juices have turned into a small amount of rich sauce.

intro.what: This slow-cooking method softens a tough cut in a tightly closed pot with little liquid.
intro.why: It teaches you how low heat and retained moisture develop texture without a large volume of broth.

mistakes.fix: Keep the pot shut and trust the low heat.
mistakes.mistake: Lifting the lid often, which lets the steam out and stretches the time.

mistakes.fix: Add only a little, well below the top of the meat.
mistakes.mistake: Adding too much liquid, so that the meat boils and the sauce is thin.

mistakes.fix: Use the lowest heat and a heavy pot.
mistakes.mistake: Setting the heat too high, so that the bottom of the pot catches.

quiz.because: The closed pot holds moisture around the meat while it softens slowly.
choices: To let liquid evaporate as quickly as possible.
To retain steam and moisture during slow cooking.
To brown the top as in an open roasting tin.
quiz.question: Why keep the pot tightly closed for most of this method?

quiz.because: This method depends on a small amount of liquid and the juices released into the closed pot.
choices: Completely submerge it as for a broth.
Reach the meat surface without leaving the top exposed.
Remain well below its top.
quiz.question: How should the added liquid relate to the meat?

quiz.because: Giving way under light fork pressure shows the softened texture this method aims for.
choices: The meat gives way under light fork pressure.
The meat remains springy and resistant.
Only a crisp surface develops.
quiz.question: Which texture change is being sought?

quiz.because: Limiting added liquid keeps the resulting juices concentrated without excessive later reduction.
choices: Add more stock to speed the softening.
Start with little liquid below the top of the meat.
Open the lid repeatedly throughout cooking.
quiz.question: The sauce is thin because too much liquid was added. What should change next time?

variant_of.differs: A braise browns the meat first, cooks it half covered in liquid and turns it now and then. Slow cooking skips the browning, uses only a little liquid, stays shut, and takes far longer at a lower heat, so the meat cooks in its own juices as much as in the liquid.

en: cook potatoes slowly in olive oil

comes_after.why: Slices of one thickness soften at one pace, so a cook has to be able to cut them even first.

cues.text: A slice breaks when it is pressed with the edge of a spoon, and bends without cracking.
The oil only shimmers and barely bubbles, and the slices stay pale, at most a light gold.
A sweet, mild smell of potato and onion, with nothing toasty about it.

technique/slow-fry-in-olive-oil.does: Cooks thin slices of potato and onion in a deep pool of olive oil that is kept well below frying heat, turning them now and then, until they are soft and silky and have taken almost no colour. The oil is poured off afterwards and kept.
how: Slice the potato thin and even, and the onion thinner. Salt them lightly and turn them over by hand, so that the salt goes through evenly.
Pour olive oil into a wide, deep pan until it comes about halfway up the food, and warm it over a medium heat until a slice dropped in bubbles gently.
Add the potato and onion, then turn the heat down at once, so that the oil only shimmers and nothing fries hard.
Turn the slices over now and then with a spoon, breaking up any that cling together, until they give way under the edge of the spoon and have hardly taken any colour.
Tip everything into a colander set over a bowl. Keep the oil, which now tastes of potato and onion, for the next frying.

intro.what: This potato-and-onion method softens thin slices gently in olive oil with little browning.
intro.why: It teaches you to distinguish gentle oil cooking from the stronger heat used for a crisp crust.

mistakes.fix: Turn the heat down until the oil only shimmers.
mistakes.mistake: Frying too hot, so that the slices crisp and brown outside and stay hard inside.

mistakes.fix: Use enough to come about halfway up the food, and turn it often.
mistakes.mistake: Using too little oil, so that the slices stick together and fry in patches.

mistakes.fix: Strain it and keep it for frying or for the next batch.
mistakes.mistake: Throwing the oil away, which wastes a flavoured oil.

quiz.because: Gentle oil heat softens the slices without the crust sought in hotter frying.
choices: Crisp browned slices.
Firm raw-textured slices in hot oil.
Soft silky slices with very little colour.
quiz.question: What texture is the aim of this potato-and-onion method?

quiz.because: Separating the slices exposes them more evenly to the warm oil.
choices: Turn them gently and separate them with a spoon.
Leave them packed together throughout cooking.
Press them into a firm layer against the base.
quiz.question: How should slices that cling together be handled?

quiz.because: Gentle bubbling indicates the softer oil-cooking approach rather than hard frying.
choices: A fierce constant frying action.
A shimmer with barely bubbling oil.
No movement because the oil is cold.
quiz.question: Which oil movement suits this method?

quiz.because: Less intense heat gives the slices time to soften before their surfaces brown.
choices: Increase the heat to deepen the crust.
Remove more oil and keep the heat high.
Lower the heat until the oil only shimmers.
quiz.question: The slices crisp outside while remaining firm inside. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The food is a shallow heap of thin slices turned in a pan and not lying under the fat. The oil is a little warmer, the cooking far shorter, and the oil is poured off and reused after it, not left round the food.

cues.text: Dried food is plump and smooth, with no wrinkles left.
A slice of bread is soft to the centre and still lifts in one piece.

technique/soak.does: Leaves food in a liquid until it has taken the liquid up, softened, or given up its salt.
how: Cover the food with plenty of liquid, as it will swell.
For dried pulses and dried fruit, use cold water and leave them until they are plump.
For salt cod, change the water several times and keep it cold.
For stale bread, turn the slices in the liquid until they are heavy with it and still hold together.

intro.what: Soaking lets food absorb liquid, soften or release excess salt before another step.
intro.why: It teaches you to match the soak to its purpose instead of treating all ingredients alike.

mistakes.fix: Use bread that is a day old or more, and lift it out as soon as the centre is soft.
mistakes.mistake: Soaking bread until it falls apart.

mistakes.fix: Soak them in the fridge.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving pulses or salt cod to soak in a warm kitchen.

quiz.because: Fresh cold water carries away released salt rather than keeping it around the fish.
choices: To let it release excess salt.
To concentrate more salt in the flesh.
To brown its outside before cooking.
quiz.question: Why might salt cod be soaked in changing water?

quiz.because: The aim is a hydrated slice that can still be lifted into the next preparation.
choices: Leave it until it disintegrates completely.
Turn it until the centre softens while it still holds together.
Wet only the crust and leave the centre dry.
quiz.question: How should stale bread be handled in a soaking liquid?

quiz.because: Absorbed liquid expands dried food and reduces its shrivelled appearance.
choices: It remains tightly wrinkled and dry.
It softens only at the surface while staying dry within.
It becomes plump and smoother.
quiz.question: Which appearance indicates dried food has absorbed water?

quiz.because: Staler bread holds its structure better, and ending the soak promptly avoids collapse.
choices: Use stale bread and lift it out once the centre softens.
Leave the next slices in longer.
Use softer fresh bread for a longer soak.
quiz.question: Soaked bread fell apart when lifted. What would you change next time?

cues.text: A grain bitten through is tender and slightly chewy, with no hard, dry core.
The grains have swelled to fill the bowl and the liquid is gone.

technique/soak-bulgur.does: Leaves fine bulgur in just enough cool liquid for the grains to swell and turn tender, with no cooking at all. The liquid can be water, lemon juice or the juice of tomatoes, and it flavours the grain as it goes in.
how: Rinse the bulgur in a sieve and let the water run off. Tip it into a bowl.
Pour over cool water, or lemon juice or tomato juice, to just cover the grains. They take up the liquid as they swell.
Leave it, and stir once or twice, until the grains are tender with a slight chew in the centre.
Tip it into a sieve, press out any liquid that is left, and fluff the grains with a fork before they meet other foods.

intro.what: Fine bulgur softens by absorbing cool water or flavourful vegetable juices.
intro.why: It teaches you how grain size and measured moisture change texture without simmering.

mistakes.fix: Use just enough to cover it, and press out the rest.
mistakes.mistake: Drowning the bulgur in a great deal of water, so that it turns soggy and the dish goes watery.

mistakes.fix: Coarse grades are simmered. Only the fine grades are soaked.
mistakes.mistake: Soaking coarse bulgur the same way, which leaves it hard.

quiz.because: Fine grains soften by this method, whereas coarse grades need a different cooking approach.
choices: Fine bulgur.
Coarse bulgur used without further cooking.
Any grade treated identically.
quiz.question: Which bulgur suits this cool-soaking method?

quiz.because: Controlled liquid absorption avoids leaving the final dish watery.
choices: Drown the grains and serve them with the excess.
Use enough to cover the grains, then press out any remaining liquid.
Add no liquid until after mixing the salad.
quiz.question: How should liquid be added?

quiz.because: A slight chew preserves texture while the dry core should have hydrated.
choices: Soft outside with a hard dry centre.
A soggy paste without separate grains.
Tender with a slight chew and no dry core.
quiz.question: Which bite suggests fine bulgur has softened?

quiz.because: Limiting free liquid prevents hydrated grains from carrying a puddle into the salad.
choices: Use less soaking liquid and drain and press the grains.
Add more liquid to loosen them further.
Mix the salad before any absorption occurs.
quiz.question: The bulgur makes the salad watery. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The grain is given only as much liquid as it can take up, or is drained and pressed afterwards, and it is never simmered. Beans, bread and dried fruit are covered in plenty of liquid.

cues.text: The mushrooms are soft and pliable, with no hard dry centre.
A deep, earthy scent rises from the bowl.
The water turns dark brown.

technique/soak-dried-mushrooms.does: Steeps dried mushrooms in warm water until they are plump and soft, and keeps the dark, fragrant soaking water, strained of grit, to flavour the dish.
how: Rinse the dried mushrooms quickly under cold water to take off loose dust.
Cover them with warm water, not hot, in a bowl, and press them down so that they stay under.
Leave them until they are plump and pliable. The time depends on the mushroom and the size of the pieces.
Lift the mushrooms out with your hands, squeezing them gently over the bowl, and rinse off any grit.
Pour the soaking water slowly through a fine sieve and leave the last spoonfuls behind in the bowl, where the grit has settled. Keep it to use as stock.
Slice or chop the mushrooms for the dish.

intro.what: Soaking restores dried mushrooms and produces a fragrant liquid that can flavour the dish.
intro.why: It teaches you to recover useful flavour while separating the grit that settles beneath it.

mistakes.fix: Strain it and use it in the dish.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring the soaking water away, when most of the flavour is in it.

mistakes.fix: Pour it slowly through a fine sieve and leave the dregs behind.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring it in unstrained, so that grit ends up in the dish.

mistakes.fix: Use warm water.
mistakes.mistake: Using hot water, which can leave the mushrooms tasting flat.

quiz.because: The liquid takes on aroma during soaking, but needs straining before use.
choices: It replaces the need to remove grit.
It carries mushroom flavour that can enrich the dish.
It makes the mushrooms unnecessary in every dish.
quiz.question: Why keep the mushroom soaking liquid?

quiz.because: Slow straining and leaving the dregs separates useful liquid from settled grit.
choices: Tip it all in quickly without straining.
Stir the sediment through it before pouring.
Pour slowly through a fine sieve and leave the sediment behind.
quiz.question: How should the soaking liquid be recovered?

quiz.because: Water must reach the dried interior for the pieces to become flexible throughout.
choices: Plump and pliable without a hard dry centre.
Soft edges around a brittle centre.
Rigid pieces that snap when bent.
quiz.question: Which feel suggests the mushrooms have rehydrated?

quiz.because: Grit is carried with the liquid unless the sediment is separated deliberately.
choices: Rinse the mushrooms but use the soaking liquid unstrained.
Strain the liquid and avoid pouring in the dregs.
Stir the soaking bowl harder before pouring.
quiz.question: Grit reached the finished sauce. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The water is warm, and the soaking water is the prize: it is strained of grit and kept to flavour the dish, while the mushrooms are squeezed and rinsed.

cues.text: The sharp, sweet scent of the sauce rises as the hot food goes in.
The crust has softened slightly and the food is juicy.

technique/soak-in-sauce.does: Steeps just-fried food in a sharp, sweet sauce while it is still hot, so that it drinks up the sauce and turns juicy and flavoured through.
how: Make the sauce ahead and have it in a shallow dish.
Fry the food and lift it out of the oil, shaking off the excess.
Put the hot food straight into the sauce and turn it once.
Leave it to steep for a while, turning it now and then, then lift out and serve.

intro.what: This method steeps freshly fried food in a sharp sweet sauce while it is hot.
intro.why: It teaches you to use absorption to flavour a crust while controlling how far that crust softens.

mistakes.fix: Put it in hot, as it comes from the oil.
mistakes.mistake: Putting the food into the sauce after it has cooled, so that it will not take it up.

mistakes.fix: Lift it out after a short while.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it in the sauce for too long, so that it turns mushy.

quiz.because: Steeping lets sauce enter the hot food rather than remaining only on its surface.
choices: A drier crust with no sauce absorbed.
A coating that must stay entirely separate.
A juicy sauce-flavoured texture.
quiz.question: What does the sauce soak contribute to fried food?

quiz.because: Add the food hot for this absorption method, after shaking off excess frying oil so it does not enter the sauce.
choices: While still hot after excess oil is shaken off.
Only after cooling completely on a tray.
While still carrying a pool of frying oil.
quiz.question: When should fried food meet the prepared sauce?

quiz.because: Some softening is intended, but the food should retain its structure.
choices: A fully dissolved crust and collapsed pieces.
A slightly softened crust with juicy food beneath.
A dry interior unchanged by the sauce.
quiz.question: Which texture is the aim after a brief steep?

quiz.because: A shorter steep limits the amount of structural softening while retaining sauce flavour.
choices: Leave them soaking longer.
Cover them with more sauce and wait.
Lift them out sooner.
quiz.question: The fried pieces became mushy. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: Hot, fried food is steeped in a seasoned sauce, not left in water, and the soak lasts only as long as the food needs to drink the sauce.

comes_after.why: The syrup goes on while the baked pastry is still hot.
The syrup is made ahead and cooled.

cues.text: A sharp hiss as the cool syrup meets the hot pastry.
The syrup sinks away from the surface and the top stays pale and crisp.

technique/soak-in-syrup.does: Pours a cool syrup over a pastry as it comes hot from the oven, so that the syrup runs into every layer and the pastry drinks it up while the top stays crisp.
how: Make the syrup ahead and let it cool fully. Hot pastry takes cool syrup. Hot syrup on hot pastry turns it soggy.
Cut the pastry into portions before it is baked, so that the syrup can run down the cuts.
Pour the syrup slowly and evenly over the pastry as it comes out of the oven, and listen for the hiss.
Stop when the syrup stands in the cuts and a little pools at the edge. It goes on sinking in as the pastry cools.
Leave the pastry uncovered until it is cold. A lid traps steam and softens the top.

intro.what: This pastry method pours cool syrup over hot baked layers and leaves them uncovered to absorb it.
intro.why: It teaches you to balance absorption with preserving the pastry’s upper crust.

mistakes.fix: Let the syrup or the pastry be cold.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring hot syrup on hot pastry, so that the layers go limp.

mistakes.fix: Leave it uncovered until it is cold.
mistakes.mistake: Covering the pastry while it is still warm, so that steam softens the top.

mistakes.fix: Stop boiling the syrup while it is still thin enough to run off a spoon.
mistakes.mistake: Using a syrup boiled too thick, which sits on top and does not soak in.

quiz.because: The cuts carry syrup downward instead of leaving it entirely on the surface.
choices: To give syrup routes into the layers.
To prevent any syrup reaching the centre.
To keep the syrup only on the top.
quiz.question: Why cut the pastry before baking in this method?

quiz.because: The cooled-syrup method encourages absorption while limiting the sogginess described for hot syrup on hot pastry.
choices: Pour hot syrup over hot pastry and cover it.
Pour cooled syrup slowly and evenly over the hot pastry.
Add a thick syrup only after sealing the surface.
quiz.question: How should syrup meet the pastry in this method?

quiz.because: The temperature contrast creates a hiss as syrup contacts the hot layers.
choices: The dry crackle of uncoated pastry alone.
The continued rolling boil of a syrup pan.
A sharp hiss.
quiz.question: What sound accompanies cool syrup meeting hot pastry?

quiz.because: A cover traps steam against the top, softening the crust that should remain crisp.
choices: Leave the pastry uncovered until cold.
Use a tighter lid to retain more steam.
Cover while it is still hotter.
quiz.question: The top softened while cooling under a lid. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The pastry is not left in a bath. The syrup is poured over the baked, hot pastry in one go, and either the syrup or the pastry must be cold, so that the layers drink it and stay crisp.

cues.text: The water turns brown or cloudy, and the pieces stay pale.
A piece tastes cleaner and less bitter than before.

technique/soak-in-water.does: Puts cut vegetables in cold water for a short time, to keep them from browning, to rinse off loose starch and to take out the harsh bitterness.
how: Fill a bowl with cold water before cutting.
Drop the pieces in as they are cut.
Leave them for a short while, and change the water when it turns cloudy or brown.
Drain and pat dry before they are cooked.

intro.what: A brief cold-water soak protects cut vegetables and removes loose starch or harshness.
intro.why: It teaches you to separate useful surface washing from soaking long enough to lose flavour.

mistakes.fix: Soak only briefly.
mistakes.mistake: Soaking for too long, so that the pieces lose taste.

mistakes.fix: Drain and pat dry.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the drain, so that water drips into the hot pan.

quiz.because: Water protects exposed surfaces and carries off loose starch or some harshness.
choices: To draw out as much vegetable flavour as possible.
To limit surface browning while removing loose residue.
To make drying unnecessary later.
quiz.question: Why put some cut vegetables straight into cold water?

quiz.because: Changing the water removes what the vegetables have released.
choices: Swirl the pieces but keep the same discoloured water.
Drain the pieces, then return them to the same water.
Change the water during the brief soak.
quiz.question: What should happen as the soaking water becomes cloudy or brown?

quiz.because: The water takes up surface residue while the cut pieces remain pale.
choices: Pale pieces in water that becomes cloudy or brown.
Dark dry edges around exposed pieces.
Browned pieces sitting in unchanged clear water.
quiz.question: Which appearance fits this soaking step?

quiz.because: Draining and drying removes free surface water before the next cooking step.
choices: Transfer more soaking water with them.
Drain and pat them dry first.
Skip draining but raise the heat.
quiz.question: The vegetables drip water into the cooking pan. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The soak is brief, in cold water, and aims to keep a cut vegetable pale and mild, not to swell or soften dried food.

comes_after.why: The rice is soaked after it has been washed.

cues.text: The grains turn from glassy to an even, chalky white.
A grain crushes easily between the fingers, with no hard core.

technique/soak-rice.does: Leaves washed rice in cold water until the grains have turned white and plump all through, so that they cook evenly and come out tender in the middle.
how: Put the washed, drained rice in the pot or in a bowl and cover it with cold water.
Leave it until the grains turn from clear to chalky white.
Drain it well and let it sit in the sieve for a short while.
Cook it in fresh measured water.

intro.what: This rice method soaks washed grains in cold water before draining and cooking in fresh measured water.
intro.why: It teaches you to recognise hydration and keep soaking separate from final cooking-liquid control.

mistakes.fix: Soak it in cold water and shorter.
mistakes.mistake: Soaking for too long in warm weather, so that the rice sours.

mistakes.fix: Drain it and add the measured water.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking it in the soaking water, so that the amount of water is wrong.

quiz.because: Absorbed water reaches into the grains before cooking begins.
choices: To dry out the grain centres.
To remove the need for cooking liquid.
To hydrate the centres for more even softening.
quiz.question: Why soak the washed rice in this method?

quiz.because: Separating the soak from cooking allows the cooking water to be controlled deliberately.
choices: Drain it and cook in fresh measured water.
Keep adding unmeasured water to the soaking bowl.
Cook it with whatever soaking water remains.
quiz.question: What happens after the rice has soaked?

quiz.because: These grains turn evenly chalky white as water reaches their interiors.
choices: Only the outside looks white while a glassy centre remains.
Glassy grains turn evenly chalky white.
Only dry white tips appear on transparent centres.
quiz.question: Which colour change shows hydration here?

quiz.because: Removing variable leftover soaking water makes the next addition more consistent.
choices: Leave the soaking liquid and top it up by eye.
Add extra water every time without draining.
Drain the soaking water before adding measured cooking water.
quiz.question: The final water amount is inconsistent after soaking. What should change?

variant_of.differs: It is a short soak of washed rice in cold water until the grains turn white, and not a long soak of dried pulses, and the water is poured off.

cues.text: An even layer, with the surface showing through at the thin places and a clear rim.
The spoon glides. If it drags, the paste is too stiff and wants more oil.

technique/spread.does: Smooths a soft paste, mash or butter over a surface in an even layer with the back of a spoon or a knife, so that every bite carries some and the edges stay clear.
how: Have the paste soft enough to move. Loosen it with a little oil or water if it is stiff.
Put a spoonful in the middle of the surface.
Push it outwards with the back of a spoon in slow circles, working towards the edge.
Stop a little short of the edge, so that the paste does not run off or burn on the pan.

intro.what: Spreading smooths a soft paste across a surface in an even layer.
intro.why: It teaches you to adjust paste consistency before applying pressure to a delicate base.

mistakes.fix: Loosen it with a little oil first.
mistakes.mistake: Spreading a paste that is too stiff, so that it tears the dough.

mistakes.fix: Push it out in circles until the layer is even, to just short of the rim.
mistakes.mistake: Piling the paste in the middle and leaving the edge bare.

quiz.because: A consistent layer gives more even coverage while a clear rim contains it.
choices: To concentrate nearly all of it in the middle.
To distribute it across bites without an overloaded centre.
To force it over the rim.
quiz.question: Why spread filling or paste evenly?

quiz.because: Gentle outward movement distributes the paste gradually without tearing the base.
choices: At the rim, pushing everything off the edge.
By pressing a stiff mound repeatedly in place.
From the middle, moving outward in gentle circles.
quiz.question: Where should spreading begin?

quiz.because: A gliding spoon indicates the paste is soft enough to distribute without excess force.
choices: It glides instead of dragging.
It catches and tears the base.
It leaves an immovable mound behind.
quiz.question: What should the spoon feel like as paste spreads?

quiz.because: Softening the paste addresses its resistance rather than transferring more force to the dough.
choices: Press harder with the back of the spoon.
Loosen the stiff paste with a little oil first.
Add dry flour to thicken the paste.
quiz.question: The paste tears the dough as you spread it. What should change?

cues.text: The flour vanishes into a thin paste that coats every piece.
The raw, dusty smell gives way to a faint smell of biscuit.

technique/sprinkle-with-flour.does: Scatters flour over food that is already cooking in fat and cooks it for a moment, so that the liquid added next thickens as it simmers.
how: Scatter the flour evenly over the hot, fat-coated food, not in a heap.
Stir until no white shows.
Cook it for a moment, stirring, to take away the raw taste.
Add the liquid little by little at first, stirring it smooth.

intro.what: This method scatters flour over food already cooking in fat before adding liquid.
intro.why: It teaches another route to thickening a sauce, with attention to even coating and cooking the flour first.

mistakes.fix: Scatter it from high up, or through a sieve.
mistakes.mistake: Tipping the flour in as a heap, which makes lumps that never dissolve.

mistakes.fix: Give it a moment on the heat first.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the liquid at once, before the flour has cooked.

quiz.because: Flour cooked on the fat-coated food thickens the liquid added next.
choices: Keep the liquid completely thin.
Thicken the liquid as it simmers.
Keep the cooking fat separate from the sauce.
quiz.question: What is the flour meant to do when liquid is added?

quiz.because: Scattering flour evenly coats the food without leaving heaps that can form lumps.
choices: As a heap left on top.
In a heap stirred in after all the liquid has been added.
Scattered evenly over hot food already coated in fat.
quiz.question: How should the flour meet the food?

quiz.because: No loose white flour should remain visible: it forms a thin paste coating the pieces.
choices: A thin paste coating the pieces, with no white flour showing.
Loose white heaps between the pieces.
Dry flour floating on liquid added immediately.
quiz.question: What appearance should follow stirring in the flour?

quiz.because: Scattering flour or using a sieve avoids heaps that turn into lumps.
choices: Add the flour all at once and rely on stirring to break it up.
Scatter the flour evenly or use a sieve.
Add all the liquid before stirring the flour.
quiz.question: A heap of flour has formed lumps. What would help prevent this next time?

variant_of.differs: The flour goes onto food already cooking in fat, so that the roux forms around the pieces and is not made on its own.

comes_after.why: Leaves are squeezed once they have wilted or boiled and let go of their water. Raw leaves hold it in.

cues.text: The ball of leaves is dense and damp but gives out no more water when squeezed.
The water that comes out is a dark green, and the leaves loosen into a dry, fluffy heap.

technique/squeeze.does: Presses the water out of cooked leaves by the handful, or in a sieve, so that they can be seasoned and mixed without turning the dish watery.
how: Let the cooked leaves cool enough to handle.
Take up a handful and close the fist, or press the leaves against the side of a sieve with a spoon.
Squeeze hard and long, turning the ball in the hand, until only a few drops come out.
Shake the leaves loose, as they will be a tight lump, and chop or season them.

intro.what: Squeezing removes retained water from cooked leaves before mixing or seasoning.
intro.why: It teaches you how excess water can dilute a dish and keep dressing from coating the leaves.

mistakes.fix: Let them cool, then squeeze hard.
mistakes.mistake: Squeezing the leaves while they are hot, which burns the hands and tempts a cook to squeeze too lightly.

mistakes.fix: Squeeze again until only a few drops come out.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the leaves wet, so that the oil and the dressing slide off them.

quiz.because: Removing free water keeps the leaves from diluting the mixture or shedding their dressing.
choices: To keep every drop of cooking liquid in the mixture.
To prevent them taking any seasoning.
To avoid adding excess water.
quiz.question: Why squeeze cooked leaves before mixing them into a dish?

quiz.because: Loosening restores an open texture so chopping and seasoning can be more even.
choices: Shake them loose before chopping or seasoning.
Keep them compressed as a hard lump.
Return them to water before dressing.
quiz.question: What should happen after squeezing leaves into a tight ball?

quiz.because: The aim is to remove free water while leaving the leaves naturally damp.
choices: A soaked ball streams water under light pressure.
Damp compact leaves release very little more water.
The surface is dry but the centre drips freely.
quiz.question: Which feel suggests enough water has been pressed out?

quiz.because: Free water prevents the intended coating and dilutes the seasoning.
choices: Add more water before the dressing.
Leave the water and double the dressing immediately.
Squeeze them again before seasoning.
quiz.question: Dressing slides off wet leaves. What should change?

cues.text: The yogurt stays smooth and creamy, with no grains and no pool of thin liquid at the sides.
The spoon meets a gentle, even drag, like a thick cream.

technique/stabilise.does: Prepares yogurt so that it can be heated and simmered without splitting into curds and thin liquid. A starch or a beaten egg white is mixed into the cold yogurt, and the yogurt is stirred one way as it heats.
how: Whisk the yogurt smooth in a pan, off the heat.
Mix a little cornstarch with cold water until smooth, or beat an egg white loose, and whisk it into the yogurt.
Set the pan over a low heat and stir all the time, always in the same direction.
Bring it slowly up to a bare simmer without letting it boil hard, and keep stirring until it is thick and smooth.
Keep it at a gentle simmer from then on.

intro.what: This yogurt method mixes in starch or egg white before gentle heating.
intro.why: It teaches you to protect a smooth texture by preparing the mixture and controlling heat.

mistakes.fix: Stabilise it first and stir in one direction only.
mistakes.mistake: Heating plain yogurt fast, or stirring it first one way and then the other, so that it breaks into curds.

mistakes.fix: Hold it at a gentle simmer.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the stabilised yogurt boil hard, which can still break it.

quiz.because: The added stabiliser and gentle heat help maintain a smooth creamy mixture.
choices: Separation into curds and thin liquid during heating.
All thickening of the yogurt.
Mixing yogurt with other liquids.
quiz.question: What does stabilising yogurt aim to prevent?

quiz.because: Mixing before heating distributes the stabiliser through the yogurt in advance.
choices: After the yogurt has boiled hard and separated.
While the yogurt is cold and off the heat.
Only after serving the hot sauce.
quiz.question: When is the stabiliser mixed into the yogurt?

quiz.because: Grains and separate liquid signal a loss of the intended continuous texture.
choices: Small curds floating in thin liquid.
A clear watery border widening around grains.
Creamy without grains or a watery pool at the sides.
quiz.question: Which appearance suggests a smooth heated yogurt sauce?

quiz.because: Stabilisation does not remove the need for gentle heat; hard boiling can still disrupt the texture.
choices: Heat gently and maintain only a bare simmer.
Boil harder to evaporate the separated liquid.
Add the stabiliser only after a vigorous boil.
quiz.question: The prepared yogurt splits during hard boiling. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The aim is not body but steadiness: a starch or egg white goes into the cold yogurt first, and the yogurt is stirred one way so that its milk proteins do not clump when it is heated. Thicken stirs a starch into a hot liquid.

cues.text: Vegetables are bright and just tender. Mussel shells gape wide open.
The lid rattles steadily.

technique/steam.does: Cooks food in the steam of a little boiling liquid under a tight lid, so that nothing of it is washed away.
how: Bring a shallow layer of water or wine to a boil in a wide pot.
Set the food in a basket above the liquid, or straight into the pot for shellfish, and cover it at once with a tight lid.
Keep the heat high and the lid on.
Sort mussels before they go in: throw away any with a broken shell, and any that stays open when it is tapped.
For mussels, shake the pot now and then, and take it off the heat as soon as the shells have opened. Throw away any mussel that stays shut.

intro.what: Steaming uses vapour retained under a lid to cook food with little boiling liquid.
intro.why: It teaches you how a closed cooking space carries heat without immersing a basket of food.

mistakes.fix: Leave it shut until the time is nearly up.
mistakes.mistake: Lifting the lid again and again, which lets the steam out and slows everything down.

mistakes.fix: Take the pot off the heat the moment most of the shells are open.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving mussels on the heat after they have opened, so that they shrink and turn rubbery.

quiz.because: The basket holds food above the liquid where rising vapour transfers heat.
choices: Only the dry metal of the lid.
Complete immersion in cold liquid.
Steam rising from the boiling liquid below.
quiz.question: What carries heat to vegetables in a steaming basket?

quiz.because: Keeping food above the liquid preserves the steaming method while the lid retains vapour.
choices: Above the boiling liquid beneath a tight lid.
Submerged fully beneath the liquid.
Above an uncovered pot with most steam escaping.
quiz.question: Where should a vegetable basket sit?

quiz.because: Boiling liquid beneath the closed lid generates the steam used in this covered-pot method.
choices: The scrape of dry food catching on the base.
A steadily rattling lid.
The crackle of an uncovered frying pan.
quiz.question: Which sound is consistent with active steaming in this covered-pot method?

quiz.because: Each opening releases steam and heat from the enclosed cooking space.
choices: Lift it even more often to vent the pot.
Leave the pot uncovered throughout.
Keep the lid closed between necessary checks.
quiz.question: Frequent lid lifting slows the steaming. What should change?

cues.text: Steam shows through the whole pile of grains before the steaming is counted.
The finished grains are tender, swollen and separate, and none sticks to the fingers.

technique/steam-couscous.does: Swells dry couscous grains in the steam of a simmering stew, in rounds, so that each grain turns light and separate. The grains are rubbed with water and oil, steamed, tipped out, sprinkled again and raked apart, then steamed once more until they are tender.
how: Tip the dry grains into a wide dish, sprinkle them with salted water and rub them between the palms until every grain is damp and nothing is clumped. Work in a little oil.

Bring the stew, or plain water, to a simmer in the base of the couscoussier. Seal the seam between the base and the top with a strip of damp cloth or a paste of flour and water, so that no steam escapes there.
Pile the damp grains loosely in the perforated top. Do not press them down, and do not cover them until steam rises through the whole pile.
Steam until the steam shows through the top, then tip the grains back into the dish.
Sprinkle them with a little cold salted water, rake them with the fingertips to break every lump, let them swell for a while, and steam them again in the same way.
Tip them out for the last time and rake in butter or smen until the grains shine. Heap them on a dish and serve with the stew.

intro.what: Traditional couscous steaming hydrates grains in stages above simmering liquid.
intro.why: It teaches you to combine loose grain handling, steam circulation and gradual wetting for separate tender grains.

mistakes.fix: Pile them loosely and let the steam find its way.
mistakes.mistake: Pressing the grains down in the top, which blocks the steam and leaves a hard core.

mistakes.fix: Seal the seam with damp cloth or a paste of flour and water.
mistakes.mistake: Letting steam leak at the seam, so that the grains stay dry and the stew goes thin.

mistakes.fix: Add water a little at a time and rake after each sprinkling.
mistakes.mistake: Sprinkling on too much water at once, which turns the grains gluey.

mistakes.fix: Keep them above the liquid, where only the steam reaches them.
mistakes.mistake: Cooking the grains in the stew liquid itself, which makes a paste.

names.fr: Cuire le couscous à la vapeur

quiz.because: The perforated upper pot exposes the grains to steam without immersing them in broth.
choices: To keep them dry throughout the process.
To soften them with steam rather than turn them into a wet paste.
To let them sit directly in the stew.
quiz.question: Why keep these couscous grains above the liquid?

quiz.because: Loose piling leaves routes for steam through the whole bed of grains.
choices: Pressed firmly into a dense block.
Wrapped tightly so steam cannot enter.
Piled loosely so steam can pass through.
quiz.question: How should the grains sit in the perforated top?

quiz.because: Steam showing through the pile demonstrates circulation rather than escape around it.
choices: Steam appears across the top of the grains.
Steam leaks only from the join below.
The surface stays dry while the base clumps.
quiz.question: Which sign confirms steam is moving through the pile?

quiz.because: Small additions and separation control absorption without creating a sticky mass.
choices: Pour on more water at once.
Sprinkle water gradually and rake apart the lumps.
Press the wet grains together before steaming.
quiz.question: The grains turn gluey after wetting. What should change?

variant_of.differs: Steam cooks fresh food in the steam of a little boiling water. Here the food is dry grain, wetted by hand between rounds, steamed over a stew in several rounds and raked apart each time, so that it never sets into a block.

comes_after.why: The stew is held at a gentle simmer, so a cook who can hold a simmer steady has the main skill.

cues.text: The broth turns dark green, glossy and a little thick, with the leaves hanging in it and not clumped.
The spoon moves through it easily. It is thick and silky and not stringy.
A deep, green scent, a little like cooked spinach.

technique/stew-jute-leaf.does: Simmers finely chopped jute leaf in hot broth, uncovered, until the leaves give up their slippery thickness and the broth turns dark green and silky. It is kept just below a boil, stirred little, and finished with a taqliyeh of garlic and coriander.
how: Strip fresh leaves from their stems, wash and dry them well, and chop them very fine. Frozen leaves go in as they are. Dried leaves are soaked briefly first.
Bring the broth to a gentle simmer and keep it hot.
Stir in the leaves, and keep the pot just below a boil, uncovered.
Cook until the leaves have sunk into the broth and thickened it to a silky stew, stirring only now and then.
Take the pot off the heat before the garlic and coriander taqliyeh and the lemon juice go in.

intro.what: This jute-leaf stew gently thickens broth with finely chopped leaves and finishes with garlic-coriander taqliyeh.
intro.why: It teaches you to control a leaf’s natural silky texture through fine cutting and gentle heat.

mistakes.fix: Keep it just below a boil, uncovered.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling it hard or putting a lid on, so that the stew turns dull and stringy.

mistakes.fix: Chop them very fine, or use leaves that are already chopped.
mistakes.mistake: Chopping the leaves coarse, so that they stay in long strings.

mistakes.fix: Add it at the end.
mistakes.mistake: Adding lemon juice early, which dulls the green.

quiz.because: The leaves disperse through the broth and give it its characteristic silky body.
choices: A dark-green silky thickness.
Separate leafy pieces that leave the broth thin.
A completely smooth puree without visible leaves.
quiz.question: What do chopped jute leaves contribute to the broth?

quiz.because: Finishing additions preserve their distinct role rather than boiling them throughout the leaf cooking.
choices: Before the broth begins heating.
After taking the pot off the heat at the end.
Only after the leaves have been strained out.
quiz.question: When are taqliyeh and lemon added in this method?

quiz.because: Fine leaves distribute through the liquid and create a smooth slippery body.
choices: Large tough strings in thin broth.
A stiff dry mass of clumped leaves.
Silky broth with suspended leaves rather than long strings.
quiz.question: Which texture is the aim?

quiz.because: Finer cutting reduces the long strands that interrupt the intended silky texture.
choices: Chop the leaves more finely before cooking.
Leave them whole and stir harder.
Add the lemon earlier instead of cutting.
quiz.question: Long leaf strings remained in the stew. What would you change before cooking the next batch?

variant_of.differs: The leaf is chopped very fine and cooked uncovered, just below a boil, until it thickens the broth itself, and it is stirred little.

cues.text: The spoon drags more heavily across the base as the mixture thickens.
The surface stays smooth, with no brown bits at the edges.
A caught, scorched smell means it was left still for too long.

technique/stir.does: Moves a spoon through food as it heats, scraping the base of the pan, so that it cooks evenly, does not catch and scorch, and stays smooth.
how: Use a spoon with a flat edge, or a wooden spoon, and a pan with a heavy base.
Keep the heat gentle and reach the whole base and the corners with each pass.
Stir in slow loops or long sweeps, and not so hard that the food breaks.
Keep going for as long as the dish thickens, since the base catches first.

intro.what: Stirring moves food gently across the pan base as it heats and thickens.
intro.why: It teaches you to sense thickening through the spoon while preventing local catching.

mistakes.fix: Stay with it and stir throughout.
mistakes.mistake: Walking away, so that the base catches and the whole pan tastes burnt.

mistakes.fix: Stir slowly and only as much as needed to stop it catching.
mistakes.mistake: Stirring a rice pudding hard, so that the grains break and turn to paste.

mistakes.fix: Turn the heat down.
mistakes.mistake: Using high heat, which scorches the base faster than the spoon can reach.

quiz.because: The base catches first, so stirring must reach the pan contact layer rather than only the top.
choices: To break every grain into paste.
To keep the surface moving while the base stays still.
To move food away from the hottest contact surface before it catches.
quiz.question: Why scrape the base while stirring a thickening mixture?

quiz.because: A broad pass moves mixture from places where it could otherwise remain still and scorch.
choices: The whole base and corners.
Only the centre of the surface.
The sides just above the base, without sweeping the bottom.
quiz.question: Which parts of the pan should each stirring pass reach?

quiz.because: A thickening mixture resists the spoon more even when its surface remains smooth.
choices: The mixture is necessarily burning.
The mixture is thickening.
The mixture has become thinner.
quiz.question: What does increasing drag on the spoon suggest?

quiz.because: Aggressive stirring breaks grains; gentler movement preserves texture while still protecting the base.
choices: Stir faster to break up the remaining grains.
Press the grains against the base.
Stir more gently, only enough to prevent catching.
quiz.question: Rice pudding became pasty under hard stirring. What would you change next time?

en: stir fry in a hot pan

comes_after.why: Stir-frying is sautéing at higher heat and greater speed, so a cook has to read a hot pan first.

cues.text: A steady, loud sizzle, which fades if the pan has been crowded.
The pieces are glossy and coloured at the edges, and none sits in a pool of liquid.
A toasty, sweet smell, and not a burnt one.

technique/stir-fry.does: Cooks small, even pieces very fast in a little hot oil in a wide pan, keeping them moving all the time with a spoon or a spatula, so that they take colour at the edges and stay crisp or just tender inside.
how: Cut everything small and even, and have it all at hand before the pan goes on, because the cooking is quick.
Heat a wok or wide pan until very hot, then add a little oil and swirl it.
Add the food that takes longest first, then the rest in order, and keep it moving the whole time.
Add sauces and seasoning at the end, so that they coat the food and do not stew it.
Take it out as soon as it is done, since it carries on cooking in the pan.

intro.what: Stir-frying cooks small pieces quickly in a hot wide pan while keeping them moving.
intro.why: It teaches you to coordinate preparation, pan space and ingredient order before cooking begins.

mistakes.fix: Cook in smaller batches and keep the heat high.
mistakes.mistake: Crowding the pan, so that the food stews in its own water.

mistakes.fix: Add the pieces in order of how long they take.
mistakes.mistake: Adding everything together, so that some pieces are raw and others limp.

mistakes.fix: Keep it moving.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the food still for long, so that it scorches.

quiz.because: Having ingredients ready lets you add them in the required order without leaving others to scorch.
choices: The ingredients must all enter at exactly the same moment.
The fast cooking leaves little time for preparation between additions.
Prepared ingredients need no attention in the pan.
quiz.question: Why prepare everything before heating a stir-fry pan?

quiz.because: Late sauce additions keep quick hot-pan cooking from becoming prolonged simmering.
choices: At the start before the pan heats.
In enough volume to submerge the ingredients throughout.
Near the end so they coat rather than stew the food.
quiz.question: When should sauces be added in this method?

quiz.because: A load of food can cool the pan, reducing the sizzle and encouraging stewing.
choices: The pan has been crowded and cooled.
Browning is necessarily complete.
The heat is reaching every piece more strongly.
quiz.question: What can a fading sizzle suggest?

quiz.because: Smaller batches preserve heat and space so released moisture does not dominate the cooking.
choices: Keep the whole batch in the pan and stir faster.
Cook smaller batches in the hot pan.
Cover tightly to retain the moisture.
quiz.question: Crowded food is stewing in pooled water. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The pan is hotter and wider, the pieces are cut smaller, and they are kept moving with a spoon or spatula and added in order of how long they take, where a sauté lets them sit to colour between tosses.

cues.text: A clear stock shows the bottom of the ladle through it.

technique/strain.does: Pours a liquid through a sieve, so that the solids stay behind and the liquid comes out clear.
how: Set a fine sieve over a pot or a bowl large enough for all the liquid.
Ladle the liquid in, a little at a time at first.
Let it drain by its own weight. For a clear stock, do not press on the solids.
For a soup or a sauce that should be thick, press the solids through with the back of a ladle.

intro.what: Straining passes liquid through a sieve while leaving solids behind.
intro.why: It teaches you to choose between clarity and a thicker texture when deciding whether to press the solids.

mistakes.fix: Ladle from the top and leave the last cloudy part in the pot.
mistakes.mistake: Tipping a full stockpot over the sieve in one go, which stirs up the sediment and clouds the stock.

quiz.because: Liquid passes through the sieve while the solids stay behind.
choices: Fat from water without using a sieve.
Only foam lifted from the surface with a ladle.
Liquid that passes through a sieve from solids that stay behind.
quiz.question: What does straining separate?

quiz.because: For a clear stock, let the liquid drain under its own weight. Pressing the solids is reserved here for a thicker soup or sauce.
choices: Under their own weight, without pressing.
By being crushed hard through the mesh.
By stirring the sediment vigorously first.
quiz.question: When straining a clear stock, how should the solids drain?

quiz.because: Seeing the bottom of the ladle through the stock is a useful cue to its clarity.
choices: Suspended sediment hides the ladle.
The bottom of the ladle can be seen through the stock.
A thick mash coats the sieve.
quiz.question: What can help you judge whether the strained stock is clear?

quiz.because: Tipping in the sediment can cloud the stock. Ladle from the top and leave the last cloudy liquid behind.
choices: Pour more slowly but still include all the sediment.
Press every solid through the mesh.
Ladle from the top and leave the last cloudy part behind.
quiz.question: Pouring the whole stockpot at once has stirred up sediment. What would you change?

cues.text: A plump, even shape with no filling showing at the seams.
It gives a little when it is pressed. It is not drum-tight.

technique/stuff.does: Fills a hollow, a pocket or a rolled slice with a seasoned mixture, which flavours the food from inside and keeps it moist.
how: Season the filling well and let it cool before it goes in.
Fill loosely. A filling swells as it cooks, and one that is packed tight bursts its wrapper.
Close the opening by folding, tying or pinning, so that the filling stays inside.
For a rolled slice, flatten the slice, spread the filling short of the edges, roll it up and tie it.
Check the centre of the filling against a trusted guide to doneness. It is the last part to heat.

intro.what: Stuffing encloses a seasoned mixture in a pocket, hollow or rolled slice.
intro.why: It teaches you to leave expansion room and close seams without overpacking the wrapper.

mistakes.fix: Leave room for it to swell.
