mistakes.mistake: Packing the filling in tightly, so that the wrapper splits as it cooks.

mistakes.fix: Cool the filling first, and stuff just before the food goes on the heat.
mistakes.mistake: Stuffing with a warm filling long before cooking.

quiz.because: A filling can expand during cooking, so a little space reduces pressure against the enclosure.
choices: Tight packing should stop the filling expanding at all.
Dense packing is needed to hold every kind of filling.
It needs room to swell without splitting its wrapper.
quiz.question: Why should a stuffing not be packed tightly?

quiz.because: Clear edges help the slice close around the filling rather than force it out.
choices: Spread short of the edges before rolling and tying.
Pile it beyond the edges before tying.
Leave the filling only along the outside seam.
quiz.question: How should filling sit on a slice that will be rolled?

quiz.because: A little give indicates room in the enclosure without leaving it open.
choices: Drum-tight and stretched.
Plump with a little give.
Loose with filling spilling from seams.
quiz.question: Which feel suits an assembled stuffed shape?

quiz.because: Less packing pressure allows expansion without forcing the wrapper apart.
choices: Pack the next filling more tightly.
Stretch a thinner wrapper around the same large filling.
Fill more loosely and leave expansion room.
quiz.question: The wrapper split as the filling swelled. What would you change next time?

cues.text: The filling lies flat and even, with none showing at the edge.
The closed bread is firm and flat under the hand, and does not slide apart.

technique/stuff-a-pita.does: Opens a round of pita and spreads a thin layer of raw, spiced meat mixture inside, then presses the bread shut, so that the filling cooks and the bread crisps and soaks up its juices on the heat.
how: Cut round the edge of the pita with a knife, or split it along one side, and open it into layers.
Spread the filling thinly and evenly over the inner face of one layer, right to the edge.
Close the pita over the filling and press it down firmly with the hand, so that the layers hold together.
Cut it in half, or leave it whole, and cook it at once.

intro.what: This arayes-style preparation spreads a thin meat filling inside pita before cooking.
intro.why: It teaches you to make a flat even filling rather than a thick mound beneath delicate bread.

mistakes.fix: Spread it thin, as thin as a finger, and even.
mistakes.mistake: Piling the filling thick in the middle, so that the bread crisps and burns before the filling is done.

mistakes.fix: Warm the bread first, so that it bends.
mistakes.mistake: Using a dry, cracked pita that splits as it is opened.

quiz.because: A thin even layer reduces the contrast between thick filling and the bread surrounding it.
choices: To avoid a thick centre beneath faster-browning bread.
To concentrate nearly all the meat in the middle.
To leave empty bread across most of the surface.
quiz.question: Why distribute the filling evenly inside pita?

quiz.because: Firm flat contact holds the layers together around the distributed filling.
choices: Leave the layers loose and sliding.
Close the bread and press it firmly flat.
Add a tall extra mound before closing.
quiz.question: What happens after spreading the filling?

quiz.because: A stable flat shape indicates that the filling and bread are in even contact.
choices: A raised loose centre under a shifting top.
A cracked shell around an uneven lump.
Flat and firm without layers sliding apart.
quiz.question: Which feel suggests the filled pita is assembled neatly?

quiz.because: A little warmth makes the bread more flexible for opening without splitting.
choices: Warm it first so it bends.
Use a drier colder piece.
Pull the brittle layers apart more sharply.
quiz.question: The pita cracks as it is opened. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The pocket is a round of bread, and the filling is raw meat spread flat as a thin layer and pressed shut so that it cooks with the bread. It is not packed into a hollow of a bird or a vegetable.

cues.text: The skin lifts easily from the flesh on a fingertip and does not tear.
The flavouring shows through the skin as an even pattern, with no bare patches.

technique/stuff-under-the-skin.does: Slides a flavouring, such as slices of truffle or a soft herb butter, between the skin and the flesh of a bird, so that it seasons the meat directly and keeps the breast moist as it cooks.
how: Dry the bird well. Start at the neck end and work a finger gently between the skin and the breast, then loosen the skin over the whole breast and a little way down the legs, without tearing it.
Season the flesh under the skin.
Slide the flavouring in flat and spread it in an even layer, then smooth the skin back down over it.
Tuck the neck skin under the bird, so that nothing slips out.
Truss the bird if it is to be poached or roasted whole, and cook it soon after.

intro.what: This method lays flavouring between a bird’s skin and flesh without tearing the skin.
intro.why: It teaches you to separate a delicate layer gently and distribute flavouring without lumps.

mistakes.fix: Work slowly with a finger and not a nail, and lay the skin back over any small tear.
mistakes.mistake: Tearing the skin, so that the flavouring leaks out and the flesh dries.

mistakes.fix: Use thin flat slices, or a soft smooth butter spread evenly.
mistakes.mistake: Pushing in a lumpy filling that leaves gaps and slides about.

quiz.because: The loosened space places flavouring directly against the flesh beneath the skin.
choices: Only inside the bird’s cavity.
Between the skin and flesh.
Only on the outer surface of the skin.
quiz.question: Where does the flavouring go in this method?

quiz.because: Slow fingertip work separates the layers while preserving a covering for the filling.
choices: Pull sharply with a fingernail.
Cut deep parallel slits through the flesh.
Work a finger gently under it without tearing.
quiz.question: How should the skin be loosened?

quiz.because: Even coverage distributes the flavouring rather than concentrating it in a moving lump.
choices: A flat pattern of flavouring without bare patches.
A large lump at the neck with empty areas below.
Loose filling protruding through skin tears.
quiz.question: Which appearance suggests even placement?

quiz.because: A flat smooth filling makes closer contact and is easier to retain under the skin.
choices: Push in larger hard pieces.
Use thin flat slices or soft butter spread evenly.
Leave the lumps near the opening.
quiz.question: Lumpy filling slides around beneath the skin. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The filling goes between the skin and the flesh and not into the hollow of the bird, so it flavours and bastes the meat directly and is never packed in.

comes_after.why: Even pieces soften together. Uneven ones leave some raw and some brown.

cues.text: A quiet, steady hiss. A loud sizzle means the heat is too high.
The onion turns glassy and limp, with no brown at the edges.
Sweet, with the raw sharpness gone.

technique/sweat.does: Softens cut vegetables in a little fat over low heat, so that they give up their water and turn sweet without browning.
how: Warm the fat in a wide pan over low heat.
Add the vegetables with a little salt and stir to coat them.
Keep the heat low and stir now and then, so that nothing sits long enough to colour.
Cover the pan to go faster: the trapped steam softens them.
Stop when the pieces are soft and glassy.

intro.what: Sweating softens cut vegetables gently in a little fat without browning them.
intro.why: It teaches you to use gentle heat and watch for softness before colour develops.

mistakes.fix: Turn the heat down and add a spoonful of water to stop the colour.
mistakes.mistake: The heat is too high, so the edges brown before the middle softens.

mistakes.fix: Use a wider pan, or let the water cook off before going on.
mistakes.mistake: Too many vegetables in a small pan, so they stew in their own water.

quiz.because: Gentle heat softens the vegetables and brings out sweetness without browning them.
choices: Softness and sweetness without browning.
A lightly browned surface while the centre stays firm.
A crisp, deeply browned surface.
quiz.question: What is the aim of sweating vegetables?

quiz.because: Low heat and occasional stirring keep the pieces from sitting long enough to colour.
choices: Use medium-high heat and stir constantly to avoid colour.
Keep it low and stir now and then.
Raise it whenever the vegetables soften.
quiz.question: How should the heat be managed in this method?

quiz.because: Glassy, limp onion without brown edges shows softening without browning.
choices: Black edges with a firm centre.
A crisp golden crust.
Glassy, limp pieces without brown edges.
quiz.question: Which onion appearance matches sweating?

quiz.because: The heat is too high if edges brown before the middle softens. Lower it and add a little water to halt the colouring.
choices: Lower the heat and add a little water to halt the colouring.
Keep the heat high but stir more frequently.
Leave the pieces unstirred over the same heat.
quiz.question: The edges are browning before the middle softens. What should you change?

cues.text: The sweetness is clear but does not drown the taste of the food.
No grains of sugar remain.

technique/sweeten.does: Adds sugar to a food a little at a time and tastes after each addition, to bring it to the right level of sweetness without hiding its own taste.
how: Cook the food until it is soft enough to take up the sugar.
Add the sugar in portions, stirring each in until it has dissolved.
Taste after each portion and stop when the sweetness is balanced.
Add a small amount of salt at the end to round the taste.

intro.what: Sweetening adds sugar gradually until it balances rather than hides the food’s own taste.
intro.why: It teaches you to dissolve additions fully and judge the result before adding more.

mistakes.fix: Add it a little at a time.
mistakes.mistake: Adding all the sugar at once, so that it is too sweet and cannot be corrected.

mistakes.fix: Cook them soft first.
mistakes.mistake: Adding sugar to dried beans before they are soft, so that they stay hard.

quiz.because: Sweetness should support the ingredient rather than overwhelm its character.
choices: The flavour of the food beneath the sugar.
Only the taste of sugar.
A gritty layer of undissolved sugar.
quiz.question: What should balanced sweetness preserve?

quiz.because: Dissolving distributes sweetness so tasting can guide the next addition accurately.
choices: Before the previous sugar has dissolved.
After stirring the previous addition until dissolved and tasting.
Only after adding all the sugar available.
quiz.question: When should the next sugar addition be judged?

quiz.because: Sugar needs to dissolve into the food rather than remain as separate gritty crystals.
choices: A pile of crystals sits at the base.
Dry sugar coats the surface.
No sugar grains remain visible.
quiz.question: Which appearance indicates the sugar has dissolved?

quiz.because: Small additions let you stop before sweetness masks the food.
choices: Add sugar gradually and taste between additions.
Add the entire amount before tasting.
Judge the sweetness before the previous addition has dissolved.
quiz.question: A batch becomes overwhelmingly sweet. What should change next time?

comes_after.why: The lentils are simmered until soft before the bulgur is stirred in.

cues.text: The liquid has gone and the mixture is thick and damp, with no dry grains left.
The grains are tender all through, with no hard core when pressed.

technique/swell-bulgur-in-hot-liquid.does: Stirs fine bulgur into a pan of hot, freshly cooked lentils or other hot liquid, covers it and leaves it off the heat until the grains have swollen and softened in the liquid and taken its flavour.
how: Cook the lentils until they are very soft, with enough water left in the pan to wet the bulgur.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the bulgur.
Cover at once and leave it to stand until the grains are swollen and the mixture is thick.
Stir it once and let it cool until it can be handled.

intro.what: Fine bulgur absorbs the remaining hot liquid in cooked lentils while standing covered off the heat.
intro.why: It teaches you to use retained heat and absorption to thicken a mixture without continued boiling.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat before the bulgur goes in.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the pan on the heat, so that the bulgur cooks to a paste.

mistakes.fix: Leave more liquid in the pan, or sprinkle on hot water and cover again.
mistakes.mistake: Using too little liquid, which leaves hard grains.

mistakes.fix: Leave it covered until the stand is over.
mistakes.mistake: Lifting the lid to look, which lets the heat out.

quiz.because: The bulgur swells as it takes up liquid, turning the mixture thick and damp.
choices: Evaporating all liquid over fierce heat.
Fine bulgur absorbing its remaining liquid.
Removing the lentils before adding grain.
quiz.question: What thickens the hot lentil mixture in this method?

quiz.because: Retained heat and liquid soften the fine grains during the covered stand.
choices: Keep the mixture at a rolling boil.
Drain away every trace of liquid.
Take the pan off the heat.
quiz.question: What should happen before adding the bulgur?

quiz.because: Absorption needs to reach the centre rather than merely wet the surface.
choices: Tender grains without a hard dry core.
A soft coating around hard centres.
Dry grains scattered through loose broth.
quiz.question: Which texture indicates the grains have hydrated?

quiz.because: Additional moisture under cover gives the grains more liquid to absorb.
choices: Keep the same dry mixture uncovered.
Sprinkle in hot water and cover again.
Press the dry grains harder into the lentils.
quiz.question: The grains remain hard because the mixture was too dry. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The liquid is hot, and the bulgur swells in the heat of a covered pan taken off the stove, instead of soaking in cool liquid with no heat at all. It takes the flavour of what was cooked in the liquid.

comes_after.why: The eggs are whisked first, and the hot liquid is whisked in.

cues.text: The bowl is warm and not hot, and the mixture is smooth with no threads of cooked egg.
The mixture is glossy and thinner than it was.

technique/temper.does: Warms eggs or yolks gently by whisking a little hot liquid into them, so that they can then join the hot liquid in the pan without turning to specks. The word here is for eggs, not for chocolate.
how: Whisk the eggs or yolks, usually with the sugar, in a bowl big enough to take the liquid.
Heat the milk or cream until it steams. It must not be boiling.
Pour a little of the hot liquid onto the eggs in a thin stream while whisking all the time.
Add a little more in the same way, until the bowl feels warm to the touch.
Tip the warmed mixture back into the pan and finish over gentle heat, stirring.

intro.what: Egg tempering gradually warms beaten eggs with hot liquid before they join the pan.
intro.why: It teaches you to control a temperature change so a creamy mixture does not become speckled egg.

mistakes.fix: Pour a thin stream while whisking hard.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring the hot liquid in all at once, which cooks the egg into specks.

mistakes.fix: Take the liquid off the heat first, and warm the eggs with a little of it.
mistakes.mistake: Tipping the eggs into liquid that is boiling.

quiz.because: Small whisked additions spread warmth through the eggs without a sudden local shock.
choices: To warm them gradually while keeping the mixture smooth.
To cook them into separate firm pieces first.
To cool the hot liquid completely before mixing.
quiz.question: What is the aim of tempering eggs?

quiz.because: A slow stream and whisking distribute heat instead of allowing hot liquid to set isolated egg.
choices: All at once without whisking.
In a thin stream while whisking continuously.
Only after pouring the eggs into boiling liquid.
quiz.question: How should the first hot liquid be added?

quiz.because: The eggs should join the liquid as a continuous mixture rather than setting into strands.
choices: Speckled with separate cooked egg pieces.
Firm curds surrounded by thin liquid.
Smooth and glossy without threads of set egg.
quiz.question: Which appearance suits tempered eggs?

quiz.because: Gradual addition avoids concentrated heat setting parts of the eggs before they mix.
choices: Add the liquid gradually while whisking.
Use a faster unwhisked pour.
Keep the eggs still so the specks settle.
quiz.question: Eggs form specks after hot liquid is poured in at once. What should change next time?

en: fry whole spices in hot fat

cues.text: Mustard seeds crackle and pop, then go quiet. A loud, steady sizzle means the fat is hot enough.
Cumin seeds turn a shade darker, the dried chilli puffs and darkens, and the curry leaves go glassy and crisp.
A warm, nutty scent rises. A sharp, acrid smell means the spices have gone too far.

technique/temper-spices-in-hot-fat.does: Fries whole seeds, dried chillies and leaves in a little very hot fat until they crackle, darken a shade and give up their scent, then pours the scented fat and the spices over the food. Done at the start it is the base that onions and vegetables cook in. Done at the end it is a last layer of flavour poured over a finished dish.
how: Heat a small amount of ghee or oil in a small pan until it shimmers and a single seed dropped in sizzles at once.
Add the slowest seeds first: mustard seed, which will crackle and jump, and any split lentils that should turn golden. Cover the pan with a lid if they leap out.
When the popping slows, add cumin, fenugreek seed, cardamom and the dried chilli, and stir for a moment.
Add the curry leaves, dry, and the asafoetida last. They burn the quickest, and wet leaves spit.
Stop the moment the seeds darken a shade and the scent rises, and take the pan off the heat.
Pour the fat and the spices straight into the food, or over a finished dish, and stir it in or leave it on top.

intro.what: Spice tempering releases the aroma of seeds and other aromatics into hot fat.
intro.why: It teaches you to stagger ingredients by how quickly they colour and carry their flavour into a dish.

mistakes.fix: Test with a single seed first. It must sizzle at once.
mistakes.mistake: Putting the spices into fat that is not hot enough, so that they soak it up and taste raw.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat the moment the scent rises and pour out at once.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the pan on the heat after the seeds have darkened, so that they scorch and turn bitter.

mistakes.fix: Add them last, with the pan off the heat or nearly so.
mistakes.mistake: Adding asafoetida or chilli powder first, so that it burns before the seeds are ready.

mistakes.fix: Pat the leaves dry first and stand back as they go in.
mistakes.mistake: Dropping wet curry leaves into the fat, which makes it spit.

quiz.because: The fragrant fat and spices are added together as a flavour base or finishing layer.
choices: To soften the spices mainly by absorbing water.
To keep the scented fat separate and discard it before serving.
To carry their released aroma into the dish.
quiz.question: Why temper spices in fat?

quiz.because: Staggering the additions avoids burning delicate ingredients while tougher seeds heat.
choices: Late, when the slower seeds have had their turn.
Before all the whole seeds over strong heat.
At the start and left while seeds finish.
quiz.question: When should fast-burning ingredients such as asafoetida be added?

quiz.because: Acrid aromas indicate scorched spices rather than the intended fragrant bloom.
choices: A warm nutty aroma.
A sharp acrid smell.
A rising fragrant spice scent.
quiz.question: Which smell signals that tempering has gone too far?

quiz.because: Both direct heat and retained pan heat can push coloured spices into scorching.
choices: Leave the spices in the hot pan after removing heat.
Keep heating until the popping becomes stronger.
Remove the pan promptly and pour out the fragrant fat.
quiz.question: The seeds darkened and turned bitter in the pan. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The spices are whole, few and cooked for a moment, in a small amount of hot fat on their own, and the scented fat is the point. A French sauce starts with spices or aromatics that cook slowly along with the vegetables, and it never pours the fat over a finished dish.
Toasting browns spices in a dry pan to be ground later. Here the spices go whole into hot fat, which carries their scent into the food, and the cooking is over in moments.

comes_after.why: Starch thickens at a simmer, so a cook has to be able to hold a liquid there.

cues.text: The liquid turns glossy and clear, or silky if it holds milk, and coats the back of a spoon.
The spoon drags a little more as it moves through.

technique/thicken.does: Gives a thin hot liquid more body by stirring in a starch, mixed smooth in a little cold liquid first, and bringing it to a simmer so that the starch swells and the liquid turns glossy and coats a spoon.
how: Mix the starch with a little cold liquid until it is smooth, with no lumps.
Bring the liquid to a gentle simmer and stir it round.
Pour the mixture in a thin stream while stirring, and keep stirring.
Let it bubble gently for a short while so that the raw taste of the starch cooks out and the body is full.
Stop when it coats the back of a spoon. It will thicken a little more as it cools, so take it off the heat while it still pours.

intro.what: This method thickens hot liquid with starch first dispersed in cold liquid.
intro.why: It teaches you to control lumps and stop before the sauce becomes too stiff on cooling.

mistakes.fix: Mix it smooth in cold liquid first.
mistakes.mistake: Adding the dry starch straight to hot liquid, which lumps.

mistakes.fix: Let it bubble gently only until it has thickened.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling hard for long, which breaks the starch down so that the liquid thins again.

mistakes.fix: Add a little at a time and stop while it still pours.
mistakes.mistake: Thickening too much at the start, since it keeps thickening as it cools.

quiz.because: Swollen starch thickens the surrounding liquid so it can coat a spoon.
choices: It removes all moisture from the pan.
It separates fat into a clear top layer.
It swells and gives the liquid more body.
quiz.question: What happens as dispersed starch heats in the sauce?

quiz.because: Cold dispersion separates the starch before heat thickens it, reducing lumps.
choices: As a smooth cold-liquid mixture poured in while stirring.
As a heap of dry powder without stirring.
Scatter dry starch over the hot surface and wait before stirring.
quiz.question: How should starch be added to the hot liquid?

quiz.because: A smooth increase in resistance indicates thickening rather than clumping.
choices: No resistance and no coating at all.
A little more drag and a coating on the back.
Hard dry lumps scraping the base.
quiz.question: Which spoon cue indicates added body?

quiz.because: Cooling can increase the apparent thickness, so the hot sauce should retain flow.
choices: Keep thickening until it barely moves while hot.
Add all the starch before checking texture.
Add starch gradually and stop while it still pours.
quiz.question: The sauce becomes too stiff after cooling. What should change next time?

comes_after.why: It asks for the same judgment as a custard: yolks thickening a liquid just short of scrambling.

cues.text: The sauce turns ivory and velvety, and coats the spoon more thickly than before.

technique/thicken-with-egg-yolk.does: Enriches and lightly thickens a hot sauce with egg yolks beaten with cream, without letting the yolks scramble.
how: Beat the yolks with the cream in a bowl.
Take the sauce off the boil.
Whisk a ladle of the hot sauce into the yolks to warm them, then another.
Pour the mixture back into the pan, stirring all the time.
Heat gently, stirring, just until the sauce thickens a little. It must not boil again.

intro.what: This method enriches a hot sauce with egg yolks beaten with cream.
intro.why: It teaches you to warm the yolks gradually and use gentle heat for a smooth, lightly thickened sauce.

mistakes.fix: Warm the yolks with a little hot sauce first.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring the yolks straight into a boiling sauce, which sets them into threads.

mistakes.fix: Keep it below a simmer. A sauce that has started to grain can sometimes be rescued through a fine sieve.
mistakes.mistake: Boiling the sauce after the yolks have gone in.

quiz.because: Yolks beaten with cream enrich and lightly thicken the sauce.
choices: Separated threads of egg in liquid.
A richer, lightly thickened sauce.
A clear, thinner broth.
quiz.question: What finish is the yolk and cream mixture meant to give?

quiz.because: Adding hot sauce gradually warms the yolks before they meet the pan, helping avoid threads of set egg.
choices: It is poured straight into a rolling boil.
It is cooked into firm pieces on its own.
Hot sauce is whisked into it gradually to warm it.
quiz.question: What happens before the yolk mixture returns to the pan?

quiz.because: A velvety sauce coating the spoon more thickly shows the intended light thickening, rather than grainy or set yolk.
choices: A velvety sauce that coats the spoon more thickly.
Visible threads of set yolk.
A grainy sauce with separated liquid.
quiz.question: Which texture matches the intended result?

quiz.because: Boiling sauce can set the yolks into threads. Take it off the boil and warm the yolks gradually before returning the mixture to gentle heat.
choices: Bring the sauce to a harder boil first.
Take the sauce off the boil and warm the yolks gradually with some sauce.
Stop stirring as soon as the yolks enter the pan.
quiz.question: Yolks formed threads when added directly to boiling sauce. What would you change next time?

en: thicken a soup with flour paste

comes_after.why: The paste goes into a soup that is already simmering, so a cook has to hold a steady simmer first.

cues.text: The soup turns from thin and clear to glossy and slightly cloudy, and coats the back of a spoon.
The raw taste of flour is gone and the soup tastes round.

technique/thicken-with-tadouira.does: Stirs a loose paste of flour and cold water into a hot soup in a slow stream, then keeps the soup at a simmer until the flour has lost its raw taste, so that the soup turns silky and gains body. Beaten egg is sometimes stirred in at the end.
how: Whisk the flour into plenty of cold water until it is as smooth and loose as cream, with no lump left.
Bring the soup to a steady simmer and keep stirring as you pour the paste in, in a thin stream.
Keep stirring until the soup comes back to the simmer, then let it bubble gently for a good while, so that the flour cooks out.
Stir in the beaten egg last, if the soup is to have it, off the boil.

intro.what: Tadouira thickens soup with a loose flour-and-cold-water paste added gradually.
intro.why: It teaches you to separate smooth mixing from cooking out flour for a silky soup.

mistakes.fix: Pour it in a thin stream while stirring.
mistakes.mistake: Tipping the paste into the soup all at once, which leaves lumps.

mistakes.fix: Always whisk the flour with cold water first.
mistakes.mistake: Mixing the flour with hot liquid, which clots it.

mistakes.fix: Let it simmer on until the taste is gone.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping as soon as the soup thickens, which leaves a taste of raw flour.

quiz.because: The dispersed flour thickens the liquid as it cooks, giving the soup more body.
choices: Flour flavour left raw at the point of serving.
Body and a silky texture.
Thickness without any need to simmer the flour.
quiz.question: What does tadouira add to soup?

quiz.because: Cold water lets the flour disperse smoothly before it meets heat.
choices: Stir dry flour directly into boiling soup.
Whisk flour directly into hot broth before checking for lumps.
Whisk flour into cold water until smooth and loose.
quiz.question: How should the flour paste first be mixed?

quiz.because: A coating on the spoon shows body developing through the liquid.
choices: It becomes glossy and coats the spoon.
It becomes thinner and leaves the spoon bare.
Dry flour lumps rise unchanged.
quiz.question: Which change accompanies the soup thickening?

quiz.because: Thickening and losing raw flour flavour are different stages, so the soup needs further gentle cooking.
choices: Remove it immediately as soon as it coats a spoon.
Continue a gentle simmer rather than stopping at the first thickening.
Stir in more uncooked flour paste at serving.
quiz.question: The soup thickens but still tastes of raw flour. What should change?

variant_of.differs: Thickening stirs a starch mixed smooth in a little cold liquid into a sauce. Tadouira uses plain wheat flour whisked into a loose paste with a good deal of cold water, poured into the soup in a thin stream, and the soup is then simmered on for a good while so that the flour cooks out. No roux is made.

cues.text: Bread is dry and pale gold. Nuts are a shade darker than they were.
A warm, nutty scent rises. An acrid smell means it has gone too far.

technique/toast.does: Dries and browns bread, nuts or spices in dry heat, which makes them crisp and wakes their scent.
how: Spread the food in a single layer on a tray or in a dry pan.
Use a moderate heat: an oven, a grill or a pan with no fat.
Turn bread once. Shake nuts and spices often.
Tip nuts and spices out of the hot pan as soon as they are done, as they go on browning in it.

intro.what: Toasting uses dry heat to crisp bread or develop the scent of nuts and spices.
intro.why: It teaches you to watch small colour changes and account for heat remaining in the pan.

mistakes.fix: Stay with them and shake the pan.
mistakes.mistake: Walking away, as nuts go from golden to burnt within moments.

mistakes.fix: Tip them onto a cold plate at once.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving toasted nuts or spices in the hot pan, where they keep browning.

quiz.because: Dry heat removes moisture and develops colour and aroma without added fat.
choices: Moist softness without colour change.
A coating of absorbed cooking fat.
Crispness and a warm toasted aroma.
quiz.question: What does dry toasting develop?

quiz.because: Residual pan heat continues browning even after direct heat is removed.
choices: Tip them onto a cold plate.
Leave them in the pan until serving.
Cover them tightly in the hot pan.
quiz.question: What should happen to nuts after toasting in a hot pan?

quiz.because: An acrid smell indicates scorching rather than desirable toasted flavour.
choices: A warm nutty scent.
An acrid smell.
A gently strengthening toasted aroma.
quiz.question: Which smell suggests toasting has gone too far?

quiz.because: Moving them onto a cooler surface stops the pan continuing to brown them.
choices: Keep them in the pan but stir less.
Cover the pan to hold the heat.
Remove them from the hot pan promptly.
quiz.question: Nuts burned after the heat was switched off. What would you change next time?

cues.text: The pieces puff and show golden patches.
A piece gives way softly when pressed.

technique/toast-mochi.does: Browns pieces of hard rice cake under a grill, in a dry pan or in an oven until they puff, blister and turn soft and stretchy inside, with a lightly crisp skin.
how: Cut the mochi into pieces and set them apart on a tray or in a dry pan.
Cook over a gentle heat and watch them, as they puff quickly.
Turn them once they swell and brown in places.
Lift them off as soon as they are puffed and soft, and eat or add them to a hot dish at once.

intro.what: Toasting mochi makes hard rice cake puff and soften beneath a lightly crisp skin.
intro.why: It teaches you to match surface browning with internal softening and leave room for expansion.

mistakes.fix: Leave a gap between them.
mistakes.mistake: Setting the pieces close together, so that they fuse.

mistakes.fix: Use a moderate heat and watch.
mistakes.mistake: Using strong heat, which scorches the outside before the inside softens.

quiz.because: Gentle toasting develops surface colour while the rice cake swells and softens.
choices: A lightly crisp skin around a soft stretchy centre.
A dark hard shell around a rigid centre.
A wet uncoloured surface throughout.
quiz.question: What contrast is sought when toasting mochi?

quiz.because: Space lets each piece expand without fusing to its neighbours.
choices: Touching closely in a packed layer.
Apart from each other on the tray or pan.
Stacked so their surfaces join.
quiz.question: How should mochi pieces be arranged?

quiz.because: Puffing and golden patches show expansion and moderate surface browning.
choices: Unchanged flat pieces with hard centres.
Blackened edges around a rigid block.
Puffed pieces with golden patches.
quiz.question: Which appearance marks the intended change?

quiz.because: Less intense heat gives the centre more time to soften before the outside burns.
choices: Use a gentler heat and watch closely.
Increase the heat to puff it faster.
Leave it untouched over the same strong heat.
quiz.question: The outside scorched before the mochi softened. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The food is a rice cake that swells and turns stretchy inside as it browns, and it is toasted gently so that the inside softens before the outside burns.

comes_after.why: The rice goes into onion that has been softened without colour.

cues.text: A dry, gentle rustle of grains in the pan, and a faint crackle when they are properly hot.
The edges of the grains turn translucent while the centre stays white.
A faint nutty scent rises from the pan.

technique/toast-rice.does: Stirs raw rice in hot fat until the outside of each grain turns translucent and the grains are hot and dry, so that they keep their shape and take up stock slowly. The Italian name for this first step of a risotto is tostatura.
how: Make the base of the dish first in the same wide pan, such as onion softened in butter, and leave it soft.
Tip in the dry, unwashed rice and stir over medium heat, so that every grain is coated in fat.
Keep stirring until the edges of the grains turn translucent, with a pearly dot left at the centre, and the rice is too hot to hold comfortably.
If wine is used, pour it in now and stir until it has been taken up and the sharp smell has gone.

intro.what: Tostatura warms dry risotto rice in fat before liquid is added.
intro.why: It teaches you to recognise a translucent grain edge without taking the rice into dark browning.

mistakes.fix: Use the rice dry, straight from the packet.
mistakes.mistake: Rinsing the rice first, which washes off the starch that makes the sauce creamy.

mistakes.fix: Stop when the edges are translucent and no more.
mistakes.mistake: Taking it too far, so that the grains brown and taste scorched.

mistakes.fix: Coat them in hot fat first.
mistakes.mistake: Skipping the step, so that the grains go soft outside before the centre is tender.

quiz.because: Tostatura heats the fat-coated rice to a translucent edge while preserving pale centres.
choices: The rice must become dark brown before stock.
The grains are coated in hot fat without being browned.
The grains are boiled in stock first.
quiz.question: What makes this rice step different from dark dry-toasting?

quiz.because: Dry rice can coat in the fat while retaining the surface starch used in risotto.
choices: Wet from rinsing and left unstirred.
Already boiled and drained.
Dry and unwashed, then stirred to coat in fat.
quiz.question: How should the rice enter the softened onion base?

quiz.because: The changing edge shows heating without the scorched taste of excessive browning.
choices: Translucent edges with a pearly centre.
Deep brown grains throughout.
Wet grains surrounded by cloudy stock.
quiz.question: Which appearance guides the end of this toasting step?

quiz.because: The intended grain change is subtle translucence rather than a browned crust.
choices: Wait for the centres to brown as well.
Stop at translucent edges before browning develops.
Leave the grains still for a darker crust.
quiz.question: The rice tasted scorched after toasting. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The grains are stirred in hot fat, in the pan they will cook in, and not dried alone in dry heat. They are taken only to translucent edges and never to colour.

cues.text: Every piece glistens, and nothing pools in the bottom of the bowl.

technique/toss.does: Coats every piece evenly with a dressing or a sauce by lifting and turning.
how: Put the food in a bowl far larger than it needs.
Add the dressing a little at a time, around the edge and not on top.
Lift from the bottom and let the pieces fall, with clean hands or a pair of spoons.
Taste a piece and adjust before serving.

intro.what: Tossing lifts and turns food so dressing coats the pieces lightly and evenly.
intro.why: It teaches you to distribute a small addition without crushing delicate ingredients.

mistakes.fix: Toss at the last moment.
mistakes.mistake: Dressing leaves long before serving, so that the acid and salt make them limp.

mistakes.fix: Add it in stages and stop when everything is lightly coated.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring on all the dressing at once, which drowns the food.

quiz.because: Lifting from below brings undressed surfaces into contact without heavy stirring.
choices: Dressing pooled beneath dry upper pieces.
Light even coating across the pieces.
A dense pile crushed into the dressing.
quiz.question: What is the aim when tossing with dressing?

quiz.because: Space permits gentle movement that distributes dressing while preserving delicate pieces.
choices: To keep the dressing away from the food.
To make pressing the leaves harder easier.
To lift and turn without compressing or spilling the food.
quiz.question: Why choose a bowl with plenty of room?

quiz.because: A light sheen indicates coating without excess free dressing.
choices: Pieces glisten without a pool at the bottom.
Dry patches remain above a deep puddle.
Dressing runs off every piece in streams.
quiz.question: Which appearance suggests enough dressing?

quiz.because: Salt and acid act on dressed leaves over time, so late tossing better preserves their texture.
choices: Dress them earlier and leave them longer.
Toss them at the last moment.
Squeeze them harder into the dressing.
quiz.question: Leaves turned limp before service. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: The pasta is taken from the pot a little early, with some of its water kept back, to finish in the sauce.

cues.text: The sauce is glossy and clings to the pasta, with no loose liquid and no dry patches in the pan.
The pieces slide freely against each other and do not clump.

technique/toss-pasta-with-sauce.does: Moves just-drained pasta into the sauce and tosses it over the heat with a splash of the starchy cooking water, so that sauce and water bind into a glossy coat that clings to every piece. The pasta is dressed in the pan and not on the plate.
how: Have the sauce ready in a wide pan before the pasta is drained, with a mug of the cooking water set aside.
Lift the pasta straight from the pot into the pan, still wet and hot, a little before it is ready.
Toss and stir over the heat, adding the cooking water a splash at a time, until the sauce turns glossy and clings in a thin coat.
For a sauce that holds egg or cheese, take the pan off the heat first, so that the egg warms into a cream and does not scramble.
Serve at once, while the sauce still flows.

intro.what: Finishing pasta in its sauce brings them together with a little starchy cooking water.
intro.why: It teaches you to adjust liquid while tossing until the sauce clings instead of pooling.

mistakes.fix: Finish the pasta in the pan with a splash of the cooking water.
mistakes.mistake: Spooning sauce on top of dry, drained pasta at the table, so that it slides off.

mistakes.fix: Take the pan off the heat and loosen with the cooking water.
mistakes.mistake: Tossing an egg sauce over strong heat, so that the egg scrambles.

mistakes.fix: Add it a splash at a time and watch the sauce.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring in all the water at once, so that the sauce turns thin.

quiz.because: Tossing with starchy water helps sauce distribute and bind around the pieces.
choices: To build a glossy coat that clings to the pasta.
To keep sauce entirely separate from the pasta.
To thicken the sauce while leaving it separate from the pasta.
quiz.question: Why finish pasta with sauce and cooking water in the pan?

quiz.because: Gradual additions let you loosen and bind the coating without flooding the pan.
choices: All at once before checking consistency.
In small splashes while watching the sauce.
Only after serving the pasta on dry plates.
quiz.question: How should reserved cooking water be added?

quiz.because: A clinging thin coating shows sauce and pasta coming together rather than remaining separate.
choices: A puddle beneath otherwise dry pasta.
A thick clump with a bare sauce-free surface.
A glossy coat without dry patches or loose liquid.
quiz.question: Which appearance is the aim?

quiz.because: Gentler residual heat helps the egg form a cream instead of separate set pieces.
choices: Take the pan off the heat before finishing that sauce.
Toss over stronger heat until the pieces disappear.
Keep the same high heat but stir more slowly.
quiz.question: An egg-based sauce formed scrambled pieces. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The pasta is tossed over heat and not in a cold bowl, and the starchy cooking water is added so that the sauce and the starch bind together.

cues.text: Clean, even surfaces with no silvery skin, no ragged flaps and no dark outer leaves.

technique/trim.does: Cuts away what will not be eaten or will not cook well: sinew, surplus fat, tough leaves, stalks and ragged edges.
how: Slide the tip of the knife under a strip of sinew, angle the blade up against it and draw the knife along, so that the sinew comes away with almost no meat.
Leave a thin, even layer of fat on a joint that will be roasted.
Snap or cut the ends off beans, and pull away any string.
For an artichoke, break off the stalk, pull away the dark outer leaves, cut off the top, pare the base smooth and scoop out the hairy choke. Rub every cut with lemon at once.
Keep meat trimmings for a stock or for rendering.

intro.idea: Remove carefully, keep the good part
intro.what: Trimming removes tough or unwanted parts while keeping useful food.
intro.why: It teaches you to follow the boundary between what should be removed and what should remain.

mistakes.fix: Keep the blade angled up against what you are taking off.
mistakes.mistake: Cutting deep and wasting good flesh along with the sinew.

mistakes.fix: Rub each cut with lemon, or drop the trimmed artichoke into water sharpened with lemon.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving a cut artichoke in the air, where it turns brown within moments.

quiz.because: Following the sinew closely avoids wasting flesh while removing a tough part.
choices: Cut away a thick layer of meat with every strip.
Leave ragged sinew attached for easier slicing.
Remove the tough layer with little useful flesh.
quiz.question: What is the aim of trimming sinew from meat?

quiz.because: An upward angle follows the unwanted layer instead of cutting deeply into useful meat.
choices: Up against the sinew being removed.
Deeply down into the meat.
Flat across a thick slice of flesh.
quiz.question: How should the blade angle when removing sinew?

quiz.because: A clean surface shows unwanted parts removed without unnecessary damage.
choices: Deep gouges beneath remaining sinew.
Clean and even without silvery skin or ragged flaps.
Tough outer leaves still attached everywhere.
quiz.question: Which surface suggests careful trimming?

quiz.because: Protecting the freshly exposed surfaces limits their rapid browning.
choices: Leave all cuts exposed until trimming is finished.
Dry the cut surfaces in warm air.
Rub cuts with lemon promptly or use lemon-sharpened water.
quiz.question: A cut artichoke browns while you work. What should change?

cues.text: A neat, plump shape with nothing sticking out, and string that is snug without cutting in.

technique/truss.does: Ties a bird or a joint into a compact shape, so that it cooks evenly and keeps its form.
how: Tuck the wing tips under the back of the bird.
Pass a length of string under the tail, cross it over the ends of the drumsticks and pull them together.
Run the string along the sides, between the legs and the breast, and tie it at the neck.
For a joint, tie loops of string along it at even spaces, snug but not tight.

intro.what: Trussing ties a bird or joint into a compact shape before cooking.
intro.why: It teaches you to control the outline with snug string while avoiding pressure that cuts into the flesh.

mistakes.fix: Pull it snug and no more.
mistakes.mistake: Tying so tightly that the string cuts into the flesh and squeezes the juice out.

mistakes.fix: Draw the legs in against the breast.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the legs splayed, so that the breast dries before the thighs are done.

quiz.because: Drawing loose parts toward the body gives the piece a more contained outline.
choices: A spread-out form with every limb extended.
A compact form with loose parts drawn in.
A deeply compressed shape with string grooves.
quiz.question: What is the shaping aim of trussing?

quiz.because: Tucking keeps the tips from projecting beyond the compact shape.
choices: Pull them outward away from the body.
Tie them tightly across the exposed breast.
Tuck them underneath the back.
quiz.question: What happens to the wing tips in this bird-trussing method?

quiz.because: The string should support the outline without compressing and marking the flesh deeply.
choices: Snug string that does not cut into the flesh.
Deep grooves where each loop bites in.
Loose loops hanging away from the surface.
quiz.question: Which appearance suggests appropriate string tension?

quiz.because: More pressure is not needed once the string holds the shape; reducing tension limits cutting.
choices: Tighten every loop further.
Pull it snug with less tension.
Add more tight loops over the same grooves.
quiz.question: The string cuts into the flesh. What should change?

comes_after.why: A vegetable is peeled before it is turned.

cues.text: Small barrels of one size, with smooth curved faces and blunt ends.

technique/turn.does: Pares a vegetable into a neat barrel with curved sides, so that every piece cooks in the same time and rolls in the pan.
how: Cut the vegetable into pieces of one length, and split large ones into halves or quarters.
Hold a piece between thumb and finger and draw a small knife from end to end in one curved stroke.
Turn the piece a little and cut again, until it has even faces and tapers at both ends.
Drop potatoes into cold water as they are done, and keep the parings for a soup or a mash.

intro.what: Turning pares vegetables into small barrels with curved faces and tapered ends.
intro.why: It teaches you consistent starting sizes and flowing knife strokes for an even finished shape.

mistakes.fix: Take each face in one long stroke, turning the wrist.
mistakes.mistake: Short, choppy cuts, which leave flat steps instead of a curve.

mistakes.fix: Cut all the pieces to one length before you start.
mistakes.mistake: Pieces of different sizes, which cook unevenly.

quiz.because: Consistent starting pieces make a matching set easier to produce.
choices: To keep every finished piece a different size.
To remove the need to judge thickness.
To make the finished barrels similar in size.
quiz.question: Why begin with vegetable pieces of matching length?

quiz.because: A continuous curved motion creates the smooth barrel face rather than a stepped surface.
choices: Draw the small knife along the piece in a flowing curved stroke.
Make short downward chops across the face.
Cut deep square steps into the sides.
quiz.question: How should each curved face be cut?

quiz.because: The turned shape has flowing sides and consistent proportions across the pieces.
choices: Uneven wedges with jagged edges.
Small matching barrels with smooth curved faces.
Flat slabs with sharp square corners.
quiz.question: Which shape is the aim?

quiz.because: A continuous stroke smooths the curve instead of accumulating separate flat cuts.
choices: Make more short abrupt cuts at the same angle.
Press down harder at the centre of each step.
Use a longer flowing stroke while turning the wrist.
quiz.question: Short cuts leave flat steps instead of a curve. What should change?

comes_after.why: The dish starts with crepes that are already cooked, so a cook has to be able to make them thin and supple first.

cues.text: The sauce is thick enough to coat a spoon and clings to the crepes in a glossy layer.
A warm smell of orange and caramel.

technique/warm-crepes-in-orange-sauce.does: Folds cooked crepes into a hot sauce of caramel, orange and butter, warms them in it and sets a spirit alight over them at the end. The crepes soak up the sauce, and the flame burns off the harshness of the spirit.
how: Make the sauce first in a wide pan: stir the orange juice, some zest and the butter into a pale caramel and simmer until it is syrupy.
Fold each crepe in half and in half again, to make a fan.
Lay the crepes in the sauce, spoon the sauce over them and turn them once so that both sides are coated and warm.
Warm the spirit in a small pan. Take the pan with the crepes off the heat and pour the spirit around the edge, never straight from the bottle.
Stand back and light it with a long match, or tilt the pan to the flame, and spoon the burning sauce over the crepes until the flame dies.
Serve at once on warm plates, with the sauce spooned over.

intro.what: This crêpes Suzette method warms folded crêpes in a glossy orange-caramel butter sauce.
intro.why: It teaches you to balance sauce concentration and brief coating so delicate pancakes absorb flavour without tearing.

mistakes.fix: Measure the spirit into a small pan first, and pour it around the edge, off the heat.
mistakes.mistake: Pouring the spirit from the bottle into the hot pan, where the flame can run back into the bottle.

mistakes.fix: Add the juice as soon as the sugar is a pale amber.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the caramel go dark and bitter before the juice goes in.

mistakes.fix: Warm them just long enough to coat them, and serve at once.
mistakes.mistake: Soaking the crepes for too long, so that they turn limp and tear.

names.fr: Réchauffer les crêpes au beurre d'orange

quiz.because: A brief warming lets the sauce cling and soak in without making the crêpes excessively limp.
choices: To coat and flavour them while preserving their structure.
To keep most of the sauce separate from their folds.
To make them crisp through prolonged heating.
quiz.question: Why warm the crêpes briefly in the sauce?

quiz.because: Gentle turning and spooning coat both sides without rough handling.
choices: Stir them vigorously into small pieces.
Spoon it over and turn the folded crêpes gently.
Leave their upper surfaces dry throughout.
quiz.question: How should the sauce coat the crêpes?

quiz.because: A syrupy sauce stays on the crêpes rather than simply running away.
choices: A thin puddle beneath bare dry crêpes.
A dark bitter coating of burnt caramel.
A glossy coating that clings to the crêpes.
quiz.question: Which appearance suits the orange sauce?

quiz.because: Delicate crêpes soften as they absorb sauce, so limiting the soak protects their structure.
choices: Warm them only long enough to coat and serve promptly.
Leave them soaking for longer.
Turn and press them more forcefully.
quiz.question: The crêpes became limp and tore in the sauce. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The flame is not used to start a pan sauce. The crepes are warmed in a finished sauce of caramel, orange and butter, and the spirit is lit at the end, over the whole dish.

en: rinse rice until the water runs nearly clear

cues.text: The washing water turns from milky to almost clear.
The grains feel smooth and separate.

technique/wash-rice.does: Rubs rice gently in cold water and pours the cloudy water away, again and again, to take off the loose starch, so that the cooked grains are separate and clean-tasting.
how: Put the rice in a large bowl and cover it with cold water. Stir quickly with your hand and pour the cloudy water away at once.
Rub the rice lightly with the heel of the hand in a circular motion.
Add fresh water, swirl, and drain again.
Repeat until the water runs nearly clear. It does not need to be perfectly clear.
Drain the rice in a sieve.

intro.what: Washing rice removes loose surface starch with repeated gentle rinsing.
intro.why: It teaches you to recognise nearly clear water without damaging the grains in pursuit of perfect clarity.

mistakes.fix: Pour off the first water at once.
mistakes.mistake: Washing slowly in the first water, which lets the rice soak up the starch.

mistakes.fix: Rub lightly.
mistakes.mistake: Rubbing hard, which breaks the grains.

quiz.because: Rinsing carries away loose surface starch rather than extracting the grain’s whole interior.
choices: All starch from the inside of every grain.
Loose starch from the grain surfaces.
The outer husk rather than loose surface material.
quiz.question: What does this rice-washing method remove?

quiz.because: Gentle rubbing loosens surface material while preserving the grains.
choices: Hard enough to break the grains.
Dry against the bowl before adding water.
Lightly with the hand rather than crushed.
quiz.question: How should the rice be rubbed?

quiz.because: The aim is to remove much of the loose starch without excessive washing or damage.
choices: Nearly clear rather than perfectly transparent.
Thick and milky with every rinse.
Clear only after the grains have broken down.
quiz.question: Which water appearance marks the intended washing endpoint?

quiz.because: Less force preserves the grains while water carries away the loosened starch.
choices: Apply harder pressure for fewer passes.
Rub more lightly.
Grind the grains firmly against the bowl.
quiz.question: The rice breaks during washing. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The rice is rubbed lightly as it is washed, and the first water is poured away at once, so that it does not soak up the starchy water.

cues.text: Glossy and smooth. A peak stands on the lifted whisk, its tip bending slightly.
The bowl can be tipped without the foam sliding.

technique/whip.does: Beats air into egg whites or cream until they hold a peak.
how: Start with a clean, dry bowl, with no trace of fat or yolk in it.
Whisk slowly at first, until the whites are a loose foam.
Speed up, lifting the whisk through the foam in big circles.
Stop as soon as the foam stands in a peak when the whisk is lifted.

intro.what: Whipping incorporates air until a foam can hold a peak; this method describes egg whites.
intro.why: It teaches you to distinguish a glossy supporting foam from a dry overworked one.

mistakes.fix: Stop at a glossy peak. Whites that have gone grainy cannot be brought back.
mistakes.mistake: Whipping past the peak, so that the foam turns dry and grainy and leaks water.

mistakes.fix: Separate each egg over a small bowl first, and wipe the mixing bowl clean.
mistakes.mistake: A trace of yolk or grease in the bowl, so that the whites never rise.

quiz.because: Whisking incorporates air into a structure that can support a peak rather than simply blend the liquid.
choices: A smooth liquid with no incorporated air.
A firm cooked sheet of egg.
An airy foam that holds a peak.
quiz.question: What does whipping egg whites build?

quiz.because: Grease or yolk interferes with the rise of an egg-white foam.
choices: Clean and dry without grease or yolk.
Lightly greased so the foam releases.
Coated with egg yolk before adding whites.
quiz.question: How should the egg-white bowl be prepared?

quiz.because: The peak should have structure while the foam retains gloss and smoothness.
choices: Dry and grainy with leaking liquid.
Glossy and smooth with a slightly bending tip.
A liquid mixture that runs flat immediately.
quiz.question: Which appearance marks the intended peak here?

quiz.because: Continuing beyond the desired peak damages the smooth foam rather than strengthening it.
choices: Keep beating until the grains disappear.
Wait for liquid to leak out before stopping.
Stop at the glossy peak instead of continuing.
quiz.question: Whites turn dry and grainy after the peak stage. What should change next time?

variant_of.differs: The aim is air. Whisking goes on until the foam holds a peak.

cues.text: No streaks. Beaten eggs are an even yellow that runs off the whisk in a thin stream.

technique/whisk.does: Beats a liquid with a whisk until it is blended and smooth.
how: Use a bowl large enough that nothing slops over.
Tilt the bowl and beat in quick strokes that cross the middle.
Keep going until the mixture is one colour and one texture.

intro.what: Whisking blends a liquid until its colour and texture are even.
intro.why: It teaches you to distinguish simple blending from whipping a foam.

mistakes.fix: Stop as soon as the streaks of white are gone.
mistakes.mistake: Whisking eggs for an omelette until they foam, which makes it spongy.

quiz.because: Whisking brings ingredients together; it need not continue until a foam forms.
choices: The tallest possible stiff foam in every mixture.
A smooth evenly blended liquid.
Separate streaks of each ingredient.
quiz.question: What is the aim of basic whisking here?

quiz.because: Strokes through the mixture distribute ingredients while a roomy bowl limits splashing.
choices: Quick strokes only at the surface without crossing the middle.
Short strokes at a single edge while leaving the bowl upright.
Quick strokes crossing the middle in a tilted roomy bowl.
quiz.question: How should strokes move through the bowl?

quiz.because: An even colour indicates the whites and yolks have combined without requiring a foam.
choices: Even yellow with the white streaks gone.
Distinct white streaks beneath a yellow surface.
A dry peak holding on the whisk.
quiz.question: Which appearance shows omelette eggs are blended?

quiz.because: For this use, blending is enough; added foam changes the intended omelette texture.
choices: Whip to a stiffer peak next time.
Stop whisking once the white streaks disappear.
Keep incorporating air after the eggs look even.
quiz.question: An omelette turns spongy after its eggs were whisked into foam. What should change?

comes_after.why: The foam is built by steady whisking, so a cook has to know how to whisk first.

cues.text: The foam is pale and thick and leaves a ribbon on its surface when the whisk is lifted.
The whisk meets a light, steady resistance, and the sides of the bowl are warm but not hot.

technique/whisk-over-a-bain-marie.does: Whisks egg yolks, sugar and a sweet wine such as Marsala in a bowl set over barely simmering water, until they swell into a thick, pale, warm foam that holds a ribbon. This is the Italian zabaione, also spelt zabaglione, served warm as it is or chilled and folded into mascarpone cream.
how: Set a heatproof bowl over a pan of water at a bare simmer. The bowl must not touch the water.
Whisk the yolks with the sugar in the bowl until pale, then add the wine.
Keep whisking steadily, scraping the sides and the bottom, as the mixture warms and swells. Lift the bowl off the heat now and then if it gets too hot.
Stop when the foam is thick and holds a ribbon on its surface.
Serve warm at once, or keep whisking over ice until it is cool.

intro.what: Italian zabaione whisks yolks, sugar and wine over gentle steam into a warm pale foam.
intro.why: It teaches you to coordinate continuous movement and indirect heat until a ribbon holds on the surface.

mistakes.fix: Keep the water at a bare simmer and lift the bowl off now and then.
mistakes.mistake: Letting the water boil hard, so that the yolks scramble into lumps.

mistakes.fix: Whisk until it holds a ribbon.
mistakes.mistake: Stopping too soon, so that the foam collapses in the bowl.

mistakes.fix: Whisk without a pause, scraping the sides.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving it still, so that the edges set against the bowl.

quiz.because: Whisking while gently warming develops an airy mixture with enough body to leave a ribbon.
choices: A thick pale foam that holds a ribbon.
A thin liquid with no lasting trail.
Separate firm curds floating in wine.
quiz.question: What is the intended texture of zabaione?

quiz.because: The water bath supplies indirect heat while keeping the bowl away from direct contact with boiling water.
choices: Immersed deeply in a rolling boil.
Above it without touching the barely simmering water.
Resting directly on the pan base without water.
quiz.question: Where should the bowl sit over the water?

quiz.because: A holding ribbon shows thickened foam rather than a mixture that is still too loose.
choices: The mixture runs like thin liquid without a mark.
Small solid egg grains collect around the edge.
A ribbon briefly remains on the surface.
quiz.question: Which whisk cue suggests the intended texture?

quiz.because: Moving mixture away from the heated bowl surfaces limits local setting.
choices: Whisk continuously, reaching the sides and bottom.
Leave the sides untouched and whisk only the centre.
Stop whisking and increase the boil.
quiz.question: Egg sets against the bowl edges while the middle stays loose. What should change?

variant_of.differs: The yolks are whisked with sugar and Marsala, and the foam is eaten warm as a dessert or folded into cream. It is not taken on to carry butter or to sauce fish.

cues.text: Dark green, glossy and limp, a fraction of the raw heap.

technique/wilt.does: Collapses tender leaves with brief heat, so that they turn soft and dark and lose most of their bulk.
how: Wash the leaves and leave the water that clings to them.
Melt a little fat in a wide pan over medium heat.
Add the leaves by the handful, turning them as they fall.
Take them off the heat as soon as the last leaf has collapsed, and press out the water.

intro.what: Wilting briefly heats tender leaves until they collapse and lose bulk.
intro.why: It teaches you to stop at a texture change instead of leaving delicate greens to release more water.

mistakes.fix: Stop the moment they collapse, and drain them.
mistakes.mistake: Leaving the leaves on the heat, so that they go on shedding water and turn slimy.

quiz.because: Brief heat softens the leaves so a large raw heap becomes a smaller limp mass.
choices: They form a crisp dry crust.
They remain rigid and unchanged.
They soften and collapse from their raw bulk.
quiz.question: What change is sought when wilting tender leaves?

quiz.because: Gradual additions and turning expose fresh leaves as the earlier ones lose volume.
choices: By handfuls, turning them as they collapse.
Pressed into a dense unmoving stack.
Dry them completely and add the whole pile without turning.
quiz.question: How should leaves be added to the pan?

quiz.because: Collapse and gloss distinguish wilting from leaving leaves raw or frying them until crisp.
choices: Pale rigid leaves holding the original heap.
Dark green glossy limp leaves with much less bulk.
Blackened crisp fragments around dry stems.
quiz.question: Which appearance fits wilted greens?

quiz.because: Continued heating beyond collapse can over-soften tender leaves and release excess liquid.
choices: Leave them heating until all structure disappears.
Cover and keep cooking after collapse.
Remove them when they collapse and drain them.
quiz.question: The leaves became slimy while continuing to shed water. What would you change next time?

cues.text: The wrapper lies snugly round the food, with the seam underneath and no gaps.
The parcel is firm and holds its shape when it is lifted.

technique/wrap.does: Encloses a filling or a piece of food in a wrapper, such as caul fat, a leaf, a thin omelette or a cloth, and closes it by folding or pulling, so that it keeps its shape and its juices as it cooks.
how: Lay the wrapper out flat and make sure it is soft enough to bend without tearing.
Set the food or the filling in the middle, with a border all round.
Fold the sides over the food, then bring the ends in and over, so that the wrapper meets itself and overlaps a little.
Turn the parcel seam side down, or tie it, so that it stays closed in the heat.

intro.what: Wrapping encloses food in a flexible leaf, sheet or other covering and secures the seam.
intro.why: It teaches you to leave a useful border and balance a snug closure with room for the filling.

mistakes.fix: Use less filling and leave a border.
mistakes.mistake: Overfilling, so that the wrapper splits when the filling swells.

mistakes.fix: Pull the wrapper snug and set it seam side down, or tie it.
mistakes.mistake: Wrapping loosely, so that the parcel falls open in the pan.

quiz.because: The clear border supplies material for a complete enclosure instead of an overfilled seam.
choices: To leave the filling exposed at every side.
To allow the wrapper to overlap and close.
To make the wrapper stretch as thin as possible.
quiz.question: Why leave a border around the filling?

quiz.because: An underside seam or tie helps the overlapping wrapper stay in place.
choices: Leave the seam loose on top.
Fold the ends without letting the wrapper edges overlap.
Set it seam down or tie it.
quiz.question: How should the finished parcel be secured?

quiz.because: A complete covering supports the shape without open routes for filling to escape.
choices: A snug covering with no gaps and the seam underneath.
A loose covering with exposed filling.
Torn corners around an overfilled centre.
quiz.question: Which appearance fits a neatly wrapped parcel?

quiz.because: A smaller filling and enough wrapper reduce strain while keeping the enclosure complete.
choices: Stretch the next wrapper tighter over more filling.
Use less filling and leave a border.
Remove the overlap to fit extra filling.
quiz.question: The wrapper split as the filling expanded. What would you change next time?

comes_after.why: The nori goes around rice that has already been shaped.

cues.text: The nori is crisp and crackles when it is bitten.
The nori clings to the rice without gaps.

technique/wrap-in-nori.does: Wraps a sheet of dried seaweed around shaped rice just before eating, so that the seaweed stays crisp and does not turn soggy against the moist rice.
how: Cut a sheet of nori into strips or squares, or fold it to fit the rice shape.
Hold the shaped rice in one hand and lay the nori against the rice.
Press it on lightly, so that it clings to the surface.
Wrap it just before it is eaten, or wrap it in a way that keeps part of the nori dry.

intro.what: Wrapping shaped rice in nori just before eating preserves the seaweed’s crisp texture.
intro.why: It teaches you how moisture moves from rice into a dry wrapper and why timing matters.

mistakes.fix: Wrap it just before eating.
mistakes.mistake: Wrapping long before serving, so that the nori turns damp and chewy.

mistakes.fix: Keep it in a closed container, and crisp it briefly over a flame if needed.
mistakes.mistake: Using nori that has gone soft in the air.

quiz.because: Contact with moist rice gradually softens a dry crisp sheet.
choices: To limit moisture softening the seaweed.
To let it become fully damp and chewy first.
To let the seaweed absorb moisture evenly before serving.
quiz.question: Why wrap rice in nori close to eating?

quiz.because: Light contact lets the sheet cling without deliberate wetting or breaking.
choices: Press hard enough to compact the rice deeply inside the sheet.
Press it lightly against the shaped surface.
Soak the sheet before wrapping.
quiz.question: How should nori be attached to the rice?

quiz.because: The crackle reflects a dry crisp structure rather than softened damp seaweed.
choices: A soft silent pull through a chewy sheet.
A wet squelch from a soaked wrapper.
A crackle when bitten.
quiz.question: Which sound matches crisp nori?

quiz.because: Reducing the time in contact with rice limits moisture transfer to the nori.
choices: Keep it separate and wrap close to eating.
Wrap earlier so it has longer contact with rice.
Dampen it before wrapping to help it cling.
quiz.question: Nori became damp and chewy before service. What would you change next time?

variant_of.differs: The wrapper is a sheet of dried seaweed, put on at the last moment to stay crisp, not a leaf or dough sealed around the food.
